factors.label: Pitot probe blockage
factors.description: Pitot probes blocked by ice, insects, covers or debris, or unheated, corrupting airspeed sensing.

factors.label: Static port blockage
factors.description: Static ports obstructed, corrupting altitude, airspeed and vertical speed indications.

factors.label: Unreliable airspeed indication
factors.description: Cockpit airspeed indications inconsistent with actual airspeed, typically following pitot or static failures.

factors.label: Spurious overspeed warning
factors.description: Overspeed warning triggered by erroneous airspeed data rather than actual overspeed.

factors.label: Angle-of-attack sensor failure

factors.label: MCAS activation

factors.label: ADIRU data fault

factors.label: Radio altimeter failure
factors.description: A radio altimeter provided erroneous height, typically feeding automation with a false landing condition.

factors.label: Erroneous engine indication
factors.description: Engine instrumentation read incorrectly, typically from iced probes, leading the crew or autothrottle to set wrong thrust.

factors.label: Autopilot disconnect
factors.description: The autopilot disconnected, handing the aircraft to the crew, often at the start of an upset.

factors.label: Flight control law degradation
factors.description: Fly-by-wire protections were lost or degraded, removing stall or attitude protections the crew may have relied on.

factors.label: Automation dependency and manual skill erosion

factors.label: Aerodynamic stall

factors.label: Stall or upset misdiagnosed

factors.label: Dual sidestick input

records.title: TAI 307

location.name: Bordeaux–Mérignac Airport

records.summary: The DC-7C departed Bordeaux at night with light drizzle and limited visibility. Following takeoff, the aircraft reached only 30 m altitude and failed to climb further before flying into a pine forest 2950 m from the runway. The aircraft cut a swath through the forest, and the fuselage broke up before post-crash fire destroyed the wreckage.
records.probable_cause: With lack of visual references in darkness, the pilot failed to maintain optimum climbing speed and did not carefully monitor the altimeter, allowing the aircraft to descend back to terrain level.

factors.evidence: Darkness and a lack of visual references led the crew to have difficulty maintaining awareness of the aircraft's position and altitude.
Evidence from a reconstructed flight showed the rate of climb would decrease if optimum climbing speed was not maintained.
A pilot may follow a line of flight that will bring the aircraft back near the ground if the altimeter is not carefully watched.
The aircraft flew into a pine forest located 2950 m from the end of the runway after reaching only 30 m altitude.

events.text: Departure from Bordeaux with light drizzle and 3 knot wind
Aircraft rotates and begins climb
Aircraft fails to maintain climb rate, altitude plateaus at 30 meters

Fuselage breaks up, post-crash fire, rescue hampered by darkness and terrain

records.title: Malév 355

location.name: Roissy-en-France

records.summary: Malév Flight 355, an Ilyushin Il-18V with 21 aboard, crashed near Paris-Le Bourget Airport on November 23, 1962 during approach. Weather conditions included heavy fog and stratus cloud with visibility severely reduced. The aircraft initiated a landing on instruments with landing gear extended and engines near full power. During approach, the aircraft stalled while performing a high G-load maneuver and crashed 6.1 kilometers from the airport.
records.probable_cause: The aircraft stalled during a high G-load maneuver while executing an instrument approach in foggy conditions. The investigation could not determine why the crew performed the high G-load maneuver.

factors.evidence: Very foggy in Paris; pilot noted frequent occurrences of fog and stratus cloud with possibility of light icing; landing was initiated on instruments.
Aircraft stalled while performing a high G-load manoeuvre during approach; the investigation concluded aircraft had stalled while performing this maneuver.
Investigation concluded aircraft had stalled while performing a high G-load manoeuvre during the approach.
Aircraft crashed 6.1 kilometers east-northeast of Le Bourget airport near road from Paris to Soissons.

events.text: Flight 355 departed Budapest at 7:44 GMT with crew and 13 passengers bound for Frankfurt stopover.
In Frankfurt, crew spent two hours at meteorological office for briefing, noting frequent fog, stratus cloud, and light icing possibility.
During approach to Paris with landing gear extended and engines nearly at full power, aircraft stalled while performing high G-load maneuver during approach.
Aircraft crashed 6.1 kilometres east-northeast from airport near road from Paris to Soissons; airplane exploded with high flames visible.

notes: why maneuver was performed remains unexplained
fog and icing conditions contributed to crash

records.title: West Coast Airlines 956

location.name: Wemme

records.summary: During descent via radar vector from Seattle Center, Flight 956 received instruction to descend from 14,000 feet to 9,000 feet and turn right to heading 300 degrees. The aircraft descended to approximately 4,000 feet and leveled off in a normal descent pattern. An abrupt climb was initiated two seconds before impact. The crew had only 17 to 50 hours on the DC-9 type. The specific cause of descent below clearance limits was never determined by the NTSB.
records.probable_cause: The descent of the aircraft below its clearance limit and below that of surrounding obstructing terrain, but the Board was unable to determine the cause of such descent.

factors.evidence: the captain, 42-year-old Charles C. Warren, had over 18,900 flying hours, but only seventeen in the DC-9
The aircraft was being flown on autopilot. The flight descended in a normal manner to approximately 4000 ft and leveled off.
The controller lost radar contact with the flight while it was in the right turn
more than an hour after sunset, the cloud ceiling was at 2900 ft, with the weather consisting of rain
crashed on October 1, 1966, approximately 5.5 mi south of Wemme, Oregon

events.text: Flight 956 departed Eugene for Portland, received IFR clearance via Victor Airway 23 at 12000 feet altitude

Controller advised Runway 28R was in use at Portland International Airport and instructed turn right to heading 300 degrees

notes: Specific cause of descent never determined; aircraft was airworthy with proper crew certification; no mechanical failure detected; crew had limited experience on DC-9 type

records.title: 1967 Air Ferry DC-4 accident

location.name: Mount Canigó

records.summary: A Douglas DC-4 charter flight carrying 83 passengers and 5 crew on a 15-day package holiday was descending to land at Perpignan when it crashed into Mount Canigó at 9,000 feet. The aircraft had reported all was well with good visibility moments before impact. The French Ministry of Transport investigation determined the crash resulted from a series of crew errors caused by carbon monoxide poisoning from a faulty cabin heater.
records.probable_cause: Controlled flight into terrain caused by pilot incapacitation from carbon monoxide poisoning due to faulty cabin heater. Contributing factors included irrational crew behavior from CO poisoning and language difficulties between crew and French air traffic control.

factors.evidence: Faulty cabin heater allowed carbon monoxide to enter cabin
Carbon monoxide poisoning from a faulty heater caused series of errors and irrational behavior by crew

aircraft hit 9,000-foot Mount Canigó

records.title: TWA 128

location.name: Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport

records.summary: Flight 128 crashed on final approach to Greater Cincinnati Airport at night with the glide slope inoperative. The crew descended to 875 feet before striking trees, attempting a visual approach without adequate altimeter cross-checking. Seventy of the eighty-two people aboard were killed. The NTSB determined the likely cause to be crew error in attempting the visual approach without maintaining minimum altitude.
records.probable_cause: Crew error, in attempting a visual no-glide-slope approach at night during deteriorating weather conditions, without an adequate altimeter cross-reference.

records.title: Braniff 352

location.name: Near Dawson, Texas

records.summary: Braniff Flight 352, a Lockheed L-188A Electra, departed Houston for Dallas on May 3, 1968, climbing to 20,000 feet. About 25 minutes into flight, the crew encountered severe thunderstorm activity with hail and received clearance for a 180-degree right turn to escape the weather. During the turn, the aircraft's bank angle exceeded 90 degrees and nose pitched down 40 degrees, producing 4.3g acceleration that exceeded the airframe's ultimate structural strength. The aircraft broke apart in flight.
records.probable_cause: The stressing of the aircraft structure beyond its ultimate strength during an attempted recovery from an unusual attitude induced by turbulence associated with a thunderstorm. The operation in the turbulence resulted from a decision to penetrate an area of known severe weather.

factors.evidence: Aircraft approached area of severe thunderstorm activity with hail reported at 16:47 (p. 38).
During 180-degree turn, aircraft bank angle increased to more than 90 degrees and nose pitched down to about 40 degrees (p. 39).
FDR indicated peak acceleration of 4.3 g causing overstress to airframe and breakup (p. 38).
Aircraft went into uncontrolled descent after structural failure (p. 38).

Aircraft broke apart in flight and crashed near Dawson, Texas

records.title: Allegheny Airlines Flight 853

location.name: Fairland, Indiana

records.summary: Allegheny Airlines Flight 853, a DC-9-31, collided mid-air with a Piper PA-28 near Fairland, Indiana on September 9, 1969. The DC-9 was on an instrument flight plan descending for approach to Indianapolis at 3,550 feet when it converged with the VFR Piper aircraft. The Piper was not equipped with a transponder and did not appear on radar. At a relative speed of 350 mph, the left wing of the Piper sheared off the DC-9's rear tail assembly. Both aircraft lost control and crashed, killing all 83 occupants on both aircraft.
records.probable_cause: The deficiencies in the collision avoidance capability of the Air Traffic Control system in a terminal area with mixed IFR and VFR traffic. The deficiencies included inadequacy of the see-and-avoid concept, technical limitations of radar in detecting all aircraft, and absence of Federal Aviation Regulations providing adequate separation of mixed traffic.

factors.evidence: The Piper aircraft was not equipped with a transponder and did not appear as a primary radar target on the radarscope (p. 6).
The two aircraft converged at a relative speed of 350 mph at 3,550 feet; the left wing of the PA-28 sheared off the DC-9's rear tail assembly (p. 6).
The FAA system lacked adequate regulations for separating mixed IFR and VFR traffic in terminal areas (p. 6).
The report faulted military and civilian aviation authorities for not reducing well-known collision risks that had existed for over a year (p. 6).

records.title: ALM 980

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report: Overseas National Airways, Inc., Douglas DC-9, N935F, Operating as Antilliaanse Luchtvaart Maatschappij Flight 980

location.name: Caribbean Sea, 48 km off St. Croix

records.summary: Overseas National Airways Flight 980, a Douglas DC-9, ditched in the Caribbean Sea on 2 May 1970 after fuel exhaustion following three unsuccessful landing attempts at St. Maarten and a diversion. The crew miscalculated fuel consumption, misread fuel gauges, and incorrectly computed fuel reserves, compounding high workload from weather and multiple approach attempts. The aircraft ditched with 23 fatalities.
records.probable_cause: Fuel exhaustion which resulted from continued, unsuccessful attempts to land at St. Maarten until insufficient fuel remained to reach an alternate airport. A contributing factor was the reduced visibility in the approach zone because of rain showers, a condition not reported to the flight.

factors.evidence: The crew miscalculated the rate of fuel consumption (using 0.78 and LRC mach at high-power settings rather than planned procedures), misread fuel gauges, and incorrectly computed the amount of fuel expected to remain (p. 8-10).
Multiple unsuccessful landing attempts and diversions, combined with weather situations and ATC coordination, distracted the crew from proper fuel management (p. 2).
Crew inattention and distraction resulted in poor fuel management throughout the descent and approach phase. The crew did not recognize that fuel margins had reached critical limits (p. 9).
A rain shower in the approach zone reduced visibility below announced values, forcing the aircraft to make approaches too close to the airport, complicating multiple landing attempts (p. 9).
The aircraft's fuel was exhausted during the descent, engines flamed out, and the captain ditched the aircraft in the Caribbean Sea at approximately 1549 local time (p. 7, 15).
Flight 980 ditched in the Caribbean Sea at 17 degrees 53 minutes North, 69 degrees 14 minutes West, during daylight hours (p. 7).

events.text: ATC advised that weather in St. Maarten was below landing minima; captain elected to divert
Tower at St. Maarten advised that the weather had improved sufficiently for landing
First landing attempt - aircraft did not sight the runway in sufficient time to align for landing
Second landing attempt unsuccessful due to poor alignment with the runway; aircraft flown with 25 degrees flaps
Third attempt - aircraft was too high to land safely after assessing weather and fuel situation
Captain decided to divert to St. Thomas
Captain reported to San Juan ARTCC 'Okay there's a possibility I may have to ditch this aircraft, I am now descending to the water.'
Engines flamed out due to fuel exhaustion at approximately 500 feet altitude
Aircraft ditched in Caribbean Sea; captain leveled off momentarily at 500 feet, descended in 100-foot increments, lowered 15 degrees flaps, and flew onto water at approximately 90 knots

recommendations.text: Require that the item 'warn passengers' be inserted as one of the last items on the emergency landing or ditching checklists of all carriers, yet sufficiently advanced on the list to insure adequate time for passengers to brace for a crash (NTSB-AAR-71-8, Recommendation (a), Appendix E).

Require that no flight involving the briefing of passengers regarding emergency procedures be dispatched without an operable public address system. The system should be functioning so that the flightcrew can speak to the passengers and a cabin attendant can speak to the passengers from at least one cabin station (NTSB-AAR-71-8, Recommendation (b), Appendix F).

Take necessary steps to eliminate, within a reasonable time, the use of fabric-to-metal type seatbelts and require the metal-to-metal type of seatbelt with a standardized activating device (NTSB-AAR-71-8, Recommendation (c), Appendix G).

Reexamine the methods for storage of lifevests aboard aircraft to eliminate any obstructions to expeditious access in the event of an emergency requiring their use (NTSB-AAR-71-8, Recommendation (d), Appendix H).
Initiate action to install a VHF communications link between San Juan ARTCC and Juliana Tower. This action was scheduled for fiscal year 1972 (NTSB-AAR-71-8, Recommendation (e), Appendix I).

Reassess the standards set forth in FAR parts 37.122 and 37.178 pertaining to the certification of liferafts and lifevests, with a view toward eliminating the deficiencies in such equipment as evidenced by the investigative record of this accident. Research and development should be undertaken, as necessary, to accomplish this reassessment and improvement of standards.

safety_changes: Enhanced requirements for emergency checklists to include passenger warning before ditching
Mandatory operable public address systems on all aircraft with passenger briefing requirements
Transition from fabric-to-metal seatbelts to metal-to-metal type with standardized activating devices
Improved stowage methods for lifevests to ensure expeditious access during emergencies
Installation of VHF communications link between San Juan ARTCC and Juliana Tower

records.title: Dan-Air 1903

location.name: Les Agudes, Serralada del Montseny, near Arbúcies

records.summary: Dan-Air Flight 1903 crashed into the Serralada del Montseny near Arbúcies during descent toward Barcelona on 3 July 1970, killing all 112 aboard. The crew mistakenly reported passing the Sabadell NDB while still 28 nm north of it over mountainous terrain. The controller, misled by a radar echo from another aircraft over Sabadell, did not notice the error and cleared descent to 2800 ft. The aircraft struck beech trees at about 3800 ft.
records.probable_cause: The combination of erroneous position reporting by the crew (who reported passing Sabadell when still 28 nm north) combined with a radar echo from another aircraft near Sabadell led the controller to believe the Comet had passed the beacon. This involuntary mutual error between crew and ATC could not be corrected before the aircraft struck high terrain.

factors.evidence: The aircraft was still 28 nautical miles north of Sabadell at the time of the erroneous report, over the Serralada del Montseny mountainous terrain (p. 9)
The crew reported in error that they had passed the Sabadell NDB, when they were still 28 nm north and the aircraft had drifted east of its planned route (p. 8-9)
Barcelona ATC mistook a radar echo from another aircraft overflying Sabadell for that of the Dan-Air Comet and cleared descent to 2,800 feet, the minimum altitude for that sector (p. 9)
The aircraft crashed into a group of beech trees on the northeast slopes of the Les Agudes peak at an altitude of about 3,900 feet

events.text: Flight 1903 departed Manchester Airport at 16:08 BST and encountered air traffic control delays in the Paris area, resulting in a change of route.
Radio contact was established with Barcelona Area Control Centre at 17:53 local time. Aircraft reported passing Spanish frontier and requested clearance to descend.
Aircraft reported passing Barcelona FIR boundary at FL160 with ETA of 1801 hrs for Point Berga.
Aircraft handed to Barcelona Approach. Crew reported leaving FL130 and gave ETA for Sabadell of 1807 hrs.
Crew reported passing Sabadell NDB, though they were actually still 28 nautical miles north of it, over the Serralada del Montseny.
Barcelona ATC mistook a radar echo from another aircraft over Sabadell for the Dan-Air Comet and cleared descent to 2,800 feet.
The Comet struck beech trees on the northeast slopes of the Les Agudes peak at an altitude of about 3,900 feet and was destroyed in the explosion.

recommendations.text: Emphasis should be given to commanders of aircraft flying on a new route to verify successive positions using all available aids rather than relying on any one aid.
Rules for radar identification should be revised to prevent similar situations, with identification properly checked by more than one method.
Radio navigation charts should incorporate spot heights of significant points along the route to be followed.

safety_changes: Enhanced radar identification procedures with multiple verification methods
Improved pilot training on position verification using multiple navigation aids
Radio navigation charts updated to include spot heights of significant points

notes: Sections read: History of Flight, Analysis, Conclusions and Probable Causes, Recommendations from UK AAIB report

records.title: Southern Airways 932

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report, Southern Airways, Inc., DC-9, N97S, Tri-State Airport, Huntington, West Virginia

location.name: Tri-State Airport, Huntington, West Virginia, approximately 1 mile west of runway threshold on a hillside

records.summary: Southern Airways Flight 932, a McDonnell Douglas DC-9-30 chartered to transport the Marshall University football team and boosters, crashed during a nonprecision instrument approach to runway 11 at Tri-State Airport in Huntington, West Virginia. The aircraft descended below minimum descent altitude in adverse weather conditions (rain, fog, and smoke) without establishing visual contact with the runway. All 75 occupants, including 37 football players, 5 coaches, and crew, were killed.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was the descent below Minimum Descent Altitude during a nonprecision approach under adverse operating conditions without visual contact with the runway environment. The National Transportation Safety Board has been unable to determine the reason for this descent, although the two most likely explanations are improper use of cockpit instrumentation data or an altimetry system error.

factors.evidence: The aircraft descended approximately 500 feet below the MDA of 1,240 feet during the approach (p. 2136-2138), continuing until impact with trees at 922 feet MSL.

Air traffic control advised that rain, fog, smoke and a ragged ceiling were at the airport, making the landing approach extremely difficult (p. 669-674). Visibility was estimated at 5 miles with low clouds.

The Catlettsburg Refinery, located approximately 2 miles from the runway with lights 300 feet higher in elevation than the airport, could have produced a visual illusion in the final approach phase (p. 2231-2270).
The crew did not make proper required callouts, did not arrest the descent at MDA, and the captain did not recognize that they had descended below minimums (p. 2365-2422).
The first officer failed to call out 500 feet above field elevation and failed to call out at MDA with a positive statement on runway visibility (p. 2365-2397).
The aircraft collided with trees on a hillside 5,543 feet west of the runway threshold, destroying the aircraft and killing all 75 occupants (p. 777-778, 774).

events.text: Southern Airways 932 established radio contact with Huntington Approach Control, descending to 5,000 feet.
Controller advised crew that rain, fog, smoke, and a ragged ceiling were at the airport; weather was 300 feet scattered, 500 feet variable broken, 1,100 feet overcast, visibility 5 miles.
Aircraft began normal descent after passing outer marker on localizer approach to runway 11.
First officer called out altitude readings during approach: 'seven hundred feet...We're two hundred above' then 'four hundred'.
Aircraft descended an additional 220 feet within 12 seconds after MDA callout and collided with tree tops on a hillside 5,543 feet short of runway threshold, burst into flames.

recommendations.text: All segments of the aviation industry should continue to focus attention on the unique demands for crew coordination and vigilance during nonprecision approaches, with particular emphasis on accelerated development of area navigation systems with vertical guidance and heads-up display systems.
Develop and install audible and visual altitude warning devices and implement procedures for their use to warn pilots when approaching selected altitudes during descents and instrument approaches.
Require that all air carrier aircraft be equipped with a functional ground proximity warning device in addition to barometric altimeters.
Establish final approach descent fixes and require pilots to maintain altitude at or above MDA until passing the descent fix, and provide VASI for each runway served by a nonprecision approach.

Revise procedures to require that pilots demonstrate, by means such as oral or written examination rather than simply signing a flight release, that they are familiar with 'off route' airports into which they will operate.

safety_changes: Development and mandate of ground proximity warning systems (GPWS) for air carrier aircraft
Enhanced altitude alerting device requirements
Improved crew coordination procedures for nonprecision approaches
Installation of VASI systems at more airports
Stricter qualification requirements for pilots operating to unfamiliar airports

notes: Read History of Flight (lines 556-725), Analysis and Conclusions (lines 2027-2425), Probable Cause (lines 3381-3400), and Recommendations sections (lines 3405-3580)
Accident was during hours of darkness with adverse weather, contributing to inability to establish visual contact with runway
CVR transcript available in Appendix D but not extracted as focus was on establishing factors and causal chain

records.title: Aviogenex 130

location.name: Rijeka Airport

records.summary: Aviogenex Flight JJ130, a Tupolev Tu-134A charter from London to Rijeka, encountered severe weather during approach. Due to an optical illusion caused by rain, dusk, and water on the runway, the crew believed they were closer and higher than they actually were. The aircraft touched down hard at 260 km/h, the right wing broke off, and the aircraft turned over and caught fire, killing 78 of 83 occupants.
records.probable_cause: Optical illusion caused by dusk, heavy rain, and water on the runway led the crew to perceive the aircraft as closer and higher than its actual position, resulting in a steep descent and hard landing that exceeded structural limits of the right wing attachment.

factors.evidence: Refraction of light on the wet cockpit windshield during dusk and rain created an optical illusion causing the crew to believe the runway was closer and lower by approximately 60 meters (p. 4-5)
The aircraft remained above the glide path despite crew efforts to reduce altitude by applying down elevator and reducing power (p. 4-5)
The aircraft touched down at 260 km/h with excessive forces: vertical load of 4.15g and side loading of 1.46g on the right landing gear (p. 5)
The right wing broke off at the landing gear attachment point due to the extreme loads from hard landing (p. 5)
Fire broke out after the right wing separation and the fuselage turned over and burned (p. 5)

events.text: Flight JJ130 took off from Gatwick for Rijeka; flight proceeded normally despite unstable weather with thunderstorms and rain over Europe
Zagreb Air Traffic Control provided instructions; Rijeka ATC warned crew of cumulonimbus above Uçka mountain range
Aircraft too high to start ILS procedure; crew flew around cumulonimbus using airborne radar, returned over Breza NDB, then followed ILS glide path and localizer normally
Approximately 4 kilometers from runway threshold at 300 meters above sea level, aircraft entered torrential rain; crew activated windscreen wipers
Fifty seconds before touchdown, aircraft was carried upward and rolled right by turbulence; crew attempted to return to ILS approach
Eighteen seconds before impact, engine power was increased and up elevator applied as captain considered discontinuing approach
Captain decided to land; power reduced to flight idle and down elevator applied when aircraft was 800 meters from runway threshold at height over 60 meters
Aircraft touched runway at 260 km/h with excessive forces; right wing broke off; aircraft turned over and caught fire

recommendations.text: Conduct more effective inspection of charter carriers
Study with pilots possible illusions that could be encountered during landing in heavy rain and optical illusions training
Enlarge the training programmes for captains
Modernize the training programmes for fire-fighting personnel
Reconsider meteorological minima at Rijeka airport

notes: Read History of Flight, Analysis section, and Conclusions (Findings and Probable Cause)
Optical illusion is central to probable cause, caused by rain, dusk, and water on runway
Landing speed of 260 km/h resulted in vertical load of 4.15g
Right wing failed at landing gear attachment due to extreme loads

records.title: Hughes Airwest 706

location.name: San Gabriel Mountains

records.summary: Hughes Airwest Flight 706, a DC-9 climbing from Los Angeles, collided in midair with a U.S. Marine Corps F-4B Phantom II over the San Gabriel Mountains. All 49 aboard the airliner and the F-4 pilot were killed; the F-4 radar intercept officer ejected and survived. The Phantom's right wing struck the DC-9's fuselage center and its vertical stabilizer sliced through the cockpit.
records.probable_cause: The failure of both crews to see and avoid each other, though they had only marginal capability to detect, assess, and avoid the collision. Contributing factors include very high closure rate, comingling of IFR and VFR traffic where ATC system limitations preclude effective separation, and failure of the Phantom crew to request radar advisory service despite having an inoperable transponder.

factors.evidence: F-4B's right wing struck center of DC-9's fuselage; vertical stabilizer sliced through cockpit; all 49 in DC-9 and F-4 pilot killed.
Neither crew sighted the other aircraft in time to initiate evasive action; very high closure rate (approximately 1000 ft/s) compromised detection capability.
F-4B operating under VFR not under ATC control; military aircraft operating in civilian airspace with reduced radar detection capability.
Lack of requirement for military aircraft to contact civilian ATC controllers operating in civilian airspace under VFR.
F-4B not detected on radar because of inoperative transponder and low-level temperature inversion affecting radar performance.

events.text: Flight 706 departed Los Angeles at 6:02 pm PDT bound for Seattle with intermediate stops.
Los Angeles ARTCC took control of flight 706 at 6:06 pm, four minutes after takeoff.
Flight 706 passed through 12,000 feet and received last radio transmission: instructed to heading 040 until Daggett VOR.
F-4B Phantom, with failed radio, returning to MCAS El Toro for diagnostic tests, approached DC-9 flight path.
F-4B's right wing struck center of DC-9 fuselage; vertical stabilizer sliced through cockpit; both aircraft destroyed in San Gabriel Mountains.

recommendations.text: Install video tape at all FAA ATC radar displays for use as investigation tool.
Install open area microphone at each terminal and center sector position to record all control position conversations.
Establish climb and descent corridors from TCA tops to APC base.
Establish more definitive procedures for controller guidance in handling Code 7700 aircraft.
Review radar performance monitoring procedures to assure all radar facilities can receive Code 7700 transponder returns.

notes: Sections read: Findings, Probable Cause, Recommendations

records.title: Alaska Airlines 1866

location.name: Haines Borough

records.summary: Alaska Airlines Flight 1866, a Boeing 727, crashed into a mountain near Juneau, Alaska while descending to Juneau airport on September 4, 1971. The crew received erroneous navigation radio indications that led them to believe they were closer to the airport than they actually were. The investigation found no mechanical cause for the misleading data, and the aircraft maintained proper configuration and crew qualifications throughout.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause was the crew's descent below safe altitude due to consistently false information from the captain's navigation radio at several points along the approach path. The specific reason for the erroneous indications could not be determined.

factors.evidence: the captain's navigation radio had apparently presented the crew with consistently false information at several points along the approach path
from the CVR recording it was determined that the crew did not use the audio identification features of the navigation radios and did not use all available navigational aids
the crew descended below safe altitude based on erroneous position reports
the aircraft crashed into a mountain in Haines Borough, about 18 miles west of Juneau

Crew reported leaving FL230 descending to 10,000 feet at PLEASANT
Controller instructed stop descent at 12,000 feet due to other traffic near Juneau
Crew reported passing PLEASANT and entering holding pattern
Crew received erroneous navigation indications suggesting closer proximity to airport than actual position
Crew descended below minimum safe altitude based on false position data
Aircraft impacted mountain near Juneau

recommendations.outcome: The appropriate approach charts for the Juneau Airport have been amended to reflect these changes.

recommendations.text: Continue tests and research into the effects of possible extraneous harmonics generated by a Doppler VOR transmitter on airborne navigational receivers and associated instrument displays.

records.title: British European Airways Flight 548

agencies.name: Air Accidents Investigation Branch
agencies.report_title: Report on the accident to Hawker Siddeley Trident 1C G-ARPI near Staines-upon-Thames, Surrey on 18 June 1972

location.name: Staines-upon-Thames, Surrey

records.summary: Hawker Siddeley Trident 1C G-ARPI crashed shortly after takeoff from Heathrow near Staines-upon-Thames. During the initial climb in noise-abatement configuration, the aircraft lost airspeed and the captain unintentionally retracted the leading edge droops at an insufficient airspeed of 162 knots (20 knots below minimum). The aircraft entered a deep stall from which recovery was impossible at the low altitude.
records.probable_cause: The captain failed to maintain adequate airspeed during climb and failed to extend the leading edge droops properly. Contributing factors included the captain's undiagnosed heart condition, limited co-pilot experience, an aircraft design vulnerable to deep stall if droops were retracted at low speed, and inadequate stall recovery system training.

factors.evidence: Captain failed to maintain airspeed above 177 knots and retracted droops at 162 knots, 20 knots below minimum speed (p. 531-544).
Captain Key had an undiagnosed heart condition that may have impaired judgment (p. 26-30).
Second officer Keighley had limited experience and was not qualified to act as pilot-flying for the aircraft (p. 37-42).
Trident T-tail design with retractable droops made it vulnerable to deep stall if droops retracted below minimum speed (p. 660-679).
Aircraft entered deep stall at second 116 after droop retraction, with stick-pusher system providing insufficient warning (p. 497-507).
Aircraft descended steeply after deep stall with no recovery possible at 1772 feet altitude (p. 506-507).
Aircraft impacted ground near Staines-upon-Thames at second 150.7 (p. 508).

events.text: Brake release, start of takeoff roll on runway 28R.
Aircraft rotates at 145 knots IAS, leaves runway 2 seconds later (p. 471-472).
Autopilot engaged at 355 feet above runway, airspeed 170 knots IAS, 7 knots below noise-abatement target (p. 472-473).
Aircraft begins 20-degree banked turn to port towards Epsom NDB (p. 474-475).
Captain reports 'Climbing as cleared', instructed to contact London ATC on 128.4 MHz (p. 476-477).
Noise-abatement procedure initiated: flaps retracted to fully up, power reduced. Airspeed 168 knots, still 9 knots below target (p. 487-489).
After thrust reduction, airspeed drops to 157 knots, 20 knots below noise-abatement target Vy of 177 knots (p. 540-541).
Droop lever selected up in 20-degree banked turn at 162 knots IAS, 1772 feet altitude, 20 knots below droop retraction minimum (p. 496-498, 543-544).
Stick-pusher stall recovery device operates at low airspeed, autopilot automatically disengages, nose pitches down (p. 498-500).
Second stick-push operates as elevator trim configuration causes pitch-up after first pitch-down (p. 503).
Third stick-push operates (p. 503).
Stall recovery system manually inhibited by pulling override lever. Aircraft pitched up rapidly, lost speed and height (p. 504-506).
Aircraft impacted field near Staines-upon-Thames, all 118 occupants killed (p. 508).

recommendations.text: Speed-operated baulk to prevent retraction of leading-edge droops or slats when airspeed is below safe limit.

Specific instruction and training on change of configuration stalls, simultaneous stick-shaker/stick-pusher operation, and implications of design differences between stick-shaker and stick-pusher mechanisms (p. 3013-3023).
Mandatory carriage of cockpit voice recorders on all civil passenger-carrying aircraft over 27,000 kg all-up weight (p. 3026-3028).
Pilot training on possibility and dangers of subtle pilot incapacitation (p. 3030-3031).
Young trainee pilots given more experience on flight deck before operating as P2 on passenger flights (p. 3033-3039).
Substitute stress-test electrocardiogram for resting ECG in pilot medicals when reliability improves (p. 3041-3043).
P4 seat occupied only by personnel with flight function or under training during critical flight phases (p. 3045-3047).

safety_changes: Cockpit voice recorders became mandatory on large aircraft

records.title: United Air Lines 553

location.name: Chicago Midway International Airport

records.summary: A Boeing 737 approaching Chicago Midway was too high on descent at the outer marker beacon. The captain extended spoilers and steepened descent to 1,550 feet per minute, well above the normal 1,000 fpm. After leveling at minimum descent altitude with engines not advanced fully and spoilers still extended, the aircraft entered an aerodynamic stall. The stick shaker activated and continued sounding until impact into a residential neighborhood. The flight data recorder was inoperative due to maintenance failure.
records.probable_cause: The captain's failure to properly manage the descent and approach profile, resulting in an unstable approach that led to an aerodynamic stall at low altitude.

factors.evidence: The stick shaker, a stall warning device, activated and continued to sound as the aircraft entered an aerodynamic stall
When Flight 553 reached the Kedzie OMB, the aircraft was still at an altitude of 2200 ft MSL
steepened the aircraft's descent rate to 1550 ft per minute
With the spoilers still extended, thrust was not enough to maintain level flight without losing speed

events.text: Flight 553 was cleared by air traffic control for a nonprecision approach
When Flight 553 reached the Kedzie OMB, the aircraft was still at 2200 ft MSL, 700 ft above minimum crossing altitude
Realizing the aircraft was too high, the captain extended the spoilers and steepened the descent rate to 1550 ft per minute
The captain leveled the plane off and increased engine power, but did not advance the throttles fully, with spoilers still extended thrust was not enough to maintain level flight
The stick shaker activated and continued to sound as the aircraft entered an aerodynamic stall

records.title: Eastern Air Lines 401

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Eastern Air Lines, Inc., L-1011, N310EA, Miami, Florida, December 29, 1972

location.name: Everglades, about 18 miles west-northwest of Miami International Airport, Florida

records.summary: On approach to Miami the nose gear down-and-locked light failed to illuminate. The crew abandoned the approach, climbed to 2,000 ft over the Everglades on autopilot and became absorbed in the indicator bulb and in checking the gear from the avionics bay. The autopilot altitude hold was inadvertently disengaged and the aircraft descended slowly and unnoticed in the dark until it struck the swamp. The gear had been down and locked all along; 101 of the 176 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The failure of the flightcrew to monitor the flight instruments during the final 4 minutes of flight, and to detect an unexpected descent soon enough to prevent impact with the ground. Preoccupation with a malfunction of the nose landing gear position indicating system distracted the crew's attention from the instruments and allowed the descent to go unnoticed.

factors.evidence: The entire crew became engaged with the burned-out nose gear indicator light and with visually checking the gear from the forward electronics bay.
The altitude hold mode was inadvertently disengaged, probably by a light force on the captain's control column, and the autopilot descended in control wheel steering mode.
The altitude alert chime sounded once at 1,750 ft and was not noticed; the autopilot mode annunciation and the split between the two autopilot channels made the mode change hard to detect.
No crew member monitored the flight instruments during the final four minutes.
No pilot was assigned to fly the aircraft while the others troubleshot the light, and duties were not delegated.
The crew believed they were still at 2,000 ft until seconds before impact.
Over the unlit Everglades at night there were no visual cues of the descent.
No minimum safe altitude warning capability existed; the controller saw an altitude readout of 900 ft but only asked how things were coming along.
The aircraft struck the Everglades in a shallow left bank while the crew were unaware of the descent.

events.text: On approach to runway 9L the landing gear is extended but the nose gear green down-and-locked light does not illuminate.
Captain discontinues the approach; tower instructs the flight to climb to 2,000 ft and turn west over the Everglades.
Autopilot engaged in altitude hold at 2,000 ft while the crew work on the indicator light.
First officer tries to remove and reseat the indicator lamp assembly, which has jammed; the captain and flight engineer join the effort.
Altitude hold is inadvertently disengaged, probably by pressure on the control column; the autopilot begins a slow descent in control wheel steering mode.
Flight engineer goes down into the forward electronics bay to check the nose gear visually through the viewing port; a company technician riding in the cockpit joins him.
Altitude alert chime sounds as the aircraft passes about 1,750 ft; no crew member reacts.
Miami approach controller, seeing a low altitude readout, asks how things are coming along; the crew reply that they would like to turn around and come back in.
First officer notices the altitude and says they did something to the altitude; the captain asks what.
First officer asks whether they are still at two thousand feet.
Captain exclaims, asking what is happening, as the radio altimeter warning sounds.
The left wingtip strikes the Everglades and the aircraft breaks up in the swamp about 18 miles west-northwest of the airport.

cvr.speaker: FO
cvr.text: We did something to the altitude.

cvr.speaker: FO
cvr.text: We're still at two thousand, right?

recommendations.text: Develop and install minimum safe altitude warning capability in terminal radar systems so controllers are alerted when an aircraft descends below a safe altitude.
recommendations.outcome: MSAW was implemented in ARTS terminal radar systems in the late 1970s.

recommendations.text: Require that autopilot mode changes and altitude hold disengagement be clearly annunciated and that altitude alerting be more conspicuous.
recommendations.outcome: L-1011 autopilot annunciation was modified.

recommendations.text: Emphasise in crew training that one pilot must continue to fly and monitor the aircraft while other crew members deal with a malfunction.
recommendations.outcome: Became a foundation of later crew resource management training.

safety_changes: Minimum safe altitude warning added to FAA terminal radar systems.
Ground proximity warning systems became mandatory on US airliners after this and other CFIT accidents in the mid-1970s.
The accident became a foundational case in crew resource management training on task management and monitoring.

notes: t0 is the approximate gear extension time of 23:32 EST; the CVR times from 23:40:38 onward are recalled from the report to within a few seconds; earlier offsets are estimates and the altitude hold disengagement is placed at its approximate time.
Fatalities: 99 died at the scene or shortly after and the widely cited total including later deaths is 101; 176 occupants (163 passengers, 13 crew).
CVR quotations are the widely published final exchange; exact punctuation may differ from the report transcript.
Recommendation numbers not recalled and are left null.

records.title: Pan Am 806

location.name: Pago Pago International Airport

records.summary: Pan Am Flight 806 departed Auckland on 30 January 1974 with 91 passengers and 10 crew for a flight to Los Angeles with stops at Pago Pago and Honolulu. On approach to Pago Pago, the aircraft encountered microburst wind shear. At 23:40:42, the 707 came into contact with trees 3865 ft short of runway 5 threshold while descending through weather. The aircraft impacted the ground 236 feet further and plowed through dense vegetation for another 539 ft before crashing into a three-foot high rock wall. All four engines were torn from the wings and a post-impact fire consumed most of the aircraft, killing 97 persons. Four crew and passengers initially survived but died later.
records.probable_cause: The flight crew's tardy identification of microburst-induced wind shear. Other factors included poor visibility, lack of altitude and airspeed callouts by the aircrew.

factors.evidence: the flight crew's tardy identification of microburst-induced wind shear
lack of altitude and airspeed callouts by the aircrew
mean rain shower at the airport with reduced visibility on final approach
aircraft came into contact with trees 3865 feet short of runway threshold
aircraft impacted ground and plowed through dense vegetation before hitting rock wall

Approach controller reported mean rain shower at the airport; wind zero three zero (30) degrees at two zero (20), gusting two five (25)
At 23:40:22 co-pilot said you're a little high and at 23:40:33 you're at minimums

Develop equipment for wind shear detection and warning systems.

records.title: TWA 841 (1974)

location.name: Ionian Sea, approximately 100 nautical miles west of Araxos, Greece

records.summary: TWA Flight 841, a Boeing 707-331B operating a scheduled international flight from Tel Aviv to New York via Athens and Rome, was destroyed by an explosive device detonated in the aft cargo compartment while cruising at 28,000 feet. The explosion disabled the aircraft's control systems, causing it to pitch up steeply, stall, and enter a death spiral from which it could not recover.
records.probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of this accident was the detonation of an explosive device within the aft cargo compartment of the aircraft which rendered the aircraft uncontrollable.

factors.evidence: An explosive device was detonated within the aft cargo compartment while the aircraft was cruising at 28,000 feet (p. 26, Finding 4).
The explosion disabled the control system of the aircraft, causing structural damage that made the aircraft uncontrollable (p. 26, Finding 5).
The explosive device was placed in the aft cargo compartment which contained baggage and cargo (p. 6).
The out-of-control aircraft executed a steep pitch-up followed by roll and descent, with apparent engine separation observed by witnesses before impact in the Ionian Sea (p. 7).

Flight 841 lands at Athens; 56 passengers deplane and baggage offloaded
Flight 841 departs Athens with 79 passengers after loading checked baggage, cargo, and mail

Aircraft rolls left to steep descent with apparent engine separation observed

International cargo security procedures
Enhanced luggage inspection protocols
Cargo compartment design improvements

Improved cargo compartment security measures and access controls
Standardization of explosive detection equipment at major airports
International aviation security standards strengthened following post-1974 reviews

records.title: Eastern Air Lines 212

location.name: Cornfield near Charlotte Douglas International Airport, Charlotte, North Carolina

records.summary: Eastern Air Lines Flight 212, a DC-9-31 operating a scheduled flight from Charleston to Chicago via Charlotte, crashed in a cornfield 3.3 statute miles short of the runway threshold while attempting to land at Charlotte. The crew became distracted by non-operational conversation during the approach and lost altitude awareness, descending far below safe altitudes despite terrain warning alerts and altitude alert tones.
records.probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of the accident was the flight crew's lack of altitude awareness at critical points during the approach due to poor cockpit discipline in that the crew did not follow prescribed procedures.

factors.evidence: The crew's nearly total lack of altitude awareness during approach, despite multiple altitude alert tones and terrain warning system activation at 1,000 feet above ground (p. 19).
The pilot monitoring did not detect or call out the excessive descent rate, and required altitude callouts were not made at critical points (p. 20).

The aircraft descended through the final approach fix altitude of 1,800 feet more than 2 miles before the fix was reached, eventually crossing at only 1,350 feet, which was 450 feet below prescribed altitude (p. 20).
The aircraft struck small trees and then impacted a cornfield about 100 feet below airport elevation, broke up, and burst into flames (p. 8).

events.text: Flight 212 departed Charleston with 78 passengers and 4 crew members
ATIS information recorded on CVR indicating weather at Charlotte
Atlanta ARTCC clears flight to descend to 8,000 feet; autopilot disconnect recorded
Crew engaged in non-operational discussion and conversation on several non-operational subjects from 0723:23 through approach
Altitude alert tone sounds, aircraft approaching 3,000 feet
Terrain warning alert activated at 1,000 feet above ground (0732:41), aural warning sounded but was silenced
Second altitude alert at 2,750 feet (0731:54)
Captain identifies Carowinds Tower as approach landmark, becomes fixated on visual acquisition
Initial impact with trees and cornfield; aircraft destroyed by impact and fire (0733:58)

recommendations.text: Initiate ways and means to improve professional standards among pilots
Continue emphasis on improving professional conduct and cockpit discipline

safety_changes: Establishment of Sterile Cockpit Rule requiring flight crews to limit non-essential conversation below 10,000 feet
Enhanced emphasis on altitude awareness and callout procedures
Standardization of terrain warning system utilization and response procedures

notes: Sections read: History of Flight (lines 836-1600), Findings (lines 4169-4300), Probable Cause (lines 4312-4325), Recommendations (lines 4357-4370)
Events constructed from CVR timeline and FDR data in History of Flight section
Recommendations extracted from NTSB safety recommendation letters dated October 8, 1974

records.title: Northwest Airlines 6231

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Northwest Airlines, Inc., Boeing 727-251, N274US, Near Thiells, New York, December 1, 1974

route.from_name: New York John F. Kennedy International

location.name: Harriman State Park near Thiells and Stony Point, Rockland County, New York

records.summary: On an evening ferry flight from JFK to Buffalo with only three crew aboard, the 727 climbed in cloud and icing with the pitot heat switched off. The pitot probes iced over, so the airspeed and Mach indications rose with altitude; the crew, believing the airplane was accelerating, reduced power and raised the nose until an overspeed warning sounded at 24,800 feet. They pulled up further, the airplane stalled, and the stick shaker and buffet were misread as Mach buffet. The airplane entered a spiral dive and struck the ground about 83 seconds later.
records.probable_cause: The loss of control of the aircraft because the flightcrew failed to recognize and correct the aircraft's high-angle-of-attack, low-speed stall and its descending spiral. The stall was precipitated by the flightcrew's improper reaction to erroneous airspeed and Mach indications which had resulted from a blockage of the pitot heads by atmospheric icing. Contrary to standard operational procedures, the flightcrew had not activated the pitot head heaters.

factors.evidence: The pitot heads iced over during the climb in cloud because the pitot heat switches had not been turned on.
Contrary to standard operating procedures the crew did not activate the pitot head heaters before takeoff; the checklist item was missed.
The airplane climbed through cloud in icing conditions, which produced the ice that blocked the unheated pitot heads.
With the pitot heads blocked and static ports open the indicated airspeed and Mach increased with altitude, reaching more than 400 knots indicated while the airplane was actually slowing.
The overspeed warning sounded at 24,800 feet as the erroneous indications passed the limit speed, confirming the crew's belief that the airplane was too fast.
The crew interpreted the stick shaker and pre-stall buffet as Mach buffet and continued to pitch up and reduce power.
The stick shaker activated as the airplane approached the stall but was misread by the crew.
The crew did not cross-check the implausible combination of high indicated airspeed, high pitch attitude, reduced power and a climb rate the airplane could not have sustained.
The report found crews were not adequately trained to recognize erroneous airspeed indications or the stall characteristics of the 727 at high altitude.
There was no warning to alert the crew that pitot heat was off; the NTSB recommended a pitot heat off indication.
The flight was at night in cloud, so the crew had no external visual references to contradict the instruments.
The airplane stalled at 24,800 feet in a nose-high, low-speed condition.
The airplane entered a descending spiral from which the crew did not recover, striking the ground in Harriman State Park.

events.text: The empty 727 departs JFK on a ferry flight to Buffalo with the captain, first officer and flight engineer aboard; the pitot heat switches are off.
The airplane climbs through cloud in icing conditions at night; ice begins to accumulate in the unheated pitot heads.
Passing about 16,000 feet the pitot heads are blocked; from here the indicated airspeed and Mach rise as the airplane climbs, although true airspeed is falling.
Believing the airplane is accelerating, the crew raise the nose and reduce power; the rate of climb increases to well above normal and the crew remark on the apparently excellent performance.
Indicated airspeed passes 340 knots and continues rising as the airplane climbs through 23,000 feet at a high pitch attitude and decreasing true airspeed.
The overspeed warning (clacker) sounds at about 24,800 feet with the airspeed indicators reading about 405 knots; the crew pull the nose up further to slow down.
The stick shaker activates and the airplane buffets; the crew interpret the buffet as Mach buffet consistent with the overspeed warning.
The airplane stalls at 24,800 feet in a nose-high attitude and rolls off into a descending spiral to the right.
The crew attempt to recover, still treating the situation as an overspeed; the captain calls to pull up as the descent rate exceeds 15,000 feet per minute.
In the spiral dive the airplane experiences high load factors and the horizontal stabilizer and elevator structure are overstressed.
The airplane strikes wooded terrain in Harriman State Park near Thiells, about 83 seconds after the stall began, and is destroyed; all three crew die.

recommendations.text: Require a warning or indication in the cockpit of transport airplanes when pitot heat is not on, or require pitot heat to be on automatically whenever the airplane is in flight.
recommendations.outcome: Later transport-category designs include pitot heat off caution lights or automatic probe heating.

recommendations.text: Require that air carrier training programs include recognition of and response to erroneous airspeed and Mach indications, using attitude, power and altitude cross-checks.
recommendations.outcome: Unreliable airspeed procedures were added to airline manuals and training.

recommendations.text: Ensure crews are trained to distinguish stall buffet and stick shaker warning from Mach buffet, and emphasize stall recognition and recovery at high altitude.
Review checklist design so that pitot heat and other critical anti-ice items are checked before takeoff in a way that is not easily omitted.

safety_changes: Boeing 727 operators revised checklists and flight manuals to emphasize pitot heat and added guidance on recognizing erroneous airspeed indications.
Pitot heat off warning annunciations became standard on subsequent transport airplane designs.
Unreliable airspeed and pitch-and-power procedures became a standard element of airline training, later reinforced by the Birgenair 301, Aeroperú 603 and Air France 447 accidents.

notes: Local date 1974-12-01 is used; in UTC the accident occurred on 1974-12-02.

t0 is set to the overspeed warning at about 19:24:42 EST because the onset of the erroneous climb cannot be pinned to an instant; that clock time and the 83-second duration of the descent are as recalled from the report and should be verified.

Altitudes at which the pitot heads blocked (about 16,000 feet) and of the stall (24,800 feet) and the maximum indicated airspeed (about 405 knots) are as recalled from the report; intermediate values are approximate.
No CVR excerpts are quoted; the crew's remarks are paraphrased as crew speech events.
Aircraft MSN and exact JT8D variant are omitted because they are not recalled with confidence; the report is not available online as a deep link so the NTSB home page is cited.

records.title: TWA Flight 514

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report—Trans World Airlines, Inc. Boeing 727-231, N54328

location.name: Mount Weather, Virginia

records.summary: TWA Flight 514, a Boeing 727 diverted from Washington National Airport to Dulles due to high crosswinds, was vectored for a VOR/DME approach to runway 12. At 1104 EST, while 44 nautical miles from the airport, the crew was cleared for the approach without altitude restrictions. The captain misinterpreted the clearance and descended to 1,800 feet, the final approach fix altitude, before the aircraft reached the intermediate approach fix at Round Hill. The aircraft impacted Mount Weather at 1,670 feet elevation at 11:09:22 EST, killing all 92 occupants.
records.probable_cause: The crew's decision to descend to 1,800 feet before the aircraft had reached the approach segment where that minimum altitude applied. The crew's decision to descend was a result of inadequacies and lack of clarity in the air traffic control procedures which led to a misunderstanding on the part of the pilots and of the controllers regarding each other's responsibilities during operations in terminal areas under instrument meteorological conditions. Nevertheless, the examination of the plan view of the approach chart should have disclosed to the captain that a minimum altitude of 1,800 feet was not a safe altitude.

factors.evidence: Crew descended to 1,800 feet before reaching Round Hill intersection where this altitude was authorized (p. 2-4).
Controller issued approach clearance at 44 nm without altitude restrictions; terminology 'cleared for approach' was ambiguous (p. 25-28).
Flight was not classified as radar arrival despite receiving radar service, so altitude restrictions not provided per 7110.8C procedures (p. 27).
Approach chart profile view did not depict intermediate fix Round Hill or its minimum altitudes, only showing 6 DME fix and final approach fix (p. 13).
Aircraft impacted west slope of Mount Weather at 1,670 feet elevation at approximately 230 knots (p. 4).

events.text: Flight reported level at 7,000 feet; cleared for VOR/DME approach to runway 12
Captain reviewed field elevation, minimum descent altitude of 1,800 feet, and final approach fix; announced 1,800 feet was 'the bottom'
First officer commented on altitude fluctuations and bouncing instrument panel
Captain noted minimum altitude to Round Hill was 3,400 feet but discussed with crew that flight was authorized to descend to 1,800 feet
Altitude alert horn sounded at 1,800 feet; captain stated 'I had ground contact a minute ago'
Altitude alert sounded again; first officer mentioned power and captain noted high sink rate
Radio altimeter warning horn sounded (500 feet above terrain)
Captain commanded 'Get some power on'
Aircraft impacted west slope of Mount Weather at 1,670 feet elevation, heading 120 degrees magnetic, approximately 230 knots

cvr.speaker: PF
cvr.text: I hate the altitude jumping around

cvr.speaker: PM
cvr.text: According to this dumb sheet it says thirty-four hundred to Round Hill --- is our minimum altitude

cvr.speaker: PM
cvr.text: I had ground contact a minute ago

recommendations.text: Issue a notice to all operators of air carrier aircraft in terminal areas to ensure that pilots understand the meaning of 'cleared for approach' and that altitude restrictions will be provided
Develop and implement a standardized lexicon of air traffic control words and phrases to be used by all controllers and pilots in the National Airspace System
Establish procedures requiring controllers to provide altitude restrictions when issuing approach clearances to aircraft operating on unpublished routes
Modify approach charts to depict all minimum altitudes associated with approach procedures on both plan and profile views
Mandate installation of ground proximity warning systems on all air carrier aircraft by December 1975

dissent.position: The flight was a radar arrival and should have received altitude protection from ATC. The failure of the controller to issue altitude restrictions in accordance with 7110.8C paragraph 1360, combined with the captain's failure to adhere to minimum sector altitude, was the probable cause.

safety_changes: Ground Proximity Warning System (GPWS) mandated on all air carrier aircraft by December 1975
FAA revised 14 CFR 91 regarding pilot responsibilities after receiving clearance for nonprecision approach
FAA established Aviation Safety Reporting Program for incident identification
FAA revised air traffic control procedures to provide altitude restrictions during nonprecision instrument approaches
ARTS III altitude deviation warning system installed at terminal radar facilities

notes: Read sections: synopsis (p. 1-2), history of flight (p. 3-5), analysis and conclusions (p. 25-40), probable cause and findings (p. 25-40), recommendations (p. 41-42)
Full CVR transcript analyzed; altitude alerts and crew decision-making clearly documented
Detailed timeline constructed from FDR data and CVR correlations
Two NTSB members formally dissented on probable cause analysis
This accident led to major changes in ATC procedures and CFIT prevention systems

records.title: Golden West Airlines Flight 261

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report: Golden West Airlines, Inc., De Havilland DHC-6, N6383 and CessnAir Aviation, Inc., Cessna 150, N11421, Whittier, California, January 9, 1975

aircraft.type: de Havilland Canada DHC-6 Twin Otter

records.operator: Golden West Airlines (Twin Otter); CessnAir Aviation (Cessna 150)

location.name: Whittier, California

records.summary: Golden West Airlines Flight 261 (De Havilland Twin Otter N6383) and a Cessna 150 (N11421) collided in flight near Whittier, California on January 9, 1975. The Twin Otter carried 10 passengers and 2 crew; the Cessna carried an instructor and student pilot. Both aircraft were destroyed, with 14 fatalities. Neither flight crew saw the other aircraft in sufficient time to avoid the collision.
records.probable_cause: The failure of both flightcrews to see the other aircraft in sufficient time to initiate evasive action. The ability of both crews to detect the other aircraft in time to avoid a collision was reduced because of the position of the sun (9 degrees above the western horizon), the closure angle of the aircraft, and the necessity for the Twin Otter's flightcrew to acquire visual contact with radar-reported traffic directly in front of them.

factors.evidence: The sun was positioned 9 degrees above the western horizon at azimuth 236 degrees (south of west), directly between the Twin Otter pilots and the Cessna, making it difficult or impossible to see the Cessna against the backdrop of the setting sun (p. 14).
The Twin Otter pilots were attempting to sight a reported helicopter traffic directly in front of them, which limited their visual search to a narrow sector ahead of the aircraft (p. 14).

Ground witnesses stated that neither aircraft made any abrupt evasive maneuvers prior to the collision, indicating neither flightcrew saw the other aircraft in sufficient time to attempt evasive action (p. 11).

The Cessna 150, not equipped with a transponder, was not observed on approach control radar because its track was tangential to the radar antenna, causing its return to be cancelled by the moving target indicator (MTI) circuitry. Flight test confirmed no primary return on controller's display (p. 13).

The Cessna struck the left side of the Twin Otter at an approximate 90-degree angle just back of the large plane's cockpit, causing a midair breakup with separation of a wing from the Twin Otter's fuselage (p. 11).

events.text: Golden West Airlines Flight 261 (Twin Otter N6383) departed Ontario International Airport on VFR flight plan to Los Angeles with 10 passengers and 2 crew
Twin Otter contacted LAX arrival radar, reported over Rose Hills, 23 nmi east of airport
Arrival controller advised Twin Otter of traffic 5.5 nmi in front, climbing from 1500 to 3000 ft (police helicopter on VFR flight)
Twin Otter crew acknowledged: "Two sixty one, we'll do it."
Controller transmitted advisory that helicopter was now at their 1130 position, 3 miles northbound. No response from Twin Otter.
Midair collision: Cessna 150 N11421 struck the left side of Twin Otter N6383 at approximately 90-degree angle at 2,200 ft, near Whittier. Both aircraft broke up in the air.

Both aircraft destroyed by collision and subsequent ground impact, with wreckage scattered over 8 to 10 city block area in Whittier. Falling debris caused substantial damage to houses and lawns but no injuries to persons on the ground.

notes: Sections read: Synopsis (p. 4), History of Flight (p. 5-10), Aircraft Information (p. 7), Meteorological Information (p. 7), Analysis and Conclusions (p. 12-15), Findings and Probable Cause (p. 15)
Collision geometry study showed aircraft on collision course with 174 knot closing speed
Sun position 9° above horizon, 236° azimuth (south of west), directly between Twin Otter pilots and Cessna
Cessna positioned 57° right of Twin Otter, outside normal scan pattern
Cessna not equipped with transponder, causing radar detection failure due to tangential effect
Twin Otter crew distracted by helicopter traffic advisory immediately before collision
No CVR transcript available in public report
No recommendations issued in this report

records.title: Eastern Air Lines 66

location.name: Jamaica, Queens

records.summary: Flight 66 descended through a microburst on approach to JFK in severe weather, striking approach lights 2400 ft from the runway threshold. The captain was aware of wind-shear reports from preceding aircraft but continued the approach, relying on visual cues rather than instruments.
records.probable_cause: The aircraft's encounter with adverse winds associated with a very strong thunderstorm resulted in high descent rate into non-frangible approach light towers. The flight crew's reliance upon visual cues rather than flight instrument reference contributed to delayed recognition. Contributing was the failure of air traffic control and the flight crew to abort the landing given severe weather conditions.

factors.evidence: aircraft entered a microburst or wind shear environment caused by the severe storms
A severe thunderstorm arrived at JFK just as Flight 66 was approaching the New York City area
flight crew's delayed recognition and correction of the high descent rate
crew's reliance upon visual cues rather than on flight instrument reference
Captain was aware of reports of severe wind shear but decided to continue the approach
aircraft struck the approach lights approximately 2400 ft from the threshold of the runway

events.text: Flight 66 contacted JFK approach controller and was sequenced into pattern for Runway 22L
Controller warned all incoming aircraft of a severe wind shift on final approach
Flight crew continued approach to Runway 22L despite receiving warnings of severe weather
Aircraft entered microburst environment on final approach and struck approach lights

notes: Extracted from official aviation authority final report
depth relabelled to sections at merge: record carries report recommendations/events beyond the summary

recommendations.text: Conduct a research program to define and classify the level of flight hazard of thunderstorms using specific criteria for the severity of a thunderstorm and the magnitude of change of the wind speed components measured as a function of distance along an airplane's departure or approach flight track and establish operational limitations based upon these criteria.

Expedite the program to develop and install equipment which would facilitate the detection and classification, by severity, of thunderstorms within 5 nmi of the departure or threshold ends of active runways at airports having precision instrument approaches.

Install equipment capable of detecting variations in the speed of the longitudinal, lateral, and vertical components of the winds as they exist along the projected takeoff and approach flightpaths within 1 nmi of the ends of active runways which serve air carrier aircraft.

Require inclusion of the wind shear penetration capability of an airplane as an operational limitation in the airplane's operations manual, and require that pilots apply this limitation as a criterion for the initiation of a takeoff from, or an approach to, an airport where equipment is available to measure the severity of a thunderstorm or the magnitude of change in wind velocity.

As an interim action, install equipment capable of measuring and transmitting to tower operators the speed and direction of the surface wind in the immediate vicinity of all runway ends and install lighted windsocks near to the side of the runway, approximately 1,000 feet from the ends, at airports serving air carrier operations.

Develop and institute procedures whereby approach controllers, tower controllers, and pilots are provided timely information regarding the existence of thunderstorm activity near to departure or approach flightpaths.
Revise appropriate air traffic control procedures to specify that the location and severity of thunderstorms be considered in the criteria for selecting active runways.
Modify or expand air traffic controller training programs to include information concerning the effect that winds produced by thunderstorms can have on an airplane's flightpath control.

Modify initial and recurrent pilot training programs and tests to require that pilots demonstrate their knowledge of the low-level wind conditions associated with mature thunderstorms and of the potential effects these winds might have on an airplane's performance.

Expedite the program to develop, in cooperation with appropriate Government agencies and industry, typical models of environmental winds associated with mature thunderstorms which can be used for demonstration purposes in pilot training simulators.

records.title: Air Manila 702

location.name: Guam

records.summary: Air Manila Flight 702, a Lockheed L-188A Electra with 33 passengers and 12 crew, crashed during takeoff from runway 6L at Naval Air Station Agana on 4 June 1976. Seconds after lifting off, engine number three propeller feathered. The captain continued the takeoff despite not yet reaching VR speed, when company policy and safety procedures required immediate abort. The aircraft reached only 75-100 feet altitude before crashing into terrain beyond the runway.
records.probable_cause: The primary cause was the flight crew's inappropriate response to the engine failure; the captain continued flight with the engine failure despite safely being able to abort takeoff before reaching VR speed.

factors.evidence: Seconds after lifting off from runway, the No. 3 propeller feathered.
The captain continued flight with engine failure despite safely being able to abort takeoff, having not yet reached VR speed, when company policy required abort.
Aircraft flew at varying altitudes between 75 and 100 feet for a distance, then flew level for 1,600 feet before crashing.
Aircraft crashed into terrain past the end of runway, dragging across a hill before stopping.

events.text: Air Manila flight 702 crashed while attempting to takeoff from runway 6L of Naval Air Station Agana at 14:47 Greenwich time on 4 June 1976.
Seconds after lifting off from the runway the No. 3 propeller feathered.
The captain continued flight with the engine failure despite safely being able to abort takeoff, having not yet reached VR speed.
After the failure the plane flew at varying altitudes between 75 and 100 feet for a while, then flew level for 1,600 feet before crashing into terrain past the end of the runway.
Aircraft dragged across a hill, pushed through a chain link fence, and struck a car on the highway before stopping in a vacant space and exploding.
