records.title: Tenerife runway collision (KLM 4805 / Pan Am 1736)

agencies.name: Comisión de Investigación de Accidentes e Incidentes de Aviación Civil
agencies.report_title: Report on the collision between KLM Boeing 747 PH-BUF and Pan Am Boeing 747 N736PA at Los Rodeos Airport, Tenerife, on 27 March 1977

location.name: Runway 30, Los Rodeos Airport, Tenerife

records.summary: Both 747s had diverted to Los Rodeos after a bomb explosion closed Las Palmas. In fog, with no ground radar, the KLM aircraft backtracked runway 30 and turned for departure while the Pan Am 747 was still taxiing along the same runway looking for its exit. The KLM captain began the takeoff roll without a takeoff clearance; a simultaneous radio transmission from Pan Am and the tower blocked the warning that Pan Am was still on the runway. The KLM aircraft struck the Pan Am 747 at about 140 kt; all 248 on the KLM aircraft and 335 of the 396 on the Pan Am aircraft were killed.
records.probable_cause: The fundamental cause was that the KLM captain took off without clearance, did not obey the tower's 'stand by for takeoff' instruction, did not interrupt takeoff on learning that the Pan Am aircraft was still on the runway, and in reply to the flight engineer's query as to whether the Pan Am aircraft had left the runway, replied emphatically in the affirmative. Contributing factors were the fog reducing visibility below the minimum for the airport to see the runway, the simultaneous radio transmissions that made the Pan Am position report inaudible in the KLM cockpit, the use of non-standard phraseology by the KLM co-pilot and the tower, the Pan Am aircraft's failure to leave the runway at the third taxiway as instructed, and the pressure on the KLM crew from duty-time limits.

factors.evidence: The KLM captain advanced the throttles and began the takeoff roll after receiving only the route clearance, before any takeoff clearance had been issued.

Non-standard phraseology ('we are now at takeoff', 'OK... stand by for takeoff') and a simultaneous transmission from Pan Am blocked the tower's instruction and Pan Am's report that it was still on the runway.
Fog reduced visibility on the runway to about 300 m, so neither crew nor the tower could see the other aircraft.
The KLM flight engineer's question whether Pan Am was clear of the runway was dismissed by the captain, and the first officer did not challenge the takeoff.
Los Rodeos had no ground surveillance radar, so the tower could not monitor the positions of the two aircraft on the runway.
The airport was congested with diverted aircraft, taxiway lighting was unserviceable, and the taxiway exits were poorly identified in the fog.
The KLM captain was under pressure from strict Dutch duty-time regulations that threatened the crew's ability to complete the return flight.
The Pan Am crew missed the third taxiway exit they had been instructed to take and continued along the runway toward the fourth.
A small tower staff was handling many diverted aircraft in poor visibility on a single frequency.
The Pan Am 747 was still backtracking on the active runway when the KLM aircraft began its takeoff.
The KLM 747, having rotated early and struck its tail on the runway, hit the Pan Am fuselage at about 140 kt and crashed back onto the runway in flames.
Both aircraft were destroyed by fire; all 248 on the KLM aircraft died and only 61 of the Pan Am occupants survived.

events.text: A bomb explosion at Las Palmas closes the airport; KLM 4805 and Pan Am 1736 are among many aircraft diverted to Los Rodeos, which becomes congested.
Las Palmas reopens; the KLM captain decides to refuel fully at Tenerife, delaying departure and blocking the Pan Am aircraft on the apron. Duty-time limits concern the KLM crew.
Tower instructs KLM to backtrack runway 30 and make a 180 degree turn at the end; fog is rolling across the airfield and visibility is falling.
Pan Am is instructed to backtrack the runway and leave it at the third taxiway; the crew are unsure which exit is the third and continue past it.
KLM completes its turn at the end of runway 30 and lines up; the captain begins to advance the throttles and the first officer says they do not yet have ATC clearance.
Tower issues the route clearance (not a takeoff clearance); the KLM first officer reads it back ending with 'we are now at takeoff'.
The KLM captain releases the brakes and begins the takeoff roll without clearance.

Tower replies 'OK... stand by for takeoff, I will call you'; simultaneously Pan Am transmits 'we are still taxiing down the runway'. The two transmissions overlap and only a squeal is heard in the KLM cockpit.
KLM flight engineer asks whether Pan Am is clear of the runway; the captain replies emphatically yes and continues the takeoff.
Pan Am crew see the KLM landing lights approaching through the fog and apply full power to turn off the runway to the left.
KLM captain sees Pan Am and rotates early, striking the tail on the runway for 20 m in an attempt to clear it.
The KLM 747, just airborne at about 140 kt, strikes the upper fuselage of the Pan Am 747 with its fuselage and engines and crashes onto the runway 150 m beyond, exploding in flames.
Fire destroys both aircraft; 583 people die and 61 on the Pan Am aircraft survive. The tower, unable to see the runway, learns of the collision only when the fire is reported.

recommendations.text: Place great emphasis on the importance of exact compliance with instructions and clearances, use standard aeronautical phraseology, and avoid the word 'takeoff' in any ATC clearance other than a takeoff clearance.
recommendations.outcome: ICAO standardised phraseology; 'takeoff' is used only in takeoff clearances and cancellations, and read-back requirements were strengthened.

recommendations.text: Install ground radar at Los Rodeos and other airports where conditions of low visibility and traffic density justify it, and improve taxiway lighting and signage.
recommendations.outcome: Tenerife South airport opened in 1978, relieving Los Rodeos; ground surveillance radar later installed.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the members of a flight crew, whatever their rank, are trained and encouraged to challenge a captain's decision when they have doubts about safety.
recommendations.outcome: The accident became a foundation case for crew resource management training worldwide.

dissent.position: The Netherlands Aviation Safety Board, while accepting the sequence of events, disagreed with the weight given to the KLM captain's actions as the fundamental cause. It emphasised that the mutual misunderstanding created by the ambiguous route clearance, the non-standard phraseology used by the tower, and the simultaneous transmissions that blocked critical messages were of equal importance, and that the KLM crew genuinely believed they had received takeoff clearance.
dissent.topic: probable cause and allocation of responsibility

safety_changes: ICAO standard phraseology reforms: 'takeoff' reserved for takeoff clearances, mandatory read-backs, use of 'departure' for route clearances.
Crew resource management training introduced across the airline industry.
Ground surveillance radar and improved low-visibility taxi procedures at major airports; opening of Tenerife South airport.

notes: The record's aircraft is the KLM 747-206B PH-BUF; the Pan Am aircraft was Boeing 747-121 N736PA. Occupants (644) and fatalities (583) combine both aircraft: KLM 248/248, Pan Am 335 of 396. Serious injuries approximate.

Clock strings are local time; seconds around the collision (about 17:06:50) are approximate reconstructions from the published CVR times and may differ by a few seconds. Earlier times are approximate.
The Spanish report date and title are approximate; Dutch comments were published as an appendix to the Spanish report.

records.title: Southern Airways 242

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report - Southern Airways Flight 242

location.name: New Hope, Georgia

records.summary: Southern Airways Flight 242 suffered total loss of thrust from both engines while descending through a severe thunderstorm with embedded cells. The aircraft encountered massive rain and hail that broke the windshield and caused both engines to ingest water and hail, resulting in compressor stalling and flameout. The crew successfully glided the aircraft unpowered to a forced landing on Georgia State Route 381.
records.probable_cause: Total loss of thrust from both engines caused by ingestion of massive amounts of water and hail during penetration of severe thunderstorm cell. The crew's misinterpretation of weather radar attenuation contributed to the decision to penetrate the storm. Contributing was thrust lever movement that induced severe stalling and major damage to the engine compressors.

factors.evidence: The aircraft descended from cruising altitude of 17,000 feet to near Rome VOR and apparently entered a thunderstorm cell, encountering a massive amount of rain and hail
The hail was so intense that it broke the aircraft's windshield
The crew was apparently misled by the radar's attenuation effect and proceeded toward what they believed was a low-intensity area, when in fact it was the peak convective activity point
The Pratt & Whitney JT8D-7A engines ingested a massive amount of water and hail causing major damage to the compressors and flameout
The crew glided the aircraft unpowered and executed a forced landing on Georgia State Route 381

events.text: Flight cleared to proceed to Rome VOR where peak convective activity was occurring
Aircraft encountered severe thunderstorm with massive rain and hail
Windshield broken by hail; both engines ingested water and hail causing compressor damage and flameout
Crew executed successful forced landing on Georgia State Route 381 in unpowered glide

safety_changes: Improved weather radar training for crews on radar attenuation effects
Enhanced severe weather avoidance procedures
Improved engine inlet protection from hail ingestion

notes: Sections read: Findings, Probable Cause, and event timeline from NTSB Report AAR-78-03

records.title: Pacific Southwest Airlines Flight 182

location.name: San Diego, California (North Park)

records.summary: Boeing 727 collided mid-air with Cessna 172 on approach to San Diego during clear VFR conditions. PSA crew lost visual contact with the Cessna despite ATC instructions to maintain visual separation but failed to report loss of sight. Both aircraft were destroyed in-flight. Seven people on the ground were killed and 22 dwellings destroyed.
records.probable_cause: Failure of PSA Flight 182 crew to comply with visual separation clearance and to report loss of visual contact. Contributing factors: ATC procedures authorizing visual separation when radar separation was available, controller failure to advise of Cessna's direction of movement, Cessna pilot failure to maintain assigned heading, and improper resolution of conflict alert.

factors.evidence: PSA crew lost sight of Cessna despite ATC clearance to maintain visual separation (p. 662-672).
First officer reported not seeing Cessna at 0900:41, but crew did not advise controller of loss of visual contact (p. 868-880).
ATC procedures authorized use of visual separation when radar clearances were available; controller did not advise of Cessna's direction of movement (p. 701-709).
PSA 727 and Cessna 172 collided at 0901:47, 2600 feet altitude, 3 miles northeast of Lindbergh Field (p. 954-965).
Both aircraft destroyed in collision and post-impact fires; 7 people killed on ground, 22 dwellings destroyed (p. 984-986).

events.text: Lindbergh tower local controller clears Cessna N7711G to maintain VFR and contact San Diego approach control after completing approaches (p. 744-745).
Approach controller advises PSA 182 'traffic at twelve o'clock, three miles, out of one thousand seven hundred' (p. 824-828).
First officer says 'Got em'', and captain informs controller 'Traffic in sight' (p. 830-836).
Approach controller clears Flight 182 to 'maintain visual separation' and contact Lindbergh tower (p. 837-839).
Flight 182 reports to Lindbergh tower downwind leg for landing; tower advises 'traffic, twelve o'clock, one mile, a Cessna' (p. 852-861).
First officer calls for 5-degree flaps, captain asks if that is the traffic being looked at; first officer responds 'Yeah, but I don't see him now' (p. 864-871).
Flight 182 tells local controller 'Okay, we had it there a minute ago' and 'I think he's pass(ed) off to our right' but does not declare loss of visual contact (p. 874-879).
First officer asks 'Are we clear of that Cessna?'; flight engineer says 'Suppose to be'; captain says 'I guess'; forward jumpseat occupant says 'I hope' (p. 901-909).
Captain says 'Oh yeah, before we turned downwind, I saw him about one o'clock, probably behind us now' (p. 916-918).
Conflict alert warning begins at San Diego Approach Control Facility indicating predicted flight paths would enter warning parameters (p. 931-939).
Flight 182 and Cessna 172 collide at 2600 feet, 3 miles northeast of Lindbergh Field; Flight 182 overtaking Cessna, Cessna pitches nose-up, impacts right wing (p. 954-965).

recommendations.text: Implement a Terminal Radar Service Area (TRSA) at Lindbergh Airport, San Diego, California
Review procedures at all airports used regularly by air carrier and general aviation aircraft to determine which areas require terminal control area or terminal radar service area
Use visual separation in terminal control areas and terminal radar service areas only when a pilot requests it, except for sequencing on final approach with radar monitoring
Re-evaluate policy with regard to use of visual separation in other terminal areas

dissent.position: Member McADAMS dissented; see dissenting statement on page 39

safety_changes: Terminal Radar Service Areas (TRSA) implemented at major airports
Restrictions on visual separation procedures in terminal areas
Enhanced conflict alert resolution procedures

notes: Read sections: narrative (p. 7-8), probable cause and amended probable cause (p. 36-38), safety recommendations (p. 38-41)

records.title: United Airlines 173

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: United Airlines, Inc., McDonnell-Douglas DC-8-61, N8082U, Portland, Oregon, December 28, 1978

location.name: Wooded residential area about 6 nm southeast of Portland International Airport, Oregon

records.summary: When the landing gear was extended on approach to Portland, an abnormal thump and yaw and a missing gear-down indication led the crew to break off the approach and hold while they troubleshot the problem and prepared the cabin for an emergency landing. The captain remained preoccupied with the gear for about an hour while the fuel state became critical; the flight engineer's and first officer's fuel advisories were not acted on decisively. All four engines flamed out from fuel exhaustion and the DC-8 crash-landed in a wooded suburb, killing 10 of the 189 on board. The accident led directly to the development of crew resource management training.
records.probable_cause: The failure of the captain to monitor properly the aircraft's fuel state and to properly respond to the low fuel state and the crewmember's advisories regarding fuel state. This resulted in fuel exhaustion to all engines. His inattention resulted from preoccupation with a landing gear malfunction and preparations for a possible landing emergency. Contributing to the accident was the failure of the other two flight crewmembers either to fully comprehend the criticality of the fuel state or to successfully communicate their concern to the captain.

factors.evidence: A corroded retract cylinder piston rod on the right main gear failed on extension; the gear fell free with a thump and the gear-down indication was lost, although the gear was actually down and locked.
The captain devoted the holding period to troubleshooting the gear indication and coordinating cabin preparation for an emergency landing.
The captain lost track of the fuel remaining and of the time needed to reach the runway.
The crew did not properly monitor and respond to the decreasing fuel quantity during about an hour of holding.
The flight engineer and first officer expressed concern about fuel but did not communicate its criticality assertively, and the captain did not respond to their advisories.
The fuel tanks ran dry after the extended hold; engine No. 4 flamed out first, followed by the others.
All four engines lost power from fuel exhaustion and the aircraft descended into trees and houses short of the airport.
The forced landing occurred after dark in a residential area.

events.text: Flight is cleared for a visual approach to runway 28 at Portland.
Landing gear extended; the crew hear a loud thump and feel a yaw, and the right main gear green light does not illuminate.
Captain breaks off the approach and requests holding to troubleshoot the gear indication; ATC clears the flight to hold southeast of the airport at 5,000 ft.
Flight engineer checks the gear visually through the viewers and consults with United maintenance by radio; the gear appears down but the indication problem is unresolved.
Captain discusses emergency landing preparations with the senior flight attendant and continues circling while the cabin is prepared.
Flight engineer reports the fuel remaining is about 5,000 lb; the crew discuss fuel but continue holding.
Flight engineer advises that a further fifteen minutes will leave the aircraft very low on fuel; the captain still does not commit to landing.
Captain says he plans to land in about five more minutes and continues briefing the emergency landing.
First officer reports that they are going to lose an engine; engine No. 4 flames out from fuel starvation.
Crew turns toward the airport and requests an immediate clearance; ATC clears the flight for a visual approach to runway 28L.
Flight engineer reports the remaining engines are flaming out.
First officer transmits a Mayday to Portland tower, reporting the engines are flaming out, the aircraft is going down and will not reach the airport.

Aircraft strikes trees and two houses in a wooded residential area about 6 nm southeast of the airport; the fuselage is torn open but there is no fire because the tanks are empty. The flight engineer, a flight attendant and eight passengers die.

recommendations.text: Issue an operations bulletin to all air carrier operations inspectors directing them to urge their assigned operators to ensure that their flightcrews are indoctrinated in principles of flightdeck resource management, with particular emphasis on the merits of participative management for captains and assertiveness training for other cockpit crewmembers.
recommendations.outcome: United Airlines introduced the first airline CRM program in 1981 and CRM training became an industry standard.

recommendations.text: Require inspection of DC-8 main landing gear retract cylinder assemblies for corrosion and require corrective action.

safety_changes: Development and adoption of Crew Resource Management (CRM) training; United's Cockpit Resource Management program began in 1981.
Greater emphasis in airline training on fuel-state awareness and time management during abnormal situations.

notes: Clock times other than 18:06:46 (first flameout) and 18:13:21 are approximate to the minute; t0 is the approximate gear extension time of 17:12 PST.
Occupants 189 (181 passengers, 8 crew) and 10 fatalities as stated by the NTSB; serious injury count of 23 is from memory and may differ.
The 5,000 lb fuel remark at about 17:46 is paraphrased from the transcript; crew speech is paraphrased rather than quoted.
Recommendation A-79-47 wording is recalled from the report; the second recommendation has no id.

records.title: American Airlines 191

location.name: Des Plaines

records.summary: American Airlines Flight 191, a McDonnell Douglas DC-10 departing O'Hare for Los Angeles, crashed on 25 May 1979 after its left engine and pylon separated during takeoff rotation, killing all 271 aboard and 2 people on the ground in the deadliest US aviation accident. The NTSB found improper maintenance procedures had damaged the pylon, and that the separating engine severed hydraulic lines, causing an uncommanded retraction of the left wing's slats while also cutting power to the captain's instruments, stick shaker, and slat-disagreement warning system.
records.probable_cause: The NTSB found the probable cause was separation of the left engine and pylon assembly during takeoff, caused by damage from improper maintenance procedures, which led to asymmetric stall and loss of control after the slats retracted and stall-warning systems lost electrical power.

factors.evidence: The engine separation was attributed to damage to the pylon structure holding the engine to the wing, caused by improper maintenance procedures at American Airlines (p. 3, 628-631).
As the aircraft was beginning its takeoff rotation, engine number one separated from the left wing, flipping over the top of the wing and landing on the runway (p. 3, 715-717).

As the engine separated it severed hydraulic lines that lock the wing's leading-edge slats in place, and aerodynamic forces resulted in an uncommanded retraction of the outboard slats (p. 3, 634-635).

The number-one electrical bus failed, causing several electrical systems to go offline, most notably the captain's instruments, his stick shaker, and the slat disagreement sensors (p. 3, 621-622, 641-643).

The disrupted and unbalanced aerodynamics caused the aircraft to roll abruptly to the left until it was partially inverted, reaching a bank angle past vertical, before crashing in an open field (p. 3, 589-597).

events.text: Flight 191 cleared for takeoff from runway 32R; captain acknowledges 'American one ninety-one under way'.
During takeoff rotation, sections of the left engine pylon structure come off the aircraft; witnesses see white smoke or vapor from the No. 1 engine pylon area.
The entire No. 1 engine and pylon assembly separate from the aircraft, go over the top of the wing, and fall to the runway.
The cockpit voice recorder captures only a thump and the first officer exclaiming 'Damn!' as the engine detaches; recording then ends due to power loss.
The separating engine severs hydraulic lines that locked the left wing's leading-edge slats, and aerodynamic forces cause an uncommanded retraction of the outboard slats.
The number-one electrical bus fails with the engine, knocking out the captain's instruments, his stick shaker, and the slat-disagreement warning system.
The aircraft lifts off about 6,000 feet down runway 32R, climbs with wings level to about 300 feet above ground.
The aircraft begins to turn and roll to the left, nose pitches down, and aircraft begins to descend.
Aircraft continues rolling left until wings are past the vertical position (inverted), with the nose well below the horizon.
Flight 191 crashes in an open field and trailer park about 4,600 feet northwest of the departure end of runway 32R; the aircraft is destroyed in the impact and ground fire.

recommendations.text: Require a fleetwide inspection of all DC-10 pylon assemblies, including checks for proper clearances, missing or loose fasteners, and structural damage.
Establish standard minimum clearance specifications for spherical bearing assemblies and aft wing clevis to prevent interference.
Enhance surveillance and reporting systems to detect and prevent improper maintenance procedures across the airline industry.
Improve communications and information sharing among operators, manufacturers, and FAA regarding maintenance damage incidents.

safety_changes: DC-10 Type Certificate suspension and subsequent restoration with enhanced inspection requirements
Fleetwide inspection and modification of DC-10 pylon attach points
Enhanced electrical system redundancy in DC-10 aircraft
Improved FAA surveillance procedures for maintenance practices at major carriers

notes: Comprehensive NTSB final report read; key sections: Synopsis (p. 560), History of Flight (p. 700-735), Wreckage and Impact (p. 1172+), and detailed maintenance analysis (p. 2200-2400)
CVR limited due to power loss at time of engine separation
Design deficiency and maintenance error clearly documented as causal factors
This was the deadliest aviation accident in US history at the time of occurrence

records.title: Dan-Air 1008

location.name: Mount La Esperanza

records.summary: Dan-Air Flight 1008 was cleared to join a nonstandard unpublished holding pattern without a chart. Following ambiguous ATC instructions, the captain turned toward terrain and struck Mount La Esperanza while flying in cloud at 13,500 feet in an area where MSA was 14,500 feet.
records.probable_cause: The pilot in command, without taking account of the altitude at which he was flying, took the aircraft into an area of high terrain and thereby failed to maintain a safe height above terrain. Contributing factors included imprecise navigation and disorientation, ambiguous ATC directions for an unpublished procedure, lack of teamwork between crew members, and the aircraft descending to an altitude inadequate for the holding pattern terrain.

factors.evidence: Aircraft struck Mount La Esperanza at 13:21:15 while flying in cloud at approximately 13,500 feet.
Pilot in command, without accounting for altitude and terrain, flew aircraft into area of high ground; failed to maintain required terrain clearance.
Tardy and ambiguous directions from ATC regarding the unpublished hold directly contributed to disorientation of the aircraft commander.
Aircraft was flying in cloud when it struck the mountain, reducing crew ability to see terrain.
Altitude clearance of 5000 feet was inadequate for this holding pattern area; MSA was 14,500 feet.
Co-pilot did not check or query the operations being carried out by the commander as required by company manual; lack of teamwork between crew.

events.text: Aircraft cleared to join unpublished holding pattern over FP beacon with limited information.
Aircraft turned right to intercept approach but failed to maintain proper heading and turned left toward high terrain.
Ground Proximity Warning System activated as aircraft descended toward high terrain.
Crew initiated climb with engines at full power in response to GPWS warning.
Aircraft struck Mount La Esperanza while in steep turn, totally destroyed; all 146 occupants killed.

recommendations.text: Flight crews should be reminded that precise navigation and adequate vertical terrain clearance are of vital importance.
When there are any doubts about ATC instructions, crews must request clarification before executing maneuvers.
ICAO should clarify ambiguities in documents regarding published holding circuits and definition of 'standard' hold.

dissent.position: ATC transmission regarding holding pattern was ambiguous and contributed directly to crew disorientation. Clearance to descend to 5000 feet was inadequate; MSA should have been 7000 feet minimum. Lack of published holding pattern contributed to accident.

notes: Sections read: History of Flight, Findings, Causes, UK Addendum

records.title: Air Florida 90

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Air Florida, Inc., Boeing 737-222, N62AF, Collision with 14th Street Bridge, Near Washington National Airport, Washington, D.C., January 13, 1982

location.name: 14th Street Bridge over the Potomac River, Washington, D.C.

records.summary: During a heavy snowstorm at Washington National the 737 was de-iced, then waited about 49 minutes in a departure queue with continuing snowfall and with engine anti-ice switched off. Ice in the engine inlet pressure probes caused the EPR gauges to read high, so the crew set what looked like takeoff thrust but was actually far less, and snow and ice on the wings degraded lift. The first officer voiced doubts about the instrument readings during the takeoff roll but the captain continued. The airplane struggled into the air, stalled, and struck the 14th Street Bridge and the frozen Potomac River. Seventy-four of the 79 on board and four people on the bridge died.
records.probable_cause: The flightcrew's failure to use engine anti-ice during ground operation and takeoff, their decision to take off with snow/ice on the airfoil surfaces of the aircraft, and the captain's failure to reject the takeoff during the early stage when his attention was called to anomalous engine instrument readings. Contributing to the accident were the prolonged ground delay between deicing and the receipt of ATC takeoff clearance during which the airplane was exposed to continual precipitation, the known inherent pitchup characteristics of the B-737 aircraft when the leading edge is contaminated with even small amounts of snow or ice, and the limited experience of the flightcrew in jet transport winter operations.

factors.evidence: Engine anti-ice was left off throughout ground operations and takeoff, and the crew departed with snow and ice on the wings after a de-icing that had been followed by 49 minutes of continued snowfall.
Ice blocked the engine Pt2 inlet pressure probes so the EPR gauges indicated the 2.04 takeoff target while the engines were producing thrust equivalent to about 1.70 EPR.
Snow and ice on the wings and leading edges increased stall speed and induced the 737's pitch-up tendency after liftoff.

The crew did not use engine anti-ice as required in icing conditions, used reverse thrust during pushback contrary to guidance, and taxied close behind another jet in an attempt to melt snow with its exhaust.
The first officer repeatedly questioned the engine indications during the takeoff roll but did not insist on rejecting the takeoff and the captain did not respond to his concerns.
Both pilots had limited experience in jet transport winter operations; neither had significant experience of taking off in snow.
The 737 had known pitch-up and roll-off characteristics when its leading edge was contaminated with even small amounts of snow or ice.
The stick shaker activated almost immediately after liftoff and continued until impact.
Air Florida's training and guidance on winter operations, de-icing and contaminated wing takeoffs was limited.
With reduced thrust and contaminated wings the airplane could not accelerate or climb and entered a stall at low altitude.
The airplane descended in a nose-high attitude and struck the bridge and the frozen river.
Survivors were in the icy river for more than 20 minutes before a helicopter rescue; the report identified deficiencies in water rescue capability at the airport.

events.text: The airplane is de-iced at the gate with a glycol mixture in heavy snow; the airport is closed for snow clearance and the flight is delayed.
During pushback the tug slips on the ice; the crew use reverse thrust to try to push back, contrary to the operator's guidance, blowing snow and slush around the airplane.
In the departure queue the crew taxi close behind a DC-9, hoping its exhaust will melt snow from the wings; engine anti-ice remains off.
Tower clears Palm 90 for takeoff on runway 36 with 'no delay on departure' because of landing traffic two and a half miles out.
Takeoff roll begins; the EPR gauges show the 2.04 target but the iced Pt2 probes mean the engines are producing far less thrust.
First officer: 'God, look at that thing. That don't seem right, does it?' and, seconds later, 'Ah, that's not right.'
Captain replies 'Yes it is, there's eighty' and continues the takeoff; the first officer says 'Naw, I don't think that's right' then 'Ah, maybe it is.'
Captain calls 'Hundred and twenty'; the first officer answers 'I don't know.' The acceleration is markedly slower than normal.
'V one' and 'V two' calls; the airplane becomes airborne about 2,000 feet from the end of the runway after a takeoff roll of some 45 seconds.
The stick shaker activates immediately after liftoff and the airplane pitches up with contaminated wings; the captain calls 'forward, forward, easy. We only want five hundred.'
'Stalling, we're falling'; the airplane reaches a maximum height of a few hundred feet and begins to descend.
First officer: 'Larry, we're going down, Larry.' Captain: 'I know it.'
The airplane strikes vehicles and the northbound span of the 14th Street Bridge and plunges through the ice of the Potomac River.
A U.S. Park Police helicopter and bystanders pull the five survivors from the river more than 20 minutes after the crash.

cvr.speaker: FO

cvr.speaker: CAPT

recommendations.text: Issue guidance and require training on the effects of wing contamination, the need to re-de-ice after holdover times are exceeded, and the use of engine anti-ice in icing conditions.
recommendations.outcome: The 'clean aircraft concept' was formalized and, after later accidents, 14 CFR 121.629 was revised in 1992 to require approved ground de-icing programs with holdover times.

recommendations.text: Require that flight crews be trained to recognize erroneous engine pressure ratio indications caused by iced inlet probes and to cross-check with N1 and fuel flow.
recommendations.outcome: Boeing and operators added cross-checks of N1 against EPR in icing conditions.

recommendations.text: Require operators to give flight crews training in assertive communication and decision-making so that a takeoff is rejected when either pilot detects abnormal indications.
recommendations.outcome: The accident became a founding case in crew resource management training adopted across U.S. airlines during the 1980s.

recommendations.text: Improve water rescue capability and response planning at airports adjacent to water.
recommendations.outcome: Washington National Airport acquired water rescue equipment and revised its emergency plan.

safety_changes: Airline de-icing practice moved toward the clean aircraft concept with holdover time tables and mandatory re-de-icing, later codified in 14 CFR 121.629.
Boeing reinforced 737 guidance on leading-edge contamination and the use of engine anti-ice, and operators added N1 cross-checks of EPR.
Crew resource management training spread across U.S. carriers, using Flight 90's cockpit exchange as a case study in monitoring and assertiveness.
Water rescue capability at Washington National and other waterside airports was upgraded.

notes: Fatalities (78) comprise 74 of the 79 aboard plus 4 people in vehicles on the bridge; 5 aboard survived with serious injuries.
CVR quotes and clock times follow the widely reproduced public transcript; individual times may be off by one to two seconds.
The ground delay of about 49 minutes between de-icing and takeoff clearance and the pushback and DC-9 taxi episodes are as described in the report; their t values are approximate.
Actual engine thrust is given in the report as about 10,750 pounds per engine versus about 14,500 expected, corresponding to an actual EPR of about 1.70 against an indicated 2.04.
Aircraft MSN is omitted because it is not recalled with confidence.

records.title: Pan Am 759

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report - Pan American World Airways, Inc., Flight 759

location.name: Kenner, Louisiana

records.summary: Pan Am Flight 759 crashed in Kenner, Louisiana, minutes after takeoff when the Boeing 727 encountered a microburst that produced a downdraft and decreasing headwind. The aircraft lifted off and climbed briefly then began to descend, striking trees. Eight people on the ground were killed.
records.probable_cause: The aircraft's encounter with microburst-induced wind shear during the liftoff and initial climb phase, which imposed a downdraft and a decreasing headwind. The effects of the wind shear were difficult for the pilot to recognize and react to in time for the aircraft's descent to be arrested before impact with trees.

factors.evidence: The aircraft experienced a decreasing headwind shear of about 38 knots and a 7 fps downdraft at 100 feet AGL caused by diverging flow from a microburst (p. 76)

At the time of Flight 759's takeoff, there were thunderstorms over the east of the airport with rainfall rates of 0.5 to 1.8 in/hr, with maximum possible rainfall rate of 5.7 in/hr near the departure end of runway 10 (p. 76)

The aircraft was not equipped with flight instrument systems designed to sense wind shear and provide instantaneous information, and the Low Level Wind Shear Alert System did not detect the wind shear until after Clipper 759 began its takeoff (p. 76)
The aircraft struck a line of trees at an altitude of about 50 feet and crashed into the residential area of Kenner

events.text: Flight 759 began its takeoff from Runway 10 at 16:07:57 in conditions where the winds were reported to be gusty and swirling.
Flight 759 lifted off the runway, climbed to an altitude of between 95 and 150 ft, and then began to descend.
About 2376 ft from the end of runway, the aircraft struck a line of trees at an altitude of about 50 ft.
The aircraft crashed into the residential area of Kenner, destroying a house at 1624 Fairway Street.

recommendations.text: Review all Low Level Wind Shear Alert System installations to identify and correct deficiencies in coverage
Make appropriate distribution to the aviation community of information regarding LLWSAS location, capabilities and limitations
Record output data from all installed Low Level Wind Shear Alert System sensors and retain for reconstruction of wind shear events
Emphasize to pilots the importance of making prompt reports of wind shear and assure ATC transmits such reports promptly
Require that Automatic Terminal Information Service advisories be amended promptly to provide current wind shear information
Evaluate methods and procedures for using weather information as criteria for delaying approach and departure operations
Study the feasibility of establishing aircraft operational limitations based on Low Level Wind Shear Alert System data
Make necessary changes to display Low Level Wind Shear Alert System wind output data as longitudinal and lateral components
Use data from Joint Airport Weather Studies Project to quantify low-level wind shear hazard and evaluate system effectiveness
Develop training aids and realistic microburst wind models, and promote development of airborne wind shear detection devices

safety_changes: Development and deployment of airborne wind shear detection and warning systems (WSOD/WSADL)
Enhanced training for pilots on wind shear recognition and recovery procedures
Improved Low Level Wind Shear Alert Systems (LLWSAS) at major airports
Doppler weather radar deployment in terminal areas for better wind shear detection

notes: Sections read: Synopsis, Findings, Probable Cause, Recommendations from NTSB Report AAR-83-02

records.title: Air Canada 143 (Gimli Glider)
records.time_reference: CDT (local); the report gives few exact clock times, so t is relative to the first fuel-pressure warning at about 20:00 CDT

agencies.name: Canadian Aviation Safety Board (predecessor of TSB)
agencies.report_title: Final Report of the Board of Inquiry Investigating the Circumstances of an Accident Involving the Air Canada Boeing 767 Aircraft C-GAUN that Effected an Emergency Landing at Gimli, Manitoba on the 23rd Day of July, 1983 (Lockwood Board of Inquiry)

location.name: Gimli Industrial Park Airport (former RCAF Station Gimli), Manitoba

records.summary: The new Boeing 767 was dispatched from Montreal with its fuel quantity indicators blank after a maintenance circuit-breaker mix-up. The fuel load was determined by dripstick, but the litres were converted to kilograms using the pounds-per-litre factor, so the aircraft carried less than half the fuel required. Both engines flamed out over Ontario at 41,000 ft; the crew glided the airliner to a dead-stick landing on a disused runway at Gimli, Manitoba, and all 69 occupants survived.
records.probable_cause: The Board of Inquiry found that the aircraft ran out of fuel because the fuel quantity was calculated with an incorrect conversion factor after the fuel quantity indicating system had been rendered inoperative, and because the aircraft was dispatched contrary to the minimum equipment list. Underlying deficiencies included the unresolved FQIS defect, confusion over the maintenance log and MEL, Air Canada's incomplete transition to metric fuel measurement on its first metric aircraft, and the absence of a clearly assigned responsibility and training for fuel-quantity calculations without a flight engineer.

factors.evidence: The fuel quantity indicating system had a known intermittent fault in one processor channel that had not been rectified; a replacement part was not available.

A technician in Edmonton had deactivated the faulty channel by pulling and tagging a circuit breaker; in Montreal another technician reset it during troubleshooting, blanking the gauges, and did not restore the earlier configuration or clearly record what he had done.
The aircraft was dispatched with blank fuel gauges although the MEL did not permit it; the captain understood from the log and discussions that it had been flown that way and was acceptable.
Neither the flight crew nor the ground personnel had been trained to perform fuel-quantity calculations by dripstick in metric units for the 767, Air Canada's first metric aircraft.
The inquiry criticised Air Canada's corporate procedures, the ambiguity over who was responsible for fuel calculations on the two-crew 767, and the handling of the FQIS defect and MEL.

The 7,682 litres measured by dripstick were converted with a factor of 1.77 (pounds per litre) instead of 0.8 (kilograms per litre), so the crew believed they had 22,300 kg when the aircraft held roughly 10,000 kg.
The fuel was exhausted in cruise at 41,000 ft near Red Lake, Ontario, well short of Edmonton.
The left engine flamed out first, followed a few minutes later by the right; the aircraft lost all generated electrical power and most instruments, leaving the ram air turbine for hydraulics.
The crew glided the aircraft to a dead-stick landing on runway 32L at the former RCAF station at Gimli, which was in use as a motor-racing venue.

events.text: The previous day in Edmonton a technician finds the fuel quantity processor's channel 2 faulty; he deactivates it by pulling and tagging a circuit breaker so the gauges work on one channel, and logs the fault with a reference to the MEL.
In Montreal a technician troubleshooting the fault resets the circuit breaker; the fuel gauges go blank. He is called away and does not pull the breaker again or make a clear log entry.

Captain Pearson sees the blank fuel gauges and the log entry; from the log and discussions with maintenance he concludes the aircraft has been flying in this condition and is dispatchable, although the MEL does not permit it.

The fuel tanks are dripsticked: 7,682 litres. Ground crew and pilots convert to mass using 1.77, the pounds-per-litre factor, instead of 0.8 kg per litre, and compute an uplift to reach 22,300 kg. The actual total after fuelling is roughly 10,000 kg.
Departs Montreal for Ottawa with the erroneous fuel figure entered manually into the flight management computer.
After a second dripstick check in Ottawa using the same wrong factor, the aircraft departs for Edmonton with 61 passengers and 8 crew.
Cruising at 41,000 ft near Red Lake, Ontario, a warning indicates low fuel pressure at the left engine's forward boost pump; the crew initially suspect a pump failure.
A second fuel-pressure warning follows; the crew decide to divert to Winnipeg.
The left engine flames out. The crew begin a descent toward Winnipeg on one engine and declare an emergency.

The right engine flames out; the 'all engines out' condition leaves the electronic flight instruments blank. The ram air turbine deploys to provide hydraulic pressure for the flight controls; only standby instruments remain.
First Officer Quintal, using DME distance and altitude, determines the aircraft cannot reach Winnipeg and proposes the former RCAF base at Gimli, where he once served, about 12 nm away.
Captain Pearson glides the aircraft at about 220 kt toward Gimli; the landing gear is released by gravity but the nose gear fails to lock.
Finding the aircraft too high and fast on final, the captain flies a forward slip to lose altitude without gaining speed.

Touchdown on Gimli runway 32L, which is in use as a drag-racing strip with people on it; the nose gear collapses and the aircraft stops short of the spectators. All 69 evacuate; 10 sustain minor injuries.

recommendations.text: Establish clear responsibility for, and training in, fuel quantity calculations for two-crew aircraft operating in metric units, and ensure MEL restrictions on the fuel quantity indicating system are unambiguous and enforced.
recommendations.outcome: Air Canada revised its fuelling and MEL procedures and metric training.

recommendations.text: Improve the reliability and support of the 767 fuel quantity indicating system and the maintenance recording practices that led to the defect being carried unresolved.

safety_changes: Air Canada revised its fuel-loading procedures, metric conversion training and MEL handling for the 767 fleet.
The accident became a standard case study in unit-conversion error and in dispatch with inoperative fuel indication.
Boeing improved the fuel quantity processor's reliability on the 767.

notes: The formal investigation was the Lockwood Board of Inquiry (report April 1985) with Transport Canada's Aviation Safety Bureau; the agency code TSB with the CASB name is used as instructed.
Event times are approximate reconstructions; the report's exact clock times were not available, so all clock fields are null and t is relative to the first fuel-pressure warning at about 20:00 CDT.
The altitude at which the second engine failed is not stated in the record because sources differ.
The actual fuel on board figure is given as roughly 10,000 kg; some accounts cite 10,100 kg or 4,916 litres uplifted.

records.title: Galaxy Airlines 203

location.name: Near Reno, Nevada

records.summary: Galaxy Airlines Flight 203, a Lockheed L-188 Electra, experienced severe vibrations shortly after takeoff from Reno. The pilots mistakenly attributed the vibrations to a faulty engine and reduced power to all four engines simultaneously. This caused loss of lift and induced an aerodynamic stall. The aircraft crashed nose-high onto Reno Field approximately 1.5 miles from the runway end.
records.probable_cause: The captain's failure to control and the copilot's failure to monitor the flight path and airspeed of the aircraft. This breakdown in crew coordination followed the onset of unexpected vibration shortly after takeoff. Contributing to the accident was the failure of ground handlers to properly close an air start access door, which led to the vibration.

factors.evidence: Ground crew failed to properly close air start access door before aircraft was taxied from service ramp (p. 2, Finding 10).
Aircraft stalled from insufficient engine power to maintain flight at too low altitude to effect recovery (p. 2, Finding 13).
Captain reacted to vibration by reducing power in all four engines, indicating belief vibration was caused by powerplants or propellers (p. 2, Finding 14).
Flightcrew did not complete required checklists prior to flight (p. 2, Finding 6).
Aircraft crashed at 105 knots in nose-high condition 1.5 miles short of runway end (p. 2).

events.text: Aircraft took off from Reno and immediately experienced significant vibrations due to open air start access door
Pilots reduced power to all four engines, misinterpreting vibrations as faulty engine
Airspeed decreased as aircraft lost thrust; aerodynamic stall developed in nose-high attitude
Aircraft crashed onto Reno Field at 105 knots in nose-high condition 1.5 miles short of runway end

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: I'm going to try a turn

recommendations.text: Issue Airworthiness Directive to modify Electra air start access door to prevent inflight opening
Until air start access doors are modified, inform operators of potential for open door to cause vibration and ensure information in recurrent pilot training
Establish and enforce procedures for adequate surveillance when carrier operations away from responsible office
Instruct Principal Operations Inspectors to verify operators' maintenance and service competence at transient locations
Provide guidance and training on cockpit resource management to all operators

safety_changes: Airworthiness Directive for Electra air start door modifications
Enhanced cockpit resource management training requirements

notes: 1986 NTSB report with clear findings (22 items) and probable cause
Sections read: History of Flight, Findings, Probable Cause, and Recommendations
Classic case of pilot error responding to maintenance-induced vibrations

records.title: Delta Air Lines 191

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Delta Air Lines, Inc., Lockheed L-1011-385-1, N726DA, Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport, Texas, August 2, 1985

location.name: Short of runway 17L, Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport, Texas

records.summary: On approach to runway 17L at DFW the L-1011 flew into a rapidly developing thunderstorm cell on the final approach course and encountered a microburst. The aircraft struck the ground in a field north of the runway, hit a car on Highway 114 killing its driver, and struck water tanks on the airport, breaking up and catching fire. Of the 163 on board, 136 died, plus one person on the ground.
records.probable_cause: The flightcrew's decision to initiate and continue the approach into a cumulonimbus cloud which they observed to contain visible lightning; the lack of specific guidelines, procedures, and training for avoiding and escaping from low-altitude wind shear; and the lack of definitive, real-time wind shear hazard information. This resulted in the aircraft's encounter at low altitude with a microburst-induced, severe wind shear from a rapidly developing thunderstorm located on the final approach course.

factors.evidence: A thunderstorm cell developed rapidly on the final approach course to runway 17L and the crew observed lightning in it before continuing the approach.
The aircraft encountered a microburst with a strong headwind-to-tailwind shear and downdraft at low altitude.
The crew continued the approach into the cumulonimbus rather than abandoning it; a go-around was commanded only after the aircraft was already sinking rapidly.
The NTSB cited the lack of specific guidelines, procedures and training for avoiding and escaping low-altitude wind shear.
No definitive, real-time wind shear hazard information was available; the airport low-level wind shear alert system did not alert before the encounter.
The lack of industry-wide wind shear guidance and detection requirements was a cited factor.
Thrust was reduced during the initial airspeed increase in the headwind and the nose was lowered as airspeed decayed, consistent with training of the time, which increased the sink rate.
The downdraft and tailwind produced a sink rate that could not be arrested before ground contact.
The aircraft broke up on striking water tanks and the wreckage was consumed by fire.

events.text: Aircraft is vectored for the ILS approach to runway 17L; a rain shower and rapidly building cell lie north of the airport on the final approach course.
First officer points out lightning coming out of the cloud ahead; the captain asks where and is told it is right ahead of them.
Aircraft enters heavy rain beneath the cell on final approach.
Airspeed increases in the microburst outflow headwind; captain tells the first officer to watch his speed and thrust is reduced.
Captain warns that the airspeed will be lost all of a sudden as the aircraft passes through the downdraft into the tailwind.
Captain calls for thrust to be pushed way up as airspeed decays and the sink rate increases.
Aircraft descends below the glideslope with a high sink rate in the downdraft and tailwind.
GPWS 'whoop whoop pull up' warning sounds.
Captain calls TOGA; full go-around thrust is applied but the aircraft is still descending.
Main landing gear strikes a plowed field about 6,300 ft north of the runway 17L threshold; the aircraft bounces.
Aircraft crosses Highway 114 and strikes a car, killing the driver, and hits a light pole.
Aircraft strikes two water tanks on the airport, breaks up and is engulfed in fire; the tail section separates and most survivors are in the rear.

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: You're gonna lose it all of a sudden, there it goes.

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: Push it up, push it way up.

recommendations.text: Expedite development and installation of terminal Doppler weather radar and improved low-level wind shear alert systems at airports prone to microbursts.
recommendations.outcome: Terminal Doppler Weather Radar was developed and installed at major US airports.

recommendations.text: Develop and require wind shear avoidance and escape training and procedures for air carrier flightcrews, including simulator training in microburst encounters.
recommendations.outcome: FAA Windshear Training Aid published in 1987; wind shear training became mandatory.

recommendations.text: Require airborne wind shear detection and warning systems on transport category aircraft.
recommendations.outcome: Airborne reactive and later predictive wind shear systems were mandated for air carrier aircraft.

safety_changes: Terminal Doppler Weather Radar (TDWR) program and enhanced LLWAS at US airports.
FAA Windshear Training Aid and mandatory wind shear escape training for airline pilots.
Requirement for airborne wind shear warning and, later, predictive wind shear radar on transport aircraft.

notes: CVR wording is from the widely published transcript, but the clock times for the lines without a clock value are approximate offsets from 18:05:05; the 18:04:18 lightning remark, 18:05:44 GPWS and 18:05:52 first ground contact are recalled from the report.
Fatalities: 134 on board died initially plus 1 on the ground; later deaths brought the total to 137, which is used here. Occupants 163 (152 passengers, 11 crew).

The inappropriate_control_input factor reflects the NTSB's discussion of thrust reduction and pitch handling during the encounter, which was consistent with the training of the time; it is not part of the probable cause statement.
Recommendation numbers not recalled and are left null.

records.title: Japan Airlines 123

agencies.name: Aircraft Accident Investigation Commission
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Investigation Report, Japan Air Lines Co., Ltd., Boeing 747 SR-100, JA8119, Gunma Prefecture, Japan, August 12, 1985

location.name: Ridge near Mount Osutaka, Ueno village, Gunma Prefecture

records.summary: Twelve minutes after leaving Haneda for Osaka, the 747SR's aft pressure bulkhead ruptured as it climbed through about 24,000 ft. The escaping cabin air blew off most of the vertical fin and severed all four hydraulic systems, leaving the crew without flight controls. They kept the aircraft airborne for 32 minutes using engine thrust before it struck a mountain ridge in Gunma Prefecture. Of the 524 people on board, 520 died; four survived.
records.probable_cause: The AAIC concluded that the bulkhead failed because a repair carried out by Boeing after a 1978 tailstrike had been performed improperly: a splice plate was fitted in a way that left only a single row of rivets carrying the load across the joint, greatly reducing the fatigue strength. Fatigue cracks propagated from the rivet holes over the following 12,318 flights and were not detected by Japan Airlines' inspections. The rupture of the bulkhead caused the loss of the vertical fin and of all hydraulic systems, making the aircraft uncontrollable.

factors.evidence: The 1978 repair of the aft pressure bulkhead by a Boeing team used a splice plate cut in two, so that only one row of rivets carried the load across the joint, contrary to the repair instructions.
The improper repair was not detected when the work was accepted, and subsequent inspections by Japan Airlines did not find the fatigue cracks growing in the bulkhead.
Multi-site fatigue cracks propagated from the rivet holes along the repaired joint over about 12,300 pressurisation cycles until the remaining structure could not hold cabin pressure.
The aft pressure bulkhead ruptured at 18:24:35 as the aircraft climbed through about 24,000 ft.
The cabin decompressed rapidly, with mist in the cabin and oxygen masks deployed.
The pressure released into the unpressurised tail blew off most of the vertical fin and damaged the tail cone and APU.
All four hydraulic systems, whose lines ran through the fin area, were severed and lost pressure.
With no hydraulic pressure the crew had no control over the ailerons, elevators, rudder or stabiliser and could influence the flight path only with engine thrust, flaps and landing gear.

The routing of all hydraulic systems through the same area of the tail allowed a single structural event to disable every system; Boeing subsequently modified the 747 with hydraulic fuses and a fin-base bulkhead.
The aircraft flew in phugoid and Dutch-roll oscillations for 32 minutes before descending into mountainous terrain.

events.text: 2 June 1978: JA8119 suffers a tailstrike on landing at Osaka that damages the aft pressure bulkhead.

Boeing repairs the bulkhead. The splice plate specified in the repair is fitted as two pieces, so only a single row of rivets carries the load across the joint. The discrepancy is not detected on inspection.
Departs Haneda for Osaka with 509 passengers and 15 crew; the aircraft has flown 12,318 flights since the repair.
Climbing through about 24,000 ft over Sagami Bay, the aft pressure bulkhead ruptures with a loud bang; the cabin decompresses.
Escaping cabin air blows off most of the vertical fin and severs all four hydraulic systems; the aircraft begins to oscillate in pitch and yaw.
Captain orders squawk 7700; the crew declare an emergency to Tokyo Control.
Crew request an immediate return to Haneda; Tokyo Control approves.
The flight engineer reports that hydraulic pressure is lost on all systems.
Crew inform Tokyo Control that the aircraft is uncontrollable; they attempt to steer using differential thrust as the aircraft wanders over the Izu peninsula and turns north.
The landing gear is lowered by the alternate (gravity) system in an attempt to damp the oscillations and slow the aircraft.
The captain remarks that the situation may be hopeless as the aircraft continues in phugoid oscillations over the mountains west of Tokyo.
The aircraft descends rapidly toward the mountains of Gunma Prefecture; the crew apply maximum power and call for the nose to be raised; GPWS sounds.
The aircraft strikes trees and a ridge near Mount Osutaka at about 5,100 ft, breaks up and burns; 520 of the 524 on board are killed, 4 survive.

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: これはだめかもわからんね

recommendations.text: Improve the quality control and inspection of major structural repairs, and the inspection procedures for pressure bulkheads, so that improper repairs and fatigue cracking are detected.
recommendations.outcome: Airworthiness directives required detailed inspections of 747 aft pressure bulkheads; JAL revised its inspection program.

recommendations.text: Modify the 747 so that a failure of the aft pressure bulkhead cannot cause the loss of the vertical fin and of all hydraulic systems.
recommendations.outcome: Boeing installed hydraulic fuses and a bulkhead at the base of the fin and improved the tail-cone venting on the 747 fleet.

safety_changes: Boeing modified the 747 with hydraulic fuses and structural changes to protect the fin and hydraulic systems from a bulkhead failure.
Airworthiness directives required detailed inspections of 747 aft pressure bulkheads and of major structural repairs.
Japan Airlines overhauled its maintenance quality control and inspection procedures; the accident remains the deadliest single-aircraft accident in history.

notes: The 1978 tailstrike and repair are placed at approximate t offsets of about seven years before the accident.

CVR times for the two quoted lines (18:24:42 and 18:46:33) are as widely published from the transcript; the times of the flight engineer's hydraulic report and the gear extension (about 18:40) are approximate.
Impact time is given as 18:56:30; the report gives a time within a few seconds of this.
The impact altitude of about 5,100 ft is approximate.
The AAIC is now part of the Japan Transport Safety Board; the JTSB home page is given as the source.

records.title: British Airtours 28M

agencies.name: Air Accidents Investigation Branch
agencies.report_title: Report on the accident to Boeing 737-236 series 1, G-BGJL at Manchester International Airport on 22 August 1985

location.name: Runway 24 / taxiway link D, Manchester International Airport

records.summary: During the takeoff roll on runway 24 at Manchester the left engine's No.9 combustor can failed; a section of the can was ejected forward and struck an underwing fuel tank access panel, releasing fuel that ignited. The crew rejected the takeoff and turned off the runway, positioning the aircraft so that a light wind carried the fire onto the fuselage. Fire penetrated the cabin during evacuation and 55 occupants died, mainly from smoke and toxic gases.
records.probable_cause: The cause of the accident was an uncontained failure of the left engine, initiated by a failure of the No.9 combustor can which had been the subject of a repair. A section of the combustor can was ejected forward and struck the underwing fuel tank access panel, rupturing it and releasing fuel which ignited. The major cause of the fatalities was the rapid incapacitation of occupants by toxic gases and smoke from the burning cabin, aggravated by evacuation difficulties, the aircraft having been stopped with the wind carrying the fire onto the fuselage, and the loss of time before exits were opened.

factors.evidence: The No.9 combustor can had been weld-repaired in a manner that did not restore its fatigue resistance, and the subsequent inspection regime did not catch the propagating crack.
The JT8D combustor can cracking problem was known to the manufacturer and operators, but the airworthiness response did not prevent recurrence.
The combustor can failed at about 125 kt during the takeoff roll, producing a thud heard by the crew who believed it to be a tyre burst.
The forward section of the can was ejected through the combustion casing and struck the wing fuel tank access panel.
The underwing fuel tank access panels were not designed to resist impact from ejected engine debris and the cabin materials produced dense toxic smoke.
Fuel escaped from the ruptured access panel and pooled on the runway, igniting against the hot engine.
A ground fire developed during the rejected takeoff (no impact), was carried onto the fuselage by the wind after the aircraft turned off the runway, and burned through the rear cabin.
The cabin furnishings burned rapidly and produced toxic smoke and gases that incapacitated occupants within minutes.
The right forward door was delayed by a jammed slide, the overwing exit was obstructed by seat pitch, and passengers were slow to leave due to the narrow bulkhead gap and smoke.
The crew stopped the aircraft with the wind blowing the fire onto the fuselage and there was a delay before the evacuation was ordered while the cause of the emergency was being assessed.

events.text: Flight KT28M cleared for takeoff on runway 24 with 131 passengers and 6 crew for a charter flight to Corfu.
About 36 seconds into the takeoff roll at about 125 kt a thud is heard as the No.9 combustor can of the left engine fails; a section is ejected forward and strikes the wing fuel tank access panel.
Commander, believing a tyre has burst, calls stop and rejects the takeoff using reverse thrust and light braking.
Tower informs the crew that there is a lot of fire on the left side; the crew request the fire services.
Fire warning for the left engine; the crew carry out the engine fire drill.
Commander turns right off the runway onto taxiway link D, placing the fire on the upwind side; a 7 kt wind carries flames onto the rear fuselage.
Aircraft stops; fire penetrates the rear fuselage and the cabin fills with thick black smoke within seconds.
Commander orders evacuation via the starboard side; the right forward door slide initially jams and the door is delayed about 25 seconds.
Passengers crowd the narrow gap beside the forward galley bulkhead; the right overwing exit is opened by a passenger after a struggle with the hatch.
Airport fire service arrives and applies foam; the fire has already breached the cabin and the rear of the aircraft is burning fiercely.
Last survivors leave the aircraft; 55 occupants die, 48 of them from the effects of toxic gases and smoke, and the aircraft is destroyed by fire.

recommendations.text: Require the fitting of floor-level emergency lighting and smoke hoods or other respiratory protection for passengers, and review cabin material flammability and toxicity standards.
recommendations.outcome: Floor proximity lighting and fire-blocking seat covers were mandated; smoke hoods were not.

recommendations.text: Review the minimum access gap beside galley bulkheads and the spacing of seats adjacent to overwing exits to improve evacuation flow.
recommendations.outcome: Regulations on exit access and minimum bulkhead gaps were introduced.

recommendations.text: Review the JT8D combustor can repair schemes and inspection intervals and make fuel tank access panels resistant to impact from ejected engine debris.
Provide guidance to flight crews on positioning the aircraft relative to wind after a ground fire and on ordering an immediate evacuation when a fire is reported.

safety_changes: Floor-level emergency lighting, fire-blocking seat materials and improved cabin material toxicity standards.
Minimum access gap requirements beside overwing exits and galley bulkheads.
Revised guidance on rejected takeoff and evacuation decision making, including stopping on the runway and evacuation drills for cabin crew.
Research programme into passenger smoke hoods and cabin water spray systems.

notes: post_impact_fire is used for a ground fire that started during the rejected takeoff; there was no impact.
Event seconds are approximate; the report gives the failure at about 125 kt roughly 36 s into the roll.
Recommendation numbers omitted; the report contained 31 recommendations.

records.title: Arrow Air 1285R

agencies.name: Transportation Safety Board of Canada
agencies.report_title: Final Report - Aviation Occurrence Arrow Air Inc. Flight MF1285R

location.name: Near Gander International Airport, approximately 0.5 miles northeast of runway 22 departure end

records.summary: Arrow Air Flight MF1285R crashed shortly after takeoff from Gander, Newfoundland on December 12, 1985. The aircraft accumulated ice contamination on the wings' leading edges and upper surfaces during the approach and refueling stop at Gander in freezing precipitation conditions. The aircraft was not de-iced prior to takeoff, and the ice buildup degraded lift and increased drag, resulting in a stall at low altitude from which recovery was not possible. All 256 passengers and crew were killed.
records.probable_cause: The most probable cause of the stall was ice contamination on the leading edge and upper surface of the wing. Other possible factors such as a loss of thrust from the number four engine and inappropriate take-off reference speeds may have compounded the effects of the contamination.

factors.evidence: Ice contamination on the leading edge and upper surface of the wing resulted from precipitation conditions favorable for ice formation and freezing and frozen precipitation (p. 10-11, 59-61).
Prior to takeoff the aircraft had not been de-iced despite exposure to freezing and frozen precipitation (p. 95).
The aircraft stalled at low altitude from which recovery was not possible, struck terrain approximately 3500 feet beyond the runway departure end (p. 95).
Underestimated onboard weight may have compounded the effects of the contamination; incorrect determination of the aircraft's weight using standard average weights (p. 95).
A non-functioning cockpit area microphone went undetected for an indeterminate number of flights, and no steps on standard checklists tested its functionality (p. 99).
The defect in the cockpit area microphone went undetected due to no testing procedure on standard checklists (p. 99).

events.text: During approach to Gander, precipitation conditions were favorable for formation of ice on wings.
After landing at Gander, aircraft remained exposed to freezing and frozen precipitation without de-icing.
Aircraft began takeoff roll on runway 22, rotated at 167 knots after 51 seconds, showing difficulty gaining altitude.
Airspeed reached 172 knots then decreased; aircraft descended after crossing Trans-Canada Highway 900 feet from runway departure end.
Aircraft struck terrain just short of Gander Lake approximately 3500 feet beyond runway departure end, broke up and exploded.

recommendations.text: Initiate a national safety campaign to ensure that all pilots are aware of the potential consequences of attempting take-off with even minor amounts of contamination on the wings.

Require all Canadian operators of McDonnell-Douglas DC-8 aircraft, and such other aircraft types which the Department deems appropriate, to establish detailed procedures for detecting ice on the wings prior to take-off.
Review the procedures currently in place with respect to functional checks of cockpit voice recorders with a view to ensuring that the serviceability of the equipment is being tested adequately.
Consider seeking parallel action in the United States to that outlined for Canada in CASB 88-09.

Consider recommending a change in U.S. Federal Aviation Regulations such that the flight-time, duty-time, and crew-rest provisions of FAR Part 121 would apply to all operations of Part 121 air carriers, including non-revenue flights.

safety_changes: Enhanced emphasis on clean wing procedures and verification before takeoff
Improved pilot training on effects of minor wing contamination on aircraft performance
Enhanced procedures for detecting upper wing ice prior to takeoff
Mandatory functional testing of cockpit voice recorders before flight
Stricter weight and balance procedures using actual weights instead of standard averages

notes: Synopsis, Factual Information, Conclusions and Causes sections read from TSB report (p. 1-50, 95-100)
De-icing procedures and recommendations sections reviewed (p. 97-105)

records.title: Aeroméxico 498

location.name: Cerritos

records.summary: Aeroméxico Flight 498 collided with a Piper PA-28 Cherokee that entered the Los Angeles Terminal Control Area without clearance. The Piper was not equipped with a Mode C transponder and was not visible to either crew or ATC radar. The DC-9 crashed in a residential neighborhood in Cerritos, killing 64 on the aircraft, 3 in the Piper, and 15 on the ground.
records.probable_cause: The limitations of the air traffic control system to provide collision protection, through both ATC procedures and automated redundancy. Contributing factors were the inadvertent and unauthorized entry of the PA-28 into the Los Angeles Terminal Control Area and the limitations of the 'see and avoid' concept to ensure traffic separation.

factors.evidence: Piper collided nearly perpendicular with DC-9, shearing top of Piper cockpit and damaging DC-9's tail surfaces; DC-9 crashed in Cerritos.
Neither pilot sighted the other aircraft; neither appeared to attempt evasive maneuvers.
Piper not equipped with Mode C transponder; LAX radar not equipped with automatic warning systems.
ATC was distracted by another unauthorized private aircraft (Grumman AA-5B Tiger) entering the Terminal Control Area.
Piper pilot entered the Los Angeles Terminal Control Area without required clearance; entry was inadvertent, not due to physiological disablement.

events.text: DC-9 Flight 498 begins descent into Los Angeles with 58 passengers and 6 crew.
Piper PA-28 collided nearly perpendicular with DC-9's upper left side of horizontal stabilizer support.
Collision sheared top of Piper's cockpit and severely damaged DC-9's tail surfaces including horizontal stabilizer, rudder, and vertical stabilizer.
DC-9 with damaged tail surfaces over-banked to right and entered steep dive; crashed in residential area of Cerritos.

recommendations.text: Expedite development, operational evaluation, and final certification of Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System (TCAS)
Amend 14 CFR Parts 121 and 135 to require TCAS installation in certificated air carrier aircraft
Implement procedures to track, identify, and take enforcement action against pilots who intrude into ARSAs without ATC communications

notes: Sections read: Findings, Probable Cause, Recommendations

records.title: 1986 Mozambican Tupolev Tu-134 crash

location.name: Mbuzini

records.summary: A Tupolev Tu-134 with President Samora Machel and 43 others departed Mbala, Zambia at 18:38 for Maputo. The navigator used Doppler navigation to turn the aircraft based on a VOR signal, but inadvertently tuned the VOR receiver to Matsapa Airport in Swaziland instead of Maputo. This placed the aircraft on a navigation path 45° off course. The crew failed to monitor the correct VOR or cross-check their position and continued the descent. The captain did not respond to ground proximity warnings. The aircraft crashed at Mbuzini, South Africa.
records.probable_cause: Loss of control and impact with terrain due to erroneous navigation caused by crew tuning the VOR receiver to the wrong frequency, inadequate monitoring of navigation systems, and failure to respond to ground proximity warnings.

factors.evidence: Poor design of VOR frequency display with no back-lighting, unusually close frequencies, and similar appearance of displayed numerals made frequency selection error more likely
Crew set first VOR receiver to Matsapa frequency instead of Maputo frequency, diverting aircraft 45 degrees off course
Second VOR receiver correctly set to Maputo but apparently not being used or monitored by crew
Board concluded captain failed to react to ground proximity warning system
crashed at Mbuzini, South Africa

events.text: Departed Mbala for non-stop return to Maputo; weather forecast favorable, estimated time of arrival 21:25
Navigator performed 37-degree turn using autopilot Doppler navigation mode after observing VOR signal indicating interception of Maputo VOR 45-degree radial
Turn placed aircraft on path following 45-degree radial from Matsapa Airport VOR in Swaziland instead of Maputo
Captain re-tuned first VOR receiver to ILS frequency; second VOR correctly displaying Maputo position but not being monitored
Aircraft descended into terrain with ground proximity warning system activated; captain did not respond appropriately

notes: detailed technical analysis provided by board of inquiry
multiple contributing factors identified
Read from text extraction of official report

records.title: Air France 296 (Habsheim)

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la sécurité de l'aviation civile
agencies.report_title: Rapport final de la Commission d'Enquête sur l'accident survenu le 26 juin 1988 à Mulhouse-Habsheim (68) à l'Airbus A320 immatriculé F-GFKC

location.name: Forest beyond runway 34R, Mulhouse-Habsheim aerodrome

records.summary: During a sightseeing charter flight the new A320 carried out a low-speed flypast at the Habsheim airshow with landing gear down and flaps at 3. The aircraft descended to about 30 ft radio altitude, well below the 100 ft planned, at maximum angle of attack with engines at flight idle. Go-around thrust was applied late and the engines had not spooled up when the aircraft flew into trees beyond the runway. Three passengers died in the ensuing fire.
records.probable_cause: The Commission concluded that the accident resulted from the combination of a flyover height lower than the surrounding obstacles, a speed which was very slow and reducing to reach the maximum possible angle of attack, engine speed at flight idle, and late application of go-around power. Contributing factors were the preparation of the flight, the late decision-making on the flypast parameters, the crew's lack of awareness of the trees at the end of the runway and their late recognition of the need to go around.

factors.evidence: The flypast was flown at about 30 ft radio height instead of the 100 ft planned and required for the aerobatic-style flyover, with the crew relying on visual judgement of height.
Speed was reduced to about 122 kt and angle of attack allowed to reach the alpha-max protection limit with the engines at flight idle.
The flight had been planned by Air France with little detail about the site, and the crew received the flypast briefing late with no clear procedures for very-low-altitude demonstration flights.
The crew were not aware of the forest at the end of the runway and recognised the need to go around too late.
The crew relied on the aircraft's angle-of-attack protections during a manoeuvre for which alpha-floor automatic thrust was inhibited below 100 ft.
The aircraft was held at maximum angle of attack with idle thrust, leaving no margin; go-around thrust was applied about five seconds before the trees.
The first officer's calls about height and the reference to the trees did not lead to a timely go-around decision.
The aircraft, wings level and under control, sank into the trees beyond the runway as the engines accelerated.
Fire broke out after the aircraft came to rest in the forest; three passengers died during the evacuation.

events.text: Crew briefed only shortly before departure for a flypast at Habsheim; the flight plan calls for a low-speed pass at 100 ft with gear and flaps down followed by a high-speed pass.
F-GFKC departs Basel-Mulhouse with 130 passengers and 6 crew for the short flight to Habsheim.
Aerodrome sighted late; the captain descends towards runway 34R, disconnecting the autothrust, with gear down and flap 3.
Descent continues through 100 ft; thrust at flight idle and speed reducing.
First officer calls the radio height; the aircraft levels at about 30 ft radio altitude over the runway.
Speed falls to about 122 kt; angle of attack reaches the alpha-max limit and pitch about 15 degrees nose-up; engines at idle.
Captain advances the thrust levers to TOGA as the trees come into view; the first officer mentions the trees.
Engines still accelerating (about 83 percent N1) when the aircraft, wings level and controlled, sinks into the trees at the end of the runway.
Aircraft comes to rest in the forest and fire breaks out on the right side.
Evacuation through the left exits; three passengers die, two of them children, and 34 are seriously injured.

recommendations.text: Define rules and minimum heights for demonstration and airshow flypasts by public transport aircraft carrying passengers, and prohibit such flights below 170 ft or with passengers unless specifically authorised.
recommendations.outcome: French regulations restricted passenger-carrying demonstration flights.

recommendations.text: Improve preparation of special flights, including site reconnaissance and timely briefing of crews.
