Improve the protection and handling of flight recorders after an accident to ensure their integrity is not questioned.

safety_changes: French rules restricting low-altitude demonstration flights carrying passengers.
Revised Air France procedures for special and demonstration flights.
Procedures for sealing and custody of flight recorders after accidents in France.

notes: There is a long-running public controversy about the custody and integrity of the DFDR and CVR recordings after this accident, raised by the captain and others; no accredited agency formally dissented, so dissent is empty.
Clock strings are UTC (local time was UTC+2, i.e. the accident occurred at about 14:45 local) and approximate; t values are estimated relative to the impact with the trees.
The N1 value at impact (about 83 percent) and the 30 ft / 122 kt values are from the published findings; other state values are approximate.
Report date and report title wording are from memory of the Commission's report and may differ slightly.

records.title: British Midland 092 (Kegworth)

agencies.name: Air Accidents Investigation Branch
agencies.report_title: Report on the accident to Boeing 737-400 G-OBME near Kegworth, Leicestershire on 8 January 1989

location.name: M1 motorway embankment near Kegworth, short of East Midlands Airport runway 27

records.summary: Climbing through FL283 the outer panel of a fan blade in the No.1 (left) engine detached, causing severe vibration, a smell of fire and fluctuating engine parameters. The crew believed the No.2 (right) engine was at fault and shut it down, after which the symptoms appeared to subside. During the diversion to East Midlands the No.1 engine lost power on final approach and the aircraft struck the M1 motorway embankment short of the runway. 47 people died.
records.probable_cause: The operating crew shut down the No.2 engine after a fan blade had fractured in the No.1 engine. This engine subsequently suffered a major thrust loss due to secondary fan damage after power had been increased during the final approach. Contributing factors: the combination of heavy engine vibration, noise, shuddering and smell of fire were outside the crew's training and experience; they reacted prematurely before fully assimilating the engine instrument readings; the cross-checks on the engine instruments were not adequate; the misleading response of the aircraft to the reduction of power on No.2 engine led them to believe they had acted correctly; and they were not informed of the flames from the No.1 engine seen by many passengers and cabin crew.

factors.evidence: The No.1 engine fan blade failed from a fatigue crack caused by a previously unrecognised blade vibration mode within the certificated power range of the newly rated CFM56-3C engine.
The blade failure caused severe vibration, compressor stalls and fluctuating N1/fuel flow on the No.1 engine.
The crew throttled back and shut down the serviceable No.2 engine while the damaged No.1 engine continued to run.
The crew did not adequately read or cross-check the engine instruments, including the vibration indicators, before identifying the failed engine.
Cabin crew and passengers who had seen flames from the left engine did not pass this information to the flight deck; the flight crew did not seek it.
The crew had not been trained for the combination of symptoms produced by this failure and had no simulator training on the 737-400 engine instrument presentation.
The new solid-state engine instrument display made vibration and other readings less conspicuous than on earlier 737s; the engine instrument layout led to misidentification.
The uprated CFM56-3C engine had been certificated without full-scale flight testing at the higher thrust rating, so the blade vibration mode was not discovered.
The severe vibration, shuddering, noise and smell of fire produced a startling situation outside the crew's experience, and they reacted prematurely.
With the remaining engine having failed on final approach, the aircraft descended into the M1 motorway embankment 900 m short of the runway.

events.text: G-OBME departs Heathrow runway 27R for Belfast with the captain as pilot flying.
Climbing through FL283 the outer panel of a No.1 engine fan blade detaches; severe vibration, shuddering, compressor stalls and a smell of fire in the cabin.
Autopilot disengaged; N1 vibration indicator for the No.1 engine at maximum, fluctuating fuel flow and EGT on No.1.
Asked by the captain which engine has failed, the first officer answers that it is the left, then the right one.
Captain orders the No.2 (right) throttle to be closed; as thrust is reduced the vibration and shuddering appear to subside, reinforcing the misidentification.
Crew request diversion; ATC offer East Midlands, the company's engineering base, and a descent is started.
No.2 engine shut down (fuel lever to cutoff) on the captain's instruction; the No.1 engine is left running at reduced thrust.
Captain briefs passengers by PA that there has been trouble with the right engine, which has been shut down; cabin crew and passengers who saw fire on the left engine do not challenge this.
Aircraft vectored for the ILS to East Midlands runway 27; landing gear lowered and flaps extended.
At 2.4 nm from the runway and 900 ft agl, as thrust is increased on the No.1 engine, it suffers an abrupt loss of power with compressor surges and fire warning.
First officer attempts to restart the No.2 engine; there is insufficient time for it to spool up.
GPWS glideslope warning as the aircraft drops below the glidepath; airspeed decays and the stick shaker operates.
Aircraft strikes the field beside the M1, crosses the motorway and comes to rest against the western embankment 900 m short of the runway 27 threshold; 47 of 126 occupants die.

recommendations.text: Require all UK-registered 737-300/400 aircraft to have engine vibration indication in the primary field of view and review the certification standards for engine instrument displays.
Require that new engine variants be flight tested at the full certificated thrust rating so that vibration and fatigue characteristics are demonstrated in service conditions.
recommendations.outcome: CFM56-3C fan blades were modified and the certification of derivative engines was reviewed.

recommendations.text: Review training so that flight crews are trained in the recognition and handling of engine failures using the engine instrument displays fitted to the aircraft, and improve cabin crew to flight deck communication of relevant observations.
Improve occupant survivability through review of seat and overhead bin attachment strength and the brace position.
recommendations.outcome: Research into 16g seats and the brace position followed.

safety_changes: Modification of CFM56-3C fan blades and revised fatigue/vibration certification testing of engine variants.
Emphasis on engine instrument presentation and vibration indication in the primary field of view.
Improved cabin crew to flight deck communication training and CRM emphasis on cross-checking engine indications before shutdown.
Research on seat strength, overhead stowage and the brace position for crash survivability.

notes: Event times are derived from published report chronology and are approximate to within tens of seconds; the report gives 20:05:05 for the blade failure and 20:24:33 for impact.
Recommendation numbers omitted; the AAIB report issued 31 recommendations.
Serious injury count reflects the report's 74 seriously injured.

records.title: United Airlines 811

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Explosive Decompression - Loss of Cargo Door in Flight, United Airlines Flight 811, Boeing 747-122, N4713U, Honolulu, Hawaii, February 24, 1989 (revised report)

location.name: Pacific Ocean south of Honolulu, Hawaii; returned to Honolulu International Airport

records.summary: Climbing through about 22,000 ft after a night departure from Honolulu, the forward lower lobe cargo door of the 747 swung open and tore away, causing an explosive decompression that ripped out a section of the cabin floor and fuselage. Nine passengers were lost from the aircraft, and debris damaged engines 3 and 4, which were shut down. The crew returned to Honolulu and landed safely. After the door was recovered from the seabed in 1990 the NTSB revised its findings to a faulty switch or wiring that drove the latches open.
records.probable_cause: The sudden opening of the forward lower lobe cargo door in flight and the subsequent explosive decompression. The door opening was attributed to a faulty switch or wiring in the door control system which permitted electrical actuation of the door latches toward the unlatched position after initial door closure and before takeoff. Contributing was a deficiency in the design of the cargo door locking mechanisms, which made them susceptible to deformation, allowing the door to become unlatched after being properly latched and locked. Also contributing was a lack of timely corrective actions by Boeing and the FAA following a 1987 cargo door opening incident on a Pan Am B-747.

factors.evidence: A faulty switch or wiring in the door control system allowed the latch actuators to be driven toward the unlatched position after the door had been closed.
The cargo door locking sectors were susceptible to deformation and could not prevent the latch cams from being back-driven open.
A 1987 Pan Am 747 cargo door opening incident had shown the vulnerability but corrective actions by Boeing and the FAA were not timely.
The FAA's airworthiness directive after the Pan Am incident allowed up to two years for compliance.
The forward lower lobe cargo door opened in flight and separated from the aircraft.
The door failure caused an explosive decompression that removed part of the fuselage side and cabin floor, ejecting nine passengers.
Debris from the fuselage damaged engines 3 and 4, which had to be shut down.
The event occurred at about 02:09 local time.
The crew descended, dumped fuel and landed the damaged aircraft back at Honolulu on two engines.

events.text: Forward lower lobe cargo door is closed and indicated latched and locked before departure; the latches are subsequently driven toward open by a fault in the door control electrics.
Flight 811 departs Honolulu for Auckland with 337 passengers and 18 crew.
Crew keep the seat belt sign on while deviating around thunderstorms during the climb.
Climbing through about 22,000 ft the forward cargo door swings open and separates, tearing away a section of the fuselage and cabin floor; explosive decompression follows.
Nine passengers and their seats are ejected from the aircraft; cabin debris strikes the right wing and engines.
Engine No. 3 suffers foreign object damage and is shut down; engine No. 4 subsequently shows fire indications and is also shut down.
Crew begin an emergency descent, don oxygen masks and declare an emergency to Honolulu Center, requesting a return.
Flight engineer manages fuel dumping to reduce landing weight while the crew assess control and flap damage.
Cabin crew move passengers away from the damaged area and prepare the cabin for an emergency landing.
Aircraft lands on runway 8L at Honolulu on two engines with flaps only partially extended.
Emergency evacuation completed on the runway; injuries occur among passengers and crew but there are no further fatalities.
In 1990 the cargo door is recovered from the Pacific seabed by the US Navy, leading the NTSB to revise the probable cause from improper latching to an electrical fault in the door system.

recommendations.text: Require modification of 747 cargo door latching and locking mechanisms so that the locks positively prevent the latch cams from being driven open, and require inspection of door electrical wiring and switches.
recommendations.outcome: Airworthiness directives required steel locking sectors and other door modifications on the 747 fleet.

recommendations.text: Evaluate cargo door designs on other transport aircraft for similar vulnerability to electrical faults and lock deformation.
Act promptly on airworthiness issues revealed by in-service incidents rather than allowing long compliance times.

safety_changes: 747 cargo doors were modified with stronger locking sectors and changes to the door control electrical system.
The NTSB revised its report in 1992 after the door was recovered, an unusual reopening of an investigation prompted in part by the parents of a victim who conducted their own inquiry.

notes: t0 is set to about 02:09 HST, the approximate time of the door separation; the departure (about 01:52) and landing (about 02:34) times are approximate; other offsets are estimates.
Altitude at the time of the decompression is recalled as between 22,000 and 23,000 ft.
The final event (door recovery in 1990) is included as a note with a nominal large t value outside the flight sequence.
Occupants 355 (337 passengers, 18 crew); the number of injured is not recalled reliably.
Recommendation numbers not recalled and are left null.

records.title: United Airlines 232

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: United Airlines Flight 232, McDonnell Douglas DC-10-10, Sioux Gateway Airport, Sioux City, Iowa, July 19, 1989

location.name: Sioux Gateway Airport, Sioux City, Iowa

records.summary: In cruise at 37,000 feet the stage 1 fan disk of the DC-10's tail-mounted number 2 engine fractured from a fatigue crack that had grown from a manufacturing defect in the titanium. Disk fragments severed the lines of all three hydraulic systems, leaving the crew with no conventional flight controls. Using only differential thrust on the two wing engines, and helped by an off-duty DC-10 instructor, the crew steered the airplane for 44 minutes to an emergency landing at Sioux City. The airplane cartwheeled and broke up on the runway; 111 of the 296 on board died and 185 survived.
records.probable_cause: The inadequate consideration given to human factors limitations in the inspection and quality control procedures used by United Airlines' engine overhaul facility which resulted in the failure to detect a fatigue crack originating from a previously undetected metallurgical defect located in a critical area of the stage 1 fan disk that was manufactured by General Electric Aircraft Engines. The subsequent catastrophic disintegration of the disk resulted in the liberation of debris in a pattern of distribution and with energy levels that exceeded the level of protection provided by design features of the hydraulic systems that operate the DC-10's flight controls.

factors.evidence: A fatigue crack grew from a hard alpha inclusion in the titanium of the stage 1 fan disk, formed during the manufacturing melt process, until the disk fractured after about 17 years in service.

The crack was large enough to be detected at the last fluorescent penetrant inspection at United's overhaul facility about 760 cycles before the accident but was missed; the report faulted the human factors of the inspection process.
The fan disk separated from the number 2 engine at high energy, shedding fragments through the horizontal stabilizer and tail structure.
Fragments severed lines of all three independent hydraulic systems where they ran close together in the tail, and all hydraulic fluid was lost.
With no hydraulic pressure the ailerons, elevators, rudder, spoilers, flaps and slats were inoperative; the airplane had no conventional flight controls.
The crew could only influence pitch and roll by varying thrust on the two wing engines, which could not arrest the phugoid oscillation or line up precisely for landing.
The DC-10's three hydraulic systems were routed through the same area of the tail without fuses or shutoff valves, so one uncontained failure could disable all of them.
Certification had assumed that hydraulic system redundancy was sufficient without fully considering the distribution and energy of uncontained rotor debris.
The airplane touched down at about 215 knots with a sink rate of about 1,620 feet per minute, right wing low; the right wing struck first and the airplane cartwheeled and broke apart.
Fire consumed the center fuselage after the breakup; most fatalities were in that section.
Despite the breakup, the crew's management of the emergency and the preparation of the airport and rescue services allowed 185 of 296 occupants to survive.
An unrestrained lap-held infant died; the NTSB reiterated its recommendation for child restraint systems.

events.text: Flight 232 departs Denver for Chicago and climbs to flight level 370.
The stage 1 fan disk of the number 2 (tail) engine fractures and separates; a loud bang and airframe shudder are felt. The engine's fragments strike the horizontal stabilizer and tail.
Flight engineer reports the number 2 engine failed; the crew begin the engine shutdown checklist and then notice all three hydraulic system pressures and quantities falling to zero.
The airplane enters a descending right turn that does not respond to control inputs; the captain and first officer find the controls have no effect.
The captain reduces thrust on the number 1 engine and increases it on number 3 to stop the right roll; the crew discover differential thrust is their only means of control.
The crew declare an emergency to Minneapolis Center and request vectors to the nearest suitable airport; Sioux City is offered.
A deadheading United DC-10 training check airman comes to the cockpit and takes over the throttles, allowing the pilots to concentrate on the phugoid and on planning the landing.

Captain tells Sioux City approach 'we have no hydraulic fluid, which means we have no elevator control, almost none, and very little aileron control'; a series of right-hand turns is flown because the airplane will not turn left.
The landing gear is extended by the alternate free-fall method; the airport, hospitals and Air National Guard units are alerted for a crash landing.
Sioux City tower clears the flight to 'land on any runway'; the captain replies 'you want to be particular and make it a runway, huh?' The airplane lines up with closed runway 22.
On short final a phugoid downswing and a right roll develop that thrust changes cannot correct; sink rate increases to about 1,620 feet per minute at about 215 knots.
The right wing and right main gear strike the runway first; the airplane cartwheels, breaks into sections and the center fuselage burns in a cornfield.
Survivors evacuate through fuselage breaks and doors; 185 of the 296 occupants survive, aided by the pre-positioned rescue services.

cvr.speaker: ATC
cvr.text: United two thirty two heavy, ... you're cleared to land on any runway.

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: You want to be particular and make it a runway, huh?

recommendations.text: Require modification of the DC-10 hydraulic systems, such as hydraulic fuses or shutoff valves, so that a single uncontained engine failure cannot cause total loss of hydraulic power for the flight controls.
recommendations.outcome: An airworthiness directive required installation of hydraulic fuses in the number 3 hydraulic system of DC-10s.

recommendations.text: Review the certification of transport airplanes to ensure that the effects of uncontained engine rotor failures on redundant flight control systems are adequately considered, including debris energy and distribution.
recommendations.outcome: FAA issued updated guidance (AC 20-128A) on designing for minimum hazard from uncontained rotor failures.

recommendations.text: Improve fluorescent penetrant and other inspection methods for titanium rotating parts, including human factors of the inspection process, and require re-inspection of CF6-6 fan disks from the same melt.
recommendations.outcome: Fan disks from the affected titanium lots were removed and inspection procedures at overhaul facilities were revised.

recommendations.text: Work with titanium producers to reduce the occurrence of hard alpha inclusions in rotor-grade titanium through improved melting and inspection processes.
recommendations.outcome: Triple vacuum-arc remelt and improved ultrasonic billet inspection became standard for rotor-grade titanium.

recommendations.text: Require approved child restraint systems for infants and small children on air carrier flights.
recommendations.outcome: The FAA declined to mandate child restraints, citing the cost of separate seats.

safety_changes: DC-10 fleets were retrofitted with hydraulic fuses to preserve some flight control capability after a line rupture in the tail.
Rotor-grade titanium melting practice moved to triple vacuum-arc remelt with improved billet ultrasonic inspection to reduce hard alpha inclusions.
FAA revised guidance on designing for uncontained engine failures (AC 20-128A) and engine manufacturers reviewed critical rotating part life limits.
The crew's cooperative use of an additional pilot became a model for crew resource management training, and research into propulsion-controlled aircraft followed.
Airport emergency planning was widely reviewed after the Sioux City response, which had been drilled for a similar scenario two years earlier.

notes: Engine failure at about 15:16 CDT and touchdown at about 16:00 CDT are as stated in the report; the seconds in the t0 and touchdown clocks are approximate and intermediate event times (emergency declaration, check airman arriving, gear extension) are approximate to within a few minutes.
Touchdown at about 215 knots with a sink rate of about 1,620 feet per minute is from the report.
Fatalities (111) include one passenger who died about a month later; serious injuries 47 as recalled.
The interval between the last inspection and the accident (about 760 cycles) and the disk's service history are as recalled from the report and should be verified.
ATC and captain exchange about landing 'on any runway' is quoted from the public transcript with the ATC wording abbreviated.

records.title: Avianca 052

location.name: Cove Neck

records.summary: Avianca Flight 052 ran out of fuel after three holding patterns and a failed landing attempt at JFK, crashing onto a hillside in Cove Neck on Long Island. Poor communication between crew and controllers, inadequate fuel management, and ATC's failure to recognize the emergency contributed to the accident.
records.probable_cause: The failure of the flightcrew to adequately manage the airplane's fuel load, and their failure to communicate an emergency fuel situation to air traffic control before fuel exhaustion occurred. Contributing factors: failure to use airline operational control dispatch system, inadequate traffic flow management by FAA, and lack of standardized terminology for fuel states.

factors.evidence: The Boeing 707 ran out of fuel and all four engines lost power while the aircraft was maneuvering for a second approach to JFK.
First officer did not adequately communicate the critical fuel situation using standard emergency terminology, instead saying 'we need priority' which controllers interpreted as a routine request.
Controllers did not recognize the emergency fuel situation because the flight crew failed to use the word 'emergency' and did not use standardized fuel emergency phraseology.
The flight was placed in three holding patterns totaling more than 1 hour, with weather-related delays due to inadequate traffic flow management at JFK.
Crew fatigue and stress contributed to the unsuccessful completion of the first approach and thus contributed to the accident.
Windshear on the approach path contributed to the captain's poor performance on the ILS approach, leading to a missed approach.
Descent below safe altitude limits during approach contributed to the difficulty of landing.
The Boeing 707 crashed on a hillside in Cove Neck, New York, after engines lost power due to fuel exhaustion.

events.text: Flight 052 departed Bogotá International Airport.
Flight landed at Medellín and was refueled for departure to JFK.
Flight 052 departed Medellín bound for JFK via oceanic route.
Flight 052 entered first holding pattern over Norfolk (ORF) at FL370.
Flight entered second holding pattern at BOTON intersection near Atlantic City.
Flight entered third holding pattern at CAMRN intersection, 39 nm south of JFK, at 14,000 feet.
First officer advised controller that aircraft can hold only 5 more minutes due to fuel situation.
Flight cleared from holding pattern and instructed to proceed to JFK via heading 040 at 11,000 feet.
Windshear advisory issued: increase of 10 knots at 1500 feet and 10 knots at 500 feet.
Captain asked first officer to tell ATC they are in an emergency.
Aircraft crashed on a hillside in Cove Neck, Long Island, New York due to loss of power from fuel exhaustion.

recommendations.text: Develop standardized glossary of definitions and terms for fuel communications
Conduct comprehensive study of Central Flow Control Facility and Traffic Management System
Require transport category airplane flight manuals to include minimum fuel procedures and ATC emergency handling criteria
Incorporate recorded broadcast of traffic management information in air route traffic control centers
Review policies on dual responsibility of dispatchers and flightcrews
Require Avianca to incorporate CRM and Line Oriented Flight Training into training program
Notify all domestic and foreign air carriers to emphasize knowledge of flight operations, ATC rules, procedures, and standard phraseology

notes: Sections read: Executive Summary, History of Flight, Findings, Probable Cause, Recommendations

records.title: British Airways 5390

agencies.name: Air Accidents Investigation Branch
agencies.report_title: Report on the accident to BAC One-Eleven, G-BJRT over Didcot, Oxfordshire on 10 June 1990

location.name: Over Didcot, Oxfordshire; diversion to Southampton

records.summary: Climbing through 17,300 ft after departure from Birmingham, the left windscreen, which had been replaced the previous night, blew out. The commander was partially sucked through the aperture and held by cabin crew while the first officer flew the aircraft to an emergency landing at Southampton. The commander survived with fractures and frostbite.
records.probable_cause: The windscreen had been fitted with 84 of 90 bolts that were of a smaller diameter than specified and the remaining six were too short; the bolts were installed by the shift maintenance manager, who worked alone, relied on visual matching of the old bolts and did not consult the parts catalogue. The installation was not subject to independent inspection, and the shift manager's inadequate practices were not detected by the airline's quality monitoring or the CAA.

factors.evidence: The shift maintenance manager fitted the windscreen with 84 bolts of the wrong (undersize) diameter and 6 bolts of the correct diameter but wrong length, having selected them by visual comparison in poor light.
The windscreen installation was not classified as a vital task requiring independent inspection, so the incorrect bolts went undetected.
Local management and quality monitoring did not detect the shift manager's inadequate working practices and the deviation from published procedures.
The CAA's product sampling did not identify the maintenance standards shortfall at the Birmingham base.
The shift manager did not use the Illustrated Parts Catalogue or the maintenance manual to identify the correct bolts, and operated the uncontrolled bolt carousel without verification.
The windscreen was fitted from the outside of the aircraft, so it relied wholly on the bolts to resist cabin pressure differential.
At about 17,300 ft the windscreen separated from the airframe under cabin pressure load.
The windscreen departure caused an explosive decompression and the commander was pulled partly through the aperture.
The commander was incapacitated, held by cabin crew, leaving the first officer to fly the aircraft alone.
The first officer landed the aircraft safely at Southampton about 22 minutes after the decompression.

events.text: During the previous night shift at Birmingham the left windscreen is replaced; the shift maintenance manager selects replacement bolts by visual comparison and fits 84 undersize A211-8C bolts and 6 too-short A211-9D bolts.
G-BJRT departs Birmingham for Málaga with 81 passengers and 6 crew; the commander is pilot flying.
Climbing through about 17,000 ft both pilots have released their shoulder harnesses; the commander has loosened his lap strap.
At 17,300 ft the left windscreen blows out with a loud bang; explosive decompression and condensation mist fill the flight deck.
The commander is pulled head-first out of the aperture, his knees caught on the control column; the flight deck door is blown onto the centre pedestal.
A cabin crew member on the flight deck grabs the commander's legs and holds him; the autopilot has disengaged.
The first officer takes control, regains control of the aircraft and initiates a rapid descent while transmitting a Mayday.
ATC initially have difficulty hearing the transmissions over the wind noise; the first officer requests a diversion and is offered Southampton.
Aircraft levels at 11,000 ft and is radar vectored towards Southampton; other cabin crew relieve the first steward holding the commander.
First officer lands the aircraft safely on Southampton runway 02 with the commander still held half out of the windscreen aperture.
Commander recovered alive with fractures to his right arm, wrist and left thumb, bruising and frostbite; a steward suffers a dislocated shoulder.

recommendations.text: Review the current classification of tasks requiring independent inspection and consider including windscreen and other pressure-critical installations.
Review quality assurance and the monitoring of engineering working practices at outstations, including the control of uncontrolled bolt stores and the use of parts catalogues.
Recognise the need for corrective glasses to be worn by engineers where required and improve product sampling of maintenance work.

safety_changes: Windscreen installation designated as a task requiring independent inspection at British Airways and reviewed by the CAA.
Widely cited as a case study for human factors in maintenance and the need for duplicate inspection of flight-critical tasks.

notes: Clock times are approximate; the report gives the decompression at 07:33 and landing at Southampton at about 07:55.
Bolt part numbers (A211-8C, A211-9D) are as reported by the AAIB; counts 84 and 6 as reported.
Recommendation numbers omitted.

records.title: USAir 1493

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Runway Collision of USAir Flight 1493, Boeing 737 and Skywest Flight 5569 Fairchild Metroliner

location.name: Los Angeles International Airport, Runway 24L

records.summary: USAir Flight 1493, a Boeing 737-300, collided with SkyWest Airlines Flight 5569, a Fairchild Metroliner, on runway 24L at Los Angeles International Airport during landing. The SkyWest aircraft was positioned at an intersection awaiting takeoff clearance. The collision was caused by loss of situational awareness by the local air traffic controller, who failed to maintain awareness of the SkyWest aircraft's position due to a misplaced flight progress strip and preoccupation with another aircraft.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause was the failure of the Los Angeles Air Traffic Facility Management to implement procedures that provided redundancy comparable to the requirements of the National Operational Position Standards, and the failure of the FAA Air Traffic Service to provide adequate policy direction and oversight to its air traffic control facility managers. These failures created an environment in the Los Angeles Air Traffic Control tower that led to the failure of the local controller to maintain awareness of the traffic situation, culminating in inappropriate clearances and the subsequent collision. Contributing to the cause was the failure of the FAA to provide effective quality assurance of the ATC system.

factors.evidence: A flight progress strip for Wings West aircraft was misplaced by the clearance delivery controller (p. 592-593), preventing the local controller from being aware of its position.
The local controller forgot she had positioned SkyWest 5569 for takeoff on runway 24L at intersection 45 due to preoccupation with another aircraft (p. 18478-18486).
Operating procedures at LAX did not provide redundancy for monitoring flight progress strips, relying on the local controller's memory (p. 18410-18443).
Airport Surface Detection Equipment radar was not available to assist the controller, though it probably would not have prevented the accident given the circumstances (p. 18574-18580).
SkyWest aircraft was positioned in takeoff position on runway 24L at intersection 45 (p. 757-761).
USAir 737 collided with SkyWest Metroliner on runway 24L, destroying both aircraft with 35 fatalities (p. 564-568, 770-781).

events.text: LAX tower instructs SkyWest 569 to taxi into position and hold on runway 24 left.
SkyWest 569 acknowledges position and hold clearance for runway 24 left.
USA 1493 requests clearance for left side runway 24 left approach.
LAX tower clears USA 1493 to land on runway 24 left (controller unaware of SkyWest aircraft on runway due to loss of situational awareness).
USA 1493 acknowledges landing clearance for runway 24 left.
USA 1493 descending out of 500 feet on approach.
Sound of impact as USA 1493 contacts the runway with SkyWest 5569 positioned at intersection 45.
USAir 737 crushes SkyWest Metroliner, destroying both aircraft. Fire and explosion at runway 24L, intersection 45.

recommendations.text: Modify Air Traffic Control procedures at LAX to segregate arrivals and departures to specific runways and provide redundancies as intended in the National Operational Position Standards in the control tower.

Undertake a thorough risk-based evaluation of air traffic control procedures at LAX, considering runway intersection takeoffs, position-and-hold clearances, displaced runway thresholds, hazards from crossing traffic, local assist controller needs, and ASDE use and maintenance.

Include in the Office of Safety Quality Assurance the authority and resources to independently evaluate facility compliance with FAA directives and audit facility evaluations to determine corrective action.
Retain the National Operational Position Standards as a separate, independent order and direct FAA Human Factors and Air Traffic Service staffs to review the order for adequacy of redundancies.
Provide Air Traffic Control Supervisors with formal training to improve their understanding of the intent, objectives and administration of the Technical Appraisal Program.
Require that interim evaluations of controller performance be retained for 2 years and utilized to track performance and training needs of air traffic controllers.

Conduct a one-time examination of airport lighting at all U.S. tower-controlled airports to eliminate or reduce restrictions to visibility from the control tower to runways and other traffic movement areas.
Redefine airplane certification coverage compliance standards for anticollision light installations to ensure visibility to pilots on adjacent runways.
Evaluate and implement suitable means for enhancing the conspicuity of aircraft on airport surfaces during night or reduced visibility, including high-intensity strobe lighting.

Direct the general aviation community and airlines to ensure pilot training programs emphasize vigilance in monitoring ATC radio frequencies for traffic conflicts, especially on active runways and during final approach.
Incorporate into the Airman's Information Manual language that will alert pilots to the need for vigilance in monitoring air traffic frequencies for traffic conflict situations.
Develop specific phraseology for use by pilots requesting intersection departures and controllers issuing position-and-hold clearances for intersection departures.

safety_changes: LAX implemented procedure changes requiring flight progress strips to be passed through ground control position
Segregation of arrivals and departures to specific runways at LAX
Enhanced aircraft conspicuity standards for airport operations

notes: Read Executive Summary, History of Flights (lines 714-851), Conclusions (lines 18300-18511), Probable Cause (lines 18780-18836), and Recommendations (lines 18842-19334)
Detailed CVR transcript available in report Appendix C but not extracted as focus was on key sections establishing causal chain

records.title: LAN Chile 1069

location.name: Puerto Williams Airport

records.summary: LAN Chile Flight 1069 was cleared for a VOR A approach to Puerto Williams on runway 26, but the captain decided to perform a direct approach to runway 08. The aircraft touched down 427 meters from the runway threshold at 112 knots on a wet runway with a negative slope and little braking action. The aircraft was unable to stop and overran the runway into the Beagle Channel. The investigation determined the probable cause was poor planning in changing runways and misapplication of the landing procedure.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause was a failure of good planning made by the pilot during the approach when he decided to change runway and misapplication of the landing procedure. The weather conditions, negative slope, wet runway, wind and little braking action led to the overrun of the runway.

factors.evidence: the captain decided to perform a direct approach to runway 08
Wind was given as 180° at 4 kn. Shortly, the air traffic controller announced the updated wind information
wet runway and little braking action
the aircraft overran the runway with insufficient braking action
the aircraft overran the runway and slid into the Beagle Channel

events.text: Flight 1069 cleared for VOR A approach to Puerto Williams runway 26
Wind information updated: 160 degrees at 6 knots
Captain decides to perform direct approach to runway 08
Aircraft touched down 427 m from runway threshold at 112 knots on wet runway
Brakes applied with insufficient action on wet, negatively-sloped runway
Aircraft overran runway, slid into Beagle Channel
Aircraft partially submerged in water, evacuation begins

Enriched with 7 timestamped events

records.title: United Airlines Flight 585

location.name: Colorado Springs Municipal Airport

records.summary: United Airlines Flight 585, a Boeing 737-291, experienced a sudden rudder hardover on final approach to Colorado Springs on March 3, 1991. Prior to the fatal accident, the rudder abruptly deflected on February 25 and again on February 27, but these incidents were not fully resolved. On March 3, the aircraft rolled over and entered an uncontrolled dive on final approach, killing all 25 aboard. The NTSB eventually determined the crash resulted from a design defect in the 737's rudder power control unit.
records.probable_cause: A loss of control of the airplane resulting from the movement of the rudder surface to its blowdown limit. The rudder surface most likely deflected in a direction opposite to that commanded by the pilots as a result of a jam of the main rudder power control unit servo valve secondary slide to the servo valve housing offset from its neutral position and overtravel of the primary slide (p. 158).

factors.evidence: The design of the 737's rudder power control unit had a flaw allowing secondary slide overtravel (p. 158).
On February 25, 1991, rudder abruptly deflected 10 degrees right; similar event occurred February 27, but not fully resolved before fatal accident (p. 139).
The aircraft experienced rudder hardover while on final approach to runway 35 (p. 139).

records.title: Atlantic Southeast Airlines 2311

location.name: Brunswick

records.summary: Atlantic Southeast Airlines Flight 2311, an Embraer EMB 120 Brasilia with 23 aboard, crashed north of Brunswick, Georgia on April 5, 1991 during approach to landing. The NTSB investigation determined that the left propeller control unit malfunctioned, allowing the left propeller to overspeed with its blades oriented nearly perpendicular to the direction of flight. This created severe asymmetric thrust with insufficient thrust on the left side, causing a left roll that exceeded pilot recovery capability. The crew did not perceive the problem until the propeller blade angle reached 22-26 degrees, at which point the aircraft became very difficult to control.
records.probable_cause: A malfunction of the left propeller control unit allowed the left propeller to overspeed, creating severe asymmetric thrust that rolled the aircraft to the left beyond the pilot's control authority to recover.

factors.evidence: Propeller control unit malfunction allowed left propeller to overspeed with blades nearly perpendicular to direction of flight, creating asymmetric thrust condition.
Crew was unable to perceive problem until propeller blade angle reached 22-26 degrees; aircraft became very difficult to control at that point.
Aircraft was in approach phase during descent to landing when propeller malfunction developed at critical phase with high workload.
Aircraft rolled to the left until wings were perpendicular to ground; descended in nose-down attitude and disappeared behind trees near airport.
Aircraft struck ground in nose-down attitude after rolling left and losing control during approach.

events.text: Flight 2311 departed Atlanta at 13:47, 23 minutes behind schedule, with no reported mechanical problems after performing round trip to Montgomery.
Just after 14:48, flight crew acknowledged to Jacksonville ATC that airport was in sight and was cleared for visual approach to runway 7.
Last transmission reported to ASA manager; propeller control unit failure caused left propeller overspeed with blades nearly perpendicular at low altitude during approach.
Aircraft suddenly rolled to the left until wings were perpendicular to ground; descended in nose-down attitude and disappeared behind trees near airport.

records.title: Lauda Air 004
records.time_reference: Thailand local time (UTC+7); clock strings approximate to the minute, t is relative to the reverser deployment at about 23:31

agencies.name: Aircraft Accident Investigation Committee
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Investigation Report, Lauda Air Luftfahrt Aktiengesellschaft, Boeing 767-300ER, Registration OE-LAV, Ban Dan Chang, Suphan Buri Province, Thailand, 26 May 1991

location.name: Phu Toei National Park, Ban Dan Chang, Suphan Buri Province

records.summary: About 16 minutes after leaving Bangkok for Vienna, the 767's left engine thrust reverser deployed in flight while the aircraft was climbing through about 24,700 ft at Mach 0.78. The reverser plume disrupted the airflow over the left wing, the aircraft rolled and pitched down, and it broke up in flight during the ensuing dive. All 223 on board died. A REV ISLN advisory light had illuminated some 20 minutes earlier, and the checklist had indicated that no action was required.
records.probable_cause: The Thai Aircraft Accident Investigation Committee determined that the probable cause was the uncommanded in-flight deployment of the left engine thrust reverser, which resulted in loss of flight path control. The specific cause of the deployment was not positively identified, but the investigation showed that the reverser could be deployed by hydraulic pressure reaching the actuator through a failure in the directional control valve or associated wiring, and that the certification assumption that an in-flight deployment was controllable was not valid at climb speed and altitude.

factors.evidence: The 767 thrust reverser system's hydraulic isolation and directional control valves could allow deployment from a single failure; Boeing subsequently added a third, independent locking system.

The design had been certificated on the assumption that an in-flight reverser deployment was controllable; Boeing's post-accident simulations showed a loss of about 25 percent of wing lift and that recovery was not possible at the accident conditions.
The REV ISLN advisory light that illuminated 20 minutes before the accident did not convey the possibility of an imminent deployment.

The quick reference handbook indicated that additional system failures might cause in-flight deployment but that normal reverser operation should be expected after landing, leading the crew to take no action.
The left engine thrust reverser deployed uncommanded during the climb at about 24,700 ft and Mach 0.78.
The aircraft rolled and pitched down into a steep dive from which the crew could not recover.
The aircraft exceeded its structural limits in the dive and broke up in flight before striking the ground.

events.text: Departs Bangkok Don Mueang for Vienna, the second leg of the flight from Hong Kong, with 213 passengers and 10 crew.
The left engine REV ISLN advisory light illuminates intermittently during the climb.

The first officer reads the quick reference handbook entry, which states that additional system failures may cause in-flight deployment and that normal reverser operation should be expected after landing; the crew conclude no action is required.
The crew discuss the light and continue the climb; the captain regards it as an advisory only.
Climbing through about 24,700 ft at Mach 0.78, the left engine thrust reverser deploys uncommanded. The first officer calls out that the reverser has deployed.
The reverser efflux disrupts airflow over the left wing; the aircraft rolls and yaws left and pitches nose-down. Autopilot disconnects.
The crew attempt to recover; the aircraft continues into a steep, accelerating dive.
The aircraft exceeds its structural limits and breaks up in flight; recorders stop.
The wreckage falls into jungle in Phu Toei National Park, Suphan Buri Province; all 223 on board are killed.

recommendations.text: Modify the 767 thrust reverser system to prevent uncommanded in-flight deployment, and review the reverser systems of other transport aircraft against the same failure modes.
recommendations.outcome: The FAA required Boeing to install an additional independent sync-lock on 767 reversers, and reverser systems on other types were reviewed and modified.

recommendations.text: Revise the certification requirements so that in-flight reverser deployment is treated as a hazardous event to be prevented rather than assumed controllable.
recommendations.outcome: FAA and JAA certification policy for thrust reversers was revised to require multiple independent locks and no reliance on controllability after deployment.

recommendations.text: Revise the REV ISLN checklist guidance and crew training so that an isolation-valve indication is treated as a warning of possible in-flight deployment.

safety_changes: Boeing 767 aircraft with PW4000 engines were restricted from using reverse thrust until an additional independent locking system was installed.
Certification requirements for thrust reverser systems were revised worldwide to require multiple independent locks and to remove the assumption that in-flight deployment is controllable.
The failure of the flight data recorder to survive the fire led to improvements in recorder crash and fire protection standards.

notes: Clock strings are approximate to the minute; the time from reverser deployment to break-up (given here as about 29 s) is approximate.
Only the first officer's 'reverser's deployed' line is quoted; other widely reported CVR lines are not included because their exact wording and timing were not verified.
The Thai AAIC report is not available at a stable URL; the NTSB (accredited representative) home page is given as the source.
The flight data recorder was destroyed by fire, so state values are limited to the altitude at deployment.

records.summary: Indian Airlines Flight 257 crashed into Thangjing Hill during descent on approach to Imphal. The pilot deliberately violated the published approach procedure by flying direct to Imphal instead of via Agartala, changed heading to 053 degrees from the planned 007 degrees, and reported a false position to ATC while failing to monitor instruments.
records.probable_cause: Pilot's deliberate non-adherence to published approach procedure; over-reliance on terrain familiarity; inadequate instrument monitoring; loss of situational awareness.

factors.evidence: The crew decided to violate the approach procedure by taking a short cut
The crew reported that they were above the supposed VOR but they were nowhere near the said location
During the approach, the crew did not adequately monitor their instruments, despite the deteriorating weather condition
Flight 257 began to deviate to heading 053, significantly off to the right from its supposed heading of 007

records.title: Air Inter 148 (Mont Sainte-Odile)

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la sécurité de l'aviation civile
agencies.report_title: Rapport de la Commission d'Enquête sur l'accident survenu le 20 janvier 1992 près du Mont Sainte-Odile (Bas-Rhin) à l'Airbus A320 immatriculé F-GGED exploité par la compagnie Air Inter

location.name: La Bloss ridge near Mont Sainte-Odile, Vosges, Bas-Rhin

records.summary: On a night VOR/DME approach to Strasbourg runway 05, after a late change of runway and approach by ATC, the crew descended from the final approach fix at about 3,300 ft/min instead of the intended 3.3 degree flight path angle. The aircraft struck the wooded ridge of La Bloss at 2,620 ft in cloud. 87 of the 96 occupants died; the wreckage was not located for several hours.
records.probable_cause: The Commission concluded that the accident was most probably due to a very high rate of descent during the final approach, the origin of which could not be determined with certainty; the most probable hypothesis was that the crew selected a vertical speed of -3,300 ft/min when they intended a flight path angle of -3.3 degrees on the FCU, whose display of the two modes was similar. Contributing factors included the crew's high workload following the late change of approach, the absence of cross-checking of the descent, the absence of a GPWS on the aircraft, the lack of an altitude check-call culture at Air Inter, and the limited radar and MSAW coverage at Strasbourg.

factors.evidence: ATC changed the expected ILS approach to runway 23 to a VOR/DME approach to runway 05 late in the descent, requiring the crew to re-plan under time pressure.
The crew were re-briefing the approach, managing the autopilot and flying a tight circuit with little time between the approach fix and the descent.
The most probable hypothesis is that the crew set -33 on the FCU in vertical speed mode (-3,300 ft/min) while intending -3.3 degrees flight path angle.
The FCU display presented flight path angle and vertical speed in a similar two-digit format with only a small mode indication, facilitating confusion.
Neither pilot monitored the vertical speed or altitude against the approach profile during the roughly one-minute descent.
There was no callout or cross-check of altitude and descent rate between the two pilots.
The aircraft was not fitted with a GPWS; Air Inter had obtained an exemption, so no terrain warning was available to the crew.
Air Inter had chosen not to equip its fleet with GPWS and did not require altitude callouts on non-precision approaches.
Strasbourg approach radar did not provide minimum safe altitude warning to the controller.
The approach was flown at night in cloud with no visual reference to the terrain.
The aircraft was in cloud with snow showers over the Vosges during the descent.
The aircraft struck the ridge at 2,620 ft in a controlled descent with no indication that the crew saw the terrain.

events.text: Flight IT148 departs Lyon for Strasbourg with 90 passengers and 6 crew; the captain is pilot flying.
Strasbourg approach informs the crew that the ILS to runway 23 is not available for them and offers a VOR/DME approach to runway 05; the crew re-brief the approach.
ATC vectors the aircraft to intercept the final approach track, which brings it to the ANDLO final fix closer in than planned.
The crew set up the descent on the FCU; the most probable hypothesis is a -33 selection in vertical speed mode rather than -3.3 degree flight path angle.
Aircraft begins descent from about 5,000 ft after ANDLO at about 3,300 ft/min, well above the expected 800 ft/min.
Controller, without MSAW, sees nothing abnormal on the radar and clears the crew to continue; no altitude alert is available.
The aircraft passes through 3,500 ft in cloud at night still descending at high rate; no callouts are made and no GPWS is fitted.
Aircraft strikes trees on the ridge of La Bloss at 2,620 ft in level flight and breaks up; 87 of 96 occupants die.
Rescuers reach the wreckage some four hours after the accident; nine survivors are recovered.

recommendations.text: Make the carriage of a ground proximity warning system mandatory on French public transport aircraft.
recommendations.outcome: GPWS became mandatory in France and Air Inter equipped its fleet.

recommendations.text: Modify the FCU so that the vertical speed and flight path angle modes are clearly distinguishable in the display.
recommendations.outcome: Airbus modified the FCU display to show vertical speed with four digits and flight path angle with two digits and a decimal point.

recommendations.text: Extend minimum safe altitude warning coverage at French approach radar facilities and review approach procedures at Strasbourg.
Introduce systematic altitude and descent rate callouts and cross-checks during non-precision approaches.
Improve the location of accident sites through ELT performance and coordination of search and rescue.

safety_changes: GPWS made mandatory in France; Air Inter equipped its A320 fleet.
Airbus FCU display modification distinguishing V/S from FPA (four digits versus two with decimal point).
Reinforced altitude callouts and approach monitoring procedures at Air Inter and improved SAR coordination.

notes: Impact at 18:20:33 UTC (19:20 local) is from the report; intermediate times and the descent initiation clock are approximate.
The ATC runway change and radar vectoring are recorded contributors but the report attributes the descent rate primarily to the probable FCU mode confusion, which could not be proved definitively.
Report reference number omitted; recommendation ids null.

records.title: USAir Flight 405

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report - USAir Flight 405

location.name: Flushing, New York

records.summary: USAir Flight 405, a Fokker F-28-4000, crashed during takeoff from runway 13 at LaGuardia Airport on March 22, 1992. Due to inadequate ground de-icing procedures and weather-related delays up to 35 minutes, significant ice accumulated on the wings and airframe. The flight crew was unaware of the extent of ice buildup. The aircraft lifted off but failed to gain altitude, veering off the runway into Flushing Bay. Of the 51 people on board, 27 were killed, including the captain and one cabin crew member.
records.probable_cause: The failure of the airline industry and the Federal Aviation Administration to provide flightcrews with procedures, requirements, and criteria compatible with departure delays in conditions conducive to airframe icing, and the decision by the flightcrew to take off without positive assurance that the airplane's wings were free of ice accumulation after 35 minutes of exposure to precipitation following deicing. The ice contamination on the wings resulted in an aerodynamic stall and loss of control after liftoff. Contributing to the cause were the inappropriate procedures used by, and inadequate coordination between, the flightcrew that led to a takeoff rotation at a lower than prescribed airspeed.

factors.evidence: Poor weather conditions at LaGuardia resulted in heavy ground traffic and delays up to 35 minutes (p. 10).
A large amount of ice had accumulated on the wings and airframe due to inadequate de-icing procedures and delays exceeding the deicing fluid holdover time (p. 10).

De-icing procedures at LaGuardia were found to be substandard by the investigation; the aircraft deiced at approximately 2026 but delays extended beyond the holdover time before takeoff at 2135 (p. 9-10).

The flight crew was unaware of the amount of ice that had built up after the jet was delayed during taxiing to the runway; the first officer said he did not see contamination when inspecting the wing (p. 10).

The aircraft began its takeoff rotation at too low a speed; the specified V_R for the F-28 at this weight and flap configuration was 124 knots, but the aircraft rotated about 2.2 seconds after the V_R callout (p. 10).
Approximately 4.8 seconds after nose strut extension, stick shaker began; stall warnings were recorded (p. 10).

The aircraft veered off the runway, struck visual approach slope-indicator posts and other obstructions, with the left wing scraping the asphalt for 110 feet before separating from the fuselage (p. 10).
The aircraft came to rest in Flushing Bay, just beyond the end of the runway, in a partially inverted position (p. 10).

events.text: Flight 405 departs Jacksonville at 1715 EST for Cleveland via LaGuardia stopover.
Aircraft lands at LaGuardia; ground delays due to poor weather conditions.
First deicing at approximately 2026; first deicing truck experiences mechanical problems.
Aircraft pushed away from gate; second deicing by single truck at approximately 2026-2100.
Crew inspects aircraft; first officer does not see contamination on wing; aircraft cleared for departure.
Aircraft taxies to runway 13; second deicing holdover time expired by takeoff.
Aircraft cleared for takeoff at 2134:51; takeoff roll commences.
First officer calls 'VR' at approximately 124 knots; aircraft rotates about 2.2 seconds later.
Stick shaker activates; stall warning beeps recorded; aircraft at ~600 feet altitude.
Left wing scrapes runway for 110 feet; aircraft veers off runway into Flushing Bay.

recommendations.text: If gate holds are required to limit deicing fluid holdover time, encourage ATC to initiate gate holds as soon as a deicing operation begins rather than after delays have exceeded 15 minutes.
Where deicing operations are conducted away from the departure runway, report taxi delays in conditions conducive to airframe icing in increments less than 15 minutes.

Require flight crewmembers and appropriate ground personnel responsible for inspection of transport-category airplanes for wing contamination receive specific periodic training on what contamination looks like and feels like.
Study the effects on performance of swept-wing turbojet airplanes when specific amounts of airspeed are added to the computed rotation speed during takeoffs when wing contamination is possible.
Require airlines to establish a way to inform flightcrews of the type of fluid and mixture used, the current moisture accumulation rate, and the available holdover time.
Require that all airports which might experience freezing conditions and that are certified under Title 14 CFR Part 139 establish deicing plans for approval.

safety_changes: Enhanced de-icing procedures and training for flight crews
Improved holdover time guidelines for de-icing fluids
More stringent requirements for wing contamination inspection

Probable Cause section fully reviewed (lines 9931-9962)
Recommendations section reviewed (lines 9969-10200)

records.title: Indian Airlines Flight 491

agencies.name: Directorate General of Civil Aviation
agencies.report_title: Civil Aviation Aircraft Accident Summary for the Year 1993

location.name: Aurangabad

records.summary: Indian Airlines Flight 491, a Boeing 737-200, took off from Aurangabad Airport with 118 persons on board. The aircraft lifted off near the end of the 6,000-foot runway with inadequate rotation. Shortly after takeoff, the left landing gear and left engine struck a truck carrying cotton bales on a road adjacent to the runway at approximately 410 feet from the runway end. The impact damaged the aircraft's left landing gear, left engine thrust reverser, and control surfaces. The aircraft continued in flight but subsequently struck high-tension power lines approximately 3 km northeast of the airport and crashed, killing 55 persons.
records.probable_cause: The captain's error in initiating late rotation and following wrong rotation technique resulted in inadequate climb performance. Additionally, the airport authorities failed to regulate mobile traffic on the Beed Road during flight operations, allowing a truck to remain in the hazard zone near the runway end.

factors.evidence: Captain's false perception of takeoff technique resulted in late rotation and failure to achieve adequate liftoff altitude before the runway end (p. 1).
Pilot did not initiate rotation at appropriate airspeed or position on runway, resulting in aircraft lifting off near end of 6,000-foot runway; error in rotation technique (p. 1).
Airport authorities failed to regulate or exclude mobile traffic from Beed Road adjacent to runway during flight operations (p. 1).
Aircraft's left main landing gear and left engine thrust reverser were severed; left elevator and horizontal stabilizer damaged by collision with truck (p. 1).
Aircraft impacted high-tension electric wires approximately 3 km northeast of runway and struck ground, resulting in destruction by post-impact fire (p. 1).

records.title: China Airlines 140
records.time_reference: JST (local, UTC+9); t0 is the GO lever activation at about 20:14, the exact second is not reproduced

agencies.name: Aircraft Accident Investigation Commission
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Investigation Report, China Airlines, Airbus Industrie A300B4-622R, B1816, Nagoya Airport, April 26, 1994

location.name: Nagoya Airport, east of runway 34

records.summary: On final approach to Nagoya the first officer inadvertently triggered the go-around (GO) lever, putting the autothrottle and flight director into go-around mode. The crew tried to continue the approach by pushing the nose down while the autopilot, engaged in go-around mode, trimmed the horizontal stabiliser fully nose-up against them. When the captain took over and added power the out-of-trim aircraft pitched up steeply, stalled at about 1,800 ft and fell onto the airport. Of 271 on board, 264 died.
records.probable_cause: The AAIC concluded that the accident resulted from the first officer's inadvertent activation of the GO lever, the crew's continued attempt to land while the autopilot was in go-around mode, and the resulting out-of-trim condition in which the trimmable horizontal stabiliser moved to its nose-up limit while the elevators were held nose-down. The captain's late takeover and the application of go-around thrust then produced a pitch-up beyond the crew's ability to control, leading to a stall. Contributing factors included the flight control computer design, under which the autopilot could not be overridden by control-column force in go-around mode, the fact that an Airbus service bulletin correcting this had not been incorporated, inadequate crew training on the autopilot's go-around behaviour, and deficient crew coordination.

factors.evidence: The first officer, as pilot flying, inadvertently activated the GO lever on final approach at about 1,070 ft, and later held the control column forward against the autopilot.
The crew did not fully understand that the autothrottle, flight director and then the autopilot were in go-around mode and continued trying to land.
The AAIC found the crew had not been adequately trained in the autopilot's behaviour in go-around mode and in the recovery from an out-of-trim condition.
In go-around mode the A300-600 autopilot could not be disengaged by force on the control column, and the automatic trim moved the stabiliser opposite to the pilots' elevator input.

Airbus had issued a service bulletin to modify the flight control computers so that the autopilot would disconnect with control-column force in go-around mode, but it was not mandatory and its urgency was not conveyed.
The service bulletin had not been incorporated on B-1816, and a similar earlier incident had not led to corrective action.
With the stabiliser trimmed to the nose-up limit, the elevators lacked the authority to counter the pitch-up when thrust was increased.
The captain's instructions to the first officer were not effective, the takeover of control was late, and neither pilot monitored the trim state.
The crew were dealing with unexpected autoflight behaviour at low altitude in the final phase of the approach.
The aircraft pitched up to over 50 degrees, lost airspeed and stalled at about 1,800 ft.
The aircraft fell tail-first onto the airport grass east of the runway.

events.text: Before the accident: Airbus service bulletin A300-22-6021, modifying the flight control computers so that control-column force disengages the autopilot in go-around mode, is available but not mandatory; it has not been incorporated on B-1816.
Night ILS approach to Nagoya runway 34; the first officer is pilot flying, the captain is pilot monitoring.
At about 1,070 ft the first officer inadvertently triggers the GO lever; the autothrottle enters go-around mode and thrust increases, and the flight director commands go-around.

The captain tells the first officer to disengage the go-around mode and continue the approach; the first officer reduces thrust manually and pushes the control column forward, but the flight director remains in go-around mode.

The autopilots are engaged while go-around mode is active. The autopilot commands nose-up while the first officer holds the column forward; the automatic trim runs the horizontal stabiliser toward the nose-up limit while the elevators are nose-down.
The stabiliser reaches its full nose-up position; the aircraft is severely out of trim, and the pilots are unaware of the trim state.
The angle of attack increases and alpha-floor protection commands go-around thrust, adding to the pitch-up tendency.
The captain takes control and decides to go around, increasing thrust; with full nose-up trim and high thrust the aircraft pitches up steeply despite forward elevator.
Pitch attitude exceeds 50 degrees and airspeed decays rapidly; the aircraft stalls at about 1,800 ft.
The aircraft falls tail-first onto the grass east of runway 34 and breaks up in flames; 264 of the 271 on board are killed, 7 survive.

recommendations.to: Ministry of Transport (Japan) / DGAC France / Airbus
recommendations.text: Make mandatory the flight control computer modification allowing the autopilot to be disengaged by control-column force in go-around mode, and review the design so that the autopilot cannot trim against sustained pilot input.
recommendations.outcome: The DGAC issued an airworthiness directive mandating the service bulletin on A300-600 and A310 aircraft.

recommendations.text: Improve crew training on autoflight mode awareness, the go-around mode behaviour of the autopilot, out-of-trim recovery and crew coordination.

safety_changes: The Airbus flight control computer modification for A300-600 and A310 aircraft was made mandatory by airworthiness directive.
Operators reinforced training on autoflight mode awareness and recovery from out-of-trim conditions.
China Airlines undertook a review of its training and operating procedures under pressure from regulators.

notes: Only the impact time (20:15:45 JST) is given as a clock string; event offsets are approximate and t0 is the GO lever activation at about 20:14.
The stabiliser trim reached the nose-up limit (about -12.3 degrees); the exact value is omitted from the state fields.
The service bulletin number is given as A300-22-6021 from memory and should be verified.
The report date (July 1996) and report number (96-5) are from memory.

Weather update: heavy rain south of field, amend altitude to maintain 3,000 feet, expect ILS approach
Cleared for ILS approach, flightcrew performs landing checklist
Captain makes contact with tower, windshear alert called by another aircraft
First officer notes weather showing buildup ahead
Captain directs 'stay heads up', first officer observes increasing wind shift
Engines advance to high power (1.82 EPR) attempting go-around
Aircraft descended despite maximum power, touched down in field 0.5 nm from runway, crashed through fence into trees

notes: Extracted from report using History of Flight section
Enriched with 15 timestamped events

records.title: USAir 427

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Uncontrolled Descent and Collision With Terrain, USAir Flight 427, Boeing 737-300, N513AU, Near Aliquippa, Pennsylvania, September 8, 1994

location.name: Hopewell Township near Aliquippa, Pennsylvania, about 6 miles northwest of Pittsburgh International Airport

records.summary: Descending through 6,000 ft on vectors for Pittsburgh, the 737 encountered the wake of a 727 ahead and rolled left. The main rudder power control unit servo valve jammed and the rudder moved to its blowdown limit opposite to the pilots' input; below the crossover airspeed the ailerons could not counter it. The aircraft rolled through inverted and dived into a ravine 28 seconds later, killing all 132 on board. The four-and-a-half-year investigation, together with United 585 and Eastwind 517, led to a redesign of the 737 rudder system.
records.probable_cause: A loss of control of the airplane resulting from the movement of the rudder surface to its blowdown limit. The rudder surface most likely deflected in a direction opposite to that commanded by the pilots as a result of a jam of the main rudder power control unit servo valve secondary slide to the servo valve housing offset from its neutral position and overtravel of the primary slide.

factors.evidence: The rudder moved to its blowdown limit, most likely reversed relative to the pilots' pedal input, after a jam in the main rudder PCU dual servo valve.
The jam of the servo valve secondary slide and overtravel of the primary slide caused an uncommanded rudder deflection.
The 737 main rudder PCU dual concentric servo valve could jam and reverse under thermal and mechanical conditions, and the rudder system lacked redundancy.

The NTSB found the 737 rudder design did not adequately consider the possibility of a servo valve jam producing a reversal, and that certification standards did not require reliably recoverable rudder failures.
The crew were surprised by the wake encounter and roll and did not recognise a rudder malfunction in the seconds available.
Pilots were not trained to recognise or recover from a rudder reversal or on the crossover airspeed at which roll control cannot overcome full rudder.
Below the crossover airspeed at flaps 1 the ailerons could not counter the full rudder deflection.
The stick shaker activated as the aircraft rolled over and the pilots pulled back on the column.
Column back pressure during the upset stalled the aircraft, deepening the loss of control.
The aircraft rolled through inverted, pitched steeply nose down and struck the ground about 28 seconds after the upset began.

events.text: Pittsburgh approach vectors the flight for runway 28R, sequenced about four miles behind a Delta 727 that is also descending.
Aircraft levels at 6,000 ft at about 190 knots with flaps 1, autopilot engaged.
Aircraft encounters the wake vortex of the 727 and rolls left; a thump is heard on the CVR and the crew exclaim in surprise.
The rudder moves to its left blowdown limit, most likely reversed relative to the pilots' right rudder input, following a jam in the main rudder PCU servo valve.
Captain tells the first officer to hang on; the autopilot disconnects and the roll continues left despite right wheel.
Left bank exceeds 70 degrees and the nose drops; the crew apply full right wheel and pull back on the control column.
Stick shaker activates as the angle of attack increases under the column back pressure.
First officer transmits an emergency call to approach control.
Captain repeatedly calls to pull as the aircraft rolls through inverted and the nose falls to about 80 degrees down.
Aircraft accelerates in a steep dive, load factor near 4 g, with the rudder still fully deflected.
Aircraft strikes a wooded hillside near Aliquippa nose down at about 300 knots; all 132 on board are killed.

recommendations.text: Require Boeing to redesign the 737 main rudder power control unit so that no single jam or failure can produce a rudder reversal or hardover, and mandate retrofit of the fleet.
recommendations.outcome: The 737 rudder PCU was redesigned with a new servo valve and later an independent standby system; the fleet was retrofitted.

recommendations.text: Require air carriers to train pilots on recognition of and recovery from uncommanded rudder deflections, including the concept of crossover airspeed and increasing airspeed before rudder events at low speed.
recommendations.outcome: Airlines adopted 737 jammed or restricted rudder procedures and unusual attitude training; minimum manoeuvring speeds were raised at flaps 1.

recommendations.text: Require flight data recorders on 737s and other transport aircraft to record more parameters, including rudder pedal and surface positions and control wheel forces.
recommendations.outcome: FDR parameter requirements were expanded by rulemaking in 1997.

recommendations.text: Revise transport category certification standards so that flight control system failures producing uncommanded surface movement are shown to be recoverable.

safety_changes: Redesign of the Boeing 737 rudder power control unit servo valve and later a redundant rudder system, retrofitted across the world fleet.
Expanded flight data recorder parameter requirements for airliners.
Introduction of jammed/restricted rudder and upset recovery training and higher flaps 1 manoeuvring speeds on the 737.

notes: t0 is the wake encounter at 19:02:57 EDT and impact at about 19:03:23; intermediate offsets are approximate.

The related accidents United 585 (Colorado Springs, 1991) and Eastwind 517 (Richmond, 1996) share the rudder PCU mechanism but are not in the record set; the NTSB revised its United 585 findings in 2001 on the basis of this investigation.
Crew speech is paraphrased rather than quoted; the stall during the upset and approximate 4 g and 300 knot impact values are recalled from the report.
Recommendation numbers not recalled and are left null.

records.title: American Eagle 4184

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: In-Flight Icing Encounter and Loss of Control, Simmons Airlines, d.b.a. American Eagle Flight 4184, Avions de Transport Regional (ATR) Model 72-212, N401AM, Roselawn, Indiana, October 31, 1994

location.name: Soybean field near Roselawn, Indiana

records.summary: Held for over half an hour at 10,000 ft in freezing drizzle while waiting for O'Hare, the ATR 72 accumulated a ridge of ice behind its deice boots. When the flaps were retracted during the descent to 8,000 ft the ice caused an aileron hinge moment reversal; the autopilot disconnected and the aircraft rolled sharply, recovered briefly, then rolled again and dived into a field. All 68 on board died. The investigation found ATR and the French DGAC had known about the aircraft's behaviour in freezing precipitation from earlier events.
records.probable_cause: The loss of control, attributed to a sudden and unexpected aileron hinge moment reversal that occurred after a ridge of ice accreted beyond the deice boots because ATR failed to completely disclose to operators, and incorporate in the ATR 72 airplane flight manual, flightcrew operating manual and flightcrew training programs, adequate information concerning previously known effects of freezing precipitation on the stability and control characteristics, autopilot and related operational procedures when the ATR 72 was operated in such conditions; the French DGAC's inadequate oversight of the ATR 42 and 72 and its failure to take the necessary corrective action to ensure continued airworthiness in icing conditions; and the DGAC's failure to provide the FAA with timely airworthiness information developed from previous ATR incidents and accidents in icing conditions. Contributing were the FAA's failure to ensure that aircraft icing certification requirements, operational requirements for flight into icing conditions and published icing information adequately accounted for the hazards of freezing rain and other conditions outside 14 CFR Part 25 Appendix C; the FAA's inadequate oversight of the ATR 42 and 72 in icing conditions; and ATR's failure to include an adequate warning in the flight manual.

factors.evidence: Supercooled large droplet freezing drizzle in the hold built a ridge of ice on the upper wing aft of the deice boots, ahead of the ailerons.
Icing certification under Appendix C did not account for supercooled large droplets, so the ATR 72 was never shown to be controllable in freezing drizzle.
The unpowered ailerons of the ATR 72 were susceptible to hinge moment reversal when ice accreted behind the boots.
ATR did not fully disclose to operators what it knew from earlier icing incidents about roll control anomalies and did not put adequate information in the AFM and training.
The French DGAC and the FAA provided inadequate oversight of the ATR fleet's continued airworthiness in icing and did not exchange airworthiness information in a timely way.
Previous ATR 42 and 72 roll control incidents in icing had not led to effective corrective action.
The autopilot masked the growing aileron forces until it disconnected, giving the crew no warning of the developing control anomaly.
The autopilot disconnected when the aileron hinge moment reversed, handing the crew an aircraft already rolling rapidly.
The reversed aileron hinge moment drove the ailerons toward full deflection against the crew's inputs.
The crew were surprised by the sudden roll and had seconds to react in a situation they had not been trained for.
The aircraft rolled through more than 70 degrees, recovered briefly, rolled again and pitched steeply nose down into the ground.

events.text: Chicago Center instructs the flight to hold at the LUCIT intersection at 10,000 ft because of delays into O'Hare.
Aircraft holds in cloud with freezing drizzle; the deice boots operate but a ridge of ice builds aft of the boots.
Crew extend flaps 15 in the hold to lower the angle of attack; the ice detection caution is noted and the crew discuss icing.
Center clears the flight to descend to 8,000 ft.
As speed increases in the descent the flap overspeed warning sounds and the flaps are retracted to 0, increasing the angle of attack of the iced wing.
Aileron hinge moment reverses; the autopilot disconnects and the aircraft rolls rapidly to the right beyond 70 degrees of bank.
Crew apply full left aileron and the aircraft rolls back toward wings level momentarily.
Aircraft rolls right again through inverted and the nose drops steeply.
Captain, as pilot monitoring, takes the controls and attempts to recover; the crew pull back on the control column as speed and g increase.
Aircraft descends in a steep dive at high speed with the nose pitched far below the horizon.
Aircraft strikes a soybean field near Roselawn in a nose-down, partially inverted attitude at high speed; all 68 on board are killed.
