recommendations.text: Revise icing certification criteria to include supercooled large droplet conditions such as freezing drizzle and freezing rain, and require aircraft to be shown controllable in those conditions or to have means to detect and exit them.
recommendations.outcome: Led to the FAA icing rulemaking and eventually 14 CFR Part 25 Appendix O supercooled large drop icing conditions in 2014.

recommendations.text: Require ATR 42 and 72 aircraft to be modified with extended deice boot coverage and revised operating procedures for freezing precipitation.
recommendations.outcome: ATR fleet was fitted with extended-chord deice boots and the AFM was revised with freezing rain procedures.

recommendations.text: Require manufacturers and foreign airworthiness authorities to share airworthiness information from incidents in a timely manner under bilateral agreements.
Require operators to provide pilots with information and training on the effects of freezing precipitation, on limiting autopilot use in icing and on recognising unusual control forces.

dissent.position: The French BEA, in comments appended to the NTSB report, disagreed with the emphasis on ATR and the DGAC and argued that the probable cause should give greater weight to the flight crew's actions, including holding at a speed and configuration outside the recommended envelope in known icing and relying on the autopilot, and to the failure of US air traffic and weather services.

safety_changes: ATR 42 and 72 fleets were modified with larger deice boots and new freezing rain procedures; the FAA temporarily prohibited ATR operations in known icing.
FAA icing certification rulemaking culminated in Appendix O supercooled large drop conditions and new requirements for detecting and exiting such icing.
Renewed research into supercooled large droplet icing and ice-induced roll control anomalies across turboprop types.

notes: t0 is the approximate autopilot disconnect time of 15:57:33 CST; the impact time of about 15:58-15:59 and intermediate offsets are approximate.
Altitude at the upset (about 9,100 ft during the descent from 10,000 ft) and the initial bank angle are recalled from the report and may be slightly off.
The BEA dissent is recorded from memory of the appended French comments; the exact wording and scope of the disagreement should be verified against the appendix.
Recommendation numbers not recalled and are left null.

records.title: Birgenair 301

agencies.name: Dirección General de Aeronáutica Civil
agencies.report_title: Final report on the accident of Boeing 757-225 TC-GEN, Birgenair flight 301, Puerto Plata, 6 February 1996

location.name: Atlantic Ocean about 26 km northeast of Puerto Plata

records.summary: Departing Puerto Plata at night after the 757 had stood unused for about three weeks, the captain noticed during the takeoff roll that his airspeed indicator was not working but continued the takeoff. His pitot probe was blocked, probably by a wasp nest, and as the aircraft climbed his airspeed indication rose falsely. The autopilot, using the same erroneous data, pitched the nose up to hold speed; an overspeed warning and the stick shaker sounded together, the crew reduced thrust, and the aircraft stalled and fell into the sea. All 189 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The Dominican commission determined the probable cause was the crew's failure to recognise the activation of the stick shaker as an imminent warning of entry into an aerodynamic stall and their failure to execute the procedures for recovery from the onset of loss of control. Before the stall the crew were confused by contradictory airspeed indications and warnings resulting from a blocked pitot tube (attributed to an obstruction, probably a mud dauber wasp nest, while the aircraft was parked without pitot covers) and by the autopilot's response to the erroneous airspeed.

factors.evidence: The captain's pitot probe was obstructed, most probably by an insect nest built while the aircraft stood parked for about 20 days without pitot covers.
The captain's airspeed indicator read low on the takeoff roll and then increasingly high in the climb while the first officer's indicator read correctly.
The captain continued the takeoff after noting his airspeed indicator was not working instead of rejecting it.
The autopilot and autothrottle were engaged using the captain's erroneous air data and pitched the nose up and reduced thrust to counter the apparent overspeed.
An overspeed warning sounded at about 7,300 ft as the erroneous indication passed 350 knots.
The crew reduced thrust in response to the overspeed indication while the stick shaker was warning of a stall, and did not identify the stall.
The first officer's correct airspeed indication and the relief pilot's prompts were not used to resolve the situation.
The stick shaker activated while the overspeed warning was still sounding.
The aircraft stalled at about 7,000 ft with the nose high and thrust reduced; an engine flamed out during the descent.
The aircraft rolled and descended out of control into the sea about five minutes after takeoff.
The takeoff and climb were made at night over the sea with no visual horizon.

events.text: Aircraft stands parked at Puerto Plata for about three weeks without pitot covers installed.
Takeoff roll begins on runway 08 at Puerto Plata.

At about 80 knots the captain remarks that his airspeed indicator is not working; the first officer reports that his is, and the captain elects to continue the takeoff using the first officer's calls.
Aircraft rotates and lifts off; the captain's airspeed indicator begins to show increasing values as the aircraft climbs.
Autopilot engaged in the climb using the captain's air data.
Rudder ratio and mach speed trim advisories appear; the captain remarks that something is wrong and the airspeed indications differ.

Passing about 7,300 ft the captain's airspeed reads about 350 knots and the overspeed warning sounds; the autopilot has raised the pitch attitude and the autothrottle has reduced thrust to hold the target speed.
Captain reduces thrust further in response to the overspeed indication.
Stick shaker activates while the overspeed warning continues; the autopilot disconnects.
First officer and relief pilot call for thrust and attitude corrections as the crew struggle to understand the contradictory warnings.
Aircraft stalls at about 7,000 ft and begins to roll and descend; full thrust is applied late and the left engine flames out.
Ground proximity warnings sound as the aircraft descends steeply toward the sea in darkness.
Aircraft strikes the Atlantic about 26 km northeast of Puerto Plata; all 189 on board are killed.

recommendations.text: Require that pitot covers be installed whenever an aircraft is parked for an extended period and that preflight procedures verify pitot-static probes are unobstructed.
recommendations.outcome: Operators reinforced pitot cover and inspection procedures.

recommendations.text: Provide clear procedures and training for rejecting takeoff when an airspeed disagreement is detected and for flying with unreliable airspeed using pitch and power.
recommendations.outcome: Unreliable airspeed procedures and training were strengthened across the industry.

recommendations.text: Improve airspeed comparison alerting so that a disagreement between captain's and first officer's airspeed is annunciated directly to the crew.
recommendations.outcome: Later Boeing aircraft and 757/767 updates added airspeed disagree alerts.

safety_changes: Reinforced procedures for pitot covers and pre-flight checks of pitot-static systems after extended parking.
Industry-wide emphasis on unreliable airspeed procedures, pitch-and-power flying and rejecting takeoff on airspeed disagreement.
Airspeed disagree alerting introduced on later Boeing aircraft.

notes: t0 is the airspeed disagreement during the takeoff roll at about 23:42 local; impact was about 23:47. Intermediate offsets are estimates and clocks are omitted.
The Dominican final report id, date and URL are unknown; the source given is the Dominican civil aviation authority site.
The 7,300 ft / 350 knot overspeed figures and the 80 knot remark are widely cited from the report; the stall altitude of about 7,000 ft and the engine flameout are recalled but less certain.
CVR lines are not quoted because exact transcript wording (English translation) is uncertain; they are paraphrased as crew_speech events.
Flight number ALW301 reflects the Alas Nacionales flight designation; some sources cite Birgenair 301.

records.title: ValuJet 592

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: In-Flight Fire and Impact With Terrain, ValuJet Airlines Flight 592, DC-9-32, N904VJ, Everglades, Near Miami, Florida, May 11, 1996

location.name: Everglades, about 17 miles northwest of Miami International Airport, Florida

records.summary: Shortly after takeoff from Miami, a fire broke out in the forward class D cargo compartment of the DC-9, started by unexpended chemical oxygen generators that maintenance contractor SabreTech had boxed without safety caps and mislabelled as empty. The fire spread rapidly, produced smoke and electrical failures in the cockpit, and about ten minutes after takeoff the aircraft dived into the Everglades. All 110 on board died.
records.probable_cause: A fire in the airplane's class D cargo compartment that was initiated by the actuation of one or more oxygen generators being improperly carried as cargo. The fire resulted in a loss of control of the airplane. Contributing were the failure of SabreTech to properly prepare, package, and identify unexpended chemical oxygen generators before presenting them to ValuJet for carriage; the failure of ValuJet to properly oversee its contract maintenance program to ensure compliance with maintenance, maintenance training, and hazardous materials requirements and practices; and the failure of the FAA to require smoke detection and fire suppression systems in class D cargo compartments. Also contributing were the FAA's failure to adequately monitor ValuJet's heavy maintenance programs and its oversight of contractors, the FAA's failure to adequately respond to prior chemical oxygen generator fires, and ValuJet's failure to ensure that its own and contract maintenance employees were aware of its no-carry hazardous materials policy and had received hazardous materials training.

factors.evidence: SabreTech employees removed unexpended oxygen generators from MD-80s, did not install safety caps, and packed them in boxes labelled as empty canisters.
One or more generators actuated in the forward class D cargo compartment, and the intense oxygen-fed fire spread to the boxes, tyres and cabin structure.
The fire burned through the cabin floor and produced smoke and electrical failures in the cockpit within minutes.
ValuJet failed to oversee its contract maintenance program and to ensure employees knew its no-carry hazardous materials policy.
The FAA had not required detection or suppression in class D compartments and had not adequately monitored ValuJet's rapidly expanding operation and contractors.
The class D compartment had no smoke detection, so the crew had no warning until electrical failures and cabin shouts of fire.
The NTSB found the FAA had not adequately responded to prior chemical oxygen generator fires, including a 1986 cargo fire on an American Trans Air DC-10.
SabreTech and ValuJet employees had not received hazardous materials training adequate to recognise the generators as hazardous.
Fire damage and smoke in the cockpit led to loss of control; the aircraft entered a steep descent and struck the Everglades.

events.text: Five boxes containing unexpended chemical oxygen generators, labelled as empty, plus three aircraft tyres are loaded into the forward class D cargo compartment as company material.
Flight 592 takes off from Miami runway 9L bound for Atlanta.
An unidentified sound is recorded on the CVR as the aircraft climbs through about 10,600 ft.
Captain asks what the sound was.
Captain reports an electrical problem as instruments and systems begin to fail.
Captain says they are losing everything and calls for a return to Miami.
First officer requests an immediate return to Miami from Miami Departure control.
Shouts of 'fire, fire, fire' from the passenger cabin are heard on the CVR.
A flight attendant tells the cockpit there is fire in the cabin and smoke is spreading.
Miami Departure turns the flight back toward the airport and clears it to descend; the crew report smoke in the cockpit and cabin.
Controller offers runway 12 and then clears the flight direct to the airport as it descends.
Flight data and cockpit voice recorders stop recording as electrical power and control are lost; radar shows the aircraft in a steep descent.
Aircraft strikes the Everglades in a steep nose-down attitude at high speed; all 110 on board are killed.

recommendations.text: Require smoke detection and fire suppression systems in class D cargo compartments of transport category aircraft.
recommendations.outcome: FAA rule of 1998 eliminated class D compartments on passenger aircraft, requiring detection and suppression by 2001.

recommendations.text: Prohibit the transportation of chemical oxygen generators as cargo on passenger aircraft and improve hazardous materials training and oversight for air carriers and their maintenance contractors.
recommendations.outcome: Oxygen generators were banned as cargo on passenger aircraft; hazmat training requirements were strengthened.

recommendations.text: Strengthen FAA surveillance of air carriers' contract maintenance and repair stations, including hazardous materials handling.

safety_changes: Class D cargo compartments were eliminated; smoke detection and fire suppression required in all cargo compartments of passenger aircraft.
Chemical oxygen generators prohibited as cargo on passenger aircraft; hazardous materials training strengthened for carriers and contractors.
FAA oversight of contract maintenance and of rapidly growing carriers was reorganised; ValuJet was grounded and later merged into AirTran.

notes: CVR clock times for the first 25 seconds after the sound and the 14:13:42 impact time are from the report; the times of the cabin fire shouts, ATC turns and recorder stop are approximate.
Crew speech is paraphrased rather than quoted verbatim.
Recommendation numbers not recalled and are left null.

records.title: TWA 800

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: In-flight Breakup Over the Atlantic Ocean, Trans World Airlines Flight 800, Boeing 747-131, N93119, Near East Moriches, New York, July 17, 1996

route.from_name: New York John F. Kennedy International

location.name: Atlantic Ocean about 8 miles south of East Moriches, Long Island, New York

records.summary: About twelve minutes after takeoff from JFK, climbing through about 13,800 feet, the 747's nearly empty center wing fuel tank exploded. The forward fuselage separated, the remainder of the airplane continued briefly before the wings failed and the burning wreckage fell into the Atlantic off Long Island. All 230 people on board died. A four-year investigation, the largest in NTSB history, ruled out a bomb or missile and attributed the explosion to ignition of flammable fuel vapor in the tank, most likely from a short circuit in fuel quantity indication system wiring.
records.probable_cause: An explosion of the center wing fuel tank (CWT), resulting from ignition of the flammable fuel/air mixture in the tank. The source of ignition energy for the explosion could not be determined with certainty, but, of the sources evaluated by the investigation, the most likely was a short circuit outside of the CWT that allowed excessive voltage to enter it through electrical wiring associated with the fuel quantity indication system. Contributing factors to the accident were the design and certification concept that fuel tank explosions could be prevented solely by precluding all ignition sources and the design and certification of the Boeing 747 with heat sources located beneath the CWT with no means to reduce the heat transferred into the CWT or to render the fuel vapor in the tank nonflammable.

factors.evidence: The most likely ignition source was a short circuit outside the tank that allowed excessive voltage into fuel quantity indication system wiring; aging wiring with cracked insulation and sulfide deposits on FQIS components were found in the fleet.
Wreckage and sooting patterns showed the center wing tank ruptured from an internal overpressure explosion of the fuel/air vapor.
Air conditioning packs beneath the center wing tank heated the small quantity of residual fuel during the long ground delay, producing a flammable vapor in the tank.
The design and certification philosophy relied solely on excluding ignition sources and did not require reducing fuel tank flammability.
The explosion severed the fuselage forward of the wing; the forward section fell away and the remaining structure broke up as it descended.
Fuel released from the ruptured wing tanks ignited, producing the fireball seen by witnesses as the wreckage descended.
After the forward fuselage separated the airplane could not be controlled and broke up in flight.

events.text: The airplane sits at the gate at JFK on a hot afternoon with air conditioning packs running beneath the nearly empty center wing tank, heating the small quantity of fuel and creating a flammable vapor.
Flight 800 departs JFK runway 22R about an hour late and climbs out over Long Island.
Captain remarks on an erratic number 4 engine fuel flow indication; the investigation did not link it to the accident.
Boston Center clears the flight to climb and maintain 15,000 feet; the crew acknowledge and set climb thrust.
The center wing tank explodes at about 13,800 feet; the CVR and FDR stop and the transponder return ceases.
The fuselage fails forward of the wing and the nose section separates and falls into the sea.
The remaining airplane, now nose-light, pitches up and climbs briefly before rolling and descending out of control.
The wings and remaining fuselage break up; fuel released from the wing tanks ignites and a fireball is seen by hundreds of witnesses on the shore and in aircraft.
Burning wreckage falls into the Atlantic Ocean about 8 miles south of East Moriches; there are no survivors.
A large search and recovery effort begins; over the following months more than 95 percent of the airplane is recovered from the seabed and reconstructed.

recommendations.text: Require the development of and implementation of design or operational changes that will preclude the operation of transport-category airplanes with explosive fuel-air mixtures in the fuel tanks, such as nitrogen inerting or reduced heat transfer to the center tank.
recommendations.outcome: FAA Fuel Tank Flammability Reduction rule (2008) required flammability reduction means, typically nitrogen inerting, on new and many in-service transport airplanes.

recommendations.text: Require a fleet-wide review of fuel tank systems, including fuel quantity indication system wiring, to identify and eliminate ignition sources, and address aging wiring and separation of FQIS wiring from higher voltage circuits.
recommendations.outcome: SFAR 88 (2001) required design reviews of fuel tank systems and led to numerous airworthiness directives; transient suppression devices were developed for FQIS wiring.

recommendations.text: Revise the transport-category certification standard for fuel tank systems so that flammability, and not only ignition source exclusion, is addressed in design.
recommendations.outcome: 14 CFR 25.981 was amended to require flammability reduction or ignition mitigation.

recommendations.text: Improve inspection, maintenance and replacement standards for aging electrical wiring on transport airplanes.
recommendations.outcome: The Enhanced Airworthiness Program for Airplane Systems (EWIS rules, 2007) established electrical wiring interconnection system requirements.

safety_changes: SFAR 88 (2001) required manufacturers and operators to conduct safety reviews of fuel tank systems, producing dozens of airworthiness directives on wiring, pumps and FQIS components.
14 CFR 25.981 was amended so that fuel tank flammability must be minimized or ignition effects mitigated in new designs.

The 2008 Fuel Tank Flammability Reduction rule required flammability reduction means, typically nitrogen inerting, on new production and most in-service large transport airplanes with heated center tanks.
Enhanced Airworthiness Program for Airplane Systems rules (2007) added electrical wiring interconnection system design, inspection and maintenance requirements for aging aircraft.
The FAA and Boeing developed and fielded onboard nitrogen generation systems for the 737, 747 and 777 families.

notes: Explosion time 20:31:12 EDT and altitude about 13,800 feet are as stated in the report; the sequence of breakup after the explosion is a reconstruction and the t values after 0 are approximate.
Takeoff time about 20:19 EDT; the captain's fuel flow remark is at about 20:29 and is paraphrased rather than quoted.

Recommendation A-96-174 was issued in December 1996 during the investigation; its wording is condensed. Other recommendation ids from the final report are not given because they are not recalled with confidence.
The FBI conducted a parallel criminal investigation and is listed as a participant, not as an investigating agency with a formal aviation role.

records.title: Aeroperú 603

agencies.name: Comisión de Investigación de Accidentes de Aviación
agencies.report_title: Informe final del accidente del Boeing 757-23A N52AW, Aeroperú vuelo 603

location.name: Pacific Ocean off Pasamayo, about 30 miles northwest of Lima

records.summary: Before a night departure from Lima, the 757's static ports had been covered with adhesive tape during washing and polishing and the tape was not removed. After takeoff the altimeters and airspeed indicators gave erroneous readings and the crew received a stream of contradictory warnings including wind shear, rudder ratio, mach trim, overspeed and stick shaker. Unable to trust their instruments and relying on ATC altitude readouts that came from the aircraft's own faulty transponder data, the crew flew a slow descending return over the sea until the aircraft struck the water in the dark. All 70 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The Peruvian commission concluded that the accident was caused by the blockage of the static ports by adhesive tape that maintenance personnel had applied during cleaning and polishing of the fuselage and failed to remove, and the failure of maintenance supervision and the flight crew's preflight inspection to detect it. The blocked ports produced erroneous altitude, airspeed and vertical speed indications and a series of contradictory warnings that, together with the dark night over the sea and the absence of reliable altitude information from ATC, prevented the crew from recognising the aircraft's true altitude before it struck the water.

factors.evidence: A worker covered the left-side static ports with protective tape during washing and polishing and did not remove it; supervision and the walk-around did not detect the tape.
The taped static ports fed erroneous static pressure to the captain's instruments and the air data computer.
Airspeed and altitude indications were erroneous from shortly after rotation and became increasingly divergent from the true values.
Overspeed warnings sounded while the stick shaker also activated, presenting the crew with contradictory indications.
Wind shear, rudder ratio, mach trim, overspeed and stick shaker warnings occurred together and were treated as unreliable, including the terrain warnings near the end.
The crew were saturated by continuous warnings while trying to determine which instruments to trust and coordinate a return.
The flight was over the sea at night with no external references to judge altitude.
The crew believed they were at about 9,700 ft, as confirmed by ATC from the aircraft's own erroneous Mode C data, when they were near the sea.
The aircraft struck the water in a controlled descent while the crew believed they had ample altitude.

events.text: During washing and polishing of the fuselage the static ports on the left side are covered with adhesive tape; the tape is not removed when the work is finished.
Preflight walk-around at night does not detect the tape on the static ports.
Flight 603 takes off from Lima for Santiago.
Altimeters and vertical speed indications behave abnormally and the airspeed indications disagree; the crew realise the instruments are unreliable.
Wind shear, rudder ratio and mach/speed trim warnings appear in succession.
Captain declares an emergency to Lima and requests vectors back to the airport, reporting that the instruments are unreliable.
Controller relays altitude and speed readouts from radar; these come from the aircraft's own transponder and air data and are equally erroneous.
Overspeed warning sounds while the stick shaker also activates; the crew cannot reconcile the two.
Crew request that another aircraft be sent to guide them and discuss the impossibility of trusting any instrument; they turn back over the sea toward Lima.
Ground proximity 'too low terrain' warnings sound; the crew consider them false because ATC still reports them at about 9,700 ft.
The left wingtip and engine strike the sea; the aircraft climbs briefly.
Aircraft strikes the Pacific inverted about 30 miles from Lima and breaks up; all 70 on board are killed.

recommendations.text: Require that protective coverings on pitot-static ports be conspicuous, logged and removed under supervision, and that preflight inspections specifically verify the static ports are clear.
recommendations.outcome: Boeing and operators reinforced procedures for covering and inspecting static ports; maintenance logging of port covers became standard.

recommendations.text: Provide flight crews with training and procedures for flight with unreliable airspeed and altitude, including use of pitch and power tables and radio altitude.
Ensure controllers understand that Mode C altitude readouts derive from the aircraft's own air data and cannot confirm altitude when the aircraft's instruments are unreliable.

safety_changes: Boeing and airlines strengthened procedures for covering, tagging and inspecting static ports and pitot probes during maintenance and washing.
Unreliable airspeed and altitude training was expanded, emphasising pitch and power flying and use of the radio altimeter.
Awareness that ATC Mode C altitude is aircraft-derived and cannot verify altitude for an aircraft with air data faults.

notes: The Peruvian final report is not widely available in English; the probable cause is condensed from published summaries and may not match the report wording.
Report id, report date and URL for the CIAA report are unknown and left null; the sources entry is the Peruvian Ministry of Transport site.
t0 is the approximate takeoff time of 00:42 local and impact about 01:11; intermediate offsets are estimates and clocks are omitted.
Crash coordinates are approximate for the sea area off Pasamayo.

records.title: Comair 3272

location.name: Raisinville Township, Monroe County

records.summary: Flight 3272 on approach to Detroit descended to 4,000 feet and was instructed to turn left to intercept the localizer. During the turn, the captain noted the low speed indicator and requested more power from the first officer. The aircraft abruptly stalled with a thin rough accretion of ice on the lifting surfaces. The aircraft rolled violently 145 degrees left, right, and left again as the crew lost control. The stall was attributed to inadequate icing procedures and failure to activate de-icing boots.
records.probable_cause: Aerodynamic stall and loss of control caused by aircraft encountering a thin rough accretion of ice on the wings while operating at a low airspeed in icing conditions. Contributing factors included inadequate FAA standards for icing operations, inadequate Comair procedures for icing conditions, crew failure to activate de-icing boots contrary to manufacturer recommendations, and operation near the lower end of the flight envelope while flaps were retracted.

factors.evidence: Aircraft accumulated thin rough accretion of ice on lifting surfaces in icing conditions
Crew did not activate deicing boots on wings contrary to manufacturer instructions; Comair procedure was incorrect due to concern over ice bridging from older aircraft no longer valid for EMB-120
Aircraft operating at low airspeed on approach with flaps retracted; captain requested power to increase speed
Crew inadequately trained for icing conditions and stall recovery in this aircraft type
Comair flight manual procedures for icing conditions were inadequate and did not follow manufacturer recommendations
Aircraft abruptly stalled during approach in icing conditions
Aircraft violently rolled 145 degrees left and right; crew lost control and crashed

events.text: Flight 3272 took off from Cincinnati; less than one hour later began approach to Detroit
Instructed aircraft to descend to 4,000 feet and turn right on heading 180 degrees
Instructed aircraft to turn left on heading 090 degrees to intercept localizer
Captain stated looks like your low speed indicator; requested increased power from first officer
Aircraft abruptly stalled; violently rolled 145 degrees left to right and back to left; crew lost control and aircraft crashed into rural field killing all 29 aboard

notes: NTSB determined clear probable cause related to icing procedures
similar accident (American Eagle 4184) noted with same causal pattern
Sections read from text report at /home/user/portfolio/blackbox/cache/text/wd_q5150488.txt: synopsis/summary, probable cause, factors, chain, events

records.title: Korean Air 801

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Controlled Flight Into Terrain, Korean Air Flight 801, Boeing 747-300, HL7468, Nimitz Hill, Guam, August 6, 1997

location.name: Nimitz Hill, about 3 nm southwest of Guam International Airport

records.summary: Flying a night non-precision localizer approach to runway 6L at Guam in rain showers, with the glideslope out of service, the fatigued captain descended below the step-down altitudes as if on a glideslope while the first officer and flight engineer failed to challenge him effectively. The 747 struck Nimitz Hill about 3 nm short of the runway near the Nimitz VOR. The FAA's minimum safe altitude warning system, which could have alerted the controller, had been inhibited. 228 of the 254 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The captain's failure to adequately brief and execute the nonprecision approach and the first officer's and flight engineer's failure to effectively monitor and cross-check the captain's execution of the approach. Contributing to these failures were the captain's fatigue and Korean Air's inadequate flight crew training. Contributing to the accident was the Federal Aviation Administration's intentional inhibition of the minimum safe altitude warning system at Guam and the agency's failure to adequately manage the system.

factors.evidence: The captain did not adequately brief the localizer-only approach and descended below the published step-down altitudes before reaching the fixes.
The aircraft descended through the 2,000 ft and 1,440 ft step-down altitudes and through the 560 ft MDA without the runway in sight.
The captain remarked during the flight that he was really sleepy; the NTSB found his fatigue degraded his performance.
The first officer and flight engineer failed to monitor and cross-check the captain's execution of the approach.
Concerns about the approach were voiced indirectly and the call for a missed approach came too late to prevent impact.
The captain apparently believed the glideslope was usable and lost awareness of the aircraft's position relative to the step-down fixes.
The NTSB cited Korean Air's inadequate flight crew training in non-precision approaches and CRM.
The FAA had intentionally inhibited the Guam MSAW system to eliminate nuisance alerts, so the controller received no warning of the descent.
The NTSB found the FAA failed to adequately manage the MSAW system at Guam.
Rain showers on the approach path intermittently obscured the runway.
The approach was flown at about 01:40 local time in darkness.
GPWS altitude and sink rate callouts were heard but the go-around was not initiated until seconds before impact.
The aircraft struck Nimitz Hill at about 660 ft elevation near the Nimitz VOR, about 3 nm from the runway.
The wreckage burned after impact; fire and delayed rescue contributed to the death toll.

events.text: During the descent the captain remarks that he is really sleepy.
Captain briefs the approach to runway 6L, referring to the ILS although the glideslope is out of service per NOTAM; the briefing does not cover the step-down fixes of the localizer approach.
Guam CERAP clears the flight for the ILS runway 6L approach, noting the glideslope is unusable, and hands the flight to Agana tower.
Crew discuss whether the glideslope is working after seeing intermittent indications; the captain appears to believe a glideslope is available.
Aircraft enters rain showers on final; the runway lights are intermittently visible.
Aircraft descends below 2,000 ft before reaching the Nimitz VOR step-down fix.
Aircraft continues descent below the 1,440 ft step-down altitude and below the 560 ft MDA; the inhibited MSAW gives the controller no alert.
GPWS radio altitude callout 'one thousand' sounds.
Flight engineer and first officer note that the runway is not in sight; GPWS 'minimums' and 'sink rate' callouts follow.
First officer calls for a missed approach.
Captain calls go around and begins to advance the throttles.
Aircraft strikes trees and terrain on Nimitz Hill near the Nimitz VOR, about 3 nm southwest of the runway 6L threshold, and breaks up; fire follows.
Rescue efforts are delayed by the terrain, a broken pipeline and coordination problems; 26 people survive.

recommendations.text: Review and correct the inhibition of MSAW systems at all ATC facilities and establish procedures to ensure MSAW is not inappropriately inhibited.
recommendations.outcome: The FAA restored full MSAW coverage at Guam and reviewed MSAW configurations nationwide.

recommendations.text: Require air carriers to provide flight crews with training and procedures for non-precision approaches, including constant-angle descent techniques.
recommendations.outcome: Constant descent final approach techniques were widely adopted for non-precision approaches.

recommendations.text: Require terrain awareness and warning systems (enhanced GPWS) on transport category aircraft.
recommendations.outcome: FAA required TAWS on turbine aircraft with six or more passenger seats by 2005.

recommendations.text: Improve Korean Air's flight crew training, CRM and fatigue management and strengthen Korean oversight of the airline.
recommendations.outcome: Korean Air overhauled its training and safety programs following this and subsequent accidents.

safety_changes: FAA restored MSAW coverage at Guam and audited MSAW inhibition at other facilities.
Korean Air restructured its flight operations, training and CRM programs after a series of accidents.
Wider adoption of constant descent angle non-precision approaches and of terrain awareness warning systems.

notes: t0 is the impact time 01:42:26 local; the GPWS 'one thousand' callout and first officer's missed approach call times are recalled from the report to within a few seconds; earlier event times are approximate.
Fatalities: the NTSB report gives 228 of 254 occupants; some sources count later deaths differently.
Korean accredited representative agency code 'KCAB' is a shorthand for the Korean Civil Aviation Bureau of the time.
Recommendation numbers not recalled and are left null.

records.title: Austral Líneas Aéreas 2553

agencies.name: Comisión Investigadora de Accidentes de Aviación
agencies.report_title: Final report on the accident to DC-9-32 LV-WEG near Nuevo Berlín, Río Negro, 10 October 1997

agencies.name: Junta de Investigación de Accidentes de Aviación Civil

location.name: Near Nuevo Berlín, Fray Bentos area, Río Negro department

records.summary: In cruise at night the DC-9 entered an area of thunderstorms and icing. The pitot probes iced and the airspeed indications fell well below the true speed. Believing the aircraft was slowing toward a stall, the crew added thrust and extended the slats at a speed far above the slat limit. The slats were damaged or deployed asymmetrically, the aircraft rolled and pitched down, and it dived into marshland near Nuevo Berlín at very high speed. All 74 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The Uruguayan commission concluded that the crew, faced with erroneous low airspeed indications caused by pitot probe icing in a thunderstorm, extended the slats at a speed well above the structural limit, which led to loss of control and an unrecoverable dive. Contributing factors included the crew's failure to identify the erroneous airspeed indications and cross-check with other parameters, inadequate training for unreliable airspeed situations, and the decision to fly through severe weather.

factors.evidence: The aircraft was flying at night through an area of thunderstorms with icing conditions when the airspeed indications became erroneous.
The commission determined that the pitot probes iced, causing the indicated airspeed to fall progressively below the true airspeed.
The indicated airspeed decreased toward values suggesting an imminent stall while the aircraft was in fact flying at normal cruise speed.
The crew believed the aircraft was slowing toward a stall and reacted to protect against it rather than recognising an instrument failure.
The crew added thrust and extended the slats at high speed, and pushed the nose down to gain speed.
The slats were extended at a true airspeed far above their limit; the aircraft then accelerated in the dive to near or above the speed of sound.
The slats were damaged by the overspeed extension, producing an asymmetric configuration and loss of lift and control.
The report found the crew had not been adequately trained to recognise and manage unreliable airspeed indications.
The accident occurred at night, removing external visual references.
The aircraft rolled and entered a steep dive from which the crew could not recover.

events.text: In night cruise at FL350 toward Buenos Aires the aircraft approaches a line of thunderstorms over the Uruguay river area.
Crew request and receive clearance to descend to avoid weather, then enter an area of cloud and icing.
The pitot probes ice and the indicated airspeed begins to fall below the true airspeed.
Crew note the decreasing airspeed indication and discuss it as a real loss of speed.
Thrust is increased in response to the low airspeed indication; the aircraft accelerates while the indication continues to decay.
With the indicated airspeed near the low-speed limit, the crew extend the slats although the true airspeed is far above the slat limit.
The slats are damaged by the aerodynamic loads and deploy asymmetrically; the aircraft rolls and pitches nose down.
The crew attempt to recover but the aircraft enters a steep dive and accelerates.
The aircraft strikes marshland near Nuevo Berlín at very high speed in a near-vertical attitude and disintegrates.

recommendations.text: Train DC-9 crews to recognise unreliable airspeed indications caused by pitot icing, to cross-check with attitude, thrust and groundspeed, and to avoid configuration changes on the basis of a suspect indication.
Reinforce guidance on avoiding penetration of thunderstorm areas and on the use and monitoring of pitot heat in icing conditions.

safety_changes: Austral and other Argentine DC-9 operators revised training on unreliable airspeed and slat operating limits following the accident.
The accident is used as a reference case for pitot icing induced unreliable airspeed leading to inappropriate configuration changes.

notes: t0 is null and clock strings are omitted: the exact UTC times from the Uruguayan report were not verified. t values are approximate offsets from the onset of pitot icing reconstructed from the published narrative. The accident occurred at about 22:10 Argentine local time on 10 October 1997 (early 11 October UTC).
The cruise altitude before the descent (FL350) and the exact slat limit speed were not verified; the state value is indicative.
Whether the pitot heat was switched off or the probes iced despite heating was not verified; the record states only that the probes iced as the commission concluded.
The Uruguayan commission's report number, date and URL are not known; the Argentine JIAAC's successor (JST) site is given as a source.
Recommendations are summarised themes, not verified verbatim recommendations.

records.title: SilkAir 185
records.time_reference: Western Indonesia time (UTC+7); clock strings approximate to the minute

agencies.name: Komite Nasional Keselamatan Transportasi
agencies.report_title: Investigation of Aircraft Accident SilkAir Flight MI 185, Boeing B737-300, 9V-TRF, Musi River, Palembang, Indonesia, 19 December 1997 (National Transportation Safety Committee)

location.name: Musi River near Sungsang, Palembang, South Sumatra

records.summary: In cruise at FL350 between Jakarta and Singapore the 737's cockpit voice recorder stopped, followed six minutes later by the flight data recorder. About a minute after that the aircraft left its cruise altitude in a near-vertical dive, exceeded the speed of sound and shed parts of its tail before striking the Musi River near Palembang. All 104 on board died. The Indonesian NTSC could not determine the cause; the NTSB, as accredited representative, concluded that the evidence was consistent with deliberate pilot action.
records.probable_cause: The Indonesian National Transportation Safety Committee concluded that the technical investigation had yielded no evidence to explain the cause of the accident and that the cause could not be determined. The NTSB, in formal comments appended to the report, stated that the accident could be explained by intentional pilot action, most likely by the captain: the sequential stopping of the recorders was consistent with their circuit breakers being pulled, the horizontal stabiliser was found trimmed nearly full nose-down, and no mechanical failure, including the rudder power control unit anomalies examined after other 737 accidents, could account for the flight path.

factors.evidence: The NTSB's position, not adopted by the NTSC: the recorder stoppages, the nose-down stabiliser trim and the flight path are consistent with intentional control inputs by a pilot, most likely the captain. The NTSC found the evidence inconclusive.
The aircraft departed FL350 in a near-vertical dive and reached supersonic speed before impact.
Parts of the horizontal stabiliser and elevator separated in flight during the dive as a result of the extreme speed.

events.text: Departs Jakarta for Singapore with 97 passengers and 7 crew.
Reaches cruise altitude FL350; the flight proceeds normally.
The cockpit voice recorder stops recording. No aircraft fault was found to explain this; the stoppage is consistent with the CVR circuit breaker being pulled.
Jakarta control has a routine exchange with the flight; nothing abnormal is reported.
The flight data recorder stops recording, again with no fault found and consistent with its circuit breaker being pulled.
Radar shows the aircraft leaving FL350 in a rapid descent. Wreckage evidence shows the horizontal stabiliser trimmed nearly full nose-down.
The dive becomes near-vertical and the aircraft exceeds the speed of sound; parts of the tail separate in flight and are found some distance from the main wreckage.
The aircraft strikes the Musi River near Sungsang at very high speed; the wreckage is deeply embedded and highly fragmented. All 104 on board are killed.

Investigation: the rudder power control unit is examined and tested for the dual servo valve jam implicated in the USAir 427 and United 585 accidents; no evidence of a rudder hardover is found. The NTSC concludes the cause is undetermined; the NTSB disagrees.

recommendations.text: Consider means to prevent flight recorders from being disabled from the cockpit, such as relocating the circuit breakers or providing independent recording of their status.
Review pilot medical, psychological and financial-stress screening and support programs.

dissent.position: In formal comments on the draft final report (December 2000) the NTSB stated that the accident sequence was consistent with, and could be explained by, intentional pilot action, most likely by the captain, and that no mechanical failure could explain the recorder stoppages, the stabiliser trim setting and the flight profile. The NTSC did not adopt this conclusion and reported the cause as undetermined.

safety_changes: The accident, together with EgyptAir 990, focused attention on pilot mental health screening and on measures to prevent flight recorders from being disabled in flight.
The rudder power control unit examination contributed to the wider 737 rudder system investigation following USAir 427.

notes: The cause of this accident is formally undetermined; deliberate_act is included on the basis of the NTSB's dissenting position and is labelled as such in the evidence.
Clock strings are given only to the minute (CVR stop about 16:05, FDR stop about 16:11, departure from FL350 about 16:12); the offsets between the recorder stoppages and the impact are approximate.

A 2004 US civil jury verdict attributing the crash to a rudder servo defect was not an official investigation finding; the NTSC and NTSB found no evidence of a rudder hardover, which is why rudder_hardover is not listed as a factor.
The Singapore accredited representative's agency code (MOC-SG) is a placeholder; Singapore had no separate investigation bureau at the time.

records.title: Swissair 111
records.time_reference: UTC (the accident occurred on 3 September UTC, 2 September local time)

agencies.name: Transportation Safety Board of Canada
agencies.report_title: In-Flight Fire Leading to Collision with Water, Swissair Transport Limited, McDonnell Douglas MD-11 HB-IWF, Peggy's Cove, Nova Scotia 5 nm SW, 2 September 1998

location.name: Atlantic Ocean off Peggy's Cove, Nova Scotia

records.summary: About 53 minutes after departing New York for Geneva, the crew of the MD-11 noticed an unusual odour and then smoke in the cockpit while cruising at FL330. They declared Pan Pan, diverted toward Halifax, began the smoke checklist and prepared to dump fuel, but a fire spreading above the cockpit ceiling progressively disabled aircraft systems. The aircraft struck the sea near Peggy's Cove about 20 minutes after the odour was first noticed, killing all 229 on board.
records.probable_cause: The TSB found that an electrical arcing event, most probably involving in-flight entertainment network wiring, ignited flammable metallised polyethylene terephthalate (MPET) cover material on thermal acoustic insulation blankets in the area above the cockpit ceiling. The fire spread along the flammable insulation and other materials, degrading aircraft systems and the cockpit environment until the crew lost control. Contributing were the absence of a fire-detection and suppression capability in that area, certification standards that allowed flammable materials, and a checklist and diversion philosophy that did not lead to an immediate landing.

factors.evidence: Arc-damaged wires, including an in-flight entertainment network power cable, were found in the area above the cockpit; the TSB concluded an arcing event was the most probable ignition source.

The IFE network installation, approved under a supplemental type certificate, was integrated into the aircraft's electrical system in a way that meant its power was not removed by the CABIN BUS switch, and the area above the cockpit had no fire detection or suppression.

MPET-covered thermal acoustic insulation blankets were easily ignited by the arc and propagated the fire; other materials such as silicone elastomeric end caps and hook-and-loop fasteners also contributed.
The MPET insulation passed the certification flammability test then in force (FAR 25.853 vertical Bunsen burner), a test the TSB found inadequate to predict in-service behaviour.
The TSB found deficiencies in regulatory oversight of the STC process and in flammability standards for materials in hidden areas.
The fire spread rearward above the ceiling and into the cockpit, damaging wiring and systems and creating smoke and heat in the cockpit.

The Smoke/Fumes of Unknown Origin checklist was designed around isolating electrical sources and did not direct the crew toward the earliest possible landing; the TSB found it unsuitable for an in-flight fire situation.

The crew, following Swissair procedures, prepared for a landing with fuel dumping and checklist actions rather than an immediate emergency descent; the TSB concluded that even an immediate diversion would probably not have allowed a landing before systems failed.
After fire-related failures of the flight recorders, autopilot and instruments, the aircraft descended and struck the water at high speed in a steep nose-down, right-wing-low attitude.

events.text: Departs New York JFK for Geneva with 215 passengers and 14 crew.
Pilots notice an unusual odour in the cockpit while cruising at FL330; it is initially assessed as an air-conditioning smell.
Smoke is seen in the cockpit; the crew agree there is a problem, don oxygen masks and decide to divert.
Crew declare Pan Pan Pan to Moncton Centre, report smoke in the cockpit and request an immediate return to a convenient airport, suggesting Boston.
Moncton Centre offers Halifax, about 56 nm closer than Boston, and clears the aircraft to descend.
Crew accept Halifax and begin the descent.
Told they are 30 nm from the Halifax runway, the crew respond that they need more distance to descend from 21,000 ft; ATC turns the aircraft to lose altitude.
Crew ask to dump fuel; ATC vectors the aircraft south over St. Margaret's Bay for the dump. The Smoke/Fumes of Unknown Origin checklist is under way.
CABIN BUS switch selected OFF as part of the smoke checklist; this does not remove power from the IFE network wiring.
Autopilot disconnects as fire damage spreads to aircraft wiring.
Crew declare an emergency, state they must land immediately and that they are starting to dump fuel.
Flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder stop as fire-related electrical failures multiply; last radio transmission received from the aircraft.
Fire continues to degrade cockpit instruments and displays; the aircraft is observed manoeuvring over St. Margaret's Bay in the final minutes.
Aircraft strikes the sea near Peggy's Cove at about 300 kt in a 20-degree nose-down, 110-degree right-bank attitude; all 229 killed.

cvr.speaker: PM
cvr.text: Swissair one eleven heavy is declaring Pan Pan Pan. We have smoke in the cockpit. Request immediate return to a convenient place, I guess Boston.

recommendations.text: Require cockpit voice recorders with a minimum recording capacity of two hours on aircraft required to carry CVRs and FDRs.
recommendations.outcome: Two-hour CVRs are now required on newly manufactured transport aircraft in Canada, the USA and Europe.

recommendations.text: Require an independent power source for CVRs and cockpit-area microphones so that recording continues after loss of aircraft electrical power.
recommendations.outcome: Recorder independent power supplies (RIPS) required on new aircraft by the FAA from 2010.

recommendations.text: Develop and adopt a flammability test regime for aircraft materials that reflects realistic in-service ignition and fire-propagation conditions, and require the removal or replacement of MPET-covered insulation blankets.
recommendations.outcome: The FAA mandated replacement of MPET insulation in affected aircraft and adopted the radiant panel test (FAR 25.856) for thermal acoustic insulation.

recommendations.text: Review and improve in-flight firefighting measures, including crew training, smoke and fire checklists that direct the crew to land as soon as possible, and fire detection and suppression in hidden areas.
recommendations.outcome: Industry smoke/fire checklists were revised to prioritise an immediate diversion and landing.

recommendations.text: Improve the certification and installation review of supplemental type certificate modifications that integrate with aircraft electrical systems, and improve circuit protection and arc-fault detection on aircraft wiring.

safety_changes: FAA airworthiness directives required removal of metallised PET (MPET) thermal acoustic insulation from affected transport aircraft.
A new radiant-panel flammability test for thermal acoustic insulation (FAR/CS 25.856) replaced the previous vertical Bunsen burner test for that material.
Two-hour CVR recording and recorder independent power supplies were mandated for new transport aircraft.
Smoke, fire and fumes checklists across the industry were rewritten to direct crews to land at the nearest suitable airport as early as possible.
The in-flight entertainment network installation was deactivated on the Swissair MD-11 fleet and STC oversight for electrical modifications was tightened.

notes: Clock times for smoke detection (t=150), ATC offer of Halifax, the fuel-dump request and the CABIN BUS switch action are approximate and reconstructed from the report narrative; other clock times are as published by the TSB.
The identity of the pilot making radio calls is given as PM without confirmation.

Only recommendation ids A99-07 and A99-08 are given with confidence; the flammability and firefighting recommendations were issued as several separate TSB recommendations whose numbers are not reproduced here.
Only the Pan Pan call from the ATC transcript is quoted; the cockpit CVR transcript was not published in full.

records.title: American Airlines 1420

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Runway Overrun During Landing, American Airlines Flight 1420, McDonnell Douglas MD-82, N215AA, Little Rock, Arkansas, June 1, 1999

location.name: Beyond the end of runway 4R, Little Rock National Airport, Arkansas

records.summary: Late at night, at the end of a long duty day, the crew of the MD-82 pressed on with an ILS approach to runway 4R at Little Rock as a severe thunderstorm moved over the airport, with wind shear alerts and a crosswind beyond company limits. After touchdown on the rain-soaked runway the spoilers, which had not been armed, did not deploy, and the captain used reverse thrust above the recommended limit, degrading directional control. The aircraft overran the runway end, struck the approach light structure for the opposite runway and broke apart. The captain and 10 passengers died.
records.probable_cause: The flight crew's failure to discontinue the approach when severe thunderstorms and their associated hazards to flight operations had moved into the airport area and the crew's failure to ensure that the spoilers had extended after touchdown. Contributing to the accident were the flight crew's impaired performance resulting from fatigue and the situational stress associated with the intent to land under the circumstances; continuation of the approach to a landing when the company's maximum crosswind component was exceeded; and use of reverse thrust greater than 1.3 engine pressure ratio after landing.

factors.evidence: A severe thunderstorm with heavy rain, lightning and strong gusty winds moved over the airport during the approach.
The tower issued wind shear alerts during the approach.
The crew did not discontinue the approach when the storm hazards moved into the airport area.
The crew had been on duty about 13.5 hours and the NTSB found their performance impaired by fatigue and the stress of getting in.
The approach continued with the crosswind above the company maximum and the spoilers were not armed before landing.
The spoilers did not extend after touchdown and neither pilot verified or manually deployed them, greatly reducing braking effectiveness.
Reverse thrust above 1.3 EPR reduced rudder effectiveness and directional control on the wet runway.
The runway was flooded by heavy rain, reducing braking and causing hydroplaning.
Heavy rain reduced visibility so that the crew lost sight of the runway during the approach.
The crew were rushing to land ahead of the storm while reconfiguring for a runway change and managing wind shear alerts.
The non-frangible approach light support structure beyond the runway end contributed to the severity of the impact.
The aircraft left the end of runway 4R and collided with the approach lighting structure and a walkway.
A fire broke out after the aircraft came to rest.

events.text: Flight departs Dallas/Fort Worth about two hours late after weather delays; the crew are near the end of a long duty day.
Crew and dispatcher discuss thunderstorms moving toward Little Rock; the crew plan to arrive before the storm.
Because of wind changes the approach is changed from runway 22L to the ILS runway 4R, adding to the crew's workload.
Tower reports a wind shear alert and strong winds; the crosswind component exceeds the company limit for a wet runway.
Heavy rain and lightning envelop the airport; the crew lose sight of the runway and continue the ILS approach.
Landing checklist is completed without the spoiler lever being armed.
Captain regains sight of the runway close in and continues to land in gusty crosswinds and heavy rain.
Aircraft touches down on the flooded runway 4R; the spoilers do not deploy and neither pilot notices.
Captain applies reverse thrust above 1.3 EPR; the aircraft begins to drift and the rudder becomes ineffective in the reverser airflow.
Aircraft hydroplanes and weathervanes on the wet runway; braking is ineffective without spoilers.
Aircraft departs the end of runway 4R at high speed and strikes the runway 22L approach lighting structure and a walkway before stopping near the Arkansas River flood plain.
Fire breaks out and the passengers evacuate the broken fuselage in heavy rain; the captain and 10 passengers die.

recommendations.text: Require air carriers to provide guidance and training on thunderstorm avoidance and on discontinuing approaches when convective weather affects the airport, and on the effects of fatigue on decision-making.
Require MD-80 operators to emphasise spoiler arming and verification of spoiler deployment after touchdown, and to limit reverse thrust use on wet runways to preserve directional control.
Require approach light support structures and other objects in runway safety areas to be frangible and to review runway safety area standards at Little Rock and similar airports.
Require automatic spoiler deployment or a warning when spoilers are not armed for landing on transport aircraft.

safety_changes: American Airlines revised its thunderstorm and wind shear operating limits and emphasised spoiler verification on the MD-80.
Runway safety areas and the approach light structure at Little Rock were improved; the accident supported later frangibility standards and duty time reform.

notes: t0 is the touchdown time of about 23:50:20 CDT recalled from the report; the departure time from DFW (about 22:40) is approximate and other offsets are estimates.
Occupants 145 (139 passengers, 6 crew) and 11 fatalities; the duty period of about 13.5 hours is recalled from the report.
The ground speed on leaving the runway (about 97 knots) is not stated in the events because the exact value is uncertain.
Recommendation numbers not recalled and are left null.

records.title: EgyptAir 990

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Brief: EgyptAir Flight 990, Boeing 767-366ER, SU-GAP, 60 Miles South of Nantucket, Massachusetts, October 31, 1999

location.name: Atlantic Ocean about 60 miles south of Nantucket, Massachusetts

records.summary: About half an hour after departing New York for Cairo, while the 767 was in cruise at FL330 and the captain had left the cockpit, the relief first officer disconnected the autopilot and applied nose-down elevator, and the aircraft entered a steep dive. The captain returned and pulled back while the relief first officer continued to push; the engines were shut down, the elevators split, and after a partial recovery the aircraft dived again into the Atlantic. All 217 on board died. The NTSB attributed the accident to the relief first officer's control inputs for undetermined reasons; the Egyptian authorities disagreed.
records.probable_cause: The NTSB determined that the probable cause was the airplane's departure from normal cruise flight and subsequent impact with the Atlantic Ocean as a result of the relief first officer's flight control inputs. The reason for the relief first officer's actions was not determined.

factors.evidence: The NTSB found that the nose-down elevator inputs and subsequent engine shutdown were made by the relief first officer while alone in the cockpit and were not the result of any mechanical failure; the reason was not determined.
Sustained nose-down elevator input and throttles to idle drove the aircraft into a dive; the split elevator inputs after the captain returned reflected opposing column forces.
The aircraft exceeded its maximum operating speed during the dive, reaching about Mach 0.99.
After a partial pull-out and climb with the engines shut down, the aircraft entered a second dive and struck the ocean.

events.text: Flight 990 departs JFK for Cairo with a double crew for the long flight.
Aircraft levels in cruise at FL330; the relief first officer takes the right seat earlier than scheduled.
Captain leaves the cockpit, leaving the relief first officer alone at the controls.
Relief first officer quietly says 'I rely on God' (Tawakkalt ala Allah), a phrase he repeats several times over the following seconds.
Autopilot is disconnected.
Elevators move nose-down and the aircraft begins to pitch over into a dive.
Throttle levers are moved from cruise power to idle; the descent steepens and the load factor approaches zero.
Captain re-enters the cockpit asking repeatedly what is happening.
Master warning sounds; airspeed exceeds Mmo and continues to increase toward about Mach 0.99.

Captain pulls back on the control column and calls for the relief first officer to pull with him; the left and right elevators move in opposite directions as one column is pulled and the other pushed.
Both engine start levers are moved to cutoff, shutting down the engines.
Flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder stop as electrical power is lost; the aircraft is passing about 16,000 ft in the pull-out.
Radar shows the aircraft climbing back to about 24,000 ft with the engines shut down.
Aircraft enters a second steep dive; some structure separates before impact.
Aircraft strikes the Atlantic Ocean about 60 miles south of Nantucket; all 217 on board are killed.

recommendations.text: The NTSB issued no new safety recommendations in the accident brief, having found no mechanical failure; earlier recommendations on cockpit voice recorder duration and flight recorder power were referenced.

dissent.position: The Egyptian Civil Aviation Authority rejected the conclusion that the relief first officer deliberately caused the dive and argued that a failure in the elevator power control units (sheared bellcrank rivets and a jammed PCU) could explain the nose-down elevator movement, the elevator split and the sequence of events. The ECAA's comments were appended to the NTSB brief and the ECAA published its own report.

safety_changes: Boeing evaluated 767 elevator PCU failure scenarios during the investigation; the NTSB found no failure mode that could produce the recorded control movements.
Renewed attention to cockpit door and crew presence policies and to psychological screening of pilots, although no formal regulatory change was directly attributed to this accident.

notes: Departure time (about 01:20 EST) and the sequence times from 01:49:45 to 01:50:36 are recalled from the aircraft accident brief to within a few seconds; the second dive, radar climb altitude and 01:52 impact time are approximate.
The peak Mach number of about 0.99 and the in-flight separation of structure during the final descent are from memory of the brief.
The NTSB issued the findings as an Aircraft Accident Brief (AAB-02/01) rather than a full AAR; the record uses the report id given by the task.
The ECAA dissent is recorded as a formal disagreement; the ECAA report and the NTSB's rebuttal are both public.

records.title: Si Fly 325

location.name: Near Pristina, Kosovo

records.summary: An ATR 42 on a shuttle flight from Rome to Pristina for UN aid workers struck a mountain during approach to Pristina on November 12, 1999. The crew, experiencing fatigue from a high flight roster, failed to execute appropriate approach procedures and descent below minimum altitudes. The faulty GPWS warning system failed to alert the crew. Combined with inadequate air traffic control vectoring, the aircraft failed to clear terrain.
records.probable_cause: Crew teamwork lacking procedural discipline and vigilance during maneuvers in mountainous region with poor visibility. Aircraft kept on track then forgotten by military controller unused to mountainous environment and preventing CFIT risk. Operator's critical dependence on lease contract favoring failure to respect procedures. Opening of aerodrome to civil traffic without advance evaluation of operating conditions.

factors.evidence: Crew experiencing fatigue from high flight roster influencing failure to execute appropriate approach procedure (p. 65).
Crew not following appropriate approach procedure; hastily conducted flight preparation without mentioning safety altitudes (p. 65).
Controller extended flight KSV3275 track and appears to have forgotten it until crew called back (p. 65).
GPWS warning alarm did not sound; system broken down or switched off (p. 65).
Aircraft at 4,600 feet crashed into mountain at 4,650 feet in area where MSA is 6,900 feet (p. 65).
Crew appeared influenced by routine flights to Pristina; did not strictly follow appropriate briefing (p. 65).
Aircraft struck mountain terrain during approach to Pristina killing all 24 aboard (p. 65).

events.text: ATR 42 departs Rome Fiumicino with 3 crew and 21 passengers, mostly UN officials and aid workers
Pristina ATC vectors aircraft to intercept ILS and instructs descent to 5,200 feet then 4,600 feet
Crew changes to visual flight rules; not following appropriate approach procedure during briefing
GPWS warns crew 17 seconds before impact; crew does not react
Aircraft struck mountain terrain at 4,650 feet during approach to Pristina, killing all 24 aboard

recommendations.text: Opening to international civil traffic of an aerodrome not under effective authority of contracting State be subject to complete ICAO audit
Apply JAR OPS regulations in shortest possible time
Exercise reinforced surveillance of companies with recently acquired air transport certificate
Make modifications mandatory which improve operation of essential equipment like GPWS
Where GPWS mode failure occurs, make aircraft takeoff subject to establishing and following alternate procedures

safety_changes: ICAO audit requirements for aerodromes opening to international civil traffic
Enhanced GPWS testing requirements

notes: 1999 BEA French investigation
Sections read: Findings, Probable Cause, and Recommendations
CFIT with complex factors including aerodrome opening without ICAO audit

records.title: Kenya Airways 431

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la sécurité de l'aviation civile

location.name: Atlantic Ocean, 1.5 nm south of Abidjan Airport

records.summary: Kenya Airways Flight 431, an Airbus A310-304, crashed into the Atlantic Ocean 33 seconds after takeoff from Abidjan on 30 January 2000. A stall warning activated during rotation at low altitude, though the aircraft was not in a true stall. The pilot flying applied only part of the stall recovery procedure by pushing the control column forward, placing the aircraft in an unintended descent. GPWS warnings were masked by priority stall and overspeed warnings, and the absence of visual references over the sea at night prevented the crew from recognizing the low altitude.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by the pilot flying applying only part of the stall recovery procedure by pushing forward on the control column to stop the stick shaker following the initiation of a stall warning during rotation, while the airplane was not in a true stall situation. The pilot flying's action put the aircraft into a descent without the crew realizing it. The GPWS warnings that could have alerted the crew to imminent contact with the sea were masked by the priority stall and overspeed warnings. The conditions for a takeoff towards the sea at night provided no external visual references.

factors.evidence: A stall warning sounded just seconds after takeoff when the first officer requested landing gear retraction. The warning did not correspond to a true stall situation. (p. 73-74)

The pilot flying pushed the control column forward immediately after stick shaker activation, applying only part of the recommended stall recovery procedure. The crew did not apply TOGA thrust as specified in the FCOM. (p. 74-75)
The pilot flying put the aircraft into a descent without the crew realizing it, despite radio altimeter callouts from 300 feet down to 10 feet. (p. 74)

The GPWS warnings that could have alerted the crew to imminent contact with the sea were not generated in the cockpit because they were not prioritized compared to the successive stall and overspeed warnings. (p. 74-75)
The conditions for a takeoff performed towards the sea at night provided no external visual references that would have allowed the crew to be aware of the proximity to the sea. (p. 75)
The aircraft descended rapidly and crashed into the Atlantic Ocean, 1.5 nautical miles south of Abidjan Airport. (p. 15)
The aircraft was completely destroyed on impact with the sea. (p. 15)

events.text: Captain applied take-off power and announced 'thrust, SRS, and runway'; V1 and Rotate announced.
Stall warning sounded less than two seconds after 'Positive rate of climb, gear up' announcement.
Automatic call out announced 300 feet.
Copilot asked 'what's the problem?'
Copilot ordered the aural warning to be cut and pushed control column forward to stop the stick shaker.
GPWS sounded the 'Whoop' alarm, followed by automatic call out of 50 feet, but GPWS warning was masked by higher priority stall and overspeed warnings.
Master warning started. Captain ordered 'Go up!' preceded by automatic call out of 10 feet.
Aircraft collided with the sea with slight nose down attitude at speed above VFE, 33 seconds after takeoff.

cvr.speaker: FO
cvr.text: Positive rate of climb, gear up

recommendations.text: Integrate into type rating and recurrent training programs for crews of all aircraft likely to be subject to false stall warnings, the elements necessary to recognize and manage such a false alarm during phases of flight close to the ground.
Ensure that Airbus harmonizes the procedures in the FCOM with those taught during type rating training.
Ensure that appropriate equipment (aerial, maritime, etc.) be put in place to ensure immediate intervention at accident sites near coastal airports.

safety_changes: Airbus revised stall recovery procedures to emphasize minimum altitude loss rather than minimum time recovery

notes: Sections read: SYNOPSIS, Summary, History of Flight, Findings, Causes of the accident, Safety Recommendations
CVR transcript from appendix 7 and crew callouts
FDR data available but detailed parameters not extracted

records.title: Alaska Airlines 261

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Loss of Control and Impact with Pacific Ocean, Alaska Airlines Flight 261, McDonnell Douglas MD-83, N963AS, About 2.7 Miles North of Anacapa Island, California, January 31, 2000

route.from_name: Puerto Vallarta Licenciado Gustavo Díaz Ordaz

location.name: Pacific Ocean about 2.7 miles north of Anacapa Island, California

records.summary: The MD-83's horizontal stabilizer jammed during climb out of Puerto Vallarta and the crew spent much of the cruise troubleshooting with Alaska Airlines maintenance and dispatch. When the crew ran the trim motors the worn threads of the jackscrew acme nut stripped and the stabilizer moved to an extreme nose-down position; the airplane dived from 31,000 feet before the crew regained control at about 24,000 feet. About ten minutes later, while diverting to Los Angeles, the jackscrew's lower stop failed, the stabilizer went beyond its limit and the airplane pitched over, inverted, and struck the Pacific Ocean. All 88 on board died.
records.probable_cause: A loss of airplane pitch control resulting from the in-flight failure of the horizontal stabilizer trim system jackscrew assembly's acme nut threads. The thread failure was caused by excessive wear resulting from Alaska Airlines' insufficient lubrication of the jackscrew assembly. Contributing to the accident were Alaska Airlines' extended lubrication interval and the FAA's approval of that extension, which increased the likelihood that a missed or inadequate lubrication would result in excessive wear of the acme nut threads, and Alaska Airlines' extended end play check interval and the FAA's approval of that extension, which allowed the excessive wear of the acme nut threads to progress to failure without the opportunity for detection. Also contributing to the accident was the absence on the McDonnell Douglas MD-80 of a fail-safe mechanism to prevent the catastrophic effects of total acme nut thread loss.

factors.evidence: The acme nut threads wore away because of insufficient lubrication of the jackscrew assembly; very little grease was found on the recovered jackscrew.
Lubrication tasks were either missed or performed inadequately, and the last end play check recorded a value near the replacement limit without the nut being replaced.
Alaska Airlines' end play check interval had been extended to about 9,550 flight hours, allowing the excessive thread wear to progress to failure undetected.

The FAA approved Alaska Airlines' extensions of both the lubrication interval and the end play check interval without adequate technical justification, and its oversight of the airline's maintenance program was deficient.
Alaska Airlines' maintenance program repeatedly extended maintenance intervals; the report cited weaknesses in the airline's maintenance and quality control.
The stabilizer jammed during the climb and, when the crew later operated the trim motors, moved rapidly nose down as the remaining acme nut threads stripped.
About ten minutes after the first dive the jackscrew's lower mechanical stop and torque tube failed, allowing the stabilizer to move beyond its normal nose-down limit.
The MD-80 jackscrew assembly had no fail-safe mechanism to prevent the catastrophic effects of total acme nut thread loss.
The original certification of the DC-9/MD-80 stabilizer trim system treated the acme nut as structurally reliable without requiring a fail-safe load path.
With the stabilizer at an extreme nose-down position the elevators could not counter the pitching moment; the crew's control column and trim inputs had no effect.
The airplane pitched over, rolled inverted and descended into the ocean.

events.text: During the climb out of Puerto Vallarta the horizontal stabilizer trim stops responding; the autopilot holds pitch with elevator and the crew begin troubleshooting a jammed stabilizer.
The crew discuss the jammed stabilizer with Alaska Airlines dispatch and maintenance control by radio and consider whether to divert to Los Angeles or continue to San Francisco.
Cruising at 31,050 feet the captain, with the autopilot disengaged, operates the primary and alternate trim switches together to try to free the stabilizer.
The remaining acme nut threads strip; the stabilizer moves rapidly to a nose-down position and the airplane pitches over and begins a steep descent.
Both pilots pull on the control columns with well over 100 pounds of force to arrest the dive.
The airplane is recovered to level flight at about 24,000 feet after losing roughly 7,000 feet; the crew declare an emergency to Los Angeles Center and request a divert to Los Angeles.
Captain tells ATC they are stabilized, slowing, and will 'do a little test flight' with slats and flaps to check controllability before landing.
Descending through about 18,000 feet the crew extend slats and flaps 11 to evaluate handling, then retract them when the pitch forces become worse.
The cockpit voice recorder records an extremely loud noise as the jackscrew's lower stop fails; the stabilizer travels past its nose-down limit and the airplane pitches over sharply.
Captain transmits 'mayday' and the crew attempt to regain control, including trying to fly the airplane inverted.
The airplane descends inverted and nearly vertically, pitching and rolling, with no pitch authority available to the crew.
End of recording; the airplane strikes the Pacific Ocean north of Anacapa Island and is destroyed.

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: push and roll, push and roll.

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: ok, we are inverted... and now we gotta get it.

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: push push push... push the blue side up.

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: at least upside down we're flyin'.

recommendations.text: Establish shorter, technically justified lubrication and end play check intervals for the DC-9/MD-80/MD-90 and 717 horizontal stabilizer jackscrew assembly and require a review of maintenance interval extensions that are not supported by data.
recommendations.outcome: FAA airworthiness directives reduced jackscrew lubrication and end play inspection intervals.

recommendations.text: Require that the jackscrew assembly design on MD-80 series airplanes, and on any transport airplane using a similar single-load-path design, be modified to be fail-safe against total acme nut thread loss.
recommendations.outcome: FAA required design reviews of jackscrew trim systems; a fail-safe retrofit was not mandated but nut wear limits and inspections were tightened.

recommendations.text: Improve FAA surveillance of air carrier maintenance programs, including scrutiny of proposed maintenance interval extensions and of the data used to justify them.
Issue guidance that flight crews facing a jammed or unresponsive stabilizer should not continue to operate the trim motors in an attempt to free it and should land at the nearest suitable airport.
recommendations.outcome: Boeing revised MD-80 series jammed stabilizer procedures.

safety_changes: FAA airworthiness directives shortened the MD-80 series jackscrew lubrication interval to about 650 flight hours and reduced the end play check interval, with new inspection and grease requirements.
Alaska Airlines' maintenance program was extensively audited and restructured after the FAA threatened to revoke its maintenance certificate.
