The FAA required manufacturers and operators to review transport-category flight control systems for single points of failure lacking fail-safe features.
Boeing revised MD-80 family procedures for a jammed horizontal stabilizer to discourage repeated trim motor operation.

notes: Local date 2000-01-31 is used; in UTC the accident occurred on 2000-02-01.

Clock of the first dive (16:09:16) and of the loud noise on the CVR (16:19:36) are as recalled from the report and may differ by a few seconds; the end of recording is given as about 16:20:57 and may be off by up to a minute.
Times of the stabilizer jam during climb and of the dispatch/maintenance discussions are approximate; those events carry rough negative t values with no clock.
CVR lines are well-known excerpts from the public transcript; their t values between 16:19:36 and the end of recording are estimated, not taken from the transcript.
Altitude at which the first dive was arrested is stated in the report as about 23,000 to 24,000 feet; 24,000 is used.

records.title: Air France 4590 (Concorde)

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la sécurité de l'aviation civile
agencies.report_title: Accident on 25 July 2000 at La Patte d'Oie in Gonesse (95) to the Concorde registered F-BTSC operated by Air France

location.name: Hotel at La Patte d'Oie, Gonesse, 9.5 km from Paris CDG

records.summary: During the takeoff roll on runway 26R at Charles de Gaulle, Concorde F-BTSC ran over a titanium alloy strip that had fallen from a Continental Airlines DC-10 minutes earlier. The strip cut the right front tyre of the left main gear, which burst; a large piece of tyre struck the underside of the wing, causing a shock wave that ruptured fuel tank 5. Leaking fuel ignited, engines 1 and 2 lost thrust, the gear could not be retracted, and the aircraft, unable to climb or accelerate, lost control and crashed onto a hotel in Gonesse. All 109 on board and 4 on the ground died.
records.probable_cause: The accident was due to: the high-speed passage of a tyre over a part lost by an aircraft that had taken off five minutes earlier and the destruction of the tyre; the ripping out of a large piece of tank 5 from the underside of the wing through a complex process of transmission of the energy from the tyre debris; ignition of the leaking fuel by an electric arc in the landing gear bay or by contact with hot parts of the engine, and the propagation of the fire; the impossibility of retracting the landing gear, which probably contributed to the loss of thrust on engine 1 and the loss of control. Contributing: the strip had been installed on the DC-10 in a non-conforming manner, and previous tyre-burst incidents on Concorde had not led to protective measures against tank rupture.

factors.evidence: The titanium wear strip on the Continental DC-10 thrust reverser cowl had been manufactured and fitted in a non-conforming manner and detached on takeoff, leaving it on runway 26R.
Concorde had suffered numerous tyre bursts and several tank penetrations since 1979 without measures adequate to prevent fuel tank rupture.
The wing fuel tanks were vulnerable to rupture from tyre debris impacts and the tyres were prone to catastrophic destruction on foreign object damage.
Certification did not address the risk of tank rupture from tyre debris at the energy levels shown to be possible.
Tank 5 was ruptured from within by a pressure wave and fuel escaped at a very high rate under the left wing.
The fuel ignited, producing a very large flame trailing from the left wing and damaging the airframe and controls.
Engine 2 surged and lost thrust and was shut down; engine 1 also lost thrust twice, the second time irrecoverably.
The landing gear could not be retracted, probably because of fire damage to gear bay wiring, preventing acceleration and climb.
With two engines lost, the gear down and the aircraft below V2, it could neither accelerate nor climb above about 200 ft.
The aircraft pitched up and rolled left beyond 100 degrees, and struck the ground at low speed and high angle of attack.
The aircraft was destroyed by impact and fire on striking a hotel in Gonesse, killing four people on the ground.

events.text: A Continental Airlines DC-10 takes off from runway 26R; a 43 cm titanium wear strip from its number 3 engine thrust reverser cowl falls onto the runway.
Concorde begins its takeoff roll on runway 26R, about a tonne over the maximum takeoff weight with a light tailwind.
At about 175 kt, after V1, the number 2 tyre on the left main gear runs over the metal strip and bursts; tyre debris strikes the wing and tank 5 ruptures.
Leaking fuel ignites; a large flame trails from under the left wing. Engines 1 and 2 surge and lose thrust.
Tower controller informs the crew that they have strong flames behind them.
Engine 2 fire alarm sounds; the captain rotates and the aircraft lifts off at about 205 kt with engine 1 recovering thrust.
Flight engineer shuts down engine 2 and pulls the fire handle; the crew call for gear retraction.
The landing gear does not retract despite the selection; the aircraft climbs slowly to about 200 ft at about 200 kt.
Crew declare an emergency and attempt to reach Le Bourget; the aircraft cannot accelerate or climb.
Engine 1 loses thrust a second time; with only engines 3 and 4 on the right the aircraft pitches up and rolls steeply left.
Aircraft strikes the Hotelissimo hotel at La Patte d'Oie, Gonesse, in a nose-high left-banked attitude; all 109 occupants and 4 people on the ground killed.

recommendations.text: Suspend the Concorde certificate of airworthiness until measures are taken to guarantee a satisfactory level of safety with respect to tyre destruction and its consequences on the fuel tanks.
recommendations.outcome: Certificates suspended in August 2000; Kevlar tank liners, new Michelin NZG tyres and armoured wiring were introduced before return to service in November 2001.

recommendations.text: Strengthen the requirements and inspection of runways for foreign object debris, and ensure that repairs on aircraft parts liable to fall on runways conform to approved data.
Study tyre-destruction models and the effects of tyre debris on aircraft structures and fuel tanks for certification of large aircraft.

safety_changes: Kevlar-rubber liners in Concorde fuel tanks, Michelin NZG near-zero-growth tyres, armoured gear bay wiring; return to service in November 2001.
Increased runway FOD inspection frequency at Paris airports and broader FOD awareness programmes.
Concorde withdrawn from service by both operators in 2003.

notes: Continental Airlines and its mechanics were prosecuted and Continental disputed the findings in court, but no accredited agency formally dissented; dissent is empty.
Clock times are UTC as used in the BEA report; intermediate event seconds are approximate (tyre burst about 14:43:13, impact about 14:44:31).
Occupants counts the 109 on board; fatalities of 113 include 4 persons on the ground.
Some speeds (175 kt at tyre burst, lift-off about 205 kt) are approximate values from the report.

records.title: Gulf Air 072

location.name: Persian Gulf

records.summary: Gulf Air Flight 072, an Airbus A320-212 flying from Cairo to Bahrain, crashed into the shallow waters of the Persian Gulf 2 km from the airport on 23 August 2000, minutes after a go-around from a failed approach to Runway 12. The captain suffered spatial disorientation, applying a large nose-down input that produced a 15-degree dive; as the aircraft descended, the crew disregarded the GPWS 'sink rate' and 'Whoop, whoop, pull up' warnings while debating flap configuration instead. The Airbus struck the sea at 280 knots, killing all 143 people on board.
records.probable_cause: The final report found non-adherence to Standard Operating Procedures and loss of spatial and situational awareness by the crew during the approach and go-around, compounded by deficient CRM training at Gulf Air and safety oversight failures by the civil aviation authority.

factors.evidence: The flight crew suffered from spatial disorientation during the go-around and crashed into the shallow waters of the Persian Gulf.
Non-adherence to a number of Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) by the aircraft crew during the approach and final phases of the flight.
Systemic factors also contributed to the accident, including deficiency in crew resource management (CRM) training by Gulf Air.
Instead of responding to the sink rate warning, the captain ordered flap retraction as the GPWS escalated to 'Whoop, whoop! Pull up!'
Safety oversights by the Directorate General Of Civil Aviation and Meteorology of Oman.
Flying with a speed of 280 knots and a nose-down pitch of 6.5 degrees, the aircraft slammed onto the sea below, instantly killing all 143 passengers and crew members.

events.text: Captain Shakeeb applied a large nose-down input, inducing a rapid descent at a pitch angle of approximately 15 degrees, the maximum permissible, as the aircraft continued to accelerate under TO/GA thrust.
As the first officer called 'flaps three,' the Ground Proximity Warning System issued a 'sink rate' alert, but instead of responding to the warning, the captain ordered flap retraction.
As the aircraft descended toward the sea, the GPWS escalated to 'Whoop, whoop! Pull up!' while the crew continued discussing flap position as the aircraft descended unchecked.
At 19:30, flying at 280 knots with a nose-down pitch of 6.5 degrees, the aircraft slammed onto the sea, instantly killing all 143 passengers and crew members.

notes: BEA final report HTML page accessed but detailed content sections not fully parsed
Summary and key findings from provided summary_record
Report table of contents indicates comprehensive analysis and recommendations present in full document
Spatial disorientation, procedural non-compliance and inadequate CRM training clearly identified as causal factors

records.title: Air Transat 236

agencies.name: Gabinete de Prevenção e Investigação de Acidentes com Aeronaves
agencies.report_title: Accident Investigation Final Report: All Engines-out Landing Due to Fuel Exhaustion, Air Transat, Airbus A330-243 marks C-GITS, Lajes, Azores, Portugal, 24 August 2001

location.name: Lajes Air Base, Terceira, Azores

records.summary: During a night crossing of the Atlantic the A330's right engine fuel line, which had been installed with inadequate clearance from a hydraulic line during an engine change five days earlier, chafed through and began leaking. The crew did not recognise a leak, opened the crossfeed to correct the resulting imbalance and fed the left tank's fuel to the leak. Both engines flamed out and the crew glided about 65 nm to Lajes Air Base in the Azores, where the aircraft landed hard with all 306 occupants surviving.
records.probable_cause: The GPIAA concluded that the fuel leak resulted from the fracture of the engine 2 fuel feed line after it chafed against the hydraulic line, a consequence of the mismatched hydraulic pump installed during the engine change without the clearance-adaptation called for by the manufacturer. The crew's failure to identify the leak and their opening of the crossfeed, contrary to the caution in the fuel imbalance procedure, allowed the remaining fuel to be lost, leading to the flame-out of both engines. Contributing were Air Transat's maintenance planning and procedures, the absence of a fuel-leak warning on the aircraft, and the ECAM and checklist presentation, which did not lead the crew to consider a leak.

factors.evidence: Air Transat's maintenance organisation proceeded with the engine installation using a hydraulic pump configuration that did not match the engine, under time pressure and without resolving the discrepancy identified by the technicians.
The report noted shortcomings in the regulatory oversight of the operator's maintenance program; Transport Canada subsequently fined Air Transat.

The replacement engine was fitted with a hydraulic pump from an earlier configuration, and the service bulletin's interim clearance adaptation was not applied, leaving the fuel line in contact with the hydraulic line.
The fuel feed line fractured from chafing at about 04:38 UTC and fuel leaked overboard at a high rate for the rest of the flight.
The A330 had no fuel-leak detection or warning; the fuel imbalance advisory was the first indication presented to the crew.
The crew attributed the unusual oil indications and the fuel imbalance to instrument or computer problems and did not consider a leak until fuel was critically low.
The report found that the ECAM fuel imbalance procedure and QRH presentation did not effectively direct the crew to consider and rule out a fuel leak before opening the crossfeed.
The crossfeed valve was opened without first confirming that the imbalance was not due to a leak, contrary to the caution associated with the procedure.
All usable fuel was lost through the leak and the crossfeed; the right engine flamed out at 06:13 and the left at 06:26 UTC.
With both engines stopped the aircraft lost normal electrical and hydraulic power, leaving the ram air turbine, and became a glider about 65 nm from Lajes.
The crew landed the aircraft without engine power on runway 33 at Lajes; the aircraft bounced, eight main-gear tyres deflated and the occupants evacuated by slides.

events.text: Five days before the flight, Air Transat maintenance in Montreal installs a replacement Trent 772B in the number 2 position. The hydraulic pump fitted is from an earlier configuration and the interim clearance adaptation in the Rolls-Royce service bulletin is not applied, leaving the fuel feed line in contact with the hydraulic line.
Departs Toronto for Lisbon with 46.9 tonnes of fuel, 293 passengers and 13 crew.
The engine 2 fuel feed line fractures where it has chafed against the hydraulic line; fuel begins leaking overboard from the right side at a high rate.

The crew notice abnormal engine 2 oil indications (low oil temperature, high oil pressure and quantity). They contact Air Transat maintenance control by satellite phone and are advised the indications are probably spurious.
ECAM FUEL IMBALANCE advisory: the right wing tank quantity is well below the left.
The crew open the crossfeed valve to balance the tanks without first considering a leak, transferring fuel from the left tank to the leaking right side.
Noting that total fuel is far below the planned quantity, the crew now suspect a fuel problem, declare an emergency and divert toward Lajes.
Crew close the crossfeed and begin the descent toward Lajes with the fuel quantity falling rapidly.
Engine 2 flames out about 150 nm from Lajes.
Engine 1 flames out about 65 nm from Lajes; all generated electrical power is lost, the ram air turbine deploys and the crew fly the aircraft in emergency electrical configuration as a glider.
With the aircraft too high for a straight-in approach, the captain flies a series of turns to lose altitude near the airfield; slats are extended and the landing gear is lowered by gravity.

Hard landing on runway 33 at Lajes at about 200 kt; the aircraft bounces, eight main-gear tyres deflate under maximum braking and it stops on the runway. The occupants evacuate by slides; two are seriously injured.

recommendations.text: Develop and install a fuel-leak detection and warning capability on the A330 and similar aircraft, and revise the fuel imbalance ECAM and QRH procedures to require a leak check before the crossfeed is opened.
recommendations.outcome: Airbus revised the fuel imbalance procedures to require the fuel leak procedure to be considered first and later introduced fuel-leak detection logic.

recommendations.text: Review Air Transat's maintenance planning, engine change procedures and configuration control, and Transport Canada's oversight of them.
recommendations.outcome: Air Transat was fined by Transport Canada and revised its maintenance procedures.

recommendations.text: Clarify the service bulletin and engine installation documentation concerning hydraulic pump configuration and fuel/hydraulic line clearance.

safety_changes: Airbus revised the fuel imbalance ECAM/QRH procedures so that a fuel leak must be considered before opening the crossfeed, and introduced fuel-leak detection logic on the A330/A340 family.
Air Transat's maintenance organisation was audited and fined by Transport Canada; engine change and configuration-control procedures were revised.
The event became the reference case for fuel-leak recognition training in airline crews.

notes: Clock times for the leak onset (04:38), oil indications (05:33), fuel imbalance advisory (05:45), engine flame-outs (06:13 and 06:26) and landing (06:45) are from the published report summary; the crossfeed opening and diversion decision times are approximate.
Fuel at departure (46.9 t) and the number of serious injuries (2) are from memory of the report and should be verified.
The report date is given as October 2004; the exact day may differ.
GPIAA is now GPIAAF; the home page is given rather than a deep report URL.

records.title: American Airlines 587

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: In-Flight Separation of Vertical Stabilizer, American Airlines Flight 587, Airbus Industrie A300-605R, N14053, Belle Harbor, New York, November 12, 2001

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la Sécurité de l'Aviation Civile

route.from_name: New York John F. Kennedy International

location.name: Belle Harbor, Queens, New York

records.summary: About 100 seconds after takeoff from JFK runway 31L, the A300-600 encountered the wake of a Japan Airlines 747 that had departed ahead of it. The first officer, who was flying, responded to the second wake encounter with a series of alternating full rudder pedal inputs. The resulting sideslip loads exceeded the vertical stabilizer's ultimate design load and it separated from the fuselage; the airplane went out of control and crashed into a residential area, killing all 260 aboard and 5 on the ground.
records.probable_cause: The in-flight separation of the vertical stabilizer as a result of the loads beyond ultimate design that were created by the first officer's unnecessary and excessive rudder pedal inputs. Contributing to these rudder pedal inputs were characteristics of the Airbus A300-600 rudder system design and elements of the American Airlines Advanced Aircraft Maneuvering Program (AAMP).

factors.evidence: The first officer made five alternating full rudder pedal inputs within about seven seconds in response to a wake turbulence encounter that required no rudder input.
Aerodynamic loads from the resulting sideslip reached about twice the vertical stabilizer's design limit load and the composite fin and rudder separated from the fuselage at its attachment lugs.
The A300-600 rudder control system's light pedal forces and small pedal travel at high speed made it unusually sensitive, so a pilot could reach full rudder deflection with little force.

Elements of American Airlines' Advanced Aircraft Maneuvering Program, including a simulator exercise that responded to rudder input unrealistically, encouraged pilots to use rudder for upset recovery.
Certification standards did not address rudder pedal sensitivity or the loads created by full alternating rudder inputs below maneuvering speed.

Prior events such as American Airlines flight 903 in 1997 and Interflug in 1991 had not led to clear communication to pilots that full alternating rudder inputs could exceed structural limits even below maneuvering speed.
Airbus had earlier expressed concern to American about the AAMP's emphasis on rudder use without effective resolution before the accident.
Without the vertical stabilizer the airplane could not be controlled; both engines separated during the descent and the airplane struck houses in Belle Harbor.
The wreckage was consumed by fire, which also destroyed several houses.

events.text: A Japan Airlines Boeing 747-400 departs runway 31L ahead of flight 587.
Flight 587 begins its takeoff roll on runway 31L about 1 minute 40 seconds behind the 747, within the required wake separation.
Departure control clears the flight to climb on the Bridge Climb; the airplane turns left toward the 747's flight path.
First wake turbulence encounter from the preceding 747; the airplane rocks briefly and the first officer responds with wheel and modest rudder inputs.
Captain remarks 'little wake turbulence, huh?'; first officer agrees.
Second, stronger wake encounter at about 250 knots; the first officer calls for 'max power'.
First officer makes full right, then alternating full left and right rudder pedal inputs together with large wheel inputs over about seven seconds.
Captain says 'hang onto it, hang onto it' as the airplane yaws and rolls.
Sideslip loads exceed the vertical stabilizer's ultimate design load; the fin and rudder separate from the fuselage. A loud bang is recorded.
First officer says 'what the hell are we into... we're stuck in it'; the airplane is now uncontrollable.
Captain says 'get out of it, get out of it'; the airplane pitches down and yaws as both engines separate from the wings in the descent.
End of recording; the airplane strikes houses in Belle Harbor and is destroyed by impact and fire.

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: hang onto it, hang onto it.

cvr.speaker: FO
cvr.text: what the hell are we into... we're stuck in it.

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: get out of it, get out of it.

recommendations.text: Modify transport-category certification standards so that rudder pedal sensitivity and the risk of structural loads from full alternating rudder inputs are addressed across the flight envelope.
recommendations.outcome: FAA and EASA adopted rulemaking on rudder control sensitivity and pedal force characteristics for new designs.

recommendations.text: Require that upset recovery training programs make clear that full or alternating rudder inputs can generate loads exceeding the structure's limits even below maneuvering speed, and that simulator exercises do not encourage such inputs.
recommendations.outcome: American Airlines revised the AAMP; industry Airplane Upset Recovery Training Aid was updated to address rudder use.

recommendations.text: Review the A300-600 and A310 rudder control system and require modifications to reduce sensitivity at high airspeed.
recommendations.outcome: Airbus incorporated a rudder pedal travel limiter warning and revised documentation; no mandatory hardware change was made to the in-service fleet.

recommendations.text: Develop guidance so that manufacturers and operators communicate clearly about aircraft handling characteristics and structural limits related to rudder use.

dissent.position: In comments appended to the report the BEA, on behalf of the French accredited representative and Airbus, disagreed that the A300-600 rudder system design characteristics should be listed as contributing, holding that the rudder system met certification requirements and that the first officer's pedal inputs alone explained the loads.

safety_changes: American Airlines revised its Advanced Aircraft Maneuvering Program to remove the emphasis on rudder use in upset recovery.

Manufacturers and the industry Airplane Upset Recovery Training Aid clarified that maneuvering speed does not protect against full alternating control inputs and that rudder should not be used to counter roll from wake turbulence.
FAA and EASA introduced certification requirements on rudder pedal sensitivity and control force characteristics for new transport airplanes.
Airbus added a rudder pedal travel limiter monitoring and warning system to the A300-600 and A310 and revised pilot documentation on rudder use.

notes: Fatalities (265) include 5 people on the ground; 260 were aboard.
CVR times are taken from the public transcript to within a second; the 747's departure time and the departure clearance are approximate.
Airspeed of about 250 knots at the second wake encounter is as stated in the report; altitude at that moment is not given here because the exact value is not recalled with confidence.
The BEA dissent entry summarizes the French comments appended to the report as recalled; verify against the appendix before relying on the wording.

records.title: Crossair 3597

agencies.name: Swiss Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau
agencies.report_title: Final Report No. 1793 of the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau concerning the accident to the aircraft AVRO 146-RJ100, HB-IXM, operated by Crossair under flight number CRX 3597, on 24 November 2001 near Bassersdorf/ZH

location.name: Wooded hill near Bassersdorf, 4 km short of Zurich runway 28

records.summary: On a night VOR/DME approach to Zurich runway 28 in snow showers and low cloud, the RJ100 descended below the minimum descent altitude of 2,390 ft without the crew having the required visual reference. The aircraft struck trees on a wooded hill near Bassersdorf and crashed, killing 24 of the 33 occupants, including the two pilots.
records.probable_cause: The accident is attributable to the fact that on the final approach to runway 28 the flight crew deliberately continued the descent below the minimum descent altitude without having the necessary prerequisites (visual contact with the approach lights or runway), and that the crew initiated the go-around too late. Contributing factors: the commander's inadequate performance and his pattern of not adhering to procedures, which the operator and the regulator had not adequately addressed; the co-pilot's failure to intervene; the crew's fatigue; the use of a standard VOR/DME approach at night in marginal weather; and the absence of an MSAW at Zurich for this approach.

factors.evidence: The commander continued the descent below the MDA of 2,390 ft QNH without visual reference to the runway or approach lights.
Snow showers and cloud with a base near or below the minima prevented the crew from seeing the runway environment.
The approach was flown in darkness, removing terrain cues during the descent over wooded hills.
The go-around was initiated only after the first officer called for it and the aircraft was already below the safe height; the terrain was struck seconds later.
The first officer did not intervene effectively when the commander descended below minimums, and only late called for a go-around.
The crew had been on duty for a long day with an early start, and the report found that fatigue may have degraded their performance.
Crossair had not acted on the commander's documented history of navigation errors and disregard of procedures, nor on earlier incidents on approach.
The Swiss Federal Office for Civil Aviation had not ensured adequate supervision of the operator's crew standards and the commander's licence history.
The commander's proficiency on the RJ100 and his general performance on non-precision approaches were found to be inadequate.
Zurich ATC had no minimum safe altitude warning for the runway 28 approach area that could have alerted the controller.
The aircraft, in controlled flight in landing configuration, struck treetops on a hill at about 1,780 ft and crashed.
The wreckage caught fire after impact; the fire contributed to the destruction of the aircraft.

events.text: Flight LX3597 departs Berlin Tegel for Zurich with 28 passengers and 5 crew; the commander is pilot flying.
Because of the night noise abatement rules ATC assigns the VOR/DME approach to runway 28 rather than the ILS to runway 14; the crew prepare the non-precision approach.
A preceding Crossair flight lands on runway 28 and reports the runway in sight late; the weather is snow showers with a low cloud base.
Aircraft established on the runway 28 VOR/DME final approach track, flying manually with the landing configuration set.
The aircraft descends towards the MDA of 2,390 ft QNH; the commander reports visual with the ground below but not with the runway.
The aircraft descends below the MDA without the required visual reference; the first officer reads out heights and mentions the minimum.
The radio altimeter reaches 300 ft over the rising wooded terrain of the hill near Bassersdorf; the aircraft is at about 1,900 ft QNH.
The first officer calls for a go-around; the commander applies go-around power and pitches up.
The aircraft strikes treetops on the hill at about 1,780 ft, about 4 km from the runway threshold, and crashes into the forest.
The wreckage catches fire; nine occupants escape, 24 including both pilots die.

recommendations.text: Ensure that operators identify and remedy crew members whose performance shows recurring deficiencies, and that the licensing authority takes into account a pilot's record when renewing licences.
Introduce a minimum safe altitude warning system at Zurich covering the non-precision approaches.
recommendations.outcome: MSAW was implemented at Zurich.

recommendations.text: Equip runway 28 with an instrument landing system or an approach with vertical guidance to reduce the risk of non-precision approaches at night in poor weather.
recommendations.outcome: An ILS was installed on runway 28 at Zurich.

recommendations.text: Strengthen CRM training so that first officers intervene decisively when minima are breached, and review crew rostering to limit fatigue.

safety_changes: ILS installed on Zurich runway 28 and MSAW implemented at Zurich approach.
Crossair (later Swiss) revised crew performance monitoring and CRM training.
Reinforced Swiss oversight of operator crew records and licence renewals.

notes: Clock strings are UTC; the accident occurred at about 21:06 UTC (22:06 local). Seconds are estimated except the approximate impact time.
Altitudes (MDA 2,390 ft QNH, impact about 1,780 ft) are from the report; the 300 ft radio altitude moment is approximate.
The role of fatigue is described by the report as a possible contributing factor; the report's report number 1793 and publication date are from memory.
Recommendation ids not reproduced.

records.title: Überlingen midair collision (Bashkirian 2937 / DHL 611)

agencies.name: Bundesstelle für Flugunfalluntersuchung
agencies.report_title: Investigation Report AX001-1-2/02: Collision of Tupolev TU154M and Boeing B757-200 near Überlingen, Lake Constance, 1 July 2002

location.name: Near Überlingen, Lake Constance, Baden-Württemberg

records.summary: A Bashkirian Airlines Tu-154M and a DHL Boeing 757-23APF (A9C-DHL) were converging at FL360 at night in Swiss-controlled airspace over southern Germany. The single controller on duty at Skyguide Zurich, working two positions with the short-term conflict alert switched off for maintenance and the telephone system degraded, noticed the conflict late and instructed the Tu-154 to descend. Seconds later TCAS commanded the Tu-154 to climb and the 757 to descend. The Tu-154 crew followed the controller's repeated descent instruction rather than the TCAS RA, and the two aircraft collided at 34,890 ft, killing all 71 people aboard both aircraft.
records.probable_cause: Immediate causes: the imminent separation infringement was not noticed by ATC in time, and the instruction for the Tu-154M to descend was given at a time when the prescribed separation could no longer be ensured; the Tu-154M crew followed the ATC instruction to descend and continued to do so even after TCAS advised them to climb, so that the manoeuvre was contrary to the TCAS resolution advisory. Systemic causes: the integration of ACAS/TCAS II into the aviation system was insufficient and did not correspond in all points with the system philosophy, with the regulations concerning ACAS/TCAS published by ICAO and the manufacturers being incomplete and partially contradictory; management and quality assurance of the air navigation service company did not ensure that during the night all open workstations were continuously staffed; and management and quality assurance tolerated for years that during times of low traffic flow at night only one controller worked and the other retired to rest.

factors.evidence: Only one controller was on duty at Zurich ACC, handling two workstations and frequencies, while his colleague was resting, as tolerated by Skyguide management.
The Skyguide short-term conflict alert (STCA) optical warning was switched off for maintenance work on the radar system, and the main telephone system was unavailable.
Skyguide management and quality assurance tolerated single-controller night operations and did not ensure safe procedures during system maintenance.

The controller noticed the conflict late, instructed the Tu-154 to descend about 44 seconds before the collision, and repeated the instruction with an incorrect traffic position ('at your 2 o'clock') after TCAS had commanded a climb.
TCAS issued a climb RA to the Tu-154 and a descend RA to the 757 seven seconds after the controller's descent instruction; the Tu-154 crew followed ATC and descended into the 757's descent.
Bashkirian Airlines' TCAS operating documentation and training were ambiguous about the priority of RAs over ATC instructions, reflecting contradictory regulations.
ICAO and manufacturer regulations on TCAS were incomplete and partially contradictory, and Swiss oversight of Skyguide's night staffing was inadequate.
In the Tu-154 cockpit the pilot-in-command in the left seat and the instructor gave conflicting comments about following TCAS or ATC, and the descent was continued.
The collision occurred at night, limiting visual acquisition; the 757 crew and the Tu-154 crew saw each other only seconds before impact.
The 757's vertical fin struck the Tu-154 fuselage at 34,890 ft; both aircraft broke up and fell near Überlingen.

events.text: At Zurich ACC the second controller retires to rest, leaving one controller working both radar positions; the STCA is switched off and the telephone system degraded for maintenance work.
The controller is busy with a delayed Aero Lloyd A320 approach to Friedrichshafen on the second frequency and attempts to telephone Friedrichshafen, without success because of the phone outage.
The Tu-154M at FL360 and the 757 at FL360 converge on crossing tracks about 45 seconds apart; both TCAS systems issue traffic advisories.
Karlsruhe upper area control's STCA alerts its controller, who tries repeatedly to phone Zurich but cannot get through.
Zurich controller instructs the Tu-154 to descend to FL350 expedite because of crossing traffic; the Tu-154 crew begin to descend.
TCAS resolution advisories: 'climb' for the Tu-154 and 'descend' for the 757. The 757 crew follow their RA and descend.
In the Tu-154 the instructor says the controller has told them to descend; the co-pilot notes that TCAS says climb; the descent is continued.
Zurich controller repeats the descent instruction, describing the traffic as at the Tu-154's 2 o'clock position (it was actually to the left); the Tu-154 crew acknowledge and increase the descent.
The 757 crew report to Zurich that they are in a TCAS descent; the transmission is not acknowledged by the controller, who is on the other frequency.
TCAS in the 757 commands 'increase descent'; in the Tu-154 TCAS commands 'increase climb', but the aircraft continues to descend.
The Tu-154 crew see the 757's lights and pull up; the 757 crew see the Tu-154 and push over. Neither manoeuvre is enough.
The two aircraft collide at 34,890 ft at almost a right angle; the 757's fin severs the Tu-154 fuselage. Both aircraft break up and fall near Überlingen; all 71 occupants (69 and 2) killed.

recommendations.text: Change the international requirements so that pilots are required to follow TCAS resolution advisories regardless of contrary ATC instructions, and clarify the regulations and training documentation accordingly.
recommendations.outcome: ICAO amended Annex 2 / PANS-OPS in 2003 to require pilots to follow RAs even when contrary to ATC instructions.

recommendations.text: Develop a TCAS RA downlink so that controllers are informed automatically when an RA has been issued, and modify TCAS logic to reverse an RA if one aircraft does not comply.
recommendations.outcome: TCAS II version 7.1 with RA reversal logic was mandated in Europe; RA downlink via Mode S was developed.

recommendations.text: Ensure that all open workstations at air navigation service units are continuously staffed, that safety-relevant technical work is coordinated with operations, and that conflict alert systems remain operational or the airspace capacity is reduced accordingly.
recommendations.outcome: Skyguide revised its night staffing and maintenance coordination procedures.

recommendations.text: Ensure that TCAS training programmes and operating manuals give unambiguous guidance that RAs take precedence over ATC instructions.

safety_changes: ICAO rule change: TCAS RAs take precedence over ATC instructions; standard phraseology for reporting RAs.
TCAS II version 7.1 with reversal logic and 'level off' advisories mandated in Europe.
Skyguide changes to night staffing, maintenance coordination and safety management; Swiss oversight strengthened.

notes: Record aircraft is the Tu-154M RA-85816 (69 occupants); the other aircraft was DHL Boeing 757-23APF A9C-DHL (2 crew). Occupants and fatalities combine both aircraft.

Key clock times (21:34:42 Karlsruhe STCA, 21:34:49 descent instruction, 21:34:56 RAs, 21:35:03 repeated instruction, 21:35:24 increase descent, 21:35:32 collision) follow the BFU report; earlier times approximate.
Recommendation ids not reproduced.

records.title: Air Midwest 5481

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Loss of Pitch Control During Takeoff, Air Midwest Flight 5481, Raytheon (Beechcraft) 1900D, N233YV, Charlotte, North Carolina, January 8, 2003

records.operator: Air Midwest (operating as US Airways Express)

location.name: US Airways maintenance hangar area, Charlotte Douglas International Airport, North Carolina

records.summary: Immediately after rotation from runway 18R at Charlotte the Beech 1900D pitched up steeply. The crew pushed the control column fully forward but the elevator's nose-down travel had been restricted to about half its range during a maintenance check two days earlier, and the airplane's center of gravity was well aft of the certified limit because of underestimated passenger and baggage weights. Pitch reached about 52 degrees, the airplane stalled at about 1,150 feet, rolled and struck a maintenance hangar 37 seconds after liftoff. All 21 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The airplane's loss of pitch control during takeoff. The loss of pitch control resulted from the incorrect rigging of the elevator control system compounded by the airplane's aft center of gravity, which was substantially aft of the certified aft limit. Contributing to the cause of the accident were (1) Air Midwest's lack of oversight of the work being performed at the Huntington, West Virginia, maintenance station; (2) Air Midwest's maintenance procedures and documentation; (3) Air Midwest's weight and balance program; (4) the Raytheon Aerospace quality assurance inspector's failure to detect the incorrect rigging of the elevator system; (5) the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) average weight assumptions in its weight and balance program guidance at the time of the accident; and (6) the FAA's lack of oversight of Air Midwest's maintenance program and its weight and balance program.

factors.evidence: During a detail-6 check at Huntington two nights before the accident, elevator control cables were re-tensioned with steps of the rigging procedure skipped, leaving the elevator's nose-down travel restricted to about 7 degrees of the normal 14.
The Raytheon Aerospace quality assurance inspector did not detect the incorrect rigging, and the required-inspection-item process was not followed.
The mechanic performing the work was receiving on-the-job training and had not previously rigged a 1900D elevator system; supervision and training at the contract station were inadequate.
Air Midwest lacked oversight of the contract maintenance work at Huntington and its maintenance procedures and documentation were deficient.

The load manifest used FAA average passenger and bag weights (175 and 20 pounds); actual weights placed the center of gravity about 5 percent MAC aft of the certified limit and the airplane about 600 pounds over its maximum takeoff weight.
FAA average weight guidance was outdated and the FAA had not adequately overseen Air Midwest's maintenance and weight and balance programs.
The misrigged elevator could not produce enough nose-down moment; full forward column reached the restricted elevator stop.
With the aft CG and restricted elevator, the crew had no ability to lower the nose despite full forward control input.
Pitch reached about 52 degrees nose up and the airplane stalled at about 1,150 feet above the ground.
The airplane rolled left after the stall and descended out of control into a hangar.
The airplane was destroyed by impact and fire.

events.text: About two days before the accident, during a detail-6 check at Huntington, West Virginia, the elevator control cables are re-tensioned; steps in the rigging procedure are skipped and the elevator's nose-down travel is left restricted.
The quality assurance inspector signs off the elevator work without detecting the incorrect rigging; the airplane is returned to service and flies several uneventful legs.
The crew complete the load manifest using FAA average passenger and baggage weights; the calculated center of gravity appears within limits although the actual CG is well aft of the limit.
Tower clears flight 5481 for takeoff on runway 18R.
Takeoff roll begins with the captain as pilot flying.
Rotation and liftoff; the nose continues to rise faster than commanded.
Both pilots apply forward control column; the column reaches the stop but the elevator is limited to about half its nose-down travel and pitch keeps increasing.
First officer reports the pitch problem to the tower and declares an emergency.
Pitch reaches about 52 degrees nose up as airspeed decays; the crew reduce power and roll in an attempt to lower the nose.
The airplane stalls at about 1,150 feet above the ground and rolls to the left.
The airplane strikes a US Airways maintenance hangar in a steep nose-down attitude and bursts into flames; the recording ends.

recommendations.text: Revise average passenger and baggage weight guidance based on current survey data and require operators to periodically validate the weights they use.
recommendations.outcome: FAA Advisory Circular 120-27E (2005) raised standard average passenger weights and required operator weight surveys.

recommendations.text: Require operators of small transport airplanes to use actual or validated weights when average weights could push the airplane outside its center of gravity envelope.
recommendations.outcome: Operators of 19-seat aircraft adopted revised loading and seating procedures.

recommendations.text: Strengthen oversight of contract and outsourced maintenance, including verification that required-inspection-item procedures, on-the-job training and work card documentation are followed.
recommendations.outcome: FAA revised guidance on surveillance of contract maintenance providers.

recommendations.text: Revise the 1900D maintenance manual so that the elevator control system rigging procedure explicitly requires a full travel check after any cable tension adjustment.
recommendations.outcome: The maintenance manual and work cards were revised and the fleet was re-inspected.

safety_changes: FAA revised standard average passenger and baggage weights (AC 120-27E, 2005), increasing them substantially and requiring operators to survey actual weights.
Operators of Beech 1900 and similar 19-seat airplanes revised loading and seating procedures to keep the center of gravity within limits.
Beech 1900D elevator control cable rigging procedures and work cards were revised; fleet inspections found other misrigged airplanes.
FAA strengthened surveillance of outsourced and contract maintenance and of on-the-job training at repair stations.

notes: The rotation clock time is estimated at about 08:46:39 EST from the 08:47:16 end of recording and the report's 37-second flight duration; t values of the takeoff sequence are approximate.

Maximum pitch of about 52 degrees and stall at about 1,150 feet are as stated in the report; the amount of overweight (about 600 pounds) and CG excess (about 5 percent MAC) are as recalled and may differ slightly.
The maintenance and inspection events are given a nominal t of about two days before the accident; the exact night of the work is 6 to 7 January 2003.
Aircraft MSN is not given because it is not recalled with confidence.

records.title: UTAGE 141

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la Sécurité de l'Aviation Civile

location.name: Cotonou Cadjèhoun Aerodrome

records.summary: Union des Transports Africains Flight GIH 141, a Boeing 727-223, took off from Cotonou on 25 December 2003 with overloaded cargo and an unknown center of gravity. During the takeoff roll, the aircraft struck a building containing the localizer 118 meters past the runway end and crashed into the sea, killing 141 people.
records.probable_cause: The crew attempted to rotate an aircraft that was significantly overloaded (approximately 85.5 tons versus the planned 78 tons) with a forward center of gravity (14% versus the planned 19%), combined with inadequate weight and balance procedures and lack of organizational oversight by the operator.

factors.evidence: The aircraft was overloaded at approximately 85.5 tons with center of gravity at 14%, far forward of the planned 19%, preventing normal takeoff performance (p. 9-10)
The operator possessed neither the material infrastructure nor the skills required to operate a large transport airplane (p. 60)
Passenger boarding and baggage loading took place in conditions of great confusion with no overall supervision or rigor; no document relating to boarding and loading could be supplied (p. 9, 61)
The Guinean civil aviation authority applied ICAO procedures but lacked detailed national regulations and means to inspect compliance (p. 60)
The aircraft struck the localizer building 118 meters past runway end and crashed into the Bight of Benin (p. 9)

events.text: Aircraft landed at Cotonou after departure from Conakry with 86 passengers; 9 disembarked, 63 new passengers checked in, 10 from Togo boarded; airplane at full capacity
Pre-flight checklist began; crew selected flaps 25°, air conditioning shut down
Flight cleared to roll; co-pilot was pilot flying
Takeoff thrust requested and brake release performed; aircraft began acceleration
Speed reached 137 knots; Captain called V1 and Vr; co-pilot applied back pressure on control column with initial minimal effect on aircraft angle of attack
Aircraft struck the localizer building at 13:59:11 UTC on the extended runway centerline, right main landing gear broke off, aircraft banked right and crashed onto beach

recommendations.text: Urgently draw up complete regulations in accordance with ICAO recommended standards and ensure possession of structures and means to enforce these regulations
Ensure that aerodromes check the loading of aircraft and that a copy of the weight and balance sheet is filed with them
Modify certification requirements to ensure presence of on-board systems to determine weight and balance on new commercial aircraft

notes: Read SYNOPSIS, History of Flight, Conclusions (Findings and Causes), and Recommendations sections
Fatality count uncertain due to identification issues; 141 bodies found
Actual weight was approximately 85.5 tons versus planned 78 tons
Center of gravity was 14% versus planned 19%

records.title: Flash Airlines 604

agencies.name: Egyptian Civil Aviation Authority
agencies.report_title: Final Report of the Accident Investigation - Flash Airlines Flight 604, Boeing 737-300 SU-ZCF, Sharm el-Sheikh, 3 January 2004

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la sécurité de l'aviation civile

location.name: Red Sea, about 15 km south of Sharm el-Sheikh

records.summary: After a night takeoff from Sharm el-Sheikh runway 22R, the 737 began a climbing left turn over the sea. The bank gradually reversed to the right and continued to increase, with the captain's control inputs failing to arrest it, until the aircraft reached about 111 degrees of right bank and descended into the Red Sea. All 148 people on board were killed.
records.probable_cause: The Egyptian investigation could not determine a conclusive cause. It found no evidence of a failure of aircraft systems that would explain the loss of control, and considered several possibilities including a flight control or autopilot anomaly and spatial disorientation of the crew, without being able to establish which applied. The BEA and the NTSB, in formal comments appended to the report, concluded that the accident was most probably caused by the captain's spatial disorientation and loss of situational awareness during the night climbing turn over the sea, with inadequate crew coordination and monitoring.

factors.evidence: The takeoff and climbing turn were made at night over the sea with no external visual references.
BEA and NTSB attributed the increasing right bank and the captain's failure to correct it to spatial disorientation; the ECAA listed it as one possibility.
The BEA analysis noted that the accelerating climb with turn could produce misleading vestibular sensations in the absence of visual references.
The captain made comments inconsistent with the aircraft's actual attitude while the bank increased beyond 40 degrees.
The first officer called the bank angle several times but did not take control or apply corrective inputs until very late.
Crew coordination broke down: the captain's requests to engage the autopilot and the first officer's warnings were not resolved into a recovery.
The autopilot was engaged briefly and disengaged during the turn, and the crew's expectations of what the automation was doing were unclear.
Right aileron inputs were recorded while the bank increased to the right; recovery inputs came only when the attitude was extreme.
The comments of the accredited representatives cited deficiencies in the operator's training on upset recovery and crew coordination.
Flash Airlines had been the subject of foreign audit findings and the report discussed the operator's oversight and crew scheduling.
Oversight of the operator by the Egyptian authority was discussed as a systemic contributor in the accredited representatives' comments.
The aircraft reached about 111 degrees of right bank and a steep nose-down attitude before striking the sea at high speed.

events.text: Flight 604 takes off from runway 22R at Sharm el-Sheikh at night with the captain as pilot flying, bound for Cairo and Paris with 135 passengers and 13 crew.
Climbing through about 2,000 ft the captain initiates the planned left turn towards the departure track over the sea.
Captain calls for the autopilot to be engaged; it engages and disengages within seconds, with the aircraft in a left bank.
Bank angle reduces from left through wings level and begins to increase to the right, with right aileron input recorded.
First officer calls the increasing bank; the captain replies with comments suggesting he believes the aircraft is turning left.
Right bank passes 40 degrees and continues to increase as the aircraft's pitch attitude falls; altitude peaks at about 5,400 ft.
First officer repeatedly calls 'overbank'; the captain finally applies left aileron and the bank momentarily reduces.
Bank angle reaches about 111 degrees right with the nose about 40 degrees below the horizon; the aircraft descends rapidly toward the sea, exceeding maximum operating speed.
Crew inputs begin to roll the aircraft back toward level, but there is insufficient height; the aircraft strikes the Red Sea at high speed about 15 km south of the airport.

recommendations.text: Reinforce training on upset recognition and recovery, spatial disorientation and crew resource management, including transfer of control procedures.
Strengthen regulatory oversight of Egyptian operators, including crew scheduling, training records and flight data monitoring.
Review the 737 autopilot engagement logic and aileron control system for any anomaly that could contribute to an uncommanded roll.
recommendations.outcome: Investigations found no system failure explaining the roll.

dissent.position: The BEA did not agree with the conclusion that no cause could be determined. It concluded that the accident was most likely due to the captain's spatial disorientation during the night climbing turn, a loss of situational awareness, and inadequate crew coordination, and criticised the report for giving undue weight to unsubstantiated technical hypotheses.

The NTSB, in its formal comments, concurred with the BEA that the available evidence pointed to the captain's spatial disorientation and inadequate crew monitoring and intervention, with no evidence of a flight control system failure.

safety_changes: Increased attention in Europe and France to third-country operator oversight; Flash Airlines ceased operations in 2004.
Renewed emphasis on somatogravic illusion and night departures over water in upset prevention training.

notes: Local clock times are approximate (takeoff about 04:42, impact about 04:45); t values are estimated from published FDR descriptions and may be off by tens of seconds.
The ECAA report date and the exact wording of the BEA and NTSB comments are paraphrased; both agencies' comments were appended to the final report.
Peak altitude (about 5,400 ft) and bank angle (about 111 degrees) are from published FDR summaries.
Lat/lon approximate; ECAA has no stable public URL for the report so agency-level sources are given.

records.title: Pinnacle Airlines 3701

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Crash of Pinnacle Airlines Flight 3701, Bombardier CL-600-2B19, N8396A, Jefferson City, Missouri, October 14, 2004

location.name: Residential area about 2.5 miles south of Jefferson City Memorial Airport, Missouri

records.summary: On a night repositioning flight with no passengers, the two pilots flew the CRJ-200 in an unprofessional manner, including a pitch-up manoeuvre and a climb to the aircraft's 41,000 ft ceiling at a low airspeed. The aircraft stalled at FL410, both engines flamed out during the upset, and the engine cores subsequently seized (core lock). The crew did not restore power or reach an airport and the aircraft crashed in a residential area near Jefferson City, killing both pilots.
records.probable_cause: The NTSB determined the probable cause was (1) the pilots' unprofessional behavior, deviation from standard operating procedures, and poor airmanship, which resulted in an in-flight emergency from which they were unable to recover, in part because of the pilots' inadequate training; (2) the pilots' failure to prepare for an emergency landing in a timely manner, including communicating with air traffic controllers immediately after the emergency about the loss of both engines and the availability of landing sites; and (3) the pilots' improper management of the double engine failure checklist, which allowed the engine cores to stop rotating and resulted in the core lock engine condition. Contributing were the core lock engine condition, which prevented at least one engine from being restarted, and the airplane flight manuals that did not communicate to pilots the importance of maintaining a minimum airspeed to keep the engine cores rotating.

factors.evidence: The pilots performed a pitch-up manoeuvre, exchanged seats in flight and climbed to FL410 at a low airspeed in vertical speed mode contrary to standard operating procedures.
The crew allowed airspeed to decay during the climb and at FL410 without recognising the approaching stall.
The stick shaker and then the stick pusher activated at FL410 as the aircraft approached and entered the stall.
The aircraft stalled at FL410 and the resulting upset disrupted airflow to both engines.
The pilots pulled against the stick pusher rather than reducing pitch attitude to recover.
Both engines flamed out during the stall and neither could be restarted; the aircraft crashed after a power-off glide.
The NTSB cited the pilots' inadequate training in high-altitude aerodynamics and stall recovery as part of the probable cause.
The crew initially told ATC only one engine had failed and did not promptly communicate the double engine failure or prepare for a forced landing.
The airplane flight manuals did not communicate the importance of maintaining a minimum airspeed to keep the engine cores rotating after a flameout.
The double engine failure checklist did not adequately guide pilots to maintain windmilling airspeed before attempting restarts.
The forced landing attempt was made at night with no power in a residential area.

events.text: Repositioning flight departs Little Rock for Minneapolis with only the two pilots on board.
Shortly after takeoff the crew performs an abrupt pitch-up manoeuvre reaching about 1.8 g.
The pilots exchange seats during the climb.
Crew decides to climb to FL410, the aircraft's maximum certificated altitude ('forty-one it'), and request the level from ATC.
Climb continued in autopilot vertical speed mode at about 500 ft/min; airspeed decays progressively as the aircraft approaches FL410.
Aircraft levels at FL410 at a low airspeed; the autopilot holds altitude while the airspeed continues to decrease.
Stick shaker activates; the autopilot disconnects.
Stick pusher activates repeatedly; the pilots pull back against the pusher and the aircraft stalls.
Both engines flame out during the upset; the aircraft is now without engine power.
Crew declares an emergency to ATC but reports the loss of only one engine.
Crew attempts windmill restarts but keeps the airspeed well below the 300 kt required by the checklist, so the engine cores do not spin up.
APU started at lower altitude; APU-assisted restart attempts fail as the engine cores have seized (core lock).
Crew finally informs ATC that both engines have failed; ATC provides vectors toward Jefferson City Memorial Airport.
Controller gives distance and heading to the airport; the crew reports they will not make the runway.
Crew remarks they are going to hit houses as the aircraft descends in darkness toward a residential area.
Aircraft strikes trees and the ground in a residential area about 2.5 miles south of the airport; both pilots are killed, no one on the ground is injured.

recommendations.text: Require CRJ operators and the manufacturer to revise flight manuals and checklists to state the minimum airspeed needed to keep engine cores rotating after a double engine failure and to address the core lock condition.
Require air carriers to provide training in high-altitude aerodynamics, stall recognition and stall recovery at high altitude, including the correct response to stick pusher activation.
Address unprofessional behaviour and non-adherence to standard operating procedures on non-revenue repositioning flights through operator oversight and pilot professionalism programs.

safety_changes: Bombardier revised CRJ flight manuals and the double engine failure checklist to emphasise maintaining airspeed to keep the engine cores rotating and to describe core lock.
Airlines added high-altitude aerodynamics and stall recovery training, and the accident became a standard case study in pilot professionalism.

notes: t0 is set to the approximate time of stick shaker activation at FL410 (about 21:54 CDT); event times other than takeoff (21:21), flameout (about 21:55) and impact (about 22:15) are approximations to the nearest few minutes.
Flight number, MSN and coordinates are approximate; coordinates mark the general crash area south of Jefferson City.
Recommendation numbers were not recalled with confidence and are left null.
No CVR quotations included; the widely reported 'forty-one it' remark is paraphrased as a crew_speech event.

records.title: Air France 358
records.time_reference: EDT (local); only the touchdown time is given to the minute, other clocks omitted

agencies.name: Transportation Safety Board of Canada
agencies.report_title: Runway Overrun and Fire, Air France, Airbus A340-313 F-GLZQ, Toronto/Lester B. Pearson International Airport, Ontario, 02 August 2005

location.name: Toronto Pearson International Airport, runway 24L overrun into Etobicoke Creek ravine

records.summary: Arriving from Paris during a severe thunderstorm, the A340 landed on Toronto's runway 24L in heavy rain with a tailwind, touching down about 3,800 ft along the 9,000 ft runway. Thrust reversers were selected late, and the aircraft left the runway end at about 80 kt, crossed the grass and came to rest in the Etobicoke Creek ravine, where it was destroyed by fire. All 297 passengers and 12 crew evacuated; 12 people were seriously injured.
records.probable_cause: The TSB found that the crew continued the approach into a thunderstorm in which the wind shifted to a tailwind and heavy rain reduced visibility. The aircraft crossed the threshold high, floated in a prolonged flare and touched down far down the wet runway; the thrust reversers were selected 12.8 seconds after touchdown and full braking was delayed, so the aircraft could not be stopped on the runway remaining. The crew had not calculated the landing distance required for the conditions, and Air France had no clear guidance requiring a go-around when a long landing developed. The absence of a runway end safety area meant the overrun ended in a ravine, and the ensuing fire destroyed the aircraft.

factors.evidence: A line of severe thunderstorms with lightning and intense rain was over the airport during the approach and landing; a ground-operations red alert was in effect at Pearson.
The wind shifted during the final approach so that the aircraft landed with a tailwind component of about 10 kt.
Intense rain on short final and in the flare reduced forward visibility; the pilot flying lost sight of the runway end environment during the flare.
Runway 24L was water-covered by heavy rain, reducing braking effectiveness.
The aircraft crossed the threshold about 40 ft high and touched down about 3,800 ft beyond the threshold of the 9,000 ft runway.
Thrust reversers were selected 12.8 seconds after touchdown and maximum braking was not applied immediately.
The crew did not consider a go-around when the landing became long; Air France procedures did not clearly require one in that situation.
The crew were managing a deteriorating weather situation, wind shifts and reduced visibility in the final seconds of the approach.
The crew did not compute the landing distance required for a wet runway with a tailwind before landing.
The end of runway 24L was not provided with a 300 m runway end safety area; the overrun terminated in the Etobicoke Creek ravine, which increased the damage and the fire.
The aircraft departed the runway end at about 80 kt and travelled across the grass into the ravine.
A fire developed after the aircraft came to rest and destroyed the aircraft.
Some exits and slides were unusable because of fire and damage, and many passengers took carry-on baggage with them, slowing the evacuation.

events.text: Severe thunderstorms approach Toronto Pearson; a red alert suspends ground operations for lightning. The crew brief the ILS approach to runway 24L, which is wet.
Preceding aircraft land; the crew are advised of the weather but are not given a reason to expect the runway to be unusable.
Established on the ILS for runway 24L with the autopilot engaged; intense rain and lightning are visible ahead. The crew continue the approach.
The wind shifts to a tailwind component of about 10 kt as the storm passes over the airport; rain intensity increases sharply.
Autopilot disconnected; the first officer flies the final approach manually in heavy rain and reduced visibility.
Aircraft crosses the runway threshold about 40 ft higher than normal.
Prolonged flare; the pilot flying loses visual reference to the runway end in the intense rain. No go-around is considered.
Touchdown about 3,800 ft beyond the threshold of the 9,000 ft runway, leaving about 5,100 ft of wet runway.
Ground spoilers deploy on touchdown.
Thrust reversers selected 12.8 seconds after touchdown; heavy braking applied late.
Aircraft leaves the end of runway 24L at about 80 kt, crosses the grass overrun area and drops into the Etobicoke Creek ravine, coming to rest about 300 m beyond the runway end.
Fire develops on the left side; evacuation begins. Some exits and slides are unusable and many passengers take carry-on baggage.
All 309 occupants are out of the aircraft within about two minutes; 12 are seriously injured. The aircraft is destroyed by fire.

recommendations.text: Require crews to establish, before landing, that a safety margin exists between the landing distance available and the landing distance required for the actual runway and weather conditions.
Require that all Code 4 runways have a 300 m runway end safety area or an equivalent means of stopping aircraft.
recommendations.outcome: Toronto Pearson subsequently extended its runway end safety areas; Transport Canada later moved to require RESAs at major airports.

recommendations.text: Require operators to provide clear guidance on go-around decisions when a landing is not proceeding as expected, including after the flare.
Address the risks posed by passengers retrieving carry-on baggage during an emergency evacuation.

safety_changes: Air France revised its approach and landing procedures and go-around policy for landings in deteriorating weather.
Toronto Pearson and other Canadian airports improved runway end safety areas; Transport Canada worked toward mandatory RESA standards.
Industry and regulators reinforced pre-landing landing-distance assessment for wet or contaminated runways and tailwinds.

notes: Event t values are approximate reconstructions from the report narrative (touchdown 3,800 ft down the runway, reversers 12.8 s after touchdown, exit from runway at about 80 kt); the report's exact clock times are not reproduced.
Threshold crossing height of about 40 ft high is from memory of the report and should be verified.
The number of usable exits and slides is not stated precisely; the record only says some were unusable.
TSB recommendation numbers from the December 2007 report (A07 series) are not given because the exact mapping to text was not verified.

records.title: Tuninter 1153

agencies.name: Agenzia Nazionale per la Sicurezza del Volo
agencies.report_title: Final report on the accident to ATR 72-202 TS-LBB, ditching off Capo Gallo (Palermo), 6 August 2005

location.name: Tyrrhenian Sea off Capo Gallo, north-east of Palermo

records.summary: The day before the accident, maintenance in Tunis replaced the aircraft's fuel quantity indicator with a unit designed for the ATR 42, which is physically interchangeable but over-reads on the ATR 72. The aircraft was refuelled on the basis of the false indication and departed Bari with far less fuel than displayed. In cruise both engines flamed out from fuel exhaustion; the crew attempted restarts and diverted toward Palermo but could not reach it, and the aircraft was ditched off Capo Gallo. The fuselage broke into three sections; 16 of the 39 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The ANSV concluded that the accident was caused by fuel exhaustion resulting from the installation of an ATR 42 fuel quantity indicator on the ATR 72, which over-read the fuel on board, so that the aircraft was dispatched with insufficient fuel. Contributing factors included the maintenance organisation's failure to verify the part number before installation and the interchangeability of the two indicators, the crew's failure to detect the discrepancy between fuel uplift, fuel used and indicated quantity, and, after the double flame-out, the crew's attempts to restart the engines rather than fly the aircraft at the optimum glide speed toward the nearest airport, which reduced the distance covered.

factors.evidence: On 5 August the fuel quantity indicator was replaced in Tunis with an ATR 42 unit whose part number differs from the ATR 72 unit; the mechanic did not verify the part number applicability.
The ATR 42 and ATR 72 fuel quantity indicators are physically interchangeable and nearly identical in appearance despite different calibrations.
The indicator over-read by more than 2,000 kg, so the crew refuelled to a displayed quantity that did not correspond to the actual fuel on board.
The report found the crew did not detect the inconsistency between the fuel uplifted, the fuel used since the last refuelling and the indicated quantity.
The right engine flamed out in cruise at FL230 followed by the left engine about 100 seconds later because the tanks were empty.
Both engines stopped and could not be restarted; the aircraft became a glider about 40 nm from Palermo.
The crew repeatedly attempted engine restarts and did not maintain the optimum glide speed or configuration, shortening the glide distance.
The ANSV found that the crew's training for a double engine failure and forced landing at sea was inadequate.
The aircraft was ditched in the sea off Capo Gallo; the fuselage broke into three sections on impact.
Several occupants died from the impact and in the water; the report examined the survival aspects, including the seats and the life jackets, after the fuselage broke up.

events.text: At Tunis on 5 August a mechanic replaces the fuel quantity indicator with an ATR 42 unit taken from stores, without verifying the part number applicability.
The aircraft is refuelled for the Tunis-Bari and Bari-Djerba sectors on the basis of the indicated quantity, which over-reads by more than 2,000 kg.
The crew at Bari accept the displayed fuel quantity without reconciling it with the fuel uplift and the fuel used on the inbound sector.
Departure from Bari for Djerba; climb to FL230.
The right engine flames out in cruise at FL230 over the Tyrrhenian Sea.
About 100 seconds later the left engine also flames out; the fuel gauge still shows fuel remaining.
The crew declare an emergency and request to divert to Palermo, about 40 nm away.
The crew make repeated attempts to restart the engines instead of establishing the optimum glide speed toward Palermo.
Recognising that Palermo cannot be reached, the captain prepares to ditch and informs ATC and the cabin.
The aircraft is ditched off Capo Gallo; the fuselage breaks into three sections. 23 occupants survive and are rescued by boats; 16 die.

recommendations.text: Make the ATR 42 and ATR 72 fuel quantity indicators non-interchangeable or clearly distinguishable, and review the associated maintenance documentation and parts identification.
recommendations.outcome: ATR issued instructions distinguishing the indicators and revised the illustrated parts catalogue.

recommendations.text: Improve maintenance procedures for part number verification and the oversight of the operator's maintenance organisation.
Reinforce crew procedures for checking fuel on board against uplift and consumption, and training for double engine failure, glide management and ditching.

safety_changes: ATR fuel quantity indicators for the ATR 42 and ATR 72 were made distinguishable and the parts documentation was revised.
A Palermo court convicted the two pilots and several Tuninter maintenance and management staff in 2009 in connection with the accident.

notes: The engine flame-out time (about 15:24 UTC) and ditching time (about 15:39 UTC) are from the published narrative to the minute; intermediate event t values are approximate offsets.
The ANSV final report number and publication date were not verified.
The over-read magnitude (more than 2,000 kg) is given from the published summary; the exact figure was not verified.
The BEA's accredited-representative role is assumed from ATR being a French-registered manufacturer.
Lat/lon are approximate for the ditching location off Capo Gallo.

records.title: Helios Airways 522

agencies.name: Air Accident Investigation and Aviation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report: Helios Airways Flight HCY522, Boeing 737-31S at Grammatiko, Hellas on 14 August 2005

agencies.name: Cyprus Air Accident and Incident Investigation Board

location.name: Hills near Grammatiko, about 33 km north of Athens

records.summary: After overnight maintenance the pressurisation mode selector was left in MANUAL and not detected by the crew during pre-flight checks. As the aircraft climbed through about 12,000 ft the cabin altitude warning horn sounded, but the crew misidentified it as a takeoff configuration warning and became confused by subsequent master caution alerts. Both pilots became incapacitated by hypoxia and the aircraft continued to Athens on autopilot, holding for over two hours until fuel exhaustion caused both engines to flame out and it crashed into hills near Grammatiko. All 121 on board died.
records.probable_cause: Direct causes: non-recognition that the cabin pressurisation mode selector was in the MANUAL position during the performance of the Preflight, Before Start and After Takeoff checklists; non-identification of the warnings and the reasons for the activation of the warnings (cabin altitude warning horn, passenger oxygen masks deployment indication, master caution); and incapacitation of the flight crew due to hypoxia, resulting in continuation of the flight via the flight management computer and autopilot, depletion of the fuel and engine flameout, and the impact of the aircraft with the ground. Latent causes: the operator's deficiencies in organisation, quality management and safety culture; the regulatory authority's inadequate execution of its oversight responsibilities; inadequate application of CRM principles; and the ineffectiveness of measures taken by the manufacturer in response to previous pressurisation incidents, particularly the similarity of the cabin altitude and takeoff configuration warning horns.

factors.evidence: During a pressurisation leak check the night before, the ground engineer left the pressurisation mode selector in MANUAL instead of returning it to AUTO.
The crew failed to detect the MANUAL selection during the Preflight, Before Start and After Takeoff checklists.
With the outflow valve partly open in manual, the cabin did not pressurise and cabin altitude climbed with the aircraft.
The cabin altitude warning horn was identical to the takeoff configuration warning horn, and the crew's confusion had been foreseen in earlier incidents.
The crew interpreted the cabin altitude horn as a takeoff configuration warning and the equipment cooling master caution as unrelated faults.
The captain and first officer, of different nationalities and with language difficulties, did not coordinate the diagnosis, and the captain left his seat to consult with the engineer on the radio.
The crew did not don oxygen masks; as cabin altitude passed 14,000 ft and higher, both pilots lost useful consciousness.
Both pilots were incapacitated by hypoxia; a flight attendant with a portable oxygen bottle entered the cockpit late in the flight but could not recover the aircraft.
The aircraft flew on autopilot to the KEA holding pattern near Athens and circled until the left, then the right engine flamed out from fuel exhaustion.
The manufacturer's measures after previous MANUAL-mode pressurisation incidents did not address the shared horn and the lack of a distinct cabin altitude alert.
Helios Airways had deficiencies in organisation, quality management, crew training and safety culture.
The Cyprus regulator's oversight of the operator was found inadequate.
After the second engine flamed out the autopilot could no longer maintain the aircraft and it descended into the hills near Grammatiko.

events.text: Overnight at Larnaca a ground engineer performs a pressurisation leak check in response to a reported rear door seal problem and leaves the mode selector in MANUAL.
Preflight and Before Start checklists performed; the pressurisation mode selector position is not detected as MANUAL.
Flight 522 departs Larnaca for Athens with 115 passengers and 6 crew; the After Takeoff checklist again fails to catch the MANUAL selection.
Passing about 12,040 ft the cabin altitude warning horn sounds; the crew believe it is a takeoff configuration warning.
Master caution: equipment cooling off lights and, passing about 14,000 ft, the passenger oxygen masks deploy; the crew contact the company operations centre to discuss the warnings.

Captain, speaking with the ground engineer by radio, asks where the equipment cooling circuit breakers are, then leaves his seat; the conversation is confused and the pressurisation is never discussed.
Last radio contact with the flight; the aircraft continues climbing on autopilot to the cruising level of FL340 with both pilots incapacitated.
Athens control fails to establish contact; the aircraft enters Greek airspace and proceeds to the KEA VOR under FMC guidance.
The aircraft enters the holding pattern at KEA at FL340 and continues to circle on autopilot.
Two Hellenic Air Force F-16s intercept the aircraft; they observe the first officer slumped over the controls, the captain's seat empty and oxygen masks hanging in the cabin.
A flight attendant, holding a portable oxygen bottle, is seen entering the cockpit and sitting in the captain's seat; the left engine flames out from fuel exhaustion at 11:49:50.
The aircraft descends; a Mayday call is transmitted from the cockpit but is not on the correct frequency. The right engine flames out.
The aircraft strikes hilly terrain near Grammatiko; all 121 on board killed.

recommendations.text: Require a distinct cabin altitude warning, with an aural and visual indication that cannot be confused with the takeoff configuration warning, on the Boeing 737 and similar types.
recommendations.outcome: Boeing introduced a cabin altitude warning light and the FAA mandated it on 737s.

recommendations.text: Revise checklists and training so that the pressurisation mode selector position is positively verified before flight and after maintenance, and that the cabin altitude warning is trained in the simulator.
Correct deficiencies in the operator's organisation, quality system, crew training and safety culture, and strengthen regulatory oversight of the operator.
recommendations.outcome: Helios Airways ceased operations in 2006.

recommendations.text: Improve procedures for handling loss of communication with a flight and coordination with air defence interception.

safety_changes: Cabin altitude warning light and revised annunciation on Boeing 737 aircraft, later mandated by FAA airworthiness directive.
Boeing checklist revisions and operator training emphasising pressurisation panel checks and hypoxia recognition.
Strengthened Cypriot civil aviation oversight following EU and ICAO audits.

notes: Clock strings are Cyprus/Greece local time (both UTC+3 that day); t0 is the cabin altitude warning at about 09:12 local. Seconds are estimated except the left engine flameout (11:49:50) and impact (12:03:32) given in the report.
The time of the right engine flameout is approximate.
The Cyprus accredited agency code is an informal label. Report reference number 11/2006 may not match the AAIASB's official numbering.
loss_of_control_inflight is used as the outcome factor for the uncontrolled descent after fuel exhaustion with no pilot at the controls.
