records.title: West Caribbean Airways 708

agencies.name: Junta Investigadora de Accidentes de Aviación Civil
agencies.report_title: Final report on the accident to McDonnell Douglas MD-82 HK-4374X, Machiques, 16 August 2005

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses
agencies.report_title: English translation of the Venezuelan final report

location.name: Near Machiques, Sierra de Perijá, Zulia

records.summary: The MD-82, on a charter flight from Panama to Martinique, climbed to FL330 with engine anti-ice selected on, an altitude at which the aircraft could not maintain speed at its weight and thrust setting. With the autothrottle in Mach hold and the autopilot holding altitude, the airspeed decayed unnoticed until the aircraft stalled. The captain, believing both engines had flamed out, held the nose up while the aircraft descended in a deep stall for more than three minutes and struck the ground near Machiques. All 160 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The Venezuelan JIAAC concluded that the crew allowed the aircraft to enter a stall at FL330 through inadequate monitoring of airspeed after climbing to an altitude above the aircraft's performance capability with engine anti-ice on, and then failed to recognise the stall and apply the correct recovery. The captain interpreted the situation as a loss of thrust on both engines and kept the aircraft nose up, sustaining a deep stall until impact. Contributing factors included the crew's inadequate crew resource management, the pilots' lack of knowledge of high-altitude performance and stall characteristics of the MD-80, and organisational deficiencies at the operator.

factors.evidence: The aircraft was flown to FL330 at a weight and with engine anti-ice on that left it unable to maintain cruise speed; airspeed decayed steadily while the autopilot held altitude.
The autothrottle was in Mach hold and the crew did not recognise that the thrust available was not sustaining the target speed.
The report found the crew did not monitor the decreasing airspeed and rising angle of attack before the stall warning.
The flight was operating in an area of convective weather and icing conditions, for which engine anti-ice had been selected on, reducing thrust available.
At FL330 the stick shaker activated and the aircraft entered a stall from which the crew did not recover.
The CVR showed the captain believed both engines had flamed out and did not identify the stall.
The captain held nose-up control input throughout the descent instead of reducing the angle of attack; the aircraft remained in a deep stall.
The first officer called out the stall but did not challenge the captain's actions effectively; the report cited deficient crew coordination.
The report found the crew's knowledge of high-altitude performance, stall recognition and recovery on the MD-80 was inadequate.
The report described the operator's financial difficulties and deficient operational control and training oversight at the time of the accident.
The aircraft descended in a stalled condition at rates exceeding 10,000 ft/min until it struck the ground.

events.text: Crew request and are cleared to climb from FL310 to FL330 with engine anti-ice on; the aircraft is near its performance ceiling for its weight.
In level flight at FL330 with the autothrottle in Mach hold, the airspeed begins a slow decay while the autopilot holds altitude.
Crew discuss weather and request descent to FL310 from ATC as the aircraft struggles to hold speed; airspeed continues to decay unremarked.
Pitch attitude rises as the autopilot trims to hold altitude with insufficient thrust; angle of attack approaches the stall.
Stick shaker activates at FL330; the aircraft stalls and begins to descend.
Autopilot disconnects; the aircraft pitches up and rolls as it enters a deep stall.
Captain states that both engines have flamed out and calls for the engine restart procedure; thrust is advanced.
First officer calls out that the aircraft is stalling; the captain continues to hold the nose up.
Captain declares an emergency to ATC, reporting a loss of both engines.
The aircraft descends at more than 10,000 ft/min with high angle of attack and nose-up column input; stall warning continues.
GPWS terrain warnings sound in the final part of the descent.
Impact with the ground near Machiques in a stalled, near-level attitude; all on board are killed.

recommendations.text: Ensure MD-80 crews are trained in high-altitude performance, the effect of engine anti-ice on climb capability, and stall recognition and recovery at high altitude.
Strengthen oversight of the operator's operational control, crew training and financial capacity to operate safely.
Review autothrottle and flight-mode annunciation and stall-warning enhancements on MD-80 series aircraft so that a decaying airspeed in cruise is more clearly presented to the crew.

safety_changes: West Caribbean Airways ceased operations after the accident and its operating certificate was suspended by Aerocivil.
The accident became a reference case in the industry's revision of stall-recovery training toward angle-of-attack reduction rather than minimising altitude loss.

notes: t0 is null: exact UTC clock times from the JIAAC report were not verified, so t values are approximate offsets from the onset of the stall warning at FL330 reconstructed from the report narrative (descent of roughly three and a half minutes).
The JIAAC-VE final report date and number were not verified; the BEA published an English translation.
Lat/lon are approximate for the Machiques area.
The vertical speed of about 12,000 ft/min and the crew statements are paraphrased from the published narrative, not quoted from the transcript.
Recommendation texts summarise themes of the report; the exact wording and addressees were not verified.

records.title: Southwest Airlines 1248

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Runway Overrun and Collision, Southwest Airlines Flight 1248, Boeing 737-7H4, N471WN, Chicago Midway International Airport, Chicago, Illinois, December 8, 2005

location.name: Chicago Midway International Airport, runway 31C overrun onto Central Avenue

records.summary: Landing on Midway's 6,522 ft runway 31C at night in a snowstorm with an approximately 8 kt tailwind and braking action reported fair to poor, the crew used autobrakes for the first time and did not deploy reverse thrust until about 18 seconds after touchdown. The 737 overran the runway, went through the blast fence and airport perimeter fence onto Central Avenue and struck vehicles, killing a 6-year-old boy in a car. All 103 people on board survived.
records.probable_cause: The pilots' failure to use available reverse thrust in a timely manner to safely slow or stop the airplane after landing, which resulted in a runway overrun. This failure occurred because the pilots' first experience and lack of familiarity with the airplane's autobrake system distracted them from thrust reverser usage during the challenging landing. Contributing were Southwest Airlines' failure to provide clear and consistent guidance and training regarding arrival landing distance calculations; the programming and design of its on-board performance computer, which did not present inherent assumptions critical to pilot decision-making; its plan to implement new autobrake procedures without a familiarization period; and its failure to include a margin of safety in the arrival assessment. Also contributing was the pilots' failure to divert given reports of poor braking action and a tailwind component of about 8 knots. Contributing to the severity was the absence of an engineering materials arresting system (EMAS) beyond the end of runway 31C.

factors.evidence: Snow was falling and the runway was contaminated; braking action had been reported fair for the first half and poor for the second half.
The crew landed on runway 31C with a tailwind component of about 8 knots.
The approach was flown at night in falling snow with reduced visibility.
Reverse thrust was not deployed until about 18 seconds after touchdown; the NTSB cited this as the primary cause.
This was the pilots' first landing using autobrakes; Southwest introduced the procedure without a familiarisation period, and guidance on landing distance assessment was inconsistent.

The on-board performance computer assumed immediate reverse thrust and did not present this assumption; with 'poor' braking entered the predicted margin would have been only about 30 ft rather than the 560 ft shown for 'fair'.
Southwest's arrival landing distance assessment did not include a safety margin to account for operational uncertainties.
The challenging night, snow and tailwind landing combined with unfamiliar autobrake operation distracted the captain from deploying the reversers.
The NTSB found the pilots should have diverted given the poor braking action reports and tailwind.
Runway 31C had a limited runway safety area and no EMAS, which contributed to the severity of the overrun.
The aircraft left the end of runway 31C, penetrated the blast fence and perimeter fence and came to rest on Central Avenue after striking vehicles.

events.text: Crew obtains weather and braking action reports for Midway: snow, low visibility, braking action fair for the first half of runway 31C and poor for the second half.

Landing distance computed on the on-board performance computer using 'fair' braking action, giving a stopping margin of about 560 ft; the computer assumed immediate reverse thrust and, with 'poor' entered, would have shown about 30 ft.
Crew elects to continue to Midway rather than divert despite the reports of poor braking action and a tailwind.
Aircraft is held briefly and then sequenced for the ILS approach to runway 31C; wind reported from the east giving a tailwind component of about 8 knots.
Autobrake MAX selected for landing; this is the first time either pilot has landed with the autobrake system under Southwest's new procedure.
Aircraft on final in snow and low visibility; runway environment acquired late.
Touchdown on runway 31C; the autobrakes engage.
Captain attempts to select reverse thrust but is unable to move the reverse levers past the interlock while attending to the unfamiliar autobrake behaviour.
First officer deploys reverse thrust about 18 seconds after touchdown; captain applies maximum manual braking.
Aircraft continues past the end of runway 31C at low speed, crosses the limited runway safety area and strikes the blast fence and perimeter fence.
Aircraft comes to rest on Central Avenue after striking vehicles; a child in one of the cars is killed and several occupants of the vehicles are injured.
Passengers and crew evacuate; there are no fatalities on board.

recommendations.text: Require operators to perform arrival landing distance assessments before every landing based on existing performance data, actual conditions and a safety margin of at least 15 percent.
recommendations.outcome: FAA issued SAFO 06012 on landing performance assessments at time of arrival and later rulemaking on runway condition reporting.

recommendations.text: Require that on-board performance computers and landing distance tools clearly present the assumptions on which their calculations are based.
Ensure that operators provide adequate familiarisation and training before introducing new landing procedures such as autobrake use.
Expedite installation of EMAS or equivalent runway safety area improvements at airports with limited safety areas.
recommendations.outcome: EMAS beds were installed at Chicago Midway.

safety_changes: FAA SAFO 06012 recommended landing distance assessments at time of arrival with a 15 percent safety margin.
EMAS arrestor beds were installed at the runway ends at Chicago Midway.
Development of the Takeoff and Landing Performance Assessment (TALPA) runway condition reporting framework.

notes: t0 is set to touchdown at about 19:14 CST; seconds not recalled. Pre-landing event times are approximate.
Occupant count of 103 (98 passengers and 5 crew) and the 560 ft / 30 ft OPC margins are from memory of the report; the 18 second reverse thrust delay is as stated by the NTSB.
Recommendation numbers not recalled and are left null; SAFO 06012 was issued before the final report.

records.title: Comair 5191

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Attempted Takeoff From Wrong Runway, Comair Flight 5191, Bombardier CL-600-2B19, N431CA, Lexington, Kentucky, August 27, 2006

location.name: Beyond the end of runway 26, Blue Grass Airport, Lexington, Kentucky

records.summary: Before dawn at Lexington, the CRJ-100 was cleared for takeoff from runway 22 but the crew taxied onto the unlit, 3,500-foot general aviation runway 26 and began the takeoff roll. The first officer remarked on the absence of runway lights but the takeoff continued; the airplane ran off the end of the runway at about 137 knots, struck a berm and trees and burned. The captain, flight attendant and all 47 passengers died; the first officer survived with serious injuries. The single tower controller on duty was performing administrative tasks and did not see the airplane take the wrong runway.
records.probable_cause: The flight crewmembers' failure to use available cues and aids to identify the airplane's location on the airport surface during taxi and their failure to cross-check and verify that the airplane was on the correct runway before takeoff. Contributing to the accident were the flight crew's nonpertinent conversation during taxi, which resulted in a loss of positional awareness, and the Federal Aviation Administration's failure to require that all runway crossings be authorized only by specific air traffic control clearances.

factors.evidence: The airplane taxied onto runway 26 (3,500 feet, unlit) instead of the assigned runway 22 (7,003 feet) and began its takeoff roll.
The crew lost positional awareness during taxi and did not use the compass heading, runway markings, signage or lack of lights to detect that they were on the wrong runway.
Neither pilot cross-checked the runway heading against the assigned runway before takeoff, and the first officer's comment about the missing lights did not prompt a rejected takeoff.
The crew held nonpertinent conversation during taxi, contrary to sterile cockpit rules, which the NTSB found contributed to the loss of positional awareness.
The crew did not follow Comair's taxi and pre-takeoff verification procedures for confirming the departure runway.
Recent taxiway construction had changed the route to runway 22, the airport diagram in the crew's charts did not reflect the changes, and runway 26 was unlit.
The accident occurred before dawn in darkness, reducing the visual cues available to identify the runway.
A single controller was handling tower and radar duties, contrary to FAA staffing guidance, and was performing an administrative traffic count while the airplane taxied onto the wrong runway.
The FAA did not require that all runway crossings be authorized only by specific ATC clearances, and had not enforced two-controller staffing at the facility.
The airplane became airborne only briefly after running off the end of runway 26, struck an earthen berm, a fence and trees.
The airplane was destroyed by impact forces and post-crash fire.

events.text: Ground control clears the flight to taxi to runway 22; the crew engage in nonpertinent conversation during the taxi.
The crew taxi along taxiway Alpha, past construction changes not shown on their airport diagram, toward the runway 26 crossing that leads to runway 22.
Tower controller clears 'Comair 191' to fly runway heading and take off; he then turns away to perform an administrative traffic count.
The captain turns the airplane onto runway 26 instead of continuing across it to runway 22, and transfers control to the first officer for the takeoff.
Takeoff thrust is set and the takeoff roll begins on the unlit 3,500-foot runway 26; the heading indicator shows about 260 degrees rather than 220.
First officer remarks 'that is weird with no lights'; the captain replies 'yeah' and the takeoff continues.
'One hundred knots' callout.
Captain calls 'V one, rotate' and then 'whoa' as the runway end approaches.
The airplane runs off the end of runway 26 at about 137 knots, strikes an earthen berm and briefly becomes airborne.
The airplane strikes the airport perimeter fence and trees, breaks apart and catches fire; the recording ends.
Airport police and rescue personnel reach the wreckage and pull the first officer, the only survivor, from the cockpit.

cvr.speaker: FO
cvr.text: that is weird with no lights.

recommendations.text: Require that all runway crossings be authorized only by a specific air traffic control clearance and prohibit taxi clearances that cross a runway without explicit instruction.
recommendations.outcome: FAA revised ATC procedures in 2010 so that explicit clearance is required for every runway crossing.

recommendations.text: Require operators to establish procedures for flight crews to confirm the assigned runway, including verification of runway heading and identification, before starting the takeoff roll.
recommendations.outcome: Operators added a line-up check of runway identification and heading to before-takeoff procedures; FAA issued guidance on wrong-runway takeoffs.

recommendations.text: Require cockpit moving map displays or automatic runway awareness systems that alert crews when they are not on the intended runway.
recommendations.outcome: Runway awareness and advisory systems were widely but voluntarily adopted.

recommendations.text: Ensure that runway and taxiway construction changes are promptly reflected in airport diagrams and NOTAMs and that closed or unlit runways are clearly marked.
Ensure air traffic control facilities are staffed so that a controller is not required to handle both tower and radar positions alone during periods of activity.
recommendations.outcome: FAA revised staffing at Lexington and similar facilities to provide two controllers during overnight and early morning hours.

safety_changes: FAA required explicit ATC clearance for every runway crossing from June 2010, ending taxi clearances that implied crossing authority.
Airlines added runway verification ('line-up check') steps to before-takeoff procedures, confirming runway identification and heading.
Runway awareness and advisory systems and electronic moving map displays were adopted across much of the U.S. airline fleet.

The FAA revised controller staffing guidance to ensure two controllers are on duty when tower and radar positions are both active, and reinforced sterile cockpit compliance through Safety Alerts for Operators.

notes: The clock for the start of the takeoff roll (t0) is estimated at about 06:06:05 EDT; the report's CVR times for 'that is weird with no lights' (06:06:24), 'one hundred knots' (06:06:31), 'V one, rotate' (06:06:33) and the end of recording (about 06:06:36) are used to place later events. t0 may be off by up to 10 seconds.
The takeoff clearance time 06:05:15 is as recalled from the report and may be off by a few seconds.
Speed at the runway end (about 137 knots) is from the report's performance study.
Aircraft MSN not given because it is not recalled with confidence.

records.title: Gol Transportes Aéreos 1907

agencies.name: Centro de Investigação e Prevenção de Acidentes Aeronáuticos
agencies.report_title: Final Report A-022/CENIPA/2008, PR-GTD and N600XL, 29 September 2006

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: NTSB comments appended to the CENIPA final report

location.name: Amazon rainforest near Peixoto de Azevedo, Mato Grosso

records.summary: An Embraer Legacy 600 business jet on its delivery flight from São José dos Campos to Manaus was cleared by ATC to FL370 and was not descended to FL360 at Brasília as its flight plan required. Its transponder inadvertently went to standby, disabling both its TCAS and the 737's ability to detect it, and Brasília ACC lost radio contact without acting on the loss of Mode C. The Legacy's winglet struck the left wing of Gol 1907, a 737-800 cruising at FL370 in the opposite direction on the same airway. The 737 broke up and crashed into the jungle with 154 dead; the Legacy landed at Cachimbo air base.
records.probable_cause: CENIPA concluded that the collision resulted from a combination of errors in the air traffic control system and by the Legacy crew: ATC issued a clearance to FL370 to Manaus that conflicted with the flight plan, failed to recognise the loss of the Legacy's transponder and its non-compliance with the planned level, did not re-establish communication or advise the Legacy to change level, and was affected by workload, staffing and training deficiencies; the Legacy crew inadvertently switched the transponder to standby, did not notice its loss for almost an hour, and did not manage the loss of communication adequately. The NTSB's appended comments placed greater weight on the ATC system.

factors.evidence: São José tower cleared the Legacy to FL370 to Manaus, contrary to the flight plan's FL360 segment after Brasília, and Brasília ACC never instructed a level change or re-established contact after the transponder and radio contact were lost.

CENIPA found deficiencies in controller training, staffing, supervision and sector handover procedures at Brasília ACC, including failure to act on the loss of the Legacy's Mode C for about 50 minutes.
The Legacy's transponder went to standby, most likely through inadvertent crew input on the radio management unit, and the crew did not notice the TCAS OFF indication for nearly an hour.
The Legacy crew remained at FL370 past Brasília instead of the planned FL360 and did not apply the loss-of-communication procedure after failing to reach Brasília ACC.
The Legacy's avionics presented the transponder standby status and TCAS OFF as small annunciations that did not attract the crew's attention.
CENIPA identified systemic deficiencies in the Brazilian ATC system's procedures, training and supervision at the time of the accident.
The Legacy crew were on their first flight in the aircraft type in Brazil with limited familiarity with the avionics and with Brazilian procedures.
The Legacy's left winglet struck the 737's left wing at FL370 at 19:56:54 UTC; the 737 lost part of its wing, broke up and crashed.

events.text: Legacy N600XL departs São José dos Campos for Manaus, cleared to FL370 by the tower; its flight plan calls for FL370 to Brasília, FL360 to TERES and FL380 thereafter.
Gol 1907 departs Manaus for Brasília and climbs to FL370 on airway UZ6, the reciprocal of the Legacy's route.
Last two-way radio contact between Brasília ACC and the Legacy; the controller gives no instruction to descend to FL360 at Brasília.
The Legacy passes over Brasília VOR and continues at FL370 rather than the planned FL360.
The Legacy's transponder goes to standby; Mode C and TCAS are lost. Brasília ACC's radar label changes to show the planned level rather than a measured altitude.
Brasília ACC controllers do not recognise or act on the loss of the Legacy's Mode C return; the sector is handed over without the discrepancy being resolved.

Brasília ACC begins attempts to contact the Legacy, without success; over the following half hour the controller makes several calls and the Legacy crew make many calls on the wrong or unresponsive frequencies.
The Legacy crew, unaware of the transponder status, continue at FL370 in radio blind; Gol 1907 at FL370 has no TCAS target to detect.
Head-on collision at FL370: the Legacy's left winglet cuts through the left wing of the 737. The 737 rolls, breaks up and falls into the jungle; all 154 aboard die.
The damaged Legacy lands at Cachimbo air base (Serra do Cachimbo); its seven occupants are uninjured.

recommendations.text: Revise ATC procedures so that clearances are consistent with filed flight plans, and that loss of transponder or radio contact with an aircraft under control triggers immediate coordinated action.
Improve controller training, staffing, supervision and the display of aircraft with lost Mode C so that predicted levels are not confused with measured altitude.
Improve the annunciation of transponder standby and TCAS OFF status on the Legacy 600 avionics so the condition is unmistakable to the crew.
Reinforce crew training on loss-of-communication procedures and on transponder and TCAS monitoring in cruise.

dissent.position: In its comments appended to the final report, the NTSB agreed that the loss of the transponder and the crew's failure to notice it were factors, but stated that the air traffic control system's errors, in particular the clearance to FL370 to Manaus, the failure to recognise the loss of Mode C and the lack of level instructions or communication, were the primary cause of the collision, and that the report placed undue weight on the Legacy crew's actions.
dissent.topic: relative weight of ATC versus Legacy crew errors

safety_changes: Brazil restructured airspace control procedures, controller training and staffing at Brasília ACC and reviewed the display of planned versus measured levels on ATC radar.
The FAA and Honeywell reviewed transponder-standby and TCAS-off annunciations on the Legacy 600 avionics.
The accident led to increased emphasis on strategic lateral offset procedures and TCAS monitoring on Brazilian airways.

notes: The collision time 19:56:54 UTC and the Legacy departure (17:51 UTC) are from the report; the transponder loss time (about 19:02 UTC) and the 18:51 last-contact time are given to the minute from the published narrative and t0 is set to the transponder loss.
Crash-site lat/lon left null: the wreckage lay in remote forest near Peixoto de Azevedo and exact coordinates were not verified.
The report number A-022/CENIPA/2008 and date 10 December 2008 are given from memory.
Recommendation ids and exact addressees were not verified.

records.title: TAM Linhas Aéreas 3054

agencies.name: Centro de Investigação e Prevenção de Acidentes Aeronáuticos
agencies.report_title: Final Report A-67/CENIPA/2009, PR-MBK, 17 July 2007

location.name: São Paulo Congonhas airport, runway 35L overrun into TAM Express building on Avenida Washington Luís

records.summary: The A320 landed on the wet, recently resurfaced and ungrooved runway 35L at Congonhas with its right thrust reverser deactivated under the MEL. At touchdown the left thrust lever was moved to reverse but the right lever remained in the CLIMB detent. Because one lever was above idle, the ground spoilers did not deploy and the autobrake did not engage, and the right engine continued to deliver climb thrust. The aircraft veered left, ran off the end of the runway, crossed a major avenue and struck a TAM Express warehouse and a fuel station, killing all 187 on board and 12 people on the ground.
records.probable_cause: CENIPA concluded that the accident resulted from the right thrust lever remaining in the CLIMB position during the landing roll while the left was in reverse, which prevented ground spoiler extension and autobrake operation and produced forward thrust on the right engine, so that the aircraft could not be stopped on the runway. Contributing factors included the crew's failure to recognise the thrust lever position, the absence of a specific alert for a thrust lever asymmetry on landing, the deactivated reverser and the procedure in use for landing with a reverser inoperative, deficiencies in crew training and CRM, the wet, ungrooved runway with poor drainage at the time, the absence of a runway end safety area, and inadequacies in the oversight of operations at Congonhas.

factors.evidence: The right engine thrust reverser had been deactivated four days earlier and the aircraft was operating under the MEL with the reverser inoperative.
The FDR showed that at touchdown the left thrust lever was moved to idle and reverse while the right thrust lever remained in the CLIMB detent.
The crew did not move the right thrust lever to idle despite the RETARD callout and the aircraft's failure to decelerate.
The reverser-inoperative landing procedure required both thrust levers to be retarded to idle; the report found the crew's actions did not comply with the procedure in force.
The ground spoiler and autobrake logic inhibited deployment with one thrust lever above idle, and no dedicated warning drew attention to a thrust lever asymmetry on the ground.
Apart from the RETARD callout, the aircraft provided no alert that the spoilers had not deployed or that one engine was producing forward thrust during the landing roll.
CENIPA found deficiencies in the operator's training on landing with a reverser inoperative and on thrust lever handling.
Neither pilot identified the cause of the failure to decelerate in the seconds available; the report cited inadequate crew coordination.
Runway 35L was wet, had recently been resurfaced without grooves, and had poor drainage at the time of the accident.
Congonhas runway 35L had no runway end safety area and ended at a busy avenue and buildings; the runway had been reopened without grooving.
The report cited deficiencies in the oversight of the runway condition and of operations at Congonhas by the regulator and the airport operator.
The aircraft left the end of the runway at high speed, crossed Avenida Washington Luís and struck the TAM Express building.
The aircraft exploded and burned on striking the building and an adjacent fuel station; all on board and 12 on the ground died.

events.text: Four days before the accident the right engine thrust reverser is deactivated and the aircraft continues in service under the MEL.
Congonhas reports runway 35L wet and slippery; the runway has recently been resurfaced and has not yet been grooved.
Crew brief the landing with the right reverser inoperative and continue the approach to runway 35L.
In the flare the RETARD callout sounds; the left thrust lever is retarded to idle but the right thrust lever stays in the CLIMB detent.
Touchdown on runway 35L about 250 m past the threshold; the ground spoilers do not deploy and the autobrake does not engage because one thrust lever is above idle.
Left thrust lever moved to reverse; the right engine, with its lever in CLIMB, spools toward climb thrust as the autothrust disengages.
First officer calls out that the spoilers have not deployed; the captain calls 'decelerate, decelerate'.
Manual braking is applied but the aircraft, with forward thrust on the right engine and no spoilers, barely decelerates and begins to veer left.
The captain calls that the aircraft cannot be stopped and tries to steer; the first officer urges him to turn.
The aircraft leaves the end of runway 35L at about 90 kt, crosses Avenida Washington Luís and strikes the TAM Express building and a fuel station.
The aircraft explodes and burns; all 187 on board and 12 people on the ground die.

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: Não dá, não dá, não dá.
cvr.translation: It can't, it can't, it can't.

recommendations.text: Develop a flight-deck warning for a thrust lever not at idle during landing when the aircraft is on the ground with the other lever in reverse, and review the ground spoiler and autobrake activation logic.
recommendations.outcome: Airbus introduced an ECAM 'ENG x THR LEVER ABV IDLE' style alert and revised procedures; the FAA and EASA issued airworthiness directives for the software update.

recommendations.text: Groove runway 35L at Congonhas, improve drainage, and establish runway end safety areas or equivalent protection.
recommendations.outcome: Runway 35L was grooved and operational restrictions on wet-runway landings at Congonhas were introduced.

recommendations.text: Revise training on landing with a thrust reverser inoperative, thrust lever handling during landing and crew monitoring of the landing roll.
Strengthen regulatory oversight of the operational conditions at Congonhas, including runway condition reporting and wet-runway operations.

safety_changes: Airbus revised the A320 family procedures for landing with a thrust reverser inoperative (both levers to idle, then reverse on the operative engine) and added an alert for a thrust lever above idle on the ground during landing.
Congonhas runway 35L was grooved and wet-runway operating restrictions were imposed; larger aircraft operations at Congonhas were reduced.
Brazil accelerated airport safety upgrades including runway end safety areas at major airports.

notes: t0 is the touchdown time to the minute (about 21:54 UTC, 18:54 local); event t values in the landing roll are approximate offsets reconstructed from the published FDR narrative (about 19 s from touchdown to impact).
The exit speed of about 90 kt and touchdown distance are from published summaries and were not verified against the report.
The report number A-67/CENIPA/2009 and date are given from memory.
CVR lines are the widely published Portuguese phrases from the released transcript; their exact times were not verified.
The fatalities figure (199) includes 187 occupants and 12 people on the ground.

records.title: British Airways 38

agencies.name: Air Accidents Investigation Branch
agencies.report_title: Report on the accident to Boeing 777-236ER, G-YMMM, at London Heathrow Airport on 17 January 2008

location.name: Undershoot area of runway 27L, London Heathrow Airport

records.summary: On final approach to Heathrow runway 27L, at about 720 ft, the right engine and then the left engine failed to respond to autothrottle commands for increased thrust, their fuel flows falling to little more than idle. The aircraft landed on the grass some 330 m short of the runway threshold; the landing gear collapsed and the aircraft was written off. There were no fatalities.
records.probable_cause: The reduction in thrust on both engines was the result of restricted fuel flow to the engine fuel-oil heat exchangers (FOHE). Ice had accreted in the fuel system during a flight through unusually cold ambient conditions, released as the aircraft approached, and accumulated on the face of the FOHE, restricting fuel flow. The FOHE was found susceptible to restriction when presented with soft ice in a fuel flow of high water concentration; certification requirements did not take account of this phenomenon.

factors.evidence: Ice formed from water in the fuel during the long cold-soaked cruise and was released as fuel flow increased on approach, restricting flow at the FOHE face on both engines.
Both engines rolled back to a fuel flow just above idle and failed to respond to commanded thrust increases at about 720 ft and 620 ft respectively.
Both engines suffered a simultaneous loss of thrust response on short final, leaving insufficient energy to reach the runway.
The fuel-oil heat exchanger design was susceptible to blockage by soft ice in fuel with high water concentration.
Certification requirements did not address the risk of ice accretion and release in fuel systems restricting flow at the FOHE.
With thrust stuck near idle the aircraft could not maintain the approach path and speed decayed toward stick shaker before touchdown.
The aircraft touched down on grass 330 m short of runway 27L; all occupants survived and evacuated.

events.text: Departure from Beijing with 79,000 kg of fuel at a fuel temperature of about -2 C.
Cruise over Siberia and Mongolia in unusually cold air; fuel temperature falls to a minimum of -34 C, remaining above the freezing point of the fuel.
Aircraft is held at Lambourne before being radar vectored for an ILS approach to runway 27L.
Aircraft established on the ILS with autopilot and autothrottle engaged; landing gear down and flap 30 selected.
Autothrottle commands a thrust increase during the approach; both engines initially respond.
At about 720 ft the right engine fails to respond to the autothrottle command; its fuel flow falls to about 6,000 pph.
About seven seconds later, at about 620 ft, the left engine also fails to respond; its fuel flow falls to about 5,000 pph.
First officer, as pilot flying, notices the reduced thrust; airspeed begins to decay below the approach speed.
Captain retracts the flaps from 30 to 25 to reduce drag and extend the glide toward the runway.
Stick shaker activates as the aircraft descends toward the ground short of the runway.
Aircraft touches down on the grass about 330 m short of the runway 27L threshold; landing gear collapses and the aircraft slides to a stop.
Emergency evacuation via the slides; one passenger seriously injured, all 152 occupants survive.

recommendations.text: Introduce interim measures for the Boeing 777 with Rolls-Royce Trent 800 engines to reduce the risk of ice formed from water in the fuel restricting fuel flow at the fuel-oil heat exchanger.
recommendations.outcome: Boeing issued revised operational procedures and Rolls-Royce redesigned the FOHE; a mandatory retrofit followed.

recommendations.text: Review the certification requirements for fuel systems to ensure that aircraft and engine fuel systems are tolerant to the potential build-up and sudden release of ice in the fuel feed system.
Review the design of the Rolls-Royce Trent 800 fuel-oil heat exchanger so that it is not susceptible to blockage by ice released from the fuel system.
recommendations.outcome: Modified FOHE with redesigned inlet introduced and mandated by airworthiness directive.

safety_changes: Redesign of the Rolls-Royce Trent 800 fuel-oil heat exchanger and mandatory retrofit across the 777 fleet.
Interim operational procedures for cold-soaked fuel on 777/Trent aircraft (periodic thrust increases, fuel temperature management).
Research into ice accretion in aircraft fuel systems and review of fuel system certification requirements.

notes: Event clock times other than the 12:41 thrust rollback and fuel flow values are approximate; t values are estimates relative to the first engine rollback.
Only the first AAIB recommendation number is given; others left null.
Location lat/lon is approximate.

records.title: Spanair 5022

agencies.name: Comisión de Investigación de Accidentes e Incidentes de Aviación Civil
agencies.report_title: Report A-032/2008: Accident involving a McDonnell Douglas DC-9-82 (MD-82) aircraft, registration EC-HFP, operated by Spanair, at Madrid-Barajas Airport, on 20 August 2008

location.name: Beyond the end of runway 36L, Madrid Barajas Airport

records.summary: After returning to the stand because of an overheating ram air temperature probe, which maintenance addressed by pulling its heater circuit breaker, the MD-82 taxied out again for a second departure. The crew did not extend the flaps and slats for takeoff and the takeoff warning system did not sound. The aircraft rotated, stalled immediately after lift-off, rolled and struck the ground beside the runway, breaking up and burning. 154 of the 172 occupants died.
records.probable_cause: The crew lost control of the aircraft as a consequence of entering a stall immediately after takeoff due to an improper aircraft configuration, with the flaps and slats retracted, following a series of mistakes and omissions, together with the absence of the takeoff configuration warning. The crew did not identify the configuration error because they did not properly use the checklists that contain the items to select and verify the position of the flaps and slats, omitting the flaps/slats item in the After Start checklist, cross-checking of it in the Takeoff Briefing, and the visual check of the flaps/slats when performing the Takeoff Imminent checklist. The TOWS did not function because of a failure whose origin could not be determined, but which was associated with the R2-5 relay and the RAT probe heating problem.

factors.evidence: The flaps and slats were not extended for takeoff; the flap handle was found in the retracted position and the FDR shows flaps at zero.
The crew omitted the flaps/slats item of the After Start checklist, did not cross-check it in the takeoff briefing and did not carry out the visual check in the Takeoff Imminent checklist.
The takeoff warning system (TOWS) did not sound when the throttles were advanced with the flaps retracted.

Maintenance action on the RAT probe overheating consisted of pulling the Z-29 circuit breaker for the probe heater without investigating the cause, which was associated with the R2-5 ground-sensing relay that also feeds the TOWS.
The RAT probe heating on the ground had been reported on earlier flights and was deferred rather than diagnosed.
The TOWS was not designed to be fail-safe and was not monitored for its own failure; the same relay affected both the RAT heater and the TOWS ground logic.
The return to the stand, delay and rushed second departure disrupted the normal flow of the crew's preparation and checklists.
The CVR recorded non-essential conversation and interruptions during the second taxi-out that disrupted checklist execution.
The operator's checklists and the way they were executed did not ensure independent verification of the takeoff configuration.
The stall warning sounded immediately after rotation; the aircraft pitched up, rolled and stalled at low height with flaps retracted.
The crew did not identify the configuration cause and their responses did not recover the aircraft in the few seconds available.
The aircraft rolled alternately right and left with a very high angle of attack and struck the ground beside the runway.
The aircraft broke up and a fuel-fed fire destroyed the fuselage; most fatalities were due to impact and fire.
The report found deficiencies in the oversight of the operator's maintenance and MEL handling and in the harmonisation of TOWS airworthiness requirements.

events.text: During the first taxi to runway 36L the crew note the RAT probe temperature indicating an excessive value on the ground and return to the stand.
Maintenance technicians pull the Z-29 circuit breaker for the RAT probe heater in accordance with the MEL and release the aircraft, without investigating the R2-5 relay.
Engines restarted; the After Start checklist is read but the flaps/slats item is skipped and the flaps remain retracted.
Second taxi to runway 36L; the takeoff briefing does not cross-check the flap setting and there is non-essential conversation in the cockpit.
Takeoff Imminent checklist read; the flaps/slats response is given without a visual check of the handle or indicators.
Throttles advanced for takeoff; the takeoff warning system does not sound although flaps and slats are retracted.
Rotation at about 154 kt; the aircraft lifts off with flaps and slats retracted.
Stall warning and stick shaker activate immediately after lift-off; a synthetic voice calls stall.
The aircraft reaches about 40 ft with a high pitch attitude, then rolls right and left with bank angles of over 30 degrees; the crew apply inputs but do not identify the configuration.
The right wing and tail strike the ground beside the runway; the aircraft skids across the terrain, breaks up and catches fire near a stream.
Fuel-fed fire destroys the fuselage; 154 of the 172 occupants die and 18 survive with injuries.

recommendations.text: Require that takeoff warning systems on transport aircraft be designed so that a failure of the system is detected and indicated to the crew, and that the TOWS is checked before every flight.
recommendations.outcome: Boeing revised MD-80 procedures to include a TOWS check before each takeoff.

recommendations.text: Reinforce checklist discipline, in particular the independent verification of flaps and slats before takeoff, and the application of sterile cockpit rules during taxi.
Improve maintenance troubleshooting and MEL application so that defects with potential links to safety systems are diagnosed rather than deferred.
Investigate the R2-5 relay and RAT probe heating faults on MD-80 series aircraft and their relationship with TOWS operation.

safety_changes: Boeing MD-80 checklist revision requiring a TOWS functional check before every takeoff.
Spanish and European emphasis on sterile cockpit discipline and takeoff configuration verification.
Review of MEL procedures and maintenance troubleshooting for the RAT probe heater circuit on MD-80s.

notes: Clock strings are local time (CEST); the accident occurred at about 14:24 local. Seconds and the earlier taxi/maintenance times are approximate.
Rotation speed (about 154 kt) and the roughly 40 ft maximum height are from the report's FDR analysis; other values approximate.
Sterile cockpit violation is included on the basis of the report's discussion of interruptions and non-essential conversation during taxi; the report did not name it as a cause.
Recommendation ids not reproduced.

records.title: Qantas 72

agencies.name: Australian Transport Safety Bureau
agencies.report_title: In-flight upset, Airbus A330-303, VH-QPA, 154 km west of Learmonth, WA, 7 October 2008

location.name: Indian Ocean, 154 km west of Learmonth, Western Australia

records.summary: Cruising at 37,000 ft off Western Australia, the A330's number 1 air data inertial reference unit began outputting intermittent spikes on many parameters. The autopilot disconnected and a stream of spurious warnings followed. Two minutes later the flight control computers, acting on spike angle-of-attack values, commanded an abrupt nose-down pitch that threw unrestrained occupants against the ceiling; a second, smaller pitch-down followed. The crew diverted to Learmonth, where the aircraft landed safely; 12 people were seriously injured and many more hurt.
records.probable_cause: The ATSB found that one of the aircraft's three ADIRUs entered a failure mode in which it output numerous spikes with incorrect data and labels, including angle-of-attack spikes. A limitation in the flight control primary computers' algorithm for processing angle-of-attack data meant that two spikes 1.2 seconds apart could pass the filtering and trigger the high-AoA protection, commanding the pitch-downs. The ADIRU failure mode's origin could not be determined; the FCPC algorithm limitation had not been identified during the design and certification safety assessment.

factors.evidence: ADIRU 1 began outputting spikes in many parameters with incorrect data and labels at 0440:28 UTC; the specific trigger for the failure mode could not be identified.
Autopilot 1 disconnected at the onset of the ADIRU failure, and the crew flew manually with numerous alerts active.
Spurious overspeed and stall warnings alternated on the flight deck as a result of the corrupted air data.
The crew received a large number of spurious warnings, cautions and fault messages that did not reflect the actual aircraft state, and no procedure existed for the ADIRU failure mode.

The FCPC angle-of-attack processing algorithm could not correctly manage a scenario with multiple spikes 1.2 seconds apart, so the spikes triggered the high-AoA protection and the pitch-down commands.
The ATSB found that the ADIRU failure mode and the FCPC algorithm's vulnerability to it were not identified in the design and certification safety assessment process.
The two pitch-down manoeuvres were commanded by the flight control system, not the crew; the first reached about -0.8 g and 8.4 degrees nose-down.
The crew dealt with continuous alerts, cabin injuries and a diversion with degraded information.
After declaring PAN and then MAYDAY, the crew landed at Learmonth about 50 minutes after the upset.

events.text: Cruising at FL370 toward Perth with 303 passengers and 12 crew; the captain is pilot flying and the first officer is on a rest break, with the second officer in the right seat.
ADIRU 1 begins outputting intermittent spikes on multiple parameters with incorrect labels; autopilot 1 disconnects and a NAV IR 1 FAULT is displayed with a master caution.
Stall and overspeed warnings alternate, and numerous spurious ECAM cautions appear; the captain's airspeed and altitude indications show momentary spikes.
The captain flies manually and the crew begin assessing the alerts; the first officer is recalled to the flight deck.

The flight control computers, acting on two angle-of-attack spikes 1.2 s apart, command an abrupt nose-down: about 8.4 degrees pitch-down and -0.8 g. Unrestrained passengers and crew strike the cabin ceiling; the aircraft loses about 650 ft.
The captain applies back-stick and the aircraft returns to about FL370; the crew make a PAN call and begin considering a diversion.
A second, smaller uncommanded pitch-down occurs; the aircraft loses about 400 ft before the crew recover.
The crew decide to divert to Learmonth, the nearest suitable airport, and declare PAN; on learning of serious cabin injuries they upgrade to MAYDAY.
Descent and approach to Learmonth flown manually with the crew treating the flight control and air data indications with caution.
The aircraft lands at Learmonth. Twelve people are seriously injured and many others hurt; ambulances and later aeromedical flights take the injured to Perth.

recommendations.text: Redesign the flight control primary computer angle-of-attack processing algorithm so that erroneous spike data cannot trigger the high angle-of-attack protection, and provide crews with a procedure for the ADIRU failure mode.
recommendations.outcome: Airbus modified the FCPC software (mandated by EASA airworthiness directive) and issued an operations engineering bulletin instructing crews to switch off the affected ADIRU.

recommendations.text: Investigate the ADIRU failure mode and improve the unit's internal data checking and built-in test so that corrupted output is detected and flagged.
recommendations.outcome: The ADIRU's failure mode could not be reproduced; the manufacturer improved the unit's data-integrity checks.

recommendations.text: Reinforce advice to passengers to keep seat belts fastened while seated, since most injuries were to unrestrained occupants.

safety_changes: Airbus redesigned the A330/A340 FCPC angle-of-attack algorithm; the modification was mandated by airworthiness directive.
An operations engineering bulletin and later a permanent procedure instruct crews to switch off an ADIRU displaying the NAV IR fault so that its data is no longer used.
The FAA and EASA issued airworthiness directives on the affected Northrop Grumman ADIRU model.
The ATSB issued safety advice on the importance of keeping seat belts fastened when seated.

notes: Clock times for the ADIRU failure (0440:28), first pitch-down (0442:27) and second pitch-down (0445:08) are as recalled from the ATSB report; the landing time (0532) is approximate.
Location latitude and longitude are an approximation of 154 km west of Learmonth over the Indian Ocean.
The report describes a subsequent reversion of the flight control law; this is omitted because the exact circumstances were not verified.
Serious injuries are given as 12 (one flight attendant and 11 passengers); over 100 occupants received some injury.

records.title: US Airways 1549

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Loss of Thrust in Both Engines After Encountering a Flock of Birds and Subsequent Ditching on the Hudson River, US Airways Flight 1549, Airbus A320-214, N106US, Weehawken, New Jersey, January 15, 2009

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la Sécurité de l'Aviation Civile

location.name: Hudson River off Weehawken, New Jersey / midtown Manhattan

records.summary: About two minutes after takeoff from LaGuardia, climbing through 2,800 feet, the A320 struck a flock of Canada geese and both engines lost almost all thrust. The captain took control, started the APU, judged that no runway was reachable and ditched on the Hudson River about three and a half minutes after the strike. All 155 occupants were rescued by ferries and emergency responders; five people were seriously injured.
records.probable_cause: The ingestion of large birds into each engine, which resulted in an almost total loss of thrust in both engines and the subsequent ditching on the Hudson River. Contributing to the fuselage damage and resulting unavailability of the aft slide/rafts were (1) the Airbus engineering assumptions in the development of A320 ditching procedures and certification, the lack of industry flight crew training and guidance on ditching techniques, and (2) the captain's resulting difficulty maintaining his intended airspeed on final approach due to the task saturation resulting from the emergency situation. Contributing to the survivability of the accident were (1) the decision-making of the flight crewmembers and their use of crew resource management during the accident sequence; (2) the fortuitous use of an airplane that was equipped for an extended overwater flight, including the availability of the forward slide/rafts, even though it was not required to be so equipped; (3) the performance of the cabin crewmembers while expediting the evacuation of the airplane; and (4) the proximity of the emergency responders to the accident site and their immediate and appropriate response to the accident.

factors.evidence: The airplane struck a flock of Canada geese at about 2,818 feet; remains of Branta canadensis were found in both engines.
Ingestion of large birds into the core of each engine caused an almost total loss of thrust in both engines within seconds.

Engine bird-ingestion certification standards at the time did not require testing for birds as large as those encountered, and A320 ditching certification assumed a descent rate and configuration (engines running, 3.5 ft/s) that could not be achieved in an all-engine-out glide.
The Engine Dual Failure checklist was written for a high-altitude event and was too long to complete before the ditching; the crew never reached the ditching items.
Task saturation during the emergency contributed to the captain's difficulty maintaining his intended airspeed on final approach.
There was no industry flight crew training or guidance on ditching techniques or on managing a dual engine failure at low altitude.
In the flare the airplane entered its alpha-protection envelope, which limited the pitch-up the captain could command and prevented him from further reducing the descent rate.
Fuselage damage let water into the aft cabin, making the aft slide/rafts unusable; some passengers evacuated without life vests and one aft door was briefly opened.
The airplane was ditched on the Hudson River at about 125 knots with a descent rate of about 12.5 ft/s, flaps 2, and remained afloat long enough for all occupants to evacuate.
The forced landing on the river was survived by all 155 occupants.

events.text: Takeoff from LaGuardia runway 4 with the first officer as pilot flying.
Captain sees a flock of birds ahead and says 'birds'.
The airplane strikes a flock of Canada geese; thumps are heard and both engines ingest birds.
Both engines roll back; the captain notes 'both of 'em rolling back' and calls for ignition and APU start.
Captain takes control ('my aircraft') and starts the APU; the first officer begins the Engine Dual Failure checklist from the QRH.
Captain declares 'mayday' to LaGuardia departure, reporting a bird strike, loss of thrust in both engines, and a turn back toward LaGuardia.
Departure controller instructs a left turn to heading 220 and begins arranging a return to LaGuardia.
Controller offers runway 13 at LaGuardia; the captain replies 'we're unable. we may end up in the Hudson'.
First officer attempts engine relights per the checklist; neither engine recovers usable thrust.
Captain asks about airports to the right in New Jersey, including Teterboro; the controller offers Teterboro runway 1.
Captain tells ATC 'we can't do it' and, shortly after, 'we're gonna be in the Hudson'.
Captain makes the cabin announcement 'brace for impact'; flight attendants begin brace commands.
Flaps 2 are selected for the ditching; the captain asks the first officer 'got any ideas?' and he answers 'actually not'.
In the flare the airplane reaches the alpha-protection boundary, limiting further nose-up pitch; airspeed is below the captain's intended speed.
The airplane touches down on the Hudson River at about 125 knots and a descent rate of about 12.5 ft/s; the aft fuselage is damaged and water enters the rear cabin.

Evacuation through the forward doors and overwing exits onto the slide/rafts and wings; the aft slide/rafts are unusable because of water in the cabin. Ferries begin rescuing occupants within minutes.

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: we got one rol- both of 'em rolling back.

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: mayday mayday mayday. this is Cactus fifteen thirty nine hit birds, we've lost thrust in both engines we're turning back towards LaGuardia.

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: we're gonna be in the Hudson.

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: got flaps two, you got any ideas?

recommendations.text: Require Airbus to develop a dual engine failure checklist usable at low altitude and require operators to train on it.
recommendations.outcome: Airbus revised the A320 Engine Dual Failure procedure and QRH.

recommendations.text: Revise engine bird-ingestion certification standards to reflect the size and numbers of large flocking birds actually encountered, including core ingestion.

Require ditching training and guidance for flight crews, including the effect of flight envelope protections on the flare, and require that ditching certification consider realistic engine-out descent rates.
Require life vests and forward slide/rafts on all airplanes regardless of route, and improve passenger briefing on life vest use and location.
Improve wildlife hazard management around airports and require wildlife hazard assessments at all Part 139 airports.
recommendations.outcome: FAA expanded wildlife hazard assessment requirements and reporting.

safety_changes: Airbus revised the A320 family Engine Dual Failure procedure to add a low-altitude branch that goes directly to the essential relight and ditching items.
FAA and EASA opened reviews of engine bird-ingestion certification standards for large flocking birds, including core ingestion.
Wildlife hazard management at Part 139 airports was strengthened, including wildlife hazard assessments and Canada goose population control around New York airports.
The event became the reference case for CRM and startle-management training on low-altitude all-engine power loss.

notes: Bird strike time 15:27:11 EST and ditching 15:30:43 EST are from the report; ATC exchange clocks (15:27:32 mayday, 15:27:49, 15:28:05, 15:28:55, 15:29:21, 15:29:25) follow the public transcript to within a second or two.
The clock time of the 'brace for impact' PA and of the flaps 2 selection are not recalled precisely; those events carry approximate t only.
Touchdown parameters (about 125 kt, about 12.5 ft/s, 9.5 degrees pitch, flaps 2) are as stated in the report's performance analysis; treat pitch as approximate.
ICAO category BIRD is not in the spec's list, so OTHR is used; the initiating event was a bird strike.

records.title: Colgan Air 3407

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Loss of Control on Approach, Colgan Air, Inc., Operating as Continental Connection Flight 3407, Bombardier DHC-8-400, N200WQ, Clarence Center, New York, February 12, 2009

location.name: Clarence Center, New York, about 5 nm from Buffalo Niagara International Airport

records.summary: During a night ILS approach to runway 23 at Buffalo in light snow and icing conditions, the crew allowed airspeed to decay while configuring the Q400 for landing. When the stick shaker activated at 131 knots the captain pulled the control column aft and added only partial power, overriding the stick pusher; the first officer retracted the flaps without being asked. The airplane stalled, rolled and pitched violently, and struck a house about 26 seconds later, killing all 49 on board and one person on the ground.
records.probable_cause: The captain's inappropriate response to the activation of the stick shaker, which led to an aerodynamic stall from which the airplane did not recover. Contributing to the accident were (1) the flight crew's failure to monitor airspeed in relation to the rising position of the low-speed cue, (2) the flight crew's failure to adhere to sterile cockpit procedures, (3) the captain's failure to effectively manage the flight, and (4) Colgan Air's inadequate procedures for airspeed selection and management during approaches in icing conditions.

factors.evidence: The stick shaker activated at 131 knots (a threshold raised by the REF SPEEDS switch) and the stick pusher subsequently fired three times; the captain overrode each pusher activation.
The captain responded to the stick shaker with a 37-pound aft column pull and only partial power instead of the trained nose-down, full-power recovery.
Aft column input drove pitch to about 31 degrees nose up and the airplane rolled 45 degrees left then 105 degrees right; the first officer retracted the flaps without coordination.
Neither pilot monitored airspeed as it decayed from about 180 to 131 knots against the rising low-speed cue on the airspeed tape.
With power near flight idle, gear extended and flaps moving to 15, airspeed fell about 20 knots below the target the crew should have been flying with the REF SPEEDS switch in the INCREASE position.
The crew held an extended nonpertinent conversation about icing experience and careers below 10,000 feet, contrary to 14 CFR 121.542.
The captain failed to effectively manage the flight; the first officer retracted the flaps and asked about raising the gear during the stall without direction.
The REF SPEEDS switch was set to INCREASE without the crew adjusting their approach speed bugs accordingly, and the captain reduced power below what the approach required.

The NTSB found both pilots were likely experiencing fatigue (the first officer had commuted overnight from Seattle; the captain slept in the crew room), though its contribution to their performance could not be conclusively determined.
The report concluded the captain was startled by the unexpected stick shaker and did not recognize the situation as an impending stall.

Colgan's stall training did not expose pilots to the stick pusher or to the rising low-speed cue behavior with the REF SPEEDS switch on, and the captain had a history of training and checkride deficiencies.
Colgan Air's procedures for airspeed selection and management in icing conditions were inadequate and the airline's oversight of the captain's training record was deficient.
FAA oversight of Colgan's training program and pilot records was found wanting; the report generated recommendations on remedial training and pilot record sharing.
The captain had about 110 hours as pilot-in-command on the Q400; the first officer had about 770 hours on type and had never flown in icing before joining Colgan.

The airplane had accreted light ice; the NTSB found its effect on stall speed was minimal, but the icing conditions led the crew to select REF SPEEDS INCREASE, which raised the stick shaker speed by about 20 knots.
The airplane entered an aerodynamic stall from which the crew did not recover.
The airplane rolled and pitched uncontrollably and struck a house in a steep nose-down attitude.

events.text: Below 10,000 feet the crew continue an extended nonpertinent conversation about their icing experience and careers, contrary to sterile cockpit rules.
REF SPEEDS switch is set to INCREASE for icing conditions; the crew do not correspondingly increase their planned approach speeds.
Buffalo approach vectors the flight onto the localizer for the ILS runway 23; the airplane levels at the 2,300 ft intercept altitude with autopilot engaged.
Captain calls for flaps 5 and reduces power toward flight idle; airspeed begins to decay steadily.
First officer lowers the landing gear on the captain's call.
Captain calls for flaps 15; the low-speed cue on the airspeed tape has risen to meet the decaying airspeed, unnoticed by either pilot.
Stick shaker activates at 131 knots; autopilot disconnects.
Captain pulls the control column aft with about 37 pounds of force and advances the power levers to about 75 percent torque rather than full power.
Pitch reaches about 31 degrees nose up; the airplane rolls to about 45 degrees left bank.
Stick pusher activates for the first time; the captain overrides it with continued aft column force.
First officer retracts the flaps from 15 toward 0 without being asked, announcing 'I put the flaps up'.
Airplane rolls through wings level to about 105 degrees right bank and pitches nose down; stick pusher activates again and is overridden.
First officer asks whether to raise the landing gear; captain replies 'gear up'.
Third stick pusher activation; the airplane is in a steep nose-down attitude with insufficient altitude to recover.
Cockpit voice recorder stops; the airplane strikes a house on Long Street, Clarence Center, and is destroyed by impact and fire.

cvr.speaker: FO
cvr.text: should I put the gear up?

recommendations.text: Require operators to provide stall recovery training that emphasizes reducing angle of attack, includes stick pusher demonstration where fitted, and covers the effects of the REF SPEEDS switch on the low-speed cue.
recommendations.outcome: FAA revised stall training guidance (AC 120-109) to prioritize AOA reduction over minimum altitude loss; full-stall and pusher training added to Part 121 training requirements.

recommendations.text: Require operators to develop and implement procedures to monitor and cross-check airspeed, including low-airspeed alerting systems in transport-category airplanes.
Address pilot fatigue arising from commuting and inadequate rest, and require operators to address commuting in fatigue risk management.
recommendations.outcome: New flight and duty time rules (14 CFR Part 117) took effect in 2014.

recommendations.text: Require air carriers to obtain and review a pilot's complete training and checkride history, including failures, before hiring, and to provide remedial training programs for pilots with repeated deficiencies.
recommendations.outcome: Pilot Records Database mandated by the Airline Safety and FAA Extension Act of 2010.

recommendations.text: Reinforce sterile cockpit compliance and leadership and professionalism training for Part 121 flight crews.

safety_changes: Airline Safety and FAA Extension Act of 2010 (Public Law 111-216) required an ATP certificate and 1,500 hours for airline first officers, a pilot records database, and new fatigue rules.
14 CFR Part 117 flight, duty and rest limitations for Part 121 pilots took effect in January 2014.

FAA stall training guidance was rewritten (AC 120-109) to emphasize immediate angle-of-attack reduction rather than minimum altitude loss, with full-stall and stick pusher training later required for Part 121 carriers.
Regional airlines and their mainline partners increased oversight of training records, remedial training and commuting policies.

notes: Accident occurred 22:17 EST on 2009-02-12; in UTC it is 2009-02-13. Local date is used in the date field.
Fatalities (50) include one person in the house struck; occupants aboard were 49 (45 passengers, 4 crew).

Clock times for the REF SPEEDS switch, flaps 5 and flaps 15 calls, the second and third stick pusher activations and several CVR lines are approximate and given as relative t only; the stick shaker (22:16:27), gear call (22:16:21), first pusher (about 22:16:34) and end of CVR (22:16:52) follow the report.
CVR lines are short excerpts from the public transcript; timing of the flap and gear exchanges is estimated to within a few seconds.

records.title: Turkish Airlines 1951

agencies.name: Dutch Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Crashed during approach, Boeing 737-800, near Amsterdam Schiphol Airport, 25 February 2009

agencies.name: Turkish Accident Investigation Board (Kaza Araştırma ve İnceleme Kurulu)

location.name: Field 1.5 km short of runway 18R, Amsterdam Schiphol

records.summary: During an ILS approach to Schiphol runway 18R the left radio altimeter erroneously indicated -8 ft, causing the autothrottle to enter RETARD mode and close the thrust levers as if for landing flare. The crew, who had been vectored to intercept the glideslope from above and were busy with a line-training approach, did not notice the decaying airspeed until the stick shaker at about 460 ft. Recovery was too late and the aircraft stalled into a field 1.5 km short of the runway; 9 people died including the three pilots.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by the erroneous left radio altimeter reading, which made the autothrottle reduce the thrust to idle in the retard flare mode during the approach, combined with the crew's failure to notice the decreasing airspeed and the abnormal autothrottle mode until the stick shaker; the subsequent recovery from the stall was not successful. Contributing factors: the aircraft intercepted the glideslope from above due to ATC vectoring, which increased workload and masked the thrust reduction; the approach was not stabilised and should have been abandoned; the crew's monitoring during the line training situation was inadequate; and Boeing had not informed operators adequately about the known radio altimeter problems and their effect on the autothrottle.

factors.evidence: The left radio altimeter system produced an erroneous -8 ft value during the approach, as it had on previous flights of the aircraft.
The same radio altimeter fault had occurred on TC-JGE in the preceding days and on other 737NGs but had not been rectified.
The autothrottle entered RETARD flare mode at about 1,950 ft and closed the thrust levers; the crew did not recognise the mode annunciation.
The autothrottle used only the left radio altimeter data with no comparison against the right unit, so a single erroneous input could drive the retard logic.
Boeing was aware of radio altimeter problems affecting autothrottle behaviour but the information had not reached Turkish Airlines' crews.

Amsterdam approach vectored the aircraft onto the localiser at 5.5 nm and 2,000 ft, above the glideslope, contrary to the standard procedure, so the crew intercepted from above with the thrust already at idle.
The approach was not stabilised at 1,000 ft; the crew continued rather than executing a go-around.
The captain was instructing the first officer under line training with a safety pilot present, adding to workload during the glideslope capture and landing checklist.
None of the three pilots noticed the airspeed falling from 144 kt toward 83 kt or the thrust levers at idle for about 100 seconds.
Airspeed decayed well below the approach speed of 144 kt with the pitch attitude increasing to maintain the glideslope.
The stick shaker activated at about 460 ft radio altitude.
The first officer pushed the thrust levers forward but the captain took control and the autothrottle, still engaged, retarded them again; full thrust was applied only after a delay.
The aircraft stalled at about 83 kt and descended into the field short of the runway.
The aircraft struck the ground tail first in a nose-high attitude and broke into three sections.

events.text: Left radio altimeter begins to indicate -8 ft; the landing gear warning horn sounds once and a master caution is triggered but the crew treat it as spurious.
Approach control vectors the aircraft to intercept the runway 18R localiser at about 5.5 nm, at 2,000 ft, above the glideslope.
Crew select landing gear down and flaps 15, then 40, and descend to capture the glideslope from above with the thrust levers at idle; the landing checklist is being run.
At about 1,950 ft the autothrottle annunciates RETARD and holds the thrust levers at idle, based on the erroneous radio height.
Glideslope captured; the autopilot pitches the aircraft up to hold the glidepath as the speed falls below the 144 kt selected approach speed.
Landing checklist completed; the crew note the aircraft is at 1,000 ft but do not remark on the speed or the thrust levers at idle.
Airspeed reaches about 105 kt with the pitch attitude rising; the autopilot remains engaged.
Stick shaker activates at about 460 ft radio altitude; the first officer advances the thrust levers.
Captain takes control; the autothrottle, still engaged in RETARD mode, pulls the thrust levers back to idle again.
Autothrottle disconnected and full thrust applied, about nine seconds after the stick shaker; the aircraft is stalled with insufficient height to recover.
The aircraft strikes a field 1.5 km short of runway 18R, tail first, at about 95 kt, breaking into three parts; 9 killed including the three pilots, 28 seriously injured.

recommendations.text: Improve the reliability of the radio altimeter system and modify the autothrottle logic so that a single erroneous radio altimeter cannot drive the retard flare mode during the approach.
recommendations.outcome: Boeing modified the autothrottle software to compare both radio altimeters and issued a flight crew operations bulletin.

recommendations.text: Inform all 737NG operators of the radio altimeter problems and their effect on the autothrottle, and include an appropriate warning in the manuals.
recommendations.outcome: Boeing issued a Multi Operator Message and revised the manuals.

recommendations.text: Ensure crews are trained on recognition of autothrottle modes, the stabilised approach criteria and go-around decision-making, and that line training approaches are adequately monitored.
Ensure that Amsterdam approach procedures provide for interception of the glideslope from below in accordance with ICAO requirements.
Review stall recovery training so that flight crews immediately disconnect the autothrottle and apply maximum thrust in response to a stick shaker.

safety_changes: Boeing 737NG autothrottle software modification comparing left and right radio altimeter data.
Turkish Airlines revised approach monitoring and stabilised approach procedures.
Renewed emphasis on go-around policy and mode awareness in the industry; Dutch review of glideslope interception practices at Schiphol.

notes: Clock strings are local time (CET) to the minute; seconds are estimated. Impact occurred at about 10:26 local.
The 1,950 ft RETARD activation, 460 ft stick shaker, 144 kt approach speed and 83 kt minimum speed are from the DSB report; other state values approximate.
Turkish accredited agency code is an informal label; no formal dissent was published.

records.title: Emirates 407
records.time_reference: AEDT (local); exact clock times not reproduced, t is relative to the first rotation attempt at about 22:30

agencies.name: Australian Transport Safety Bureau
agencies.report_title: Tailstrike and runway overrun, Airbus A340-541, A6-ERG, Melbourne Airport, Victoria, 20 March 2009

location.name: Melbourne Airport, runway 16

records.summary: During pre-flight preparation the first officer entered the A340's take-off weight into the laptop performance tool as 262.9 tonnes instead of 362.9 tonnes. The resulting reduced thrust and low reference speeds went undetected through the crew's checks. On take-off from Melbourne's runway 16 the aircraft failed to lift off at the computed rotation speed, struck its tail on the runway, and became airborne only after the captain applied full thrust, beyond the end of the runway, hitting the localiser antenna and lights. The crew dumped fuel and returned safely; nobody was injured.
records.probable_cause: The ATSB found that the take-off weight was inadvertently entered 100 tonnes low in the electronic flight bag performance application, producing take-off speeds and a flex thrust setting that were too low for the actual weight, and that the crew's cross-checks did not detect the error. The design of the performance and flight management systems provided no effective gross-error check, and the operator's procedures for checking take-off performance data were vulnerable to a single undetected error. Distraction and time pressure during pre-flight contributed to the error not being caught.

factors.evidence: The take-off weight was entered as 262.9 t instead of 362.9 t, giving V speeds well below those required and a flex temperature that reduced thrust.
The captain's check of the first officer's performance calculation and the subsequent FMGS entry checks did not detect the 100 t discrepancy.
The ATSB found that the operator's take-off data verification procedure was not fully carried out as intended, and that the procedure itself was not robust against the error.
The crew were subject to distractions and time pressure during the pre-flight period when the data were calculated and checked.

Neither the EFB performance software nor the aircraft's flight management system contained a reasonableness or gross-error check that would flag take-off speeds inconsistent with the aircraft's weight.
When the aircraft did not lift off at the computed rotation speed and pitch was increased, the tail contacted the runway, causing substantial damage to the rear fuselage.
The aircraft became airborne beyond the end of runway 16 and struck the localiser antenna array and a strobe light.
After declaring PAN, holding and dumping fuel, the crew returned to Melbourne and landed safely.

events.text: During pre-flight the first officer enters the take-off weight into the laptop performance application as 262.9 t instead of 362.9 t; the resulting V speeds and flex temperature (74 degrees C) are calculated for an aircraft 100 t lighter.
The captain checks the first officer's figures and the crew enter the speeds into the FMGS; the checks compare values derived from the same wrong input and the error is not detected.
The loadsheet confirms a take-off weight of about 362.9 t, but the comparison against the performance data does not reveal the discrepancy.
Take-off roll on runway 16 (3,657 m) with the reduced flex thrust setting; acceleration is lower than normal but not recognised as abnormal.
At the computed rotation speed the first officer rotates; the aircraft does not lift off. As pitch is increased the tail strikes the runway.
The captain selects TOGA thrust.
The aircraft becomes airborne beyond the end of the runway, striking the localiser antenna array and a strobe light in the overrun area, then climbs away.
Cabin crew report a loud bang and smell during the take-off; the flight crew suspect a tail strike and stop the climb at a safe altitude.
Crew declare PAN, review the aircraft's condition with the cabin crew and decide to return after dumping fuel to reduce landing weight.
Fuel dumping carried out in a holding pattern; approach briefing for the return to Melbourne.
The aircraft lands back at Melbourne about an hour after departure; substantial damage to the rear lower fuselage is found. No injuries.

recommendations.text: Incorporate independent gross-error or reasonableness checks in take-off performance calculation tools and flight management systems so that speeds inconsistent with aircraft weight are flagged.
recommendations.outcome: Airbus developed a take-off securing function in the FMS that checks entered speeds against the aircraft's weight.

recommendations.text: Revise take-off performance procedures so that the calculation is independently performed and cross-checked by both pilots, and manage pre-flight distractions.
recommendations.outcome: Emirates changed its procedures to require independent calculations by each pilot and a comparison of results.

recommendations.text: Pursue the development of take-off performance monitoring systems capable of warning crews of inadequate acceleration during the take-off roll.
