safety_changes: Emirates revised its take-off performance calculation and cross-check procedures.
Airbus introduced a take-off securing (TOS) function in the flight management system to detect inconsistent take-off speeds and weights.
The event added impetus to regulatory and industry work on take-off performance monitoring systems and on the design of EFB performance tools.

notes: All event times are approximate offsets; the report's exact clock times are not reproduced.
The distance beyond the runway end at which the aircraft became airborne (reported as about 115 m) is omitted from the events because it was not verified.
The ATSB discussed possible crew fatigue; it is not listed as a factor because the report's conclusion on it was not verified.
Occupant count of 275 (257 passengers, 18 crew) is from memory of the report.

records.title: Air France 447

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la sécurité de l'aviation civile
agencies.report_title: Final Report on the accident on 1st June 2009 to the Airbus A330-203 registered F-GZCP operated by Air France flight AF 447 Rio de Janeiro - Paris

agencies.name: Centro de Investigação e Prevenção de Acidentes Aeronáuticos

location.name: Atlantic Ocean, about 570 nm north-east of Natal, Brazil

records.summary: In cruise at FL350 near the intertropical convergence zone the Pitot probes were obstructed by ice crystals, the airspeed indications became inconsistent and the autopilot and autothrust disconnected, with the flight control law reverting to alternate. The pilot flying applied nose-up inputs and the aircraft climbed to about 38,000 ft, where the stall warning sounded and the aircraft stalled. The stall was never recognised and the aircraft descended for 3 minutes 30 seconds, striking the ocean at 02:14:28 with all 228 occupants killed.
records.probable_cause: The accident resulted from the temporary inconsistency between the measured airspeeds, likely as a result of the obstruction of the Pitot probes by ice crystals, which led to autopilot disconnection and reconfiguration to alternate law; inappropriate control inputs that destabilised the flight path; the crew not making the connection between the loss of airspeed indications and the appropriate procedure; the late identification by the PNF of the deviation from the flight path and insufficient correction by the PF; the crew not identifying the approach to stall, the lack of an immediate response and exit from the flight envelope; and the crew's failure to diagnose the stall situation and consequently the lack of inputs that would have made recovery possible. Contributing factors included the absence of training in manual aircraft handling at high altitude and in the approach to stall procedure, the ergonomics of the stall warning and the absence of an angle of attack display, the lack of a clear display of airspeed inconsistency, the crew task-sharing and CRM weaknesses after the captain left the cockpit, and the known Pitot icing issue that had not yet led to replacement of the probes.

factors.evidence: The aircraft entered a region of ice crystals at the top of convective cloud in the ITCZ; the crew had made only a small deviation around the weather.
The Thales C16195AA Pitot probes were obstructed by ice crystals, producing a sudden fall in indicated airspeed on the left and standby instruments.
Inconsistency between the three airspeed sources caused rejection of the ADR data; airspeed indications were lost for up to about a minute.
The autopilot and autothrust disconnected at 02:10:05 as a consequence of the airspeed inconsistency.
Flight controls reverted to alternate 2 law, removing angle-of-attack protection and leaving the aircraft in a mode with which the crew were unfamiliar.
Pitot icing events on the A330/A340 with Thales AA probes were known to Airbus, Air France and the authorities; the replacement programme was in progress but F-GZCP had not yet received new probes.
The sudden autopilot disconnection, warnings and unusual conditions surprised the crew and degraded their response.
The PF made abrupt, predominantly nose-up sidestick inputs that took the aircraft into a steep climb to about 38,000 ft at over 6,000 ft/min.
Numerous ECAM messages, warnings and the need to hand-fly at altitude saturated both pilots; neither called the unreliable airspeed procedure.
The captain had left for rest without a clear designation of relief responsibilities; task sharing and communication between the two co-pilots broke down.
The PNF noticed the climb late and did not effectively challenge the PF's inputs or take control.
Stall warning sounded continuously from 02:10:51; angle of attack exceeded 40 degrees and the aircraft descended at about 10,000 ft/min in a stalled condition.
Neither pilot referred to the stall warning or identified the stall; the aircraft's behaviour was not understood.
The PF held the sidestick back and applied TOGA thrust; nose-down inputs were never sustained and the trimmable stabiliser reached 13 degrees nose-up.
The PNF and captain intervened with sidestick inputs without a clear takeover, producing dual inputs in the final minute.
The stall warning stopped when indicated airspeed fell below 60 kt and resumed when the nose was lowered, giving misleading feedback; no angle of attack was displayed.
Air France crews received no training in manual handling at high altitude or in approach-to-stall in alternate law.
The report noted the erosion of manual handling skills in highly automated operations as a contributor to the crew's inability to control the aircraft.
The crew lost awareness of the aircraft's energy state and attitude, and the captain on his return could not diagnose the situation from the available indications.
The aircraft remained stalled until impact with the ocean at 02:14:28.

events.text: Captain leaves the cockpit for rest; the junior co-pilot in the right seat is PF, the more experienced co-pilot takes the left seat as PNF.
PNF suggests turning a little to the left; the crew alter heading about 12 degrees left to avoid returns on the weather radar and reduce speed to Mach 0.80 with engine anti-ice on.
Turbulence increases slightly and a noise of ice crystals is heard on the windshield; the aircraft is in ice crystals at the top of convective cloud.
Autopilot and autothrust disconnect; the left PFD speed falls from 274 kt to 52 kt in a few seconds. Flight control law reverts to alternate.
PF takes control and applies a nose-up, left-roll sidestick input; the aircraft rolls right then left and pitches up.
Stall warning sounds twice briefly as angle of attack momentarily exceeds the alternate-law threshold; the vertical speed reaches about 7,000 ft/min.
PNF announces that the speeds have been lost and that they are in alternate law; ECAM actions begin but the unreliable airspeed procedure is not called.
PNF says several times to go back down, noting the climb; pitch reaches about 11 degrees nose-up as the aircraft passes FL360.
Left PFD airspeed indication becomes valid again, showing 223 kt; the standby (ISIS) speed follows later; no comment is made by the crew.
Stall warning sounds continuously; the aircraft is at about 37,500 ft with angle of attack increasing beyond 6 degrees.
PF advances the thrust levers to TOGA and maintains nose-up sidestick; the trimmable horizontal stabiliser begins to move nose-up from 3 to 13 degrees over the following minute.
Aircraft reaches its maximum altitude of about 37,924 ft with pitch about 16 degrees nose-up; it then begins to descend while still pitched up as the stall develops.
Captain returns to the cockpit; the aircraft is descending through about 35,000 ft with angle of attack above 40 degrees and vertical speed near -10,000 ft/min, and rolls of up to 40 degrees.
As indicated airspeed falls below 60 kt the angle of attack values are considered invalid and the stall warning stops; it sounds again whenever the nose is lowered and speed increases.
PF says he no longer has any indication; PNF says they have no valid indications. Thrust levers are briefly reduced to idle and speedbrakes momentarily extended.
PF reveals he has been holding the sidestick fully back for some time; the captain and PNF respond that he must not climb. PNF takes over briefly, with dual inputs.
PF resumes nose-up inputs; the aircraft descends through about 4,000 ft; GPWS 'pull up' and sink rate warnings sound.
PF calls that they are going to hit; last recorded values show pitch about 16 degrees nose-up, roll 5 degrees left, ground speed 107 kt, vertical speed about -10,900 ft/min.
Aircraft strikes the ocean surface in a stalled condition; recordings stop. All 228 occupants killed.

cvr.speaker: PF
cvr.translation: I don't have any more indications.

cvr.speaker: PF
cvr.text: Mais je suis à fond à cabrer depuis tout à l'heure.
cvr.translation: But I've been at full nose-up for a while.

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: Non non non ne remonte pas.

recommendations.text: Review the certification criteria for Pitot probes in icing conditions, including high-altitude ice crystals, and require probe replacement where standards are not met.
recommendations.outcome: Thales AA probes were replaced fleet-wide by airworthiness directive; ice crystal icing certification requirements were revised.

recommendations.text: Make mandatory the triggering of the flight data recorder ULB with extended transmission time and study deployable recorders and regular position transmission for aircraft over remote areas.
recommendations.outcome: ICAO standards on flight recorder locating, 90-day ULBs and autonomous distress tracking followed.

recommendations.text: Require training in manual aircraft handling at high altitude, approach-to-stall recognition and recovery in degraded flight control laws, and startle effect, for airline pilots.
recommendations.outcome: Upset prevention and recovery training (UPRT) became mandatory; stall recovery procedures were revised to prioritise reducing angle of attack.

recommendations.text: Study the inclusion of an angle of attack indicator on transport aircraft and improve the stall warning logic so that it remains consistent with the aircraft state at very low airspeed.
Review the ergonomics and the logic of the flight director bars during unreliable airspeed and stall warning, and the display of dual sidestick inputs.
Define criteria for relief crew composition and the handover of command when the captain leaves the cockpit, and reinforce CRM in a two-co-pilot configuration.

safety_changes: Fleet-wide replacement of Thales AA Pitot probes on A330/A340 and revised ice crystal icing certification criteria for probes.
Revised stall recovery procedures from Airbus, Boeing and regulators emphasising reduction of angle of attack over thrust application.
Mandatory upset prevention and recovery training and high-altitude manual handling training.
Extended 90-day underwater locator beacons, low-frequency airframe beacons and ICAO autonomous distress tracking requirements.
Air France changes to relief crew designation and captain handover procedures.

notes: CVR clock times are those given in the BEA final report to within a second or two; wording of the French lines follows the report transcript and translations are the BEA's or close paraphrases.
Recommendation ids left null: BEA issued FRAN-2009, FRAN-2011 and FRAN-2012 series recommendations, but individual numbers are not reproduced to avoid mis-attribution.
Some intermediate altitudes (e.g. 35,000 ft at the captain's return) are approximate readings from the FDR plots.
The fdr field refers to a separate FDR keyframe file to be supplied.

records.title: Yemenia 626

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses
agencies.report_title: Final Report

location.name: Indian Ocean near Moroni, Comoros

records.summary: Yemenia Flight 626, an Airbus A310-324 flying from Sanaa to Moroni, crashed into the Indian Ocean on 30 June 2009 after a botched go-around. While climbing away from a failed approach, the crew's control inputs caused the autopilot to set thrust to idle; saturated by workload and lacking training, the crew made repeated nose-up inputs and failed to recover from the resulting aerodynamic stall, ignoring the aircraft's warnings. All but one of the 153 aboard were killed; a 12-year-old girl survived by clinging to wreckage.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by inappropriate crew actions on flight controls leading to an aerodynamic stall that was not recovered. The crew, saturated by workload during an unstabilized visual approach and lacking training, failed to properly respond to multiple alarms and recover from the stall.

factors.evidence: The crew executed an unstabilized visual approach which they then abandoned for a go-around (p. 36).
During the go-around climb, crew control inputs caused the autopilot to set thrust to idle, decreasing airspeed (p. 73).
The crew was saturated by workload managing the aircraft trajectory and locating the runway while multiple alarms were triggered (p. 73).
The crew lacked adequate training and briefing for the Moroni MVI procedure and for handling emergency situations (p. 73).
The crew's control inputs and thrust reduction led to an aerodynamic stall that developed during the climb (p. 72-73).
The crew failed to properly recover from the stall, continuing to make nose-up inputs (p. 73).
The crew did not properly respond to multiple GPWS SINK RATE and PULL UP warnings (p. 38-39).
The aircraft entered an unrecoverable stall and impacted the Indian Ocean at 65 ft altitude with 185 kt airspeed and 15° nose-up pitch (p. 40-41).

events.text: The crew decided to abandon the unstabilized approach and execute a go-around.
Autopilot 2 disconnected; first officer initiates right turn at 1000 ft altitude.
GPWS SINK RATE alarm triggered; aircraft at 548 ft radio altitude with -2000 ft/min descent and 27° right bank.
Crew levels wings to 0° and increases pitch to 12° in response to GPWS warnings.
GPWS TOO LOW TERRAIN alarm at 230 ft altitude with -1000 ft/min descent and 29° right bank.
Crew levels wings and increases pitch to 17°; aircraft reaches minimum altitude of 161 ft radio altitude.
Landing gear retracted; gear not down warning triggers for 16 seconds.
LVL/CH mode engaged at 700 ft with 2000 ft altitude selected; autothrottle commands TOGA power.
Stall alarm recorded in FDR at 13° angle of attack; airspeed rapidly decreasing from 185 kt while climbing.
Alpha Floor protection triggered at 12.1° angle of attack and 191 kt; thrust lever speed increases to 8°/s.
Autopilot disconnected; altitude 653 ft; pitch and angle of attack continue to increase; stall alarm continues.
Pilot applies full nose-down pitch input at 698 ft altitude (only occurrence after stall began); airspeed is 170 kt.
Crew applies go-lever thrust command at 1034 ft altitude while in high-altitude stall condition with 15-23° angle of attack.
AP instinctive disconnect alarm ends; continuous stall warning continues until impact.
Aircraft strikes Indian Ocean at pitch angle 15° nose-up, 21° right bank, 185 kt, 65 ft altitude.

recommendations.text: Establish permanent dedicated search and rescue means adapted to the search for and rescue of aircraft accident survivors at sea near aerodromes.
Ensure that all crews performing flights to Moroni are properly trained in execution of the MVI procedure.
Review pilot training conditions for Yemenia, particularly their ability to react to emergency situations.

notes: Full BEA final report read; sections 2.1 (scenario), 3.2 (causes), and 4 (recommendations) extensively reviewed
Detailed flight data timeline from FDR analysis with specific altitudes, airspeeds, pitch angles and angles of attack
CVR content not explicitly transcribed in sections read but event times precisely match FDR timestamps
Report clearly identifies inappropriate crew actions leading to stall and inadequate recovery despite multiple warnings

records.title: Pel-Air Westwind VH-NGA
records.time_reference: UTC; clock times not reproduced, t is relative to the ditching (t=0) with earlier events negative

agencies.name: Australian Transport Safety Bureau
agencies.report_title: Ditching of Israel Aircraft Industries Westwind 1124A, VH-NGA, 6 km SW of Norfolk Island Airport, 18 November 2009 (re-opened investigation, final report 2017)

records.operator: Pel-Air Aviation (air ambulance flight for CareFlight)

location.name: Pacific Ocean about 6 km south-west of Norfolk Island

records.summary: An air ambulance Westwind carrying a patient from Apia to Melbourne via a refuelling stop at Norfolk Island departed at night with fuel for the island but no alternate. Weather at Norfolk Island deteriorated below the landing minima after departure and the crew did not obtain the updates in time to divert. After four unsuccessful instrument approaches in cloud and rain, with fuel critical, the pilot in command ditched the aircraft in the sea near the island. All six on board escaped the sinking aircraft and were rescued about 90 minutes later.
records.probable_cause: The ATSB's re-opened investigation found that the pilot in command's pre-flight planning did not adequately consider the possibility of weather deterioration at Norfolk Island and that the flight departed without an alternate or additional fuel to cope with it, which the operator's procedures and the regulations then in force permitted. Updated forecasts and reports showing conditions below the minima were not obtained by the crew until the aircraft had passed the point at which a diversion was possible. Contributing were deficiencies in Pel-Air's operational risk controls and fuel planning guidance for its air ambulance operations, and shortcomings in CASA's oversight of the operator.

factors.evidence: The re-opened investigation found Pel-Air's risk controls for long over-water air ambulance flights, including fuel planning and in-flight decision guidance, were inadequate.
The ATSB found that CASA's surveillance of Pel-Air's operations had not identified the operator's deficiencies, and that the regulations did not require an alternate for the flight.
The pilot in command's flight planning did not make adequate provision for weather deterioration at an isolated aerodrome; the flight departed without an alternate or fuel to reach one.
The crew did not obtain the updated Norfolk Island weather in time and did not recognise the deteriorating situation until diversion was no longer possible.
Cloud and rain at Norfolk Island were below the landing minima on arrival; the crew could not see the runway on four instrument approaches.
The approaches and the ditching took place at night.
With fuel critical and no landing possible, the pilot in command elected to ditch while engine power remained available.
The aircraft was ditched in the sea about 6 km south-west of the airport, broke up on impact and sank; all six occupants escaped.

events.text: Pre-flight planning at Apia: the forecast then available indicates Norfolk Island conditions above the alternate minima, so no alternate is planned and no extra fuel is carried beyond the operator's requirement.
Departs Apia at night for Norfolk Island with the patient, a doctor, a nurse, the patient's partner and two pilots on board.
After departure, updated Norfolk Island observations and forecast amendments show deteriorating cloud and visibility; the crew do not obtain them at this stage.
The crew obtain the Norfolk Island weather en route; conditions are now below the landing minima but the aircraft has passed the point from which a diversion to another aerodrome is possible.
First instrument approach to Norfolk Island; no visual reference at the minima; missed approach.
Second approach, also unsuccessful; the crew consider options as fuel decreases.
Third approach unsuccessful in cloud and rain.
Fourth approach unsuccessful; fuel is now critical.
The pilot in command decides to ditch while fuel and engine power remain; a MAYDAY is transmitted and the cabin is prepared.
The aircraft is ditched at night in the sea about 6 km south-west of the airport; the fuselage is damaged on impact and the aircraft sinks. All six occupants escape.
After about 90 minutes in the water the survivors are located and rescued by a local vessel.

recommendations.text: Strengthen fuel, alternate and in-flight re-planning requirements for flights to isolated aerodromes, particularly for air ambulance and passenger-carrying charter operations.
recommendations.outcome: CASA revised the fuel and alternate requirements applying to such operations and to remote island destinations.

recommendations.text: Improve operational risk controls, fuel planning guidance and crew decision-support for long over-water air ambulance flights.
Improve the effectiveness of regulatory surveillance so that operator deficiencies of this kind are identified.

safety_changes: CASA introduced stricter fuel and alternate requirements for air ambulance and passenger charter flights to isolated aerodromes.

The original 2012 ATSB report was criticised by a Senate inquiry and an independent review; the ATSB re-opened the investigation and published a revised report in 2017 with broader organisational findings.
Pel-Air revised its long-range over-water operating procedures.

notes: All event times are approximate offsets relative to the ditching; the report's clock times and the sequence of the four approaches (types and exact timing) were not verified.

The re-opened report also discussed possible fatigue of the pilot in command and the handling of weather information by air traffic services; these are not listed as factors because their exact findings were not verified.
Injury details for the occupants are not given (injuries_serious null).

records.title: UPS Airlines 6

agencies.name: General Civil Aviation Authority
agencies.report_title: Air Accident Investigation Sector final report, Uncontained cargo fire leading to loss of control inflight and uncontrolled descent into terrain, Boeing 747-44AF N571UP, Dubai, 3 September 2010

location.name: Nad Al Sheba military area, about 10 km south of Dubai International

records.summary: About 22 minutes after departure from Dubai, climbing through the Bahrain FIR, a fire warning sounded for the main deck cargo compartment, where a shipment including lithium batteries had ignited. The crew turned back toward Dubai. Smoke filled the cockpit and the captain's oxygen supply failed; he left his seat and was incapacitated. The first officer flew alone, unable to see the instruments or tune the radios, communicating through relay aircraft, and with degraded pitch control from fire-damaged cables. The aircraft overflew Dubai, could not be positioned for a landing, and struck the ground south of the airport. Both pilots died.
records.probable_cause: The GCAA concluded that a large fire developed in the palletised cargo on the main deck, most probably originating in a shipment containing lithium batteries, and that the resulting smoke entered the flight deck. The fire damaged the control cables, limiting pitch control, and the captain's oxygen supply was interrupted, leading to his incapacitation. The first officer, with severely reduced visibility of the instruments, no direct communication with Dubai and limited control authority, was unable to land the aircraft. Contributing factors included the lack of a requirement to declare lithium batteries as hazardous in cargo, the class E cargo compartment's lack of fire suppression, the inadequate smoke barrier between the main deck and the flight deck, and the absence of a supplementary oxygen supply that could be used without leaving the seat.

factors.evidence: A fire developed in palletised cargo on the main deck containing lithium batteries and other flammable material; the fire warning sounded about 22 minutes after takeoff.
The shipment contained lithium batteries in quantities that did not require declaration as hazardous goods, in proximity to combustible packaging.
The fire spread rapidly through the main deck; the class E compartment had no active fire suppression.
The smoke barrier between the main deck and the flight deck did not prevent smoke ingress, and the crew oxygen system did not provide a portable supply usable without leaving the seat.
The regulations in force did not require lithium batteries in the quantities carried to be declared, packaged or segregated as dangerous goods.
The captain's oxygen supply ceased; he left his seat to find a portable bottle and was incapacitated by smoke and fumes.
The fire damaged the control cables on the main deck, degrading pitch control; the first officer relied on the autopilot for control.
With fire-damaged cables and unreliable elevator response the first officer had limited ability to control pitch during the final descent.
The first officer alone flew the aircraft, managed the emergency, and relayed communications through other aircraft because he could not tune the radios.
Unable to see the instruments through the smoke, the first officer overflew the airport and could not establish the aircraft's position for an approach.
The aircraft descended into the ground south of Dubai while the first officer attempted to return to the airport.
The aircraft was destroyed by impact forces and fire.

events.text: Takeoff from Dubai runway 30R for Cologne with a main-deck cargo load that includes lithium batteries.
Fire warning for the main deck cargo compartment while climbing through about FL320 in the Bahrain FIR.
The crew declare an emergency to Bahrain ACC and elect to return to Dubai rather than divert to Doha, which is closer.
Crew run the fire checklist; the main deck is depressurised and the aircraft turns back toward Dubai.
Smoke enters the flight deck and rapidly reduces visibility of the instruments and the outside.
The autopilot is used for control; pitch control through the column becomes limited as the fire damages the control cables.
The captain's oxygen supply fails; he leaves his seat to find a portable oxygen bottle and is overcome by smoke and fumes.
The first officer, flying alone, cannot see the radio panel to tune Dubai frequencies and communicates with Bahrain ACC through relay aircraft.
The aircraft descends toward Dubai; the first officer, unable to read the instruments, passes over the airport at about 4,000 ft without seeing the runway.
Relayed instructions to turn toward Sharjah are received; the aircraft turns but continues to descend with limited pitch authority.
GPWS warnings sound as the aircraft descends toward the ground.
The aircraft strikes the ground at the Nad Al Sheba military area about 10 km south of Dubai International and is destroyed by impact and fire.

recommendations.text: Review the classification, packaging, quantity limits and declaration requirements for lithium batteries carried as cargo, and prohibit or restrict their carriage in bulk on aircraft without suppression.
recommendations.outcome: ICAO prohibited lithium metal batteries as cargo on passenger aircraft in 2015 and lithium-ion batteries in 2016, with state-of-charge limits on cargo aircraft.

recommendations.text: Improve fire detection and suppression for class E main-deck cargo compartments, and the smoke barrier between cargo compartment and flight deck.
recommendations.outcome: Industry development of fire-resistant containers and fire containment covers; FAA fire-safety research on class E compartments.

recommendations.text: Provide flight crews with full-face oxygen masks and smoke-vision systems or equivalent means to see the instruments in dense smoke, and a portable oxygen supply usable without leaving the seat.
recommendations.outcome: UPS installed full-face oxygen masks and Emergency Vision Assurance Systems on its fleet.

recommendations.text: Train crews to divert to the nearest suitable airport in the event of an uncontrolled cargo fire.

safety_changes: ICAO banned the carriage of lithium metal batteries as cargo on passenger aircraft (2015) and lithium-ion batteries as cargo on passenger aircraft (2016), with a 30 percent state-of-charge limit on cargo flights.
UPS fitted its fleet with full-face oxygen masks, Emergency Vision Assurance Systems and fire-resistant cargo containers and fire containment covers.
The FAA issued guidance on lithium battery transport and accelerated research on class E cargo compartment fire protection.

notes: Times are given to the minute from the GCAA report narrative (takeoff 14:51, fire warning about 15:12, impact about 15:41 UTC); intermediate event t values are approximate offsets.
The report number is not given because the GCAA case reference was not verified.
The cfit outcome factor is used as instructed; the GCAA described the impact as an uncontrolled descent into terrain after loss of control, so loss_of_pilot_control_authority is also listed.
Crash-site lat/lon are approximate for Nad Al Sheba.

records.title: Qantas 32

agencies.name: Australian Transport Safety Bureau
agencies.report_title: In-flight uncontained engine failure, Airbus A380-842, VH-OQA, overhead Batam Island, Indonesia, 4 November 2010

agencies.name: Air Accident Investigation Bureau of Singapore

location.name: Over Batam Island, Indonesia, shortly after departure from Singapore

records.summary: About four minutes after take-off from Singapore, the number 2 Trent 900 engine of the A380 suffered an uncontained failure of its intermediate-pressure turbine disc. Disc fragments punctured the wing and fuel tanks and severed wiring and hydraulic lines, degrading many aircraft systems. The five-pilot crew spent about 50 minutes working through the ECAM messages, assessed landing performance and returned to Changi for an overweight landing, stopping with about 150 m of runway remaining. Nobody was injured.
records.probable_cause: The ATSB found that an oil feed stub pipe in the engine's HP/IP bearing structure had been manufactured with a misaligned counter-bore, leaving a thin wall that cracked by fatigue. Oil released through the crack ignited in the buffer space, and the fire heated the IP turbine drive arm until the disc separated from the shaft, overspeed and burst. Rolls-Royce's manufacturing quality processes had not detected the non-conforming pipes, and when the non-conformance was identified in service the company's risk assessment did not lead to the affected engines being removed.

factors.evidence: An oil feed stub pipe was manufactured with a misaligned counter-bore, a non-conformance that produced a thin wall section susceptible to fatigue cracking.
Rolls-Royce's manufacturing inspection and quality processes did not detect the misaligned counter-bore before the pipe entered service.

Non-conforming stub pipes had been identified in other engines before the accident, but the retrospective risk assessment did not recognise the fatigue-cracking hazard, so engines with the defect remained in service.
A fatigue crack developed through the thin wall of the stub pipe, releasing oil into the HP/IP bearing chamber buffer space.
The leaking oil ignited and the resulting internal fire heated the IP turbine drive arm, leading to the separation of the disc from the shaft.
The IP turbine disc overspeed and burst into three main fragments that penetrated the engine casing, the wing and the fuselage.
Disc fragments punctured left-wing fuel tanks, causing a large fuel leak and preventing fuel transfer, which produced a lateral imbalance.
The green hydraulic system was lost, along with parts of the electrical system, degrading brakes, spoilers, flaps, gear and other services.
The crew processed dozens of ECAM messages over about 50 minutes while holding, and had to assess landing performance with degraded systems.
The aircraft landed overweight at Changi at about 166 kt with a computed stopping margin of about 100 m, stopping with about 150 m of runway remaining.

events.text: Departs Singapore Changi runway 20C for Sydney with 440 passengers and 29 crew, including five pilots (the operating crew plus a check captain and a supervising check captain).
Climbing through about 7,000 ft over Batam Island, the engine 2 IP turbine disc fails; fragments penetrate the left wing, fuel tanks and fuselage.

Multiple ECAM warnings begin, including engine 2 failure and fire indications, fuel leak and transfer faults, green hydraulic system loss, electrical bus losses, and degradations of brakes, spoilers and flight controls.
Crew declare PAN, level off and request a holding area east of Singapore to process the ECAM actions.
Engine 2 fire warning: the crew discharge both fire extinguisher bottles into engine 2, without confirmation of discharge.
The crew work through the ECAM procedures; fuel cannot be transferred or jettisoned, fuel is leaking from the left wing and a lateral imbalance develops.
Landing performance is computed with the landing distance performance application for the degraded configuration, giving a stopping margin of about 100 m on runway 20C.
Crew perform a controllability check in the landing configuration at low speed, then commence the approach to Changi.

Overweight landing on runway 20C at about 166 kt with limited braking and spoilers; the aircraft stops with about 150 m of runway remaining. Brake temperatures reach about 900 degrees C and four tyres deflate.
Fuel leaks from the left wing near the hot brakes; airport fire services apply foam. The crew keep passengers on board while the area is made safe, then disembark them by stairs.
Engine 1 cannot be shut down from the cockpit because its control wiring was severed; it is finally stopped about two hours after landing by drowning it with fire-fighting foam.

recommendations.text: Address the manufacturing quality-control deficiencies that allowed non-conforming oil feed stub pipes to enter service, and improve the process for assessing the risk of identified non-conformances.
recommendations.outcome: Rolls-Royce revised its quality management and non-conformance risk assessment processes; affected engines were removed or modified.

recommendations.text: Mandate inspection and, where necessary, replacement of Trent 900 HP/IP bearing structure oil feed stub pipes, and require IP turbine overspeed protection.
recommendations.outcome: EASA emergency airworthiness directives required repetitive inspections and engine changes; Rolls-Royce introduced an IP turbine overspeed protection software modification.

safety_changes: EASA emergency airworthiness directives required inspection and replacement of affected Trent 900 oil feed stub pipes across the fleet.
Rolls-Royce introduced an IP turbine overspeed protection system that shuts the engine down if the turbine begins to overspeed.
Rolls-Royce revised its manufacturing quality and non-conformance risk assessment processes.
Airbus and operators reviewed ECAM presentation and crew procedures for managing multiple system failures on the A380.

notes: Take-off (0156), failure (0201) and landing (0346) times are to the minute; intermediate event times are approximate offsets.
The time engine 1 was finally shut down (about two hours after landing) is approximate.
ATSB safety recommendation numbers for this investigation were not verified, so ids are null.

records.title: First Air 6560
records.time_reference: CDT (local); intermediate clock times are not reproduced, so t is relative to impact (t=0) with earlier events negative

agencies.name: Transportation Safety Board of Canada
agencies.report_title: Controlled Flight into Terrain, Bradley Air Services Limited (First Air), Boeing 737-210C C-GNWN, Resolute Bay, Nunavut, 20 August 2011

location.name: Hill about 1 nm east of runway 35T, Resolute Bay, Nunavut

records.summary: The chartered 737 combi was flying an ILS approach to runway 35T at Resolute Bay in low cloud when it struck a hill about 1 nm east of the runway. The autopilot had not captured the localizer and the aircraft flew a track diverging to the right of the approach course; the first officer repeatedly voiced concern and called for a go-around, but the captain continued the approach until seconds before impact. Twelve of the 15 people on board were killed.
records.probable_cause: The TSB found that the autopilot did not transition to localizer-capture mode and the aircraft diverged to the right of the localizer while the crew tried to reconcile conflicting heading, localizer and GPS indications; the captain believed the localizer indication might be erroneous. The approach was unstable and below the required standard, and the crew's coordination broke down: the first officer's concerns and go-around calls were not acted on until it was too late. Contributing factors included the crew's high workload, the compass and mode indications that were not understood, low cloud at the approach minima, and First Air's standard operating procedures and crew resource management training, which did not provide effective defences.

factors.evidence: The autopilot remained in a heading/roll mode instead of capturing the localizer, which the crew did not recognise in time.
The aircraft flew a track diverging to the right of the localizer course; heading and compass indications available to the crew were not reconciled with the localizer and GPS information.
The captain believed the localizer indication might be erroneous and did not appreciate that the aircraft was off course and heading toward rising terrain east of the runway.
The crew were dealing with an unresolved navigation discrepancy, approach configuration and communications during the final approach.
The first officer expressed concern several times and called for a go-around; the captain did not respond effectively and the two pilots did not share a common understanding of the situation.
The aircraft was not established on the localizer and did not meet the operator's stabilized-approach criteria.
The approach was continued although the criteria for a go-around had been met.
A go-around was not initiated until about two seconds before impact, too late to avoid the terrain.
Low cloud and reduced visibility at Resolute Bay prevented the crew from seeing the terrain or the runway in time.
First Air's crew resource management training was of the older, less effective type; the TSB recommended contemporary CRM training for all commercial operators.
The aircraft struck a hill about 1 nm east of the runway threshold in controlled flight.

events.text: Crew brief the ILS approach to runway 35T at Resolute Bay; weather is low cloud with reduced visibility near the approach minima. A military exercise is under way at the airport and a temporary military control unit is in operation.

The aircraft turns toward the final approach course with the autopilot engaged, but the autopilot does not transition to localizer-capture mode and the aircraft continues on a heading-based track that diverges to the right of the localizer.
The first officer notes that the localizer indication is not centred and points out the discrepancy between the heading and the GPS track.
The captain, recalling earlier experiences of erroneous ILS indications, doubts the localizer and continues descending on the glideslope while offset right of the course.
The captain disconnects the autopilot and attempts to correct toward the localizer while continuing the approach; workload is high and the crew's understanding of the situation diverges.
The first officer suggests a go-around; the captain does not act on the suggestion.
The first officer again calls for a go-around as the aircraft continues below cloud toward terrain east of the runway.
The captain calls for a go-around and advances the thrust levers about two seconds before impact.
The aircraft strikes a hill about 1 nm east of the runway 35T threshold and breaks up; 12 of the 15 occupants are killed, 3 are seriously injured.

recommendations.text: Require commercial air operators to provide contemporary crew resource management training for pilots of air taxi and commuter operations (CAR 703 and 704).
recommendations.outcome: Transport Canada introduced a contemporary CRM training standard applying to all Canadian commercial air operators in 2019.

recommendations.text: Require operators to implement measures that ensure unstable approaches are recognised and result in a go-around.

safety_changes: Transport Canada mandated contemporary CRM training for all Canadian commercial air operators.
First Air revised its standard operating procedures, stabilized-approach criteria and go-around policy, and updated its CRM training.
The TSB placed unstable approaches that are continued to a landing on its Watchlist of key safety issues.

notes: Only the impact time (about 1641 CDT) is given; all other event times are approximate offsets reconstructed from the report narrative.
The precise nature of the compass/heading discrepancy described in the TSB report (its magnitude and origin) is not reproduced; the record describes it generically.
GPWS alerts in the final seconds are not itemised because their exact timing was not verified.
Recommendation A14-01 text is paraphrased; a second TSB recommendation from this investigation exists but its number and exact wording were not verified.

records.title: UTair Flight 120

location.name: Near Roshchino International Airport

records.summary: UTair Flight 120, an ATR 72-201, crashed during takeoff from Roshchino on April 2, 2012, in snow and rain with ice and snow accumulated on the aircraft. Despite visible contamination, the flight crew decided not to de-ice the aircraft before takeoff. After takeoff at low airspeed, flaps were retracted at 139 knots in conditions requiring 160 knots minimum, triggering an aerodynamic stall. The crew failed to recognize the stall and apply appropriate recovery procedures, resulting in loss of control and impact with an open field near the runway.
records.probable_cause: The aircraft departed without de-icing treatment despite visible ice and snow contamination on the surfaces. The flap retraction at 139 knots instead of the required 160 knots in icing conditions caused an aerodynamic stall. The crew failed to recognize the stall and apply appropriate recovery procedures, instead pulling back on the control column until impact. Contributing factors included shortcomings in ground handling, inadequate crew training on stall recognition, and deficiencies in the airline's safety management system.

factors.evidence: Ice and snow accumulated on the aircraft surfaces; the aircraft had been parked for hours in snowy conditions without being de-iced (p. 1).
The crew of the flight were aware that ice and snow had accumulated on the aircraft but decided not to de-ice it despite para. 2.14 of FAP-128 and AFM requirements (p. 193).
Aircraft stall occurred at operational angles of attack right after flaps retraction with engaged autopilot, caused by loss of wing lift effectiveness (p. 193).
The crew seemed to have trouble identifying the problem with increasing stress as the situation developed; stall warning appeared but crew became confused (p. 1).
Crew applied ailerons and rudder but were unable to counteract subsequent left roll; pilots were pulling back on the control column until impact (p. 193).
The first officer's tone suggested high levels of stress during the emergency; crew preoccupation with banking and buffeting (p. 1).
Aircraft began uncommanded roll and eventually crashed at a left bank of 55 degrees and nose-down angle of 11 degrees (p. 1).

events.text: Flight 120 crew arrives at aircraft in snowy conditions; visible snow and ice on surfaces.
Crew decides not to de-ice despite visible contamination and crew awareness of ice/snow accumulation.
Aircraft departs from gate and begins taxi to runway for takeoff.
Flight 120 takes off from Roshchino at 07:33 local time with visible ice/snow on aircraft.
Aircraft reaches about 600 feet altitude; autopilot engaged; flaps retracted at 139 knots.
Stall warning sounds as aircraft loses lift due to wing contamination.
Aircraft begins uncommanded roll to the right; first officer asks 'what is this buffeting'; crew disengages autopilot.
Crew applies ailerons and rudder but cannot counteract left roll at 40-55 degree bank angles.
Aircraft crashes into open field near runway at 55 degree left bank and 11 degree nose-down angle.

recommendations.text: Develop Federal Aviation Regulations for aircraft maintenance and ground handling.
Develop guidance on aircraft ground icing protection and training for de-icing personnel.
Assure compliance with de-icing/anti-icing procedures and personnel training requirements.
Organize conferences to share experience of ATR 42/72 aircraft operation and safety issues.
Improve simulator training programs for stall prevention and recovery procedures.

safety_changes: Enhanced de-icing procedures and regulatory framework in Russia (State Standard GOST R 54264-2010 effective July 2012)
Improved crew training on stall recognition and recovery
Mandatory compliance with Clean Aircraft Concept

notes: Read summary from input record and Causes section (lines 8923-8995)
Safety Recommendations section reviewed (lines 9029-9122)
Key finding: PIC decision to take off without de-icing despite visible contamination
Crew failed to recognize stall and apply recovery procedures
Systemic issues in ground handling and crew training

records.title: SCAT Airlines 760

location.name: Kyzyltu

records.summary: SCAT Airlines Flight 760, a Bombardier CRJ200, was on final approach to Almaty International Airport in thick fog and poor visibility when it initiated a go-around at 13:13 local time on 29 January 2013. Fourteen seconds after initiating the go-around, the aircraft experienced a nose-down elevator deflection and crashed 1.6 km short of the runway near Kyzyltu. The subsequent investigation was unable to determine the cause of the elevator deflection, though a possible scenario involved pilot incapacitation from a heart attack.
records.probable_cause: Nose-down elevator deflection during go-around; cause undetermined but possibly pilot incapacitation from heart attack

factors.evidence: aircraft was on final approach in thick fog and poor visibility
go-around initiated due to weather conditions being below minimums
possible scenario that Captain Evdokimov may have experienced a heart attack and collapsed onto the yoke; postaccident autopsy revealed he had coronary artery disease
nose-down elevator deflection resulted in a steep dive and impact with the ground

events.text: Aircraft on final approach to Almaty International Airport in thick fog and poor visibility
Go-around initiated due to weather conditions being below minimums
During the missed approach procedure, a nose-down elevator deflection was recorded
Resulting in a steep dive and impact with the ground
Aircraft crashed 1.6 km short of the runway near the village of Kyzyltu

records.title: Asiana Airlines 214

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Descent Below Visual Glidepath and Impact With Seawall, Asiana Airlines Flight 214, Boeing 777-200ER, HL7742, San Francisco, California, July 6, 2013

agencies.name: Aviation and Railway Accident Investigation Board

location.name: Runway 28L seawall, San Francisco International Airport, California

records.summary: On a daytime visual approach to runway 28L at San Francisco (glideslope out of service), the 777 was high and fast. The pilot flying selected flight level change, then disconnected the autopilot and pulled the thrust levers to idle, which placed the autothrottle in HOLD so that it no longer protected speed. The crew did not notice the decaying airspeed until the airplane was below 200 feet and initiated a go-around only seconds before the main gear and tail struck the seawall. Three passengers died and 49 people were seriously injured.
records.probable_cause: The flight crew's mismanagement of the airplane's descent during the visual approach, the pilot flying's unintended deactivation of automatic airspeed control, the flight crew's inadequate monitoring of airspeed, and the flight crew's delayed execution of a go-around after they became aware that the airplane was below acceptable glidepath and airspeed tolerances. Contributing were (1) the complexities of the autothrottle and autopilot flight director systems that were inadequately described in Boeing's documentation and Asiana's pilot training, which increased the likelihood of mode error; (2) the flight crew's nonstandard communication and coordination regarding the use of the autothrottle and autopilot flight director systems; (3) the pilot flying's inadequate training on the planning and executing of visual approaches; (4) the pilot monitoring/instructor pilot's inadequate supervision of the pilot flying; and (5) flight crew fatigue, which likely degraded their performance.

factors.evidence: Moving the thrust levers to idle after selecting FLCH SPD transitioned the autothrottle to HOLD; the pilot flying believed the autothrottle would still maintain the selected speed.
The crew did not recognize that the autoflight system's mode combination left neither autopilot nor autothrottle managing airspeed.
The pilot flying relied on the autothrottle to protect airspeed and was uncomfortable hand-flying a visual approach without the ILS glideslope.
None of the three pilots monitored airspeed, which fell about 30 knots below the 137-knot approach speed before anyone called it out.
The airplane reached a minimum airspeed of 103 knots with idle thrust and a high sink rate, well below the glidepath.
The airplane was above the glidepath and fast at 1,600 feet, then below it and slow below 500 feet; the approach never met stabilized criteria.
The go-around was delayed until about three seconds before impact, when the airplane was below 100 feet with thrust only just advancing.
Communication and coordination about autoflight mode use were nonstandard, and the instructor pilot did not adequately supervise the pilot flying.
The pilot flying's training on planning and executing visual approaches was inadequate, and Asiana's training did not adequately explain the autothrottle HOLD behaviour.
The NTSB concluded that fatigue from the overnight trans-Pacific flight and circadian disruption likely degraded the crew's performance.
The complexity of the 777 autothrottle and autopilot flight director system interactions increased the likelihood of mode error.
Boeing's documentation inadequately described the autothrottle HOLD mode and the conditions under which speed protection is not available.
The pilot flying was transitioning to the 777 with about 35 hours on type and the instructor pilot was on his first flight as an instructor.
The low-airspeed alerting available did not provide timely enough warning; the NTSB recommended improved low-energy alerting for transport airplanes.
Evacuation was delayed about 90 seconds while the cabin manager consulted the cockpit, two slides inflated inside the cabin, and one ejected passenger was struck by a rescue vehicle.
The main landing gear and then the aft fuselage struck the seawall; the tail section separated.
A fire developed in the fuselage after the airplane came to rest, destroying the cabin.

events.text: Approach control vectors the flight for a visual approach to runway 28L; the ILS glideslope is out of service and the crew are asked to maintain 180 knots to 5 nm.
The airplane is above the desired glidepath and fast; the pilot flying uses vertical speed mode and then increases the descent rate to regain the path.
At about 1,600 feet the pilot flying selects FLCH SPD with the MCP altitude set at 3,000 feet; the autopilot begins to command a climb.
Pilot flying disconnects the autopilot and moves the thrust levers to idle; the autothrottle transitions to HOLD and no longer controls airspeed.
Autothrottle mode annunciation changes to HOLD on the flight mode annunciator; the change is not called out by either pilot.
The pilot flying hand-flies the descent using the PAPI as reference; thrust remains at idle and airspeed decays through the 137-knot approach speed.
The airplane passes 500 feet slightly below glidepath at about 134 knots with sink rate increasing; the PAPI shows three red lights shortly afterwards.
Passing about 200 feet the instructor pilot notices the four-red PAPI indication and low airspeed and calls for more speed; airspeed is about 118 knots.
Instructor pilot calls 'sink rate' as the airplane passes about 100 feet; the pilot flying pulls the nose up without adding thrust.
Thrust levers are advanced toward full thrust about seven seconds before impact; engines begin to spool up from idle.
Stick shaker activates about four seconds before impact.
Airspeed reaches its minimum of 103 knots about three seconds before impact; the instructor pilot calls for a go-around.
Main landing gear and aft fuselage strike the seawall short of the runway 28L threshold; the tail separates and the airplane slides and spins before coming to rest.
After a delay of about 90 seconds while the cabin manager checks with the cockpit, an evacuation is ordered when fire is seen outside; two slides have inflated inside the cabin.

recommendations.text: Require Boeing to revise 777 flight crew documentation and training to clearly describe the autothrottle HOLD mode and the conditions under which the autothrottle will not maintain the selected airspeed.
recommendations.outcome: Boeing revised 777 Flight Crew Training Manual and Operations Manual material on autothrottle modes.

recommendations.text: Convene a panel of human factors, aviation operations and design experts to evaluate the current Boeing autoflight design philosophy and recommend changes that would minimize mode confusion.
Develop a standard for low-energy alerting on transport-category airplanes so that crews receive timely warning of a low airspeed, high sink rate condition.
Revise training to require pilots to hand-fly visual approaches and to reinforce standard callouts, monitoring and go-around decision-making, including for instructor pilots.
recommendations.outcome: Asiana revised its training program and increased manual flying practice.

recommendations.text: Improve aircraft rescue and firefighting training and procedures for vehicle operation near an accident site and for interior firefighting of large aircraft.

dissent.position: In its formal comments on the draft report the Korean ARAIB argued that the autothrottle and autopilot flight director system design and Boeing's documentation should carry greater weight in the probable cause rather than being listed only as contributing factors.
dissent.topic: probable cause weighting of autoflight design

safety_changes: Boeing clarified 777 documentation and training material on autothrottle HOLD mode and speed protection.
Asiana Airlines revised its pilot training program, adding manual flying and visual approach practice and stronger instructor pilot standards.
FAA renewed emphasis on manual flight skills and monitoring (SAFO 13002 and Operational Use of Flight Path Management Systems working group follow-up).
San Francisco International Airport and other ARFF services revised procedures for vehicle movement and passenger accounting at accident sites.

notes: The precise clock time of the autothrottle HOLD transition is not recalled exactly; t0 is set to about 11:26:35 PDT (impact about 11:27:50) and may be off by roughly 15 seconds. Most event clocks are therefore left null and t values are relative estimates from the report's narrative (500 ft at 134 kt, 200 ft at about 118 kt, thrust advanced about 7 s before impact, stick shaker about 4 s before, minimum 103 kt about 3 s before).
Serious injuries (49) per the NTSB report; 187 minor.
Dissent entry reflects the Korean ARAIB's comments appended to the report as best recalled; verify wording against the report appendix.
Aircraft MSN not stated; engine model PW4090 as fitted to Asiana's 777-28E ER fleet.

records.title: UPS Airlines 1354

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Crash During a Nighttime Nonprecision Instrument Approach to Landing, UPS Flight 1354, Airbus A300-600, N155UP, Birmingham, Alabama, August 14, 2013

location.name: About 1 mile north of the runway 18 threshold, Birmingham-Shuttlesworth International Airport, Alabama

records.summary: Before dawn, with Birmingham's main runway closed, the UPS A300 crew flew the localizer non-precision approach to the shorter runway 18. The flight management computer was not properly set up so the vertical profile did not capture; the captain selected a 1,500 ft/min vertical speed descent and, expecting to break out at 1,000 ft, continued an unstabilized approach below the minimum descent altitude without either pilot noticing. The aircraft struck trees and terrain about a mile short of the runway, killing both pilots.
records.probable_cause: The flight crew's continuation of an unstabilized approach and their failure to monitor the aircraft's altitude during the approach, which led to an inadvertent descent below the minimum approach altitude and subsequently into terrain. Contributing were the flight crew's failure to properly configure and verify the flight management computer for the profile approach; the captain's failure to communicate his intentions to the first officer once it became apparent the vertical profile was not captured; the flight crew's expectation that they would break out of the clouds at 1,000 ft above ground level due to incomplete weather information; the first officer's failure to make the required minimums callouts; the captain's performance deficiencies likely due to factors including fatigue, distraction, or confusion, consistent with performance deficiencies exhibited during training; and the first officer's fatigue due to acute sleep loss resulting from her ineffective off-duty time management and circadian factors.

factors.evidence: The FMC was not properly configured and verified for the profile approach, so the vertical profile did not capture and the captain switched to vertical speed mode without announcing it.
The approach was continued with a 1,500 ft/min descent rate below the profile, contrary to stabilized approach criteria.
Neither pilot monitored the altitude against the MDA; the first officer did not make the required minimums callouts.
The aircraft descended through the MDA and continued toward terrain without the runway in sight.
The captain did not communicate his intentions after the profile failed to capture, and the first officer did not challenge the continued descent.
The first officer had acute sleep loss and the captain's performance deficiencies were likely related to fatigue, distraction or confusion.
The crew expected to break out at 1,000 ft agl based on incomplete weather information and did not recognise their proximity to terrain.
Required callouts were omitted and the approach was not flown according to the profile procedure.
Variable low clouds around 1,000 ft agl obscured the approach path; the crew had not received the latest observation indicating lower cloud.
The approach was flown before dawn at about 04:47 local time.
The EGPWS 'sink rate' caution occurred only seconds before impact; the NTSB recommended updated terrain awareness software with earlier alerting.
The aircraft struck trees and then terrain about 1 mile north of the runway 18 threshold in controlled flight.
The wreckage was consumed by fire after impact.

events.text: Crew learn that runway 6/24 at Birmingham is closed and plan the localizer runway 18 non-precision approach, briefing it as a profile (constant-angle) approach.
First officer sets up the FMC for the approach but the flight plan is not properly sequenced and verified, leaving the vertical profile unable to capture.
Approach control clears the flight for the localizer 18 approach; the crew have weather indicating a cloud base near 1,000 ft agl but not the latest observation of lower, variable cloud.
Passing the final approach fix the autopilot does not capture the vertical profile because the FMC was not configured correctly.
Captain selects vertical speed mode with a descent rate of about 1,500 ft/min without telling the first officer why the profile was not captured.
First officer calls one thousand feet, instruments cross-checked, but does not make the approaching-minimums or minimums callouts as the descent continues.
Aircraft descends through the minimum descent altitude with the descent rate unchanged and the runway not in sight.
Captain reports the runway in sight as the aircraft emerges from cloud well below the MDA and close to terrain.
EGPWS 'sink rate' caution sounds.
Captain begins to reduce the descent rate, remarking on the sink rate, but the aircraft is already among the trees.
Aircraft strikes trees and then terrain about 1 mile north of the runway 18 threshold, breaks up and catches fire; both pilots are killed.

recommendations.text: Require operators to install and use the latest EGPWS terrain awareness software that provides earlier alerting on non-precision approaches.
recommendations.outcome: Honeywell released updated EGPWS terrain clearance floor software; the FAA issued guidance encouraging updates.

recommendations.text: Emphasise in training the requirement to verify FMC configuration for profile approaches, to announce automation mode changes and to go around from an unstabilized approach.
Ensure that flight crews receive the most current weather observations and that dispatch procedures deliver updated terminal weather before approach.
Address pilot fatigue through fatigue risk management and education on effective use of rest periods.

safety_changes: Updated EGPWS terrain clearance floor software with earlier alerting was released and adopted by operators.
UPS revised its non-precision approach procedures and fatigue risk management; the accident featured in debate on the cargo carve-out from FAA flight duty time rules.

notes: t0 is the approximate impact time of 04:47 CDT; all other event times are estimated offsets and no clock values are given for them.
The MDA value, the exact EGPWS alert sequence and the first officer's callouts are paraphrased from memory of the report.
Recommendation numbers not recalled and are left null.

records.title: Tatarstan Airlines 363

agencies.name: Interstate Aviation Committee
agencies.report_title: Final report on the investigation of the accident to Boeing 737-53A VQ-BBN at Kazan, 17 November 2013

location.name: Kazan International Airport, near runway 29

records.summary: On a night approach to Kazan the crew found the aircraft displaced from the localiser course and, at about 270 m (900 ft), initiated a go-around with TOGA thrust. On the 737-500 a single-channel go-around disconnects the autopilot, and the captain, who had never flown a go-around in the aircraft outside the simulator, did not manage the pitch: it rose to about 25 degrees and the speed decayed, after which he pushed the column forward and the aircraft pitched to about 75 degrees nose down. It struck the ground near the runway about 45 seconds after the go-around began. All 50 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The MAK concluded that the accident resulted from the crew's loss of spatial orientation and inability to fly a go-around manually at night, which led to a steep dive and impact with the ground. The captain's inadequate skills, the deficiencies in the airline's pilot training and qualification, and the first officer's failure to monitor and intervene were identified as causes. Systemic contributing factors included deficiencies in the training and licensing of the crew (the captain's licence had been issued on the basis of training records found to be doubtful), the operator's lack of a functioning safety management and flight data monitoring system, and inadequate oversight by the aviation authority.

factors.evidence: The approach was flown with a significant lateral displacement from the localiser and the crew elected to go around at about 270 m.
Pressing TOGA on the 737-500 disconnected the autopilot; the crew did not appear to expect to be flying manually and did not control the pitch.
After the pitch rose to about 25 degrees and the speed decayed, the captain pushed the control column fully forward and the pitch decreased to about 75 degrees nose down.
The MAK concluded that the captain lost spatial orientation at night in cloud during the go-around.
The report considered the acceleration under TOGA thrust as a source of the false sensation of pitch-up that led to the nose-down input.
The go-around was flown at night in instrument conditions without external references.
The captain had never performed a go-around in the 737 in actual flight and had limited manual flying experience on the type.
The MAK found that the crew's training and checking at the operator did not develop manual go-around skills and that the captain's initial licence training was deficient.
The airline lacked an effective safety management system and flight data monitoring that could have detected the crew's deficiencies.
The report cited deficiencies in the authority's oversight of pilot licensing and training organisations, including the doubtful basis of the captain's licence.
The first officer did not monitor the pitch or intervene when the captain's input drove the aircraft into a dive.
The aircraft struck the ground near the runway in a near-vertical nose-down attitude at high speed.

events.text: Night approach to runway 29 at Kazan; the aircraft is displaced from the localiser course and the crew try to correct.
The crew discuss the map shift and the displacement from the approach course.
At about 270 m (900 ft) the captain calls a go-around and presses TOGA; the autopilot disconnects and thrust increases.
The pitch attitude rises to about 25 degrees as the aircraft climbs; the airspeed begins to decay.
Flaps retracted to 15 and gear raised; the aircraft climbs to about 700 m (2,300 ft) with the speed decreasing.
The captain pushes the control column forward; the pitch attitude decreases rapidly through level flight into a dive.
The pitch attitude reaches about 75 degrees nose down; the airspeed increases rapidly and the aircraft descends at a very high rate.
The first officer does not intervene effectively; the captain begins to pull but the height is insufficient.
The aircraft strikes the ground near the runway at about 450 km/h in a near-vertical attitude and disintegrates; all 50 on board die.

recommendations.text: Verify the training records and licences of pilots trained at the flight training organisations concerned and strengthen oversight of pilot licensing.
Include manual go-arounds from intermediate heights, at night and with autopilot disconnection, in recurrent training, and address somatogravic illusion.
Implement effective safety management and flight data monitoring programmes so that crew performance deficiencies are detected.
Review the 737 Classic single-channel go-around logic and the associated crew guidance on autopilot disconnection at TOGA.

dissent.position: The Russian Federal Air Transport Agency (Rosaviatsia) disagreed with the MAK's conclusions, arguing that a possible malfunction of the elevator control system had not been excluded, and recommended a suspension of 737 operations pending checks; the MAK rejected this and Rosaviatsia's representatives recorded a dissenting opinion on the investigation's findings.
dissent.topic: aircraft elevator control versus crew performance

safety_changes: Rosaviatsia audited pilot training organisations and revoked a number of pilot licences issued on the basis of deficient training records.
Tatarstan Airlines' operating certificate was revoked in December 2013.
Russian operators were required to include manual go-around training at night and from intermediate heights in recurrent training.

notes: t0 is null: the exact UTC time of the go-around was not verified (the accident occurred at about 19:24 local time, 15:24 UTC). Event t values are approximate offsets from the go-around initiation reconstructed from the MAK narrative (about 45 seconds to impact).
The pitch values (about +25 and -75 degrees), altitude (about 700 m), and impact speed (about 450 km/h) are from the MAK interim findings as recalled.
The MAK final report number and publication date (believed to be December 2015) were not verified.
The dissent entry records Rosaviatsia's public disagreement with the MAK conclusions; whether it is formally appended to the report as a dissenting opinion was not verified.

records.title: Air Algérie 5017 (Swiftair)

agencies.name: Commission d'Enquête sur l'accident du vol AH5017
agencies.report_title: Rapport final - Accident survenu le 24 juillet 2014 au MD-83 immatriculé EC-LTV exploité par Swiftair S.A. (vol AH5017)

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la sécurité de l'aviation civile
Comisión de Investigación de Accidentes e Incidentes de Aviación Civil

location.name: Near Gossi, Gourma-Rharous region, northern Mali

records.summary: In cruise at FL310 at night, skirting a line of convective cloud, the MD-83 entered ice crystal conditions with engine anti-ice not selected. Ice obstructed the engine inlet pressure (Pt2) sensors, causing the EPR indications to over-read; the autothrottle reduced thrust to hold the target while the autopilot held altitude, and airspeed decayed over several minutes until the aircraft stalled. Recovery was not achieved and the aircraft struck the ground in a steep spiral descent with the loss of all 116 occupants.
records.probable_cause: The accident resulted from the obstruction of the Pt2 pressure sensors by ice crystals while the engine anti-ice system was not activated, leading to erroneous EPR values and a reduction in thrust commanded by the autothrottle, the resulting decrease in speed not being detected by the crew, and the autopilot holding altitude until the aircraft stalled. The crew's late and inappropriate reaction to the buffet and stall, with nose-up inputs and no stall recovery, led to the loss of control. Contributing factors included the crew's inadequate monitoring of flight parameters, the absence of a low-speed warning at the onset, the ambiguity of the engine anti-ice procedures, and the crew's weather avoidance strategy.

factors.evidence: The flight was routing along and through the upper part of a large mesoscale convective system over Mali at night.
Ice crystals at FL310 in the anvil of the convective system accreted on the engine inlet pressure probes.
The crew did not activate the engine anti-ice system, which would have heated the Pt2 sensors.
The obstructed Pt2 sensors caused the EPR indications for both engines to become erroneously high.
The autothrottle, in Mach hold, reduced thrust in response to the over-reading EPR, and the crew did not perceive that thrust was decaying.
Airspeed fell from about 290 kt to about 200 kt over several minutes while the autopilot maintained FL310 by increasing pitch.
Neither pilot noticed the airspeed decay, the decreasing N1 or the increasing pitch attitude.
The aircraft stalled at about 1.1 of the initial speed margin; buffet and roll oscillations were followed by autopilot disconnection.
The crew's control inputs after the stall were predominantly nose-up and left, with no application of the stall recovery procedure.
The aircraft entered a steep, rapidly rolling descent from FL310 and struck the ground about a minute later.
Procedures for using engine anti-ice in icing conditions at cruise, and the effects of Pt2 icing on EPR, were not sufficiently explicit in the operator's documentation.
The flight was at night, with no external visual cues during the upset.

events.text: Flight AH5017 departs Ouagadougou for Algiers with 110 passengers and 6 crew.
Crew request a deviation to the left to avoid weather returns; the aircraft continues its climb to FL310.
Aircraft level at FL310 at about 290 kt with autopilot and autothrottle engaged in Mach hold; engine anti-ice is off.
Aircraft enters the upper part of the convective system; ice crystals begin to obstruct the engine Pt2 sensors.
EPR indications for both engines begin to rise erroneously; the autothrottle retards the thrust levers to hold the EPR target.
Airspeed decays steadily as the autopilot raises the pitch attitude to hold FL310; N1 falls towards a low value.
Speed reaches about 200 kt with pitch attitude above 5 degrees; no comment from the crew, who are still discussing the weather.
Aircraft begins to buffet and roll; the autopilot disengages as the aircraft stalls.
Crew inputs are mostly nose-up and left; the aircraft rolls sharply left and enters a steep descent with increasing bank.
The aircraft descends in a spiral at a very high rate with bank angles beyond 60 degrees; no recovery.
Aircraft strikes the ground near Gossi with a high rate of descent and bank; all 116 occupants killed.

recommendations.text: Require that the effects of ice crystal icing on engine pressure sensors and the resulting erroneous EPR indications be addressed through design or through clear operational procedures and warnings.
Clarify the operating procedures for engine anti-ice activation in cruise icing conditions on the MD-80 family.
Study the introduction of a low-speed or low-energy alert in cruise on aircraft not equipped with one, so that crews are warned before an approach to stall.
Reinforce crew training on monitoring of flight parameters in cruise, on the effects of ice crystals on engine sensors and on stall recovery at high altitude.

safety_changes: Boeing revised MD-80 documentation on engine anti-ice use and the effect of Pt2 probe icing on EPR.
Industry attention to ice crystal icing effects on engine sensors and to low-energy alerting in cruise.

notes: Clock times other than departure are approximate; the final loss of control occurred around 01:45-01:47 UTC. t values are estimated.
Airspeed values (about 290 kt decaying to about 200 kt) are approximate readings from the published FDR analysis.
Lead investigative body is the Malian Commission d'Enquête with BEA carrying out the technical investigation on delegation; report publication date is approximate.
MSN and lat/lon are approximate.

records.title: Indonesia AirAsia 8501

agencies.name: Komite Nasional Keselamatan Transportasi
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Investigation Report, PT. Indonesia Air Asia, Airbus A320-216, PK-AXC, Karimata Strait, Republic of Indonesia, 28 December 2014

agencies.name: Air Accident Investigation Bureau of Singapore

location.name: Java Sea (Karimata Strait), off Pangkalan Bun, Central Kalimantan

records.summary: In cruise at FL320 over the Java Sea the A320's rudder travel limiter fault recurred four times, a problem that had appeared 23 times in the previous year because of a cracked solder joint. After the fourth warning the captain pulled the circuit breakers of both flight augmentation computers. The autopilot and autothrust disengaged and the flight controls reverted to alternate law; the aircraft rolled to 54 degrees before the first officer reacted, then pitched up into a steep climb. The aircraft stalled at about 38,000 ft and descended into the sea, killing all 162 on board.
records.probable_cause: The KNKT found that a cracked solder joint in the rudder travel limiter unit caused repeated AUTO FLT RUD TRV LIM SYS failures, which the airline's maintenance system had not resolved. The crew's action of pulling the FAC circuit breakers in flight, which was not an approved procedure, disengaged the autopilot and degraded the flight control law, and the subsequent delayed and inappropriate crew inputs, including a sustained nose-up sidestick command and simultaneous inputs from both pilots after the captain's ambiguous 'pull down' instruction, led to an upset from which the crew did not recover. The crew had not received upset recovery training.

factors.evidence: The rudder travel limiter fault had occurred 23 times in the previous 12 months, with increasing frequency, without the root cause being identified.
Repeated troubleshooting reset the system rather than finding the cracked solder joint on the RTLU electronic module; the airline's reliability monitoring did not escalate the repetitive defect.
The captain pulled the FAC 1 and FAC 2 circuit breakers in flight to reset the system, an action not provided for in the flight crew procedures.
De-energising both FACs disengaged the autopilot and autothrust.
Loss of both FACs caused the flight controls to revert to alternate law, removing the yaw damper and rudder travel limiting and the normal-law protections.
The aircraft rolled left for about nine seconds to 54 degrees of bank before the first officer, as pilot flying, made any input.
The first officer applied a sustained nose-up sidestick input that took the aircraft into a climb of up to 11,000 ft/min and a stall.
The captain's instruction 'pull down' was ambiguous and the first officer continued to pull back; there was no clear transfer of control.
Both pilots made sidestick inputs simultaneously without the priority push-button being used, so the inputs were summed.
The nose-up inputs were maintained through the stall warning and the aircraft remained stalled during the descent.
The airline's training program did not include upset prevention and recovery training for this scenario.
The stall warning activated as the aircraft climbed through about FL370 and the aircraft stalled near 38,000 ft.
The aircraft descended in a stalled condition for about three minutes until it struck the sea.

events.text: Over the preceding year the AUTO FLT RUD TRV LIM SYS fault occurs 23 times on PK-AXC with increasing frequency; maintenance repeatedly resets the system without finding the cracked solder joint in the rudder travel limiter unit.
Departs Surabaya for Singapore with 155 passengers and 7 crew; the first officer is pilot flying.
First master caution in cruise at FL320: AUTO FLT RUD TRV LIM SYS. The crew carry out the ECAM actions and the fault clears.
The fault recurs a second time; ECAM actions repeated.
The fault recurs a third time; ECAM actions repeated.
Fourth master caution; the fault persists after the ECAM actions.

The captain pulls the FAC 1 and then the FAC 2 circuit breakers on the panel behind his seat to reset the system. Both FACs de-energise; autopilot and autothrust disengage and the flight controls revert to alternate law.
Without yaw damping the aircraft rolls left; no sidestick input is made for about nine seconds and the bank reaches 54 degrees.
The first officer applies right roll and sustained nose-up sidestick; the aircraft climbs from FL320 at up to 11,000 ft/min.
Stall warning activates as the aircraft climbs through about FL370 with airspeed decaying.
The captain repeatedly says 'pull down'; the first officer continues to pull back. The captain applies nose-down on his own sidestick without taking priority, and the two inputs are summed.
The aircraft reaches about 38,000 ft, stalls and begins a rapid descent in a nose-up, stalled attitude.
Stall warning continues; nose-up inputs are maintained and the aircraft remains stalled through the descent.
The flight recorders stop as the aircraft strikes the Java Sea; all 162 on board are killed.

recommendations.text: Improve the maintenance reliability program so that repetitive defects are identified and resolved, and provide flight crews with upset prevention and recovery training.
