recommendations.outcome: The airline introduced upset recovery training and revised its repetitive-defect handling.

recommendations.text: Ensure operators' maintenance and training programs address repetitive defects and upset recovery, and improve surveillance.

Reinforce guidance to operators that circuit breakers are not to be pulled in flight as a troubleshooting action, and review procedures and training for dual sidestick input and alternate law handling.

safety_changes: Indonesia AirAsia introduced upset prevention and recovery training and revised its handling of repetitive defects.
The Indonesian DGCA audited the airline and tightened oversight of maintenance reliability programs.
The accident reinforced industry-wide adoption of upset prevention and recovery training and the prohibition on in-flight circuit breaker resets for troubleshooting.

notes: The clock for the fourth master caution (23:15:36) and the end of recording (23:20:35) are as recalled from the KNKT report; times of the first three faults are to the minute and the times of the circuit-breaker pulls, roll, climb and stall are approximate offsets.
The maximum altitude reached (about 38,000 ft) and the climb rate (up to 11,000 ft/min) are from the report summary; peak descent rate is omitted.
The captain's 'pull down' line is quoted without an exact time.
Wreckage coordinates are approximate.

records.title: TransAsia Airways 235

agencies.name: Aviation Safety Council
agencies.report_title: Aviation Occurrence Report: 4 February 2015, TransAsia Airways Flight GE235, ATR72-212A, Loss of Control and Crashed into Keelung River Three Nautical Miles East of Songshan Airport

location.name: Keelung River, Nangang, Taipei, about 3 nm east of Songshan Airport

records.summary: Shortly after take-off from Taipei Songshan, the ATR 72-600's automatic take-off power control system auto-feathered the number 2 engine following an intermittent signal from its auto-feather unit. The captain, as pilot flying, misidentified the failed engine, retarded the operating number 1 engine to idle and then shut it down. With no thrust, the aircraft stalled at low altitude, rolled steeply, clipped a taxi on an elevated road and crashed inverted into the Keelung River. Forty-three of the 58 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The ASC found that the number 2 engine auto-feathered because of an intermittent signal discontinuity in its auto-feather unit, and that the captain then reduced power on the operating engine and shut it down without following the engine failure procedure or confirming the failed engine with the other pilot, leaving the aircraft with no thrust. The crew did not respond effectively to the stall warnings and lost control. Contributing were the captain's demonstrated weaknesses in handling engine failures, inadequate crew coordination, TransAsia's deficient flight crew training and safety management, and inadequate regulatory oversight.

factors.evidence: About 37 seconds after take-off the ATPCS auto-feathered the number 2 engine following an intermittent signal from its auto-feather unit; the engine itself was serviceable.
The failure occurred at about 1,200 ft during the initial climb, with a master warning and the need for immediate single-engine handling.
The captain retarded the number 1 (operating) engine's power lever to idle and later moved its condition lever to fuel shut-off, shutting down the only engine producing thrust.
The crew did not carry out the engine flame-out at take-off procedure as trained, which requires identification and confirmation of the failed engine before any lever is moved.
The pilot monitoring did not challenge the captain's actions on the wrong engine and the two pilots did not cross-check before the operating engine was shut down.
The captain's training records showed difficulties in handling engine failures after take-off; he had failed a simulator check on this before later passing.
TransAsia's ATR 72-600 differences training and its handling of pilots with unsatisfactory performance were found deficient.
The ASC found systemic deficiencies in TransAsia's flight operations management and safety management system.
The report found that the Civil Aeronautics Administration's oversight had not identified or corrected the operator's deficiencies.
The captain did not recognise until seconds before impact that he had pulled back the wrong engine.
The stall warning and stick shaker activated repeatedly and the stick pusher operated as airspeed decayed; the crew did not recover.
With both propellers producing no thrust the aircraft stalled at low altitude.
The aircraft rolled steeply left, struck a taxi and the parapet of an elevated road and crashed inverted into the river.

events.text: Take-off from Songshan runway 10 with the captain as pilot flying, a first officer as pilot monitoring and a third pilot in the observer's seat.
Climbing through about 1,200 ft, the ATPCS auto-feathers the number 2 propeller after an intermittent signal from the auto-feather unit; master warning 'ENG 2 FLAME OUT AT TAKE OFF'.
The captain announces he will pull back the number 1 power lever and begins retarding the operating engine's power lever toward idle, without confirming the failed engine.
The pilot monitoring makes callouts and reads the warning but does not challenge the action on the wrong engine; no cross-check is made.
With number 2 feathered and number 1 at low power the aircraft stops climbing; airspeed begins to decay and the autopilot is disconnected.
The captain moves the number 1 condition lever to fuel shut-off; the operating engine shuts down and the aircraft has no thrust.
Stall warning and stick shaker activate repeatedly as airspeed decays; the stick pusher operates.
The crew declare MAYDAY, reporting an engine flame-out, and attempt to restart the number 1 engine.
The captain exclaims that he pulled back the wrong side throttle.

The aircraft rolls steeply left, its left wing strikes a taxi and the parapet of the elevated Huandong Viaduct, and it crashes inverted into the Keelung River. 43 of the 58 on board die; 15 survive, and two people in the taxi are injured.

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: Wow, pulled back the wrong side throttle.

recommendations.text: Review and strengthen flight crew training on engine failure after take-off, crew coordination and the management of pilots with unsatisfactory performance records, and improve the airline's safety management system.
recommendations.outcome: TransAsia retrained its ATR crews after the accident; the airline ceased operations in November 2016.

recommendations.text: Improve the oversight of operators' flight crew training, checking and safety management.
Address the auto-feather unit signal discontinuity that triggered the uncommanded auto-feather, including inspection of units in service.
recommendations.outcome: The manufacturer issued service information on auto-feather unit inspection and replacement.

safety_changes: Taiwan's CAA ordered proficiency checks for all TransAsia ATR pilots immediately after the accident; some pilots failed and were grounded.
TransAsia's oversight and training were overhauled; the airline ceased operations in 2016.
The auto-feather unit's soldering defect led to inspections and replacements across the ATR fleet.

notes: The auto-feather time (10:52:38) and the captain's final remark (10:54:34) are as recalled from the ASC report; intermediate event offsets are approximate.
The CVR line is given in the report's English translation; the original Mandarin wording is not reproduced.
The number of seriously injured survivors is not given (null).
The Aviation Safety Council is now the Taiwan Transportation Safety Board; its home page is used as the source.

records.title: Germanwings 9525

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la sécurité de l'aviation civile
agencies.report_title: Final Report - Accident on 24 March 2015 at Prads-Haute-Bléone (Alpes-de-Haute-Provence, France) to the Airbus A320-211 registered D-AIPX operated by Germanwings

agencies.name: Comisión de Investigación de Accidentes e Incidentes de Aviación Civil

location.name: Massif des Trois-Évêchés, Prads-Haute-Bléone, Alpes-de-Haute-Provence

records.summary: Shortly after the aircraft reached cruise at FL380 the captain left the cockpit. The first officer, alone at the controls, locked the cockpit door, set the selected altitude to 100 ft and initiated a continuous descent. He did not respond to calls from ATC or to the captain's attempts to re-enter the cockpit. The aircraft struck a mountainside in the French Alps about ten minutes later, killing all 150 on board.
records.probable_cause: The collision with the ground was due to the deliberate and planned action of the co-pilot, who decided to commit suicide while alone in the cockpit. The process for medical certification of pilots, in particular self-reporting in case of decrease in medical fitness, did not succeed in preventing the co-pilot, who was experiencing mental disorder with psychotic symptoms, from exercising the privilege of his licence. Contributing factors were the co-pilot's probable fear of losing his ability to fly if he declared his condition, the potential financial consequences, the lack of clear guidelines in German regulations on when a threat to public safety outweighs medical confidentiality, and cockpit door locking requirements designed for security threats that made it impossible to enter the flight compartment before the aircraft impacted the terrain.

factors.evidence: The co-pilot, alone in the cockpit, deliberately set the selected altitude to 100 ft and flew the aircraft into terrain; he had rehearsed altitude selections on the outbound flight.

Medical certification relied on self-declaration; the co-pilot's psychiatric history and current treatment were not known to the authority or the operator, and German rules on breaking medical confidentiality lacked clear guidance.
The reinforced cockpit door and its lock, designed against hostile entry, could be kept locked from inside and prevented the captain from regaining access.
The co-pilot was experiencing a mental disorder with psychotic symptoms and had been prescribed medication incompatible with flying.
The aircraft descended under control at about 3,500 ft/min and collided with the mountainside at about 6,000 ft.

events.text: Flight 4U9525 departs Barcelona for Düsseldorf; the first officer is pilot flying.
Aircraft levels at cruise flight level FL380 under autopilot.
Captain tells the first officer he is leaving the cockpit and asks him to take over radio communications; the cockpit door is heard closing.
Selected altitude on the FCU changed from 38,000 ft to 100 ft; the autopilot begins a descent in OPEN DESCENT mode.
Aircraft descending at about 3,500 ft/min; the first officer adjusts the selected speed and the autopilot remains engaged.
Marseille control calls the aircraft several times and receives no reply; the first officer's breathing is recorded and regular throughout the descent.
Cockpit door access buzzer sounds as the captain requests entry; no response. The keypad emergency access request is later refused from inside.
Captain knocks on the door and asks the first officer to open it; the interphone and the emergency door code are unsuccessful.
Violent blows on the cockpit door are heard on the CVR as the captain tries to break in; French air defence is alerted and a fighter is scrambled.
GPWS terrain alerts and master warning sound as the aircraft descends below 7,000 ft toward the mountains.
Aircraft collides with the mountainside at about 6,000 ft and disintegrates; all 150 occupants killed.

recommendations.text: Require operators to include in their medical assessment of pilots a systematic psychiatric evaluation where there is a history of psychological trouble, and define conditions for pilots with such a history to be followed up.
recommendations.outcome: EASA introduced psychological assessment before employment and support programmes.

recommendations.text: Define clear rules to require health care providers to inform the authorities when a specific patient's health is very likely to affect public safety, including when the patient refuses to consent, while balancing patient confidentiality.
Promote the implementation of peer support programmes for pilots and mitigate the socio-economic risks of loss of licence for medical reasons, for example through loss-of-licence insurance.
recommendations.outcome: EU regulation 2018/1042 introduced mandatory pilot support programmes and psychological assessment.

recommendations.text: Analyse the risks of the cockpit door locking system and evaluate the relevance of a minimum of two crew members in the cockpit at all times.
recommendations.outcome: EASA issued a safety information bulletin recommending two persons in the cockpit; later relaxed after risk assessment.

safety_changes: Temporary two-persons-in-the-cockpit recommendation across European operators.
EU regulation 2018/1042 requiring psychological assessment of pilots, pilot support programmes and alcohol testing.
Review of medical confidentiality rules and aeromedical data sharing among European authorities.

notes: Timeline seconds after t0 (09:30:53, selected altitude change) are approximate except impact at 09:41:06; the intermediate clock strings are estimated to within about a minute.
BEA report reference number and recommendation ids not reproduced with confidence; ids set to null.
Category SEC used for a deliberate act; factor cfit used as the outcome because the aircraft was under control until impact.

records.title: Shoreham Airshow Hawker Hunter

agencies.name: Air Accidents Investigation Branch
agencies.report_title: Report on the accident to Hawker Hunter T7, G-BXFI near Shoreham Airport on 22 August 2015

location.name: A27 road near Shoreham Airport, West Sussex

records.summary: During a display at the Shoreham Airshow the Hunter entered a loop-type manoeuvre from too low a height and at too low an airspeed. At the apex the aircraft was at 2,700 ft, below the minimum required to complete the manoeuvre, and the pilot did not fly an escape manoeuvre. The aircraft descended into traffic on the A27 dual carriageway, killing 11 people on the ground; the pilot survived.
records.probable_cause: The aircraft did not achieve sufficient height at the apex of the accident manoeuvre to complete it before impacting the ground, because the combination of low entry speed and low engine thrust in the upward half of the manoeuvre was insufficient. An escape manoeuvre was not carried out, despite the aircraft not achieving the required minimum apex height. The pilot either did not perceive that an escape manoeuvre was necessary or did not realise one was possible at the speed achieved at the apex. Contributing: the display sequence had been planned for a different aircraft type, the pilot had not practised the sequence in the Hunter, and the regulatory and organisational oversight of displays did not ensure adequate risk management for the public outside the display site.

factors.evidence: The loop was entered at about 185 kt and 200 ft, lower and slower than required, with the throttle not advanced to full power during the pull-up.
The pilot did not recognise at the apex that the aircraft was 800 ft below the required gate height and that an escape manoeuvre was needed.
The pilot had not practised the display sequence in the Hunter, and the escape manoeuvre had not been practised or trained.
The CAA's oversight of flying displays did not require adequate risk assessment for areas outside the display site, and display authorisation evaluation was limited.
The display organiser's and operator's risk assessments did not adequately consider third parties outside the airfield boundary or enforce the gate heights in the pilot's display plan.
The pilot's recent display experience was predominantly on the Jet Provost, with limited recent flying on the Hunter.
The aircraft struck the A27 road in a nose-up attitude at about 100 kt below the speed at which recovery was possible, colliding with vehicles.
A fireball followed the impact, contributing to the deaths of persons on the road.

events.text: G-BXFI departs North Weald for the Shoreham display.
Pilot commences the display with a run-in and a series of aerobatic manoeuvres over the display line.
Following a turn to the north, the pilot positions for a bent loop with a quarter clover at the top, entering from the east of the display line.
Pull-up into the loop starts at about 185 kt and about 200 ft agl, below the 350 kt / 500 ft entry parameters in the pilot's plan; throttle not advanced to full.
Aircraft climbs inverted; engine at less than full power throughout the upward half of the manoeuvre.
Apex of the manoeuvre reached at about 2,700 ft, 800 ft below the 3,500 ft minimum gate height, at about 105 kt.
No escape manoeuvre (rolling upright and recovering) is flown; the pilot continues the downward half of the loop.
Recognising the aircraft is low, the pilot applies increasing back stick; the aircraft reaches maximum g but is unable to arrest the descent.
Aircraft strikes the A27 westbound carriageway in a nose-high attitude, colliding with vehicles and breaking up; a fireball follows.
Eleven people on the road are killed; the pilot is thrown clear of the wreckage and seriously injured.

recommendations.text: Introduce measures to ensure that flying displays are not conducted over areas where members of the public may be present unless the risk is acceptable; a review of the risk to third parties outside display sites.
recommendations.outcome: CAA introduced restrictions on aerobatics by vintage jets over land and enhanced display risk assessment requirements.

recommendations.text: Require that display pilots' authorisations are evaluated for the specific aircraft type and manoeuvres they intend to fly, and that escape manoeuvres are trained and practised.
Require the recording of flight data on ex-military jets used for displays and improve the maintenance standards oversight for such aircraft.

safety_changes: CAA restricted vintage jet displays over land to flypasts pending review, and later introduced new display risk assessment requirements (CAP 403 revisions).
Enhanced oversight of display authorisation evaluations and requirements for display sequences to be practised on type.
Increased separation distances between display lines and the public, including areas outside the airfield boundary.

notes: Entry and apex speeds/heights are the AAIB's derived values (approximately 185 kt / 200 ft entry, 2,700 ft / 105 kt apex, 3,500 ft required gate).
Event clock times are approximate relative to the 12:22 impact; the seconds are estimated.
Only one recommendation number (2015-039) is given; others left null. MSN is uncertain.

records.title: Flydubai 981

agencies.name: Interstate Aviation Committee
agencies.report_title: Final report on the investigation of the accident to Boeing 737-8KN A6-FDN at Rostov-on-Don, 19 March 2016

location.name: Rostov-on-Don airport, runway 22

records.summary: After a first go-around from an approach to Rostov-on-Don in strong gusting wind and windshear, the crew held for about two hours and made a second approach at night. At about 220 m (720 ft) the captain initiated a second go-around; with TOGA thrust at light weight the aircraft pitched up steeply. The captain, subject to a somatogravic illusion and without outside references, pushed the control column forward and applied nose-down stabilizer trim for about 12 seconds. The aircraft pitched to a steep dive and struck the runway at high speed about 40 seconds after the go-around began. All 62 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The MAK concluded that the accident was caused by an incorrect aircraft configuration and crew piloting during the go-around, leading to the captain's loss of situational awareness under the effect of a somatogravic illusion at night in instrument conditions, an inappropriate nose-down control input and prolonged nose-down stabilizer trim, and a dive from which recovery was not possible. Contributing factors included the presence of turbulence and windshear, the crew's fatigue after a long night duty, the lack of specific training for go-arounds from intermediate heights with high thrust and light weight, inconsistencies in the flight director cues during the go-around, and deficiencies in the crew's resource management and in the captain's psychological state during the second approach.

factors.evidence: Strong gusting wind and windshear warnings led to the first go-around and were present during the second approach.
The second approach and go-around were flown at night in cloud with no external visual references.
The crew had been on duty since the evening and the accident occurred at about 03:40 local time after two hours of holding; the MAK cited fatigue as contributing.
The second approach was flown in turbulent conditions with speed and path deviations before the go-around decision at about 220 m.
The report found that the flight director pitch command during the go-around did not correspond to the crew's expectation and contributed to the captain's confusion.
The MAK concluded that the acceleration under TOGA thrust produced a false sensation of excessive pitch-up which led the captain to push the nose down.
The captain lost awareness of the aircraft's attitude and did not use the attitude indicator to recover from the dive.
The captain pushed the control column forward and applied nose-down stabilizer trim for about 12 seconds, pitching the aircraft into a steep dive.
The first officer did not intervene effectively when the captain applied the nose-down input and the aircraft entered the dive.
The MAK found that go-arounds from intermediate heights with full thrust at light weight, and somatogravic illusion, were not adequately addressed in the operator's training.
The report identified loss of situational awareness by the captain as the central element of the sequence.
The aircraft struck the runway in a steep nose-down attitude at high speed about 40 seconds after the go-around was initiated.

events.text: First approach to runway 22 abandoned at about 1,100 ft after a windshear warning; the aircraft climbs away and enters a holding pattern.
The crew hold for about two hours awaiting improvement in the wind, discussing whether to divert; the captain decides on a second approach.
Second ILS approach to runway 22 at night in gusting wind and turbulence with the autopilot disengaged.
At about 220 m (720 ft) the captain calls a go-around and presses TOGA; the thrust increases toward full and the aircraft pitches up.
With full thrust at light weight the pitch attitude rises to about 18 degrees and the aircraft accelerates and climbs rapidly; the flight director pitch cue differs from the crew's expectation.
Flaps retracted to 15 and landing gear raised; the pitch and climb rate remain high.
Under a somatogravic illusion the captain pushes the control column forward; the pitch attitude decreases and passes through level flight.
The captain applies nose-down stabilizer trim for about 12 seconds; the pitch attitude continues to decrease into a dive.
The first officer calls out and pulls back on the column; the captain's input and the nose-down trim dominate.
The aircraft is in a steep nose-down dive with airspeed increasing; GPWS warnings sound.
The aircraft strikes runway 22 at high speed in a steep nose-down attitude about 40 seconds after the go-around began; all 62 on board die.

recommendations.text: Include in training the recognition of and recovery from somatogravic illusion during go-arounds with high thrust and light weight, and go-arounds from intermediate heights.
Review the flight director go-around pitch guidance and its transitions on the 737 so that the cues are consistent during a go-around initiated above the normal decision height.
Review crew rostering and fatigue risk management for long night duties with extended holding, and the decision-making guidance for diversion in adverse weather.
Reinforce crew resource management training on monitoring and intervention by the pilot monitoring during go-arounds.

safety_changes: Flydubai revised its go-around training, fatigue management and diversion decision-making guidance after the accident.
The accident reinforced industry attention (including the Flight Safety Foundation and EASA) on go-around safety and somatogravic illusion at night.

notes: t0 (about 00:40:50 UTC, the start of the second go-around) and the first go-around time (about 22:42 UTC) are given from the MAK narrative as recalled; the exact seconds were not verified. Event offsets within the final 40 seconds are approximate.
The final pitch attitude and impact speed are deliberately not given as numbers because the exact figures were not verified.
The MAK final report was published in November 2019; the exact report number was not verified.
The accredited representative list (GCAA, NTSB) is based on the states of registry and manufacture.

records.title: Emirates 521

agencies.name: General Civil Aviation Authority
agencies.report_title: Air Accident Investigation Sector final report, Runway impact during attempted go-around, Boeing 777-31H A6-EMW, Dubai International Airport, 3 August 2016

location.name: Dubai International Airport, runway 12L

records.summary: Landing on runway 12L at Dubai in hot conditions with a reported windshear, the 777 experienced a shift to a tailwind in the flare and floated well beyond the touchdown zone. After the main gear touched down the crew initiated a go-around, but because the aircraft was on the ground the TOGA switches were inhibited and the autothrottle left the thrust levers at idle, which the crew did not notice. The aircraft became airborne on pitch alone, the gear was retracted, and it sank back onto the runway with the engines still at idle. The fuselage slid to a stop and caught fire; all 300 occupants evacuated, but a firefighter was killed when the centre fuel tank exploded.
records.probable_cause: The GCAA concluded that the aircraft impacted the runway during an attempted go-around because the flight crew did not realise that the autothrottle had not responded to the TOGA switch presses, which were inhibited by the on-ground logic, so that the thrust levers remained at idle and the aircraft could not sustain flight after it became airborne. Contributing factors included the crew's reliance on automation and lack of awareness of the TOGA inhibit logic, the absence of a flight-deck alert or procedural guidance for a go-around after touchdown, the crew's ineffective monitoring of the flight mode annunciations and engine thrust during the go-around, the long landing resulting from a headwind-to-tailwind shift, and the decision to retract the landing gear before a positive rate of climb was established with thrust.

factors.evidence: A windshear warning had been broadcast; in the flare the wind shifted from a headwind to a tailwind of about 16 kt, extending the float.
The tailwind component in the flare increased the groundspeed and the landing distance.
The aircraft floated and the main gear touched down about 1,100 m beyond the threshold, well past the touchdown zone; the RAAS 'LONG LANDING' aural alert sounded.
The crew pressed the TOGA switches after touchdown, when they were inhibited by the weight-on-wheels logic, and did not recognise that the go-around mode had not engaged.
The autothrottle remained in its landing idle mode and the thrust levers stayed at idle for about 12 seconds after the go-around was called; the crew expected the autothrottle to advance them.
Neither pilot monitored the flight mode annunciations or engine indications; the thrust levers were advanced manually only about 3 seconds before impact.
The TOGA switch inhibit after touchdown and the absence of an alert when a go-around is attempted with the switches inhibited were identified as contributing to the crew's lack of awareness.
No flight-deck alert indicated that TOGA had not engaged or that thrust remained at idle during the attempted go-around.
The crew had not been trained for a go-around after touchdown and the operator's procedures did not address the TOGA inhibit logic.
After the aircraft came to rest, fire from the separated right engine spread to the fuselage; the centre tank exploded about nine minutes later, killing a firefighter.
Several slides were unusable in the wind, and passengers retrieving cabin baggage slowed the evacuation.
The aircraft sank back onto the runway with the gear retracting, struck the runway on its underside, and slid about 800 m before stopping.

events.text: Dubai ATIS and tower report windshear on approach to runway 12L; the aircraft is on a stabilised approach in hot conditions.
Below about 100 ft the wind shifts from a headwind to a tailwind of about 16 kt.
The aircraft floats in the flare along the runway with the thrust levers at idle under autothrottle control.
Right main gear touches down about 1,100 m beyond the threshold, followed by the left main gear; the aircraft is on the ground with idle thrust.
RAAS 'LONG LANDING, LONG LANDING' aural alert sounds.
The commander decides to go around and presses the TOGA switches; they are inhibited by the on-ground logic and the autothrottle does not advance the thrust levers.
The commander pitches the aircraft up and it becomes airborne on residual speed alone; the pilot monitoring calls a positive rate of climb.
Landing gear selected up on the commander's command; the flaps are set to 20.
The tower clears the aircraft to climb straight ahead to 4,000 ft, adding to the crew's workload during the go-around.
The aircraft reaches a maximum height of about 85 ft with the thrust levers still at idle and the airspeed decaying; it begins to sink.
The thrust levers are advanced manually about 3 seconds before impact; the engines have not yet accelerated.
The aircraft strikes the runway on its underside with the gear in transit; the right engine separates and the aircraft slides about 800 m before stopping.
Fire spreads from the separated engine along the right side; evacuation is ordered; some slides are unusable in the wind and some passengers take cabin baggage.
About nine minutes after the aircraft stopped, the centre wing fuel tank explodes; a firefighter is killed.

recommendations.text: Review the go-around logic so that a TOGA request after touchdown is either honoured or clearly annunciated to the crew, and provide guidance and alerting for a go-around initiated after touchdown.
recommendations.outcome: Boeing issued operator communications and flight crew training material on go-arounds after touchdown and TOGA inhibit logic.

recommendations.text: Include go-around after touchdown scenarios in training and emphasise the flight crew's responsibility to verify thrust lever position and flight mode annunciations during every go-around.
Reinforce guidance on the retraction of the landing gear only after a positive rate of climb has been established with thrust.
Review airport rescue and firefighting procedures for aircraft with fuel tank fire exposure and the guidance to firefighters on the risk of tank explosion.
Address the retrieval of cabin baggage during evacuations through passenger briefing and cabin crew procedures.

safety_changes: Boeing issued a flight operations bulletin and training material to 777 operators on go-arounds initiated after touchdown and the TOGA inhibit logic.
Emirates revised its go-around training and procedures, including scenarios with a bounced or long landing and a go-around after touchdown.
The accident became a reference case for the industry's guidance on cabin baggage retrieval during evacuations.

notes: t0 (first main gear touchdown at 08:37:19 UTC) and the impact time (08:37:38) are given from memory of the GCAA report timeline and may be off by a few seconds; intermediate offsets follow the report narrative (about 85 ft maximum height, thrust levers advanced about 3 s before impact).
The emergency_landing outcome factor is used as instructed to represent the aircraft settling back onto the runway; the ICAO category ARC (abnormal runway contact) is used.
The tailwind value (16 kt) and touchdown distance (about 1,100 m) are from the report narrative as recalled; the exact figures were not verified.
Recommendation ids were not verified; the GCAA report contains numbered safety recommendations to Boeing, the FAA, Emirates and the airport.

records.title: Saratov Airlines 703

agencies.name: Interstate Aviation Committee
agencies.report_title: Final report on the investigation of the accident to An-148-100B RA-61704

location.name: Near Stepanovskoye, Ramensky district, Moscow region

records.summary: The crew took off from Domodedovo without switching on the pitot probe heaters. About two and a half minutes after takeoff, in the climb through about 1,300 m, the pitot probes iced and the captain's and first officer's airspeed indications began to disagree. The autopilot was disconnected at about 2,000 m and the crew, acting on the erroneous decreasing airspeed indication, pushed the aircraft into a steep descent; it struck the ground near Stepanovskoye about six minutes after takeoff. All 71 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The MAK concluded that the accident was caused by the crew's erroneous actions in the climb after the pitot heaters had not been switched on before takeoff, which led to icing of all three pitot probes, disagreement of the airspeed indications, disconnection of the autopilot and loss of spatial/situational awareness. The crew pushed the aircraft into a steep descent in reaction to the erroneous airspeed indications and did not recover. Contributing factors included deficiencies in the crew's training and CRM, non-compliance with the checklist that included the pitot heating item, and the crew's failure to recognise and apply the unreliable airspeed procedure.

factors.evidence: The flight data showed the pitot probe heating was not switched on before takeoff, contrary to the checklist.
With the heaters off, all three pitot probes iced in the climb through cloud.
About 2.5 minutes after takeoff, at about 1,300 m, the captain's and first officer's airspeed indications began to diverge; the captain's indication fell toward zero.
The autopilot was disconnected at about 2,000 m when the airspeed disagreement developed.
The crew interpreted the falling airspeed indication as a real loss of speed and did not recognise the indications as erroneous.
The crew pushed the aircraft into a descent of 30 to 35 degrees nose down in response to the low airspeed indication.
The MAK found the crew did not coordinate their actions or clearly identify the failure, and neither pilot called for the unreliable airspeed procedure.
The report concluded the crew lost situational awareness as to the aircraft's true speed and attitude during the descent.
The MAK cited deficiencies in the crew's training for unreliable airspeed and in the operator's crew training and monitoring.
The report noted that the aircraft did not provide a clear alert that the pitot heating was off before takeoff and that the disagree indication was not sufficiently attention-getting.
The aircraft struck the ground at high speed in a steep nose-down attitude.

events.text: Before-takeoff checks completed without the pitot probe heaters being switched on.
Takeoff from Domodedovo in snow conditions; pitot heating remains off.
About 2.5 minutes after takeoff at about 1,300 m and 465 to 470 km/h, the captain's and first officer's airspeed indications begin to disagree as the pitot probes ice.
Airspeed disagree alerting is presented to the crew; the indications continue to diverge.
At about 2,000 m the autopilot is disconnected and the crew fly manually.
Believing the aircraft is losing speed, the pilot flying pushes the nose down; the aircraft transitions from climb to descent.
The captain's airspeed indication drops to zero while the first officer's shows a different, also erroneous, value.
The pilots exchange confused remarks about the speed and the aircraft's behaviour; no unreliable airspeed procedure is called for.
The aircraft is descending with 30 to 35 degrees nose down pitch; ground proximity warnings sound.
The crew pull back in the final seconds but the aircraft does not recover.
Impact with the ground near Stepanovskoye at a speed in excess of 800 km/h in a steep nose-down attitude.

recommendations.text: Reinforce flight crew training on unreliable airspeed recognition and the memory items for the procedure, including in simulator training.
Review the An-148 pitot heating switching logic and crew alerting so that takeoff with pitot heating off is prevented or clearly annunciated.
Improve checklist discipline, crew resource management and flight operations quality monitoring at the operator.

safety_changes: Russian operators of the An-148 issued additional guidance on pitot heating checks and unreliable airspeed procedures after the MAK preliminary findings.
Saratov Airlines' operating certificate was revoked by Rosaviatsia in May 2018.

notes: Times are from the MAK preliminary information (takeoff about 14:21 Moscow time, disagreement about 2.5 minutes after takeoff, autopilot disconnected at about 2,000 m); event t values between those anchors are approximate offsets and clock strings are omitted where not stated.
The MAK final report publication date and report number were not verified and are left null.
The warning_system_deficiency factor reflects the report's discussion of the absence of a clear pitot-heat-off alert; its exact wording was not verified.
Altitudes in state objects are converted from the metric values in the report (1,300 m, 2,000 m).

records.title: Lion Air 610

agencies.name: Komite Nasional Keselamatan Transportasi
agencies.report_title: Final Aircraft Accident Investigation Report, PT. Lion Mentari Airlines Boeing 737-8 (MAX) PK-LQP

location.name: Java Sea off Karawang, West Java

records.summary: A replacement angle-of-attack sensor fitted the previous day had been miscalibrated by about 21 degrees during repair, and the same fault had produced a stick shaker and repeated automatic nose-down trim on the previous flight, which the crew countered with the trim cutout switches but did not fully record. On flight 610 the stick shaker activated at rotation and, after flap retraction, MCAS repeatedly trimmed the stabilizer nose down. The captain countered with electric trim for several minutes, then handed control to the first officer, whose shorter trim inputs did not keep up; the aircraft dived into the Java Sea about 12 minutes after takeoff.
records.probable_cause: The KNKT identified nine contributing factors: the MCAS design's reliance on a single AOA sensor and the assumptions made about pilot response during development; the AOA sensor that had been miscalibrated during repair by Xtra Aerospace; the installation test that failed to detect the miscalibration; the AOA DISAGREE alert that was not functional on the aircraft; the absence of MCAS information in the flight manuals and pilot training; the incomplete documentation of the previous flight's defects, which meant the aircraft was dispatched with an unresolved problem; the multiple alerts, repetitive MCAS activations and distractions which were not effectively managed; and the crew's ineffective communication and coordination, in the context of the first officer's demonstrated difficulty in handling the aircraft.

factors.evidence: The left AOA sensor installed at Denpasar on 28 October had been miscalibrated by about 21 degrees during repair at Xtra Aerospace, and the post-installation test did not detect the bias.
From rotation the FDR recorded a left-right AOA difference of about 20 degrees that persisted to the end of the recording.

The previous flight (Denpasar to Jakarta) had experienced the same stick shaker and automatic trim; the crew wrote up IAS and ALT disagree and the feel differential pressure light but not the stick shaker or trim runaway, so the aircraft was dispatched.
The left stick shaker activated during rotation and continued for most of the flight.
The erroneous AOA corrupted the left-side airspeed and altitude, producing IAS DISAGREE and ALT DISAGREE indications.
After flap retraction the FDR recorded repeated automatic nose-down stabilizer trim, more than 20 activations, which stopped only while the flaps were re-extended.
MCAS relied on a single AOA input and could repeatedly command stabilizer motion; the report cited the design and development assumptions about pilot reaction as contributing.
The report found that the assumptions used in MCAS's functional hazard assessment about pilot recognition and response were not consistent with the accident crew's actual response.
The AOA DISAGREE alert was not functional on the aircraft because the optional AOA indicator had not been purchased, a fact Boeing had not communicated to operators.
MCAS was not described in the flight crew operations manual or training and the non-functional AOA DISAGREE alert had not been disclosed.
The flight crew had received no information or training on MCAS and were expected to treat its effects as a runaway stabilizer.
The report found ineffective communication and coordination between the pilots, including when control was transferred to the first officer without a clear briefing of the trim problem.
Multiple alerts, repetitive MCAS activations, ATC communication and checklist reading distracted the crew and were not effectively managed.
The first officer's shorter nose-up trim inputs did not fully counter the automatic nose-down trim and the stabilizer moved toward full nose down; aft column force could not stop the dive.
The aircraft entered a steep dive and struck the sea at high speed about 12 minutes after takeoff.

events.text: At Denpasar on 28 October the left AOA sensor is replaced with a unit repaired by Xtra Aerospace; the installation test does not reveal a 21-degree calibration bias.

On the previous flight (Denpasar to Jakarta) the stick shaker activates at rotation and automatic nose-down trim occurs after flap retraction; the crew set the stabilizer trim cutout switches and continue to Jakarta, recording IAS/ALT DISAGREE and the feel differential pressure light but not the stick shaker or trim.
Takeoff from runway 25L; during rotation the left stick shaker activates and the FDR records a left-right AOA difference of about 20 degrees.
First officer asks ATC to confirm the aircraft's altitude, then at 23:21:28 reports a flight control problem.
Flaps retracted; shortly afterwards the FDR records automatic nose-down trim for about 10 seconds followed by crew nose-up electric trim.
Flaps re-extended to 5; the automatic nose-down trim stops.
First officer asks ATC for the aircraft's speed as displayed on radar and requests a holding point; ATC assigns altitudes and headings while the crew work the problem.
Flaps retracted to 0 again; automatic nose-down trim resumes and the captain repeatedly counters each activation with nose-up electric trim, more than 20 cycles.
Captain asks the first officer to run the non-normal checklist for airspeed unreliable; the checklist reading is interrupted by ATC communications.
Captain hands control to the first officer without describing the trim problem, and takes over the radio and checklist.
The first officer's nose-up trim inputs are shorter than the automatic nose-down inputs; the stabilizer moves progressively nose down and the aircraft begins to descend.
First officer reports he cannot hold the aircraft up; both pilots pull on the control columns.
End of FDR recording; the aircraft strikes the Java Sea at high speed in a steep nose-down attitude.

recommendations.text: Redesign MCAS so that it is not vulnerable to a single erroneous AOA input and consider the effect of all flight-deck alerts and indications on flight-crew recognition and response.
recommendations.outcome: MCAS was redesigned to compare both AOA sensors and to limit activation and authority; FAA AD 2020-24-02.

recommendations.text: Review the assumptions used in the aircraft certification process about pilot recognition and reaction time to flight control system failures.
Improve the reporting of technical defects by flight crews and the hazard identification and risk assessment of reported problems so that aircraft are not dispatched with unresolved defects.
Ensure that AOA sensor repair and calibration procedures and their oversight prevent the release of miscalibrated units.
recommendations.outcome: The FAA revoked Xtra Aerospace's repair station certificate in October 2019.

recommendations.text: Improve crew resource management training, including the handover of control and the management of multiple simultaneous alerts.

safety_changes: FAA Emergency Airworthiness Directive 2018-23-51 (November 2018) reminded 737 MAX crews of the runaway stabilizer procedure for erroneous AOA conditions.
After the Ethiopian Airlines 302 accident the 737 MAX was grounded worldwide until MCAS was redesigned and recertified in November 2020.
The FAA revoked the repair station certificate of Xtra Aerospace, which had repaired the accident AOA sensor.

notes: The accident date is 29 October 2018 local time (WIB); in UTC the flight departed at 23:20 on 28 October, which is why t0 is on 2018-10-28.
t0 is the departure time to the minute as stated in the report; events without a clock string are placed by approximate offset from the report narrative.
The count of MCAS activations (more than 20) is from the report narrative; individual activation times are not listed.
Recommendation ids are not given because the KNKT numbering was not verified.
The report contains a CVR transcript, but no lines are quoted here because exact wording was not verified.

records.title: Atlas Air 3591

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Rapid Descent and Crash into Water, Atlas Air Inc. Flight 3591, Boeing 767-375BCF, N1217A, Trinity Bay, Texas, February 23, 2019

records.operator: Atlas Air (operating for Amazon Prime Air)

location.name: Trinity Bay near Anahuac, Texas

records.summary: Descending toward Houston through turbulence and cloud around a line of weather, the 767 freighter's go-around mode was inadvertently triggered, most likely when the first officer's wrist bumped the go-around switch while he was manipulating the speedbrake lever. The autopilot pitched up and thrust increased; the first officer, experiencing a somatogravic illusion that the airplane was pitching up steeply and stalling, pushed the nose down to nearly 50 degrees. The captain did not take control in time and the airplane struck Trinity Bay about 30 seconds later, killing the two pilots and a jumpseat passenger.
records.probable_cause: The inappropriate response by the first officer as the pilot flying to an inadvertent activation of the go-around mode, which led to his spatial disorientation and nose-down control inputs that placed the airplane in a steep descent from which the crew did not recover. Contributing to the accident was the captain's failure to adequately monitor the airplane's flightpath and assume positive control of the airplane to effectively intervene. Also contributing were systemic deficiencies in the aviation industry's selection and performance measurement practices, which failed to address the first officer's aptitude-related deficiencies and maladaptive stress response. Also contributing to the accident was the Federal Aviation Administration's failure to implement the pilot records database in a sufficiently robust and timely manner.

factors.evidence: The go-around mode was most likely activated inadvertently when the first officer's wrist or watch contacted the go-around switch on the thrust lever while he was moving the speedbrake lever in turbulence.
Neither pilot recognized that go-around mode had engaged; the resulting pitch-up and thrust increase were not understood as an automation mode change.
The unexpected pitch-up and acceleration startled the first officer, triggering a maladaptive stress response.
The forward acceleration from go-around thrust in cloud produced a false sensation of steep pitch-up; the first officer believed the airplane was pitching up excessively and stalling.
The first officer became spatially disoriented and did not use the attitude indicator to correct his perception of the airplane's attitude.
The first officer called out that the airplane was stalling although airspeed was increasing and angle of attack was low.
The first officer pushed the control column forward, driving pitch to about 49 degrees nose down with thrust still high.
The airplane was deviating around a line of convective weather in instrument conditions with light to moderate turbulence, removing outside visual references.
The captain did not adequately monitor the flightpath as the airplane pitched down and did not recognize the developing upset for several seconds.
The captain did not assume positive control of the airplane in time; his eventual aft column inputs were too late to recover.
Atlas Air's hiring process did not obtain the first officer's full training history, which included repeated training failures at previous employers that he had not disclosed.
The FAA had not implemented the pilot records database required by the 2010 Airline Safety Act in a sufficiently robust and timely manner, so his record was not available to Atlas.
Industry pilot selection and performance measurement practices did not identify or address the first officer's aptitude-related deficiencies during training.
The airplane entered a steep dive at high speed and struck the water about 32 seconds after go-around mode activation.

events.text: Houston approach clears the flight to descend and coordinates deviations west around a line of thunderstorms; the airplane is in cloud with turbulence.
The first officer, as pilot flying with the autopilot engaged, calls for flaps 1 as the airplane descends through about 6,300 feet and prepares for a turn toward the approach.
The first officer moves the speedbrake lever with his left hand; turbulence jostles the airplane.
Go-around mode activates, most likely from inadvertent contact with the go-around switch on the thrust lever; the autothrottle advances thrust and the autopilot commands a pitch-up.
Thrust increases toward go-around power; the airplane accelerates and begins to pitch up about 4 degrees.
Feeling a strong sensation of pitching up, the first officer pushes the control column forward, overriding the autopilot; he says something to the effect that the airplane is stalling.
The autopilot disconnects; pitch passes through nose-down and continues toward 49 degrees nose down with thrust near maximum; airspeed rises rapidly.
The captain, who had been handling the radios and the flap selection, expresses confusion about what is happening; he does not take control.
The airplane breaks out of cloud in a steep dive over the bay; the ground proximity warning sounds.
Both pilots pull aft on the control columns; pitch begins to recover toward about 20 degrees nose down but the airplane is too low and too fast.
The airplane strikes the shallow water of Trinity Bay at high speed and is destroyed; all three occupants die.

recommendations.text: Complete implementation of the pilot records database so that air carriers can obtain a pilot's complete training and employment history, including records from previous employers, before hiring.
recommendations.outcome: The Pilot Records Database final rule was issued in 2021 and became mandatory for carriers.

recommendations.text: Require air carriers to include in pilot training a scenario-based understanding of inadvertent go-around mode activation and of somatogravic illusion, with practice in recognizing and recovering from resulting unusual attitudes.
Develop pilot selection and performance measurement methods that identify aptitude-related deficiencies and maladaptive stress responses during training and before pilots enter line operations.
Evaluate the location and activation force of go-around switches on the 767 and similar types to reduce the likelihood of inadvertent activation.

safety_changes: The FAA published the Pilot Records Database final rule in 2021, requiring carriers to report and check pilot training and employment records.
Atlas Air and other carriers revised hiring practices to obtain complete training histories and strengthened monitoring of pilots with repeated training failures.
Operators added training on inadvertent go-around mode activation, somatogravic illusion and upset recovery in instrument conditions.
The report reinforced pilot monitoring and intervention guidance for captains when the first officer is pilot flying.

notes: Go-around mode activation is placed at about 12:38:31 CST and impact about 32 seconds later; both are as recalled from the report and could be off by several seconds.
Altitude at go-around activation (about 6,200 feet) and the maximum nose-down pitch (about 49 degrees) are as stated in the report; intermediate pitch values are approximate.
The first officer's stall remark and the captain's expressions of confusion are paraphrased as crew speech events rather than quoted, because the exact wording is not recalled with confidence.
Aircraft MSN is omitted because it is not recalled with confidence.

records.title: Ethiopian Airlines 302

agencies.name: Ethiopian Civil Aviation Authority Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau Investigation Report on Accident to the B737-MAX8 Reg. ET-AVJ operated by Ethiopian Airlines

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: NTSB comments on the AIB-ET final report

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses
agencies.report_title: BEA comments on the AIB-ET final report

location.name: Near Bishoftu (Ejere), Oromia, about 28 nm south-east of Addis Ababa

records.summary: Shortly after lift-off from Addis Ababa the left angle-of-attack sensor failed and recorded about 74.5 degrees, triggering the left stick shaker and erroneous left-side airspeed and altitude. With flaps up and autopilot disengaged, MCAS repeatedly trimmed the stabilizer nose down. The crew cut out the electric stabilizer trim but, at high speed with takeoff thrust still set, could not trim manually, re-engaged electric trim, and a final MCAS activation drove the aircraft into a dive from which it did not recover. All 157 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The AIB-ET concluded that repetitive and uncommanded airplane-nose-down inputs from MCAS, due to erroneous AOA input, and its unrecoverable activation system made the airplane dive close to the ground and was the most probable cause. Contributing factors included MCAS's reliance on a single AOA sensor and its unlimited repetitive authority, the absence of MCAS information and training for flight crews, the lack of an AOA DISAGREE alert on the aircraft, and the multiple simultaneous warnings and high workload the design imposed on the crew.

factors.evidence: Seconds after lift-off the left AOA value deviated from the right and reached 74.5 degrees while the right AOA stayed near 15 degrees; the left value stayed erroneous to the end of the recording.
The left stick shaker activated at the AOA failure and remained active until near the end of the recording.
Left-side airspeed, altitude and flight director pitch bar deviated from the right side; the left overspeed clacker later sounded while the left IAS read lower than the right.

After flap retraction and autopilot disconnect the FDR recorded automatic nose-down stabilizer trim at 05:40:00 (9 s), 05:40:20, 05:40:41 (no motion, cutout) and a final activation at 05:43:20 that moved the stabilizer from 2.3 to 1.0 units.
The autopilot disengaged at 05:39:55; MCAS operates only with the autopilot off and flaps up, and the first automatic nose-down trim followed five seconds later.
MCAS took input from a single AOA sensor and could re-activate repeatedly with full authority; the report identified the design as a contributing factor.
The report found that the MCAS safety assessment and certification did not adequately account for a single erroneous AOA input and for pilot reaction assumptions.
The AOA DISAGREE alert was not functional on this aircraft and multiple simultaneous alerts (stick shaker, master caution, overspeed, GPWS) did not identify the failure.
The report found that MCAS was not described in the flight crew operations manual and that information provided to operators after the Lion Air accident was insufficient.
The report cited shortcomings in FAA oversight of the MCAS certification and in the post-Lion Air continued airworthiness decisions.
The crew had received no simulator training on MCAS or on runaway stabilizer at high speed; the report cited the lack of MCAS training as contributing.

Engine thrust remained at the takeoff setting of about 94 percent N1 throughout; indicated airspeed rose to and beyond VMO (340 kt), making manual trim impossible and finally exceeding 458 kt (left) and 500 kt (right).
With the stabilizer trim cut out, the first officer reported the manual trim wheel was not working at high speed; aft column force on both columns could not overcome the mistrimmed stabilizer.
The crew handled stick shaker, unreliable airspeed, GPWS DON'T SINK, master caution, overspeed warning and ATC communications simultaneously during the first minutes after takeoff.
After the final MCAS activation the pitch reached about 40 degrees nose down and the aircraft struck the ground at very high speed.

events.text: Takeoff roll on runway 07R; engines stabilise at about 94 percent N1, which they hold for the rest of the flight.
Shortly after lift-off the left AOA value deviates from the right, reaching 74.5 degrees; left stick shaker activates and stays on; left airspeed and altitude begin to read low.
Left autopilot engaged at about 1,000 ft radio altitude; it disengages about 33 seconds later.
Captain requests flaps up; flap lever moved from 5 to 0.
Autopilot disengages.
First automatic nose-down stabilizer trim (MCAS) for 9 seconds; trim moves from 4.60 to 2.1 units; the climb is arrested and the aircraft descends slightly.
GPWS 'DON'T SINK' sounds for 3 seconds.
Manual electric trim nose up recorded; stabilizer moves to 2.4 units. Pitch about 2 degrees nose down.
Second automatic nose-down trim; stabilizer reaches 0.4 units. Three more GPWS 'DON'T SINK' warnings follow.
Manual electric trim nose up; stabilizer reverses and reaches 2.3 units.
First officer calls 'stab trim cut-out' twice; captain agrees and the stabilizer trim cutout switches are set to cutout.
Third automatic nose-down trim command with no stabilizer motion, consistent with the cutout switches being in cutout.
First officer asks ATC to maintain 14,000 ft and reports a flight control problem; ATC approves.
Right overspeed clacker sounds and remains active to the end. Left IAS has risen from about 305 kt toward 340 kt with aft force held on both columns.
Captain asks whether the trim is functional; the first officer says it is not working and tries the manual trim wheel, then reports at 05:41:54 that it is not working.
Both pilots call out 'left alpha vane' after a master caution.

Two momentary manual electric nose-up trim inputs are recorded at about 13,400 ft pressure altitude, indicating the trim cutout switches had been returned to normal; stabilizer moves from 2.1 to 2.3 units.
Final automatic nose-down trim moves the stabilizer from 2.3 to 1.0 units in about 5 seconds; the aircraft pitches nose down despite aft force on both columns, reaching about 40 degrees nose down.
End of recording; impact near Bishoftu. Left IAS about 458 kt and right IAS about 500 kt; last recorded pressure altitude 5,419 ft (left).

recommendations.text: Ensure that the 737 MAX flight control system (MCAS) is redesigned so that it does not rely on a single AOA input and cannot repeatedly command stabilizer motion with full authority, and that the redesign is certified and validated before return to service.
recommendations.outcome: FAA AD 2020-24-02 (November 2020) mandated flight control software using both AOA sensors, single MCAS activation per event and limited authority, plus an AOA DISAGREE alert.

recommendations.text: Provide flight crews with full system information and simulator training on MCAS and on runaway stabilizer and high-speed manual trim before the aircraft returns to service.
recommendations.outcome: Simulator training on MCAS-related scenarios became mandatory for 737 MAX pilots before return to service.

recommendations.text: Review the certification process for the MCAS system and for flight-crew reaction assumptions in the aircraft safety assessment.
recommendations.outcome: US Aircraft Certification, Safety, and Accountability Act (December 2020) reformed delegated certification.

recommendations.text: Improve flight-deck alerting so that a single AOA failure and the resulting cascade of warnings can be quickly recognised by the crew.

dissent.position: In comments published after the final report, the NTSB stated that the report did not adequately address the flight crew's performance, in particular that thrust was left at takeoff power for the entire flight, that the crew did not perform the runaway stabilizer procedure completely or promptly, and that the crew had been trained on the MCAS-related emergency AD after the Lion Air accident. The NTSB also stated that the left AOA sensor was most likely damaged by a bird or foreign object rather than by a production quality or electrical defect as the report suggested.

The BEA published comments stating that the report should have given weight to the crew's handling of the situation: thrust remaining at takeoff setting leading to an overspeed, the incomplete application of the runaway stabilizer procedure, the re-engagement of electric trim, and crew resource management; the BEA also considered the AOA vane most likely separated after a bird strike.

safety_changes: Worldwide grounding of the Boeing 737 MAX fleet from March 2019 until the redesigned flight control software was certified (FAA return-to-service November 2020).
MCAS redesigned to use both AOA sensors, activate only once per high-AOA event, and never command more stabilizer movement than the crew can counter with the control column.
AOA DISAGREE alert made standard on all 737 MAX aircraft and mandatory simulator training on MCAS scenarios for MAX pilots.
US Aircraft Certification, Safety, and Accountability Act (2020) reformed FAA delegation of certification work to manufacturers.

notes: Timeline clock times and stabilizer units are taken from the AIB-ET preliminary and final report narrative; the takeoff-roll event time (t=-70) is approximate.
Recommendation ids are not given because the exact AIB-ET numbering was not verified; the text reflects the report's key recommendations.
The NTSB docket URL is given from memory (DCA19RA101); the AIB-ET report URL is the agency home page.
CVR lines are the short callouts quoted in the report narrative, not a verbatim transcript.

records.title: Aeroflot 1492

agencies.name: Interstate Aviation Committee
agencies.report_title: Final Report on the Air Accident Investigation

location.name: Sheremetyevo International Airport

records.summary: Aeroflot Flight 1492 was struck by lightning during climb-out on 5 May 2019, suffering electrical failure. The aircraft returned to Sheremetyevo for an emergency landing. It bounced on landing and touched down hard, causing the landing gear to collapse and fuel to spill. A fire erupted in the rear cabin, killing 41 of the 78 occupants.
records.probable_cause: At 15:08 UTC, the aircraft was struck by lightning at flight level 89, causing primary radio and autopilot to become inoperative. The flight control mode changed to DIRECT, a degraded mode of operation. The captain attempted to land with excessive crosswind and the aircraft bounced, touched down hard, causing the landing gear to collapse and fuel spillage from the wings.

factors.evidence: The aircraft was struck by lightning at flight level 89, causing primary radio and autopilot to become inoperative
The flight control mode changed to DIRECT, a degraded, more challenging mode of operation
The aircraft bounced on landing and touched down hard, causing the landing gear to collapse
Fuel spilled out of the wings following the hard landing and landing gear collapse
A fire erupted and engulfed the rear of the aircraft, killing 41 of the 78 occupants

events.text: Flight 1492 took off from runway 24C at Sheremetyevo International Airport, bound for Murmansk Airport.
At 15:08 UTC, the aircraft was struck by lightning at flight level 89 and primary radio and autopilot became inoperative.
The captain assumed manual control of the aircraft and the transponder code was changed to indicate emergency.
The aircraft bounced on landing and touched down hard, causing the landing gear to collapse and fuel to spill out of the wings.
A fire erupted and engulfed the rear of the aircraft, killing 41 of the 78 occupants.

safety_changes: Enhanced procedures for in-flight lightning strike management
Improved training for degraded mode operations
Enhanced emergency evacuation procedures for post-landing fires

notes: Sections read: Factual Information, Analysis of Crew's Condition and Actions, Analysis of Aviation Equipment from MAK final report

records.title: Sriwijaya Air 182

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Committee
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Investigation Report

location.name: Java Sea, approximately 11 nm NW of Jakarta

records.summary: Boeing 737-500 crashed into Java Sea four minutes after takeoff from Jakarta during a climb to 11,000 feet. The aircraft experienced thrust asymmetry when the autopilot commanded reduced power: the left engine thrust decreased as directed, but the right engine thrust lever remained stuck at climb power due to excessive mechanical friction in the throttle cable. The resulting yaw and roll to the left caused the autopilot to reach maximum deflection. When the autopilot disengaged following the pilot's activation of the stabilizer trim switch, the aircraft entered an upset and descended rapidly into the sea. The pilots were unable to recognize the asymmetric thrust condition or recover from the upset.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by a faulty autothrottle system that was unable to move the right thrust lever due to friction or binding within the mechanical control cable system. The thrust asymmetry resulting from this mechanical failure, combined with pilot error in failing to recognize and correct the aircraft's developing roll and yaw, and inadequate upset prevention and recovery training, led to loss of control and impact with the Java Sea.

factors.evidence: The autothrottle attempted to move the throttle levers back when the aircraft reached 11,000 feet on ATC instruction, but the right lever remained stuck at climb power due to excessive friction in the throttle control cable (p. 1-2)
The right engine thrust lever remained stuck at climb power due to excessive friction, while the left lever moved backward as commanded, creating an asymmetric thrust condition (p. 1-2)
The autothrottle problem had been reported 65 times since 2013 and was never resolved; maintenance troubleshooting did not identify the mechanical friction in the throttle cable (p. 131)
The pilots did not recognize the thrust lever asymmetry or the aircraft's deviation from the intended flight path before it developed into an upset condition (p. 135)
When the bank angle reached 37 degrees, the Enhanced GPWS Bank Angle warning activated, startling the pilots (p. 1-2)
Automation complacency and confirmation bias led to reduced active monitoring of the thrust levers and flight path (p. 135)
Sriwijaya Air's upset recovery training program lacked detail and guidelines to ensure pilots had adequate knowledge to prevent and recover from upset conditions effectively (p. 135)
The aircraft entered an upset condition and descended rapidly into the Java Sea approximately 4 minutes after takeoff (p. 1)

events.text: Flight SJ182 departed from Runway 25R, Jakarta in daylight conditions with 62 occupants (2 pilots, 4 flight attendants, 56 passengers) aboard
Autopilot engaged at approximately 1,800 feet in LNAV mode and MCP SPD mode
At altitude 5,400 feet and 220 knots, pilot changed autopilot directional control from LNAV to HDG SEL mode
Autopilot vertical control changed to V/S mode and autothrottle changed from N1 mode to MCP SPD mode, requiring less engine thrust
At altitude 7,950 feet, left thrust lever began decreasing while right thrust lever remained at 46 degrees due to mechanical friction
ATC instructed aircraft to stop climbing at 11,000 feet
At altitude approximately 10,250 feet, aircraft turned left instead of right as intended due to thrust asymmetry, with calculated spoiler deflection of 3.7 degrees
Enhanced GPWS Bank Angle warning activated when bank angle reached 37 degrees to the left
Pilot called out 'ONE THREE ZERO' in response to new climb clearance to 13,000 feet
Aircraft entered upset condition with excessive bank angle; overspeed warning sounded; CVR recording ended as aircraft descended into Java Sea

recommendations.text: Include a requirement of UPRT (Upset Prevention and Recovery Training) in the CASR Part 121 and develop detailed guidance to increase the effectiveness of upset prevention and recovery training implementation

Review the requirements of notification of rescue coordination center in the CASR Part 170 to ensure compliance with ICAO Annex 11 standards, specifically including the alternative conjunction (or) in the determination of emergency states
recommendations.outcome: DGCA reviewed and amended CASR Part 170 to align with ICAO Annex 11

records.title: Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky Air 251 (2021)

location.name: Palana

records.summary: Flight 251 departed Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky at 12:56 local time for Palana. The controller informed the crew that cloud base was 720 m and recommended a land-side approach using navigation beacons. The crew rejected this, stating no published procedure existed and proceeded with a visual seaward approach. In deteriorating fog, the aircraft descended below minimums, strayed from the proper approach path, and struck a 260 m coastal cliff while at 200 m altitude.
records.probable_cause: Crew performed a visual seaward approach contrary to controller recommendation, descended below published minimums without required visual references in low visibility conditions, and struck terrain.
