records.title: Yeti Airlines 691
records.time_reference: Nepal time (UTC+5:45); clock strings approximate to the minute, t is relative to the movement of the condition levers at about 10:56

agencies.name: Aircraft Accident Investigation Commission
agencies.report_title: Final Report on the Accident Investigation of 9N-ANC ATR 72-212A (ATR 72-500), Yeti Airlines Flight 691, Pokhara, Nepal, 15 January 2023

location.name: Seti River gorge, about 1.5 km from the runway 12 threshold, Pokhara

records.summary: On a visual approach to runway 12 at the newly opened Pokhara International Airport, the pilot flying called for flaps 30. The pilot monitoring, an instructor captain, instead moved both condition levers to the feather position, feathering both propellers and removing all thrust. Neither pilot noticed; the aircraft decelerated in the turn onto final, the stick shaker activated and the aircraft stalled and rolled at low altitude, crashing into the Seti River gorge. All 72 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The AAIC concluded that the probable cause was the inadvertent movement of both condition levers to the feather position by the pilot monitoring, which resulted in the feathering of both propellers and a loss of thrust that led to an aerodynamic stall and collision with terrain. Contributing were high workload and stress during a non-standard visual approach to a newly opened airport, the failure of the crew to monitor and cross-check the aircraft's configuration and performance, inadequate crew coordination and non-compliance with standard operating procedures, and shortcomings in the operator's training and the validation of the visual approach procedure.

factors.evidence: When flaps 30 was called, the pilot monitoring moved the condition levers, located next to the flap lever on the centre pedestal, to FEATHER instead of moving the flap lever.
The crew were flying a visual approach at low altitude to a new airport with a non-standard circuit, in a supervised familiarisation flight.
The approach was not flown according to a briefed and validated procedure, and the before-landing checks were not completed as required by the SOPs.
Neither pilot detected that the flaps had remained at 15 and that both engines' torque had dropped to zero after the levers were moved.
There was no effective cross-check of the configuration change, and the exchange between the pilots did not identify the loss of thrust.
The crew did not understand why the aircraft was not responding to power lever movement until the stall warning activated.
The report identified deficiencies in the operator's training and in the preparation of crews for operations at the new airport.
The stick shaker activated twice at low altitude; the crew did not recover before the aircraft rolled.
With both propellers feathered the airspeed decayed in the turn to final and the aircraft stalled.
The aircraft rolled sharply left and struck the ground in the gorge.

events.text: Departs Kathmandu for Pokhara. The captain in the left seat is pilot flying on a familiarisation flight to the new airport; an instructor captain in the right seat is pilot monitoring.
The crew request and are cleared for a visual approach to runway 12 instead of runway 30; the approach is flown at low altitude on a non-standard path without a validated procedure.
Flaps 15 selected and landing gear extended on the downwind leg.

The pilot flying calls for flaps 30. The pilot monitoring moves both condition levers to FEATHER instead of the flap lever; both propellers feather and engine torque drops to zero. The flap lever remains at 15.
The pilot monitoring reads the flaps as set; neither pilot notices the feathered propellers or the zero torque, and the before-landing checklist is not completed.
Flaps 30 is subsequently selected; the aircraft continues the turn toward final with the propellers feathered and airspeed decreasing.
The pilot flying reports that the engines are not producing power; the power levers are advanced but, with the propellers feathered, no thrust results.
Stick shaker activates at low altitude in the turn to final.
Stick shaker activates a second time; the aircraft rolls sharply to the left.
The aircraft strikes the ground in the Seti River gorge about 1.5 km from the runway 12 threshold and catches fire; all 68 passengers and 4 crew are killed.

recommendations.text: Ensure that visual approach procedures for new airports are properly designed, validated and published, and that operators' crews are trained on them before operations begin.

Strengthen SOP compliance, crew coordination and monitoring, including cross-verification of configuration changes and completion of checklists, and review training and supervision on familiarisation flights.
Consider design or procedural measures to reduce the risk of confusing the condition levers with the flap lever on the ATR 72 pedestal.

safety_changes: The Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal revised its approach procedures and crew training requirements for Pokhara International Airport.
Yeti Airlines revised its SOPs on configuration changes and checklist discipline.

notes: Clock strings are given only to the minute; event offsets are approximate reconstructions of the roughly 50-second sequence from the lever movement to impact.
The pilot monitoring's exact words when the levers were moved are paraphrased.

The report's findings on regulatory oversight and on the airport's procedure validation are summarised in the probable cause but regulatory_oversight is not listed as a factor because the exact wording was not verified.
The Nepal AAIC report is published through the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation; its home page is used as the source.

records.title: 2025 Potomac River mid-air collision

location.name: Potomac River, Washington DC

records.summary: American Airlines Flight 5342, a CRJ700 regional jet, collided in mid-air with a U.S. Army UH-60L Black Hawk helicopter over the Potomac River near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport. The collision occurred at 8:47 p.m. at an altitude of about 300 feet. Both aircraft were in communication with air traffic control, and the helicopter crew reported visual contact, though it remains unclear whether they were monitoring the correct aircraft. All 67 occupants of both aircraft perished.
records.probable_cause: The Federal Aviation Administration's placement of a helicopter route in close proximity to a runway approach path; their failure to regularly review and evaluate helicopter routes and available data, and their failure to act on recommendations to mitigate midair collision risk near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport; as well as the air traffic system's overreliance on visual separation without consideration for the limitations of the see-and-avoid concept. Also causal was the lack of effective pilot-applied visual separation by the helicopter crew. Additional causal factors were the tower team's loss of situation awareness and degraded performance due to high workload from combined helicopter and local control positions.

factors.evidence: Part of transmission advising CRJ was circling not captured by helicopter CVR; radio push-to-talk switch blocked controller instruction to pass behind (p. 1-6).
TCAS resolution advisories disabled by design below 900 ft AGL (p. xxii).
Helicopter crew reported visual contact with airliner and visual separation twice though unknown if monitoring correct aircraft (p. 1-7).
CRJ700 airliner and UH-60L helicopter collided in mid-air; all 67 aboard both aircraft killed (p. xxi).

events.text: Flight 5342 makes initial contact with Reagan National control tower for Mount Vernon Visual Approach to runway 1
Controller advises PAT25 of CRJ at 1200 feet south of Woodrow Wilson Bridge; helicopter crew reports visual contact and requests visual separation
Conflict alert begins on controller's display; Flight 5342 receives TCAS traffic advisory at 448 feet radio altitude
Controller instructs helicopter to pass behind but transmission blocked by radio push-to-talk; helicopter crew claims aircraft in sight and requests visual separation
Aircraft collide in mid-air over Potomac River at approximately 300 feet altitude about 0.5 miles from DCA runway 33 threshold

recommendations.text: Develop and implement time-on-position limitations for supervisory air traffic control personnel
Conduct safety risk management process to evaluate modifications to helicopter route structure near DCA
Amend helicopter route design criteria to ensure vertical separation from airport approach paths
Require existing and new TCAS I/II and airborne collision avoidance system X installations to integrate directional traffic symbols
Require all aircraft in ADS-B Out airspace to also be equipped with ADS-B In with display
Revise training procedures for flight crews assigned to Washington DC area operations
Prohibit operations on Helicopter Route 4 between Hains Point and Wilson Bridge when runways 15 and 33 in use
Designate alternative helicopter route for use between Hains Point and Wilson Bridge when Route 4 closed

safety_changes: FAA reviews helicopter routes near major airports
Enhanced TCAS requirements at low altitudes

records.title: Air India 171

location.name: Ahmedabad

records.summary: Air India Flight 171, a Boeing 787-8 flying from Ahmedabad to London Gatwick, crashed 32 seconds after takeoff on 12 June 2025 into a medical college hostel near the airport, killing 241 of 242 occupants and 19 people on the ground. The AAIB's preliminary report found the front flight recorder showed both engines lost thrust after their fuel control switches moved from RUN to CUTOFF three seconds after liftoff; the reason for the switch movement had not been established.
records.probable_cause: The AAIB's preliminary report attributes the crash to loss of thrust in both engines after the fuel control switches transitioned from RUN to CUTOFF three seconds after liftoff; the reason the switches moved had not been determined as of the preliminary report.

factors.evidence: The front flight recorder indicated loss of thrust in both engines after their fuel control switches transitioned from RUN to CUTOFF three seconds after liftoff at 08:08:42-43 UTC (p. 14).
Flight recorder data showed the aircraft reached a maximum airspeed of 180 knots after a 62-second takeoff roll, leaving little margin to recover from the thrust loss (p. 14).
The aircraft began to lose altitude before crossing the airport perimeter wall and crashed into the hostel block of the B. J. Medical College campus 0.9 nmi from the runway (p. 14).
Several college buildings were severely damaged by the impact and subsequent fire, including student accommodation and the resident doctors' hostel (p. 6).

events.text: The Boeing 787-8 lifted off from runway 23 at Ahmedabad at 08:08:39 UTC after a 62-second takeoff roll, with light winds of 6 knots and visibility of 6 km.
Three seconds after liftoff, Engine 1 and Engine 2 fuel control switches transitioned from RUN to CUTOFF, causing loss of thrust in both engines according to the front flight recorder.
One pilot asked the other why he cut off; the other pilot responded that he did not do so.
The Ram Air Turbine (RAT) deployed during initial climb as both engines N2 values passed below minimum idle speed and the RAT hydraulic pump began supplying hydraulic power.
Engine 1 fuel control switch transitioned from CUTOFF to RUN at 08:08:52 UTC, and FADEC automatically initiated a relight and thrust recovery sequence.
The APU inlet door began opening at 08:08:54 UTC, consistent with APU auto-start logic.
Engine 2 fuel control switch transitioned from CUTOFF to RUN; both engines attempted relight with Engine 1 recovering and Engine 2 struggling to maintain core speed.
One of the pilots transmitted MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY; the ATCO did not get a response but observed the aircraft crashing outside the airport boundary.

After 32 seconds of flight the aircraft crashed into the hostel block of B. J. Medical College 0.9 nmi from the runway, initially striking trees and a chimney before impacting the building at a nose-up attitude of about 8 degrees.
The aircraft fragmented across five buildings with extensive thermal damage; the vertical stabilizer separated and came to rest 200 feet away; both engines were found in different buildings.

notes: AAIB preliminary report only; the reason the fuel control switches moved to CUTOFF had not been determined at time of writing

records.title: UPS Airlines 2976

location.name: Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport

records.summary: UPS Airlines Flight 2976, an MD-11F cargo aircraft, suffered separation of its left engine during takeoff roll from runway 17R. The engine, with most of its pylon still attached, separated and tumbled over the wing. The aircraft descended rapidly, struck multiple buildings and vehicles, and crashed into an industrial area. All three crew and twelve ground occupants were killed.
records.probable_cause: During takeoff, shortly after rotation, the left engine, with most of its pylon still attached, separated from the wing. NTSB revealed that Boeing asked the FAA to increase the inspection interval for lugs from 19,900 to 29,200 flight cycles even though it had received five reports of the spherical bearing fracturing long before the aircraft reached its designated inspection interval.
